## Introduction

The third edition of this textbook has been updated to take into account the new Leaving Certificate Chemistry curriculum specification introduced into schools in September 2025. All the material for Higher and Ordinary level students is included in this textbook. All Higher Level material is indicated by a vertical line drawn down the left-hand side of the margin.

All topics are covered to the depth indicated in the published curriculum specification. We hope that the numerous Worked Examples will help students to gain an understanding of the key topics on the course as well as an appreciation of the type of answer required in Leaving Certificate examination papers. We are very fortunate to have copies of SEC Sample Examination Papers to inform us of the style and format of examination questions that will be used when designing future examination papers. The numerous Worked Examples are available not only in the textbook but are also available online. These online Worked Examples are signposted throughout the textbook.

As in Chemistry Live 2nd Edition, some topics (chapters 23-26) are included in the accompanying Assessment and Exam Guide. The inclusion of these chapters in the Assessment and Exam Guide has enabled us to ensure that the correct depth of treatment has been applied to all chapters in both the textbook and in the Assessment and Exam Guide.

All the Student Experiments listed on the syllabus are included in this textbook. The key points of each experiment are included in the textbook and full step-by-step instructions are given in the accompanying Student Laboratory Notebook. A full list of Student Experiments in the order in which they appear in the textbook is given on the following pages.

In keeping with the learning outcomes in the Unifying Strand, throughout the textbook and online materials we have emphasised the importance of Science, Technology and Society (STS) and included references to the contributions that famous scientists have made to scientific discoveries and their impact on society. We also give students an appreciation of how scientists work and how scientific ideas are modified over time as required by the curriculum specification.

We have not assumed any previous knowledge of chemistry among the students for whom this textbook is written. For this reason, the opening chapters of the book introduce students to the fundamental concepts of chemistry before moving on to some of the major areas of the curriculum.

The use of the letters [LCH] and [LCO] after a question indicates that this question is taken either from a past Leaving Certificate Higher or Ordinary level paper, respectively. It is strongly recommended that students use the Assessment and Exam Guide in conjunction with the textbook. Questions in the Assessment and Exam Guide are prefixed by the letter W . These questions play an important role in testing the student and in preparing him/her for the Leaving Certificate examination. The permission of the State Examinations Commission to reproduce questions from past Leaving Certificate examination papers is gratefully acknowledged.

Writing this textbook has been a very challenging and enjoyable task and we are extremely grateful to our many friends and colleagues who have given us so much support and encouragement. In particular, we wish to express our sincere thanks and deep gratitude to those who proof-read some or all of the manuscript and made very useful suggestions and comments on the material. The comments of the proof-readers have helped us greatly in the production of the final draft of this textbook. We also wish to thank Lennox Laboratory Supplies and PASCO Scientific for their assistance in providing equipment for use in the online videos and photographs included in this publication.

A special word of thanks to our families for their help and support in writing this textbook.
Last but not least we wish to express our sincere thanks and appreciation to the staff at Folens with whom it has been a pleasure to work: Conor Walker, Ciarán Deane, Michael Plunkett and Clodagh Quinn; as well as Emma Farrell and Rónán Vaughan at Dog's-ear. Their hard work and dedication has ensured that the Chemistry Live teaching package is of the highest possible standard.

We wish all students who use this textbook and the accompanying resources every success with their studies. Bail ó Dhia ar an obair!

Declan Kennedy, Ryan Gallagher

## Laboratory Practical Work

Chemistry is a subject that involves a lot of practical work. The experiments in this book will help you to develop many practical skills and to gain confidence in working in the laboratory. Practical work also provides an opportunity for you to work with your classmates as part of a team. Above all, practical work will help to maintain your interest in chemistry, enhance your understanding of the subject and make chemistry more enjoyable for you.

## Laboratory Safety

When carrying out experiments in the laboratory, safety is of the utmost importance. Even though most accidents that occur in school laboratories are of a minor nature, there is the potential in school laboratories for serious accidents to occur. To avoid accidents, it is important that you follow the laboratory rules and that you understand the safety symbols associated with the chemicals that you use in the laboratory.

## Laboratory Rules

Most laboratory rules are based on normal common sense and are designed to ensure that the laboratory is a safe and healthy environment in which to work. The following set of suggested laboratory rules should be studied carefully. Your teacher may wish to modify these rules to make them more appropriate to the circumstances of your own school.

1. Follow all directions exactly as given by your teacher.
2. Perform only those experiments assigned to you by your teacher.
3. Safety glasses should be worn during all practical classes unless your teacher indicates otherwise.
4. When heating a liquid in a test-tube, place the test-tube in a beaker of warm water rather than heating it over a Bunsen burner.
5. If heating a test-tube, never look into the mouth of the test-tube. Never point the mouth of the test-tube in the direction of any other person during the heating process.
6. Never use a naked flame to heat a flammable liquid, e.g. alcohol.
7. Never force glass tubing into or out of rubber stoppers or tubing. Use a small amount of glycerine or Vaseline as a lubricant. Always ensure that your hand is protected by a thick cloth or suitably thick gloves.
8. Regard all laboratory chemicals as poisonous. Chemicals should never be tasted. If you get something into your mouth, spit it out immediately, wash out your mouth with water and report the accident to your teacher.
9. Test for odours of gases by wafting your hand over the sample and sniffing cautiously.
10. Take care when handling corrosive liquids (e.g. concentrated acids) and only use these liquids under the direct supervision of your teacher.
11. Never rush around the laboratory. This can be very dangerous.
12. Do not bring coats into the laboratory. Put your bag in a place where it will not cause somebody to fall over it.
13. Always co-operate with your teacher and fellow students. As well as learning about chemistry, it is important that you learn to work as part of a team.
14. Any accident or injury, however slight, must be reported to your teacher.
15. Before you leave the laboratory, wash any glassware you have used, make sure that all the apparatus has been put back in its correct place and leave the bench clean and dry.

## Safety Symbols

As you use various chemicals in this course, you will observe safety symbols on the containers in which these chemicals are stored. The relevant safety symbols are also printed next to the experiments described in this book and in the Chemistry Live Student Laboratory Notebook. These symbols will remind you of the safety precautions you must adopt when using these substances. You must learn to recognise these symbols and understand their meaning. # 1 The Nature of Science

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-015.jpg?height=1124&width=1258&top_left_y=504&top_left_x=328)

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of how scientists work.
- To ensure that students know the key points about science as a global enterprise.
- To give students an appreciation of the role of science in society.


### 1.1 Introduction

The word 'science' comes from the Latin word scientia which means 'knowledge'. Science is the study of the natural world around us. Scientists try to provide accurate explanations of how the natural world works.

The branches of science that study the natural world around us are referred to as the natural sciences. On the other hand, the branches that study human behaviour and society are called the social sciences. The natural sciences are divided into physical science and biological science. Physical science is that branch of science that deals with inanimate (non-living) things. It is subdivided into subjects such as physics, chemistry, astronomy, geology and computer science. Biological science is that branch of science which deals with living things. It is subdivided into botany (the study of plants), zoology (the study of animals) and microbiology (the study of micro-organisms).

In this course, we will be studying the subject of chemistry in some detail. Chemistry describes the substances found in nature. It investigates what these substances are made of, how they react with one another, and how new substances are produced. Without the ability of chemists to make new substances, we would have no medicines to keep us healthy, no colourful clothes to wear, no soap to keep us clean - and no deodorant or perfume or aftershave to help us smell nice!

### 1.2 How scientists work

Similar to all scientists, chemists are curious people - they want to understand how the world works. To do this, they follow a logical and organised process called the scientific method, Figure 1.1. This is a step-by-step approach that helps us test ideas, answer questions and discover new knowledge.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-015.jpg?height=1395&width=1176&top_left_y=2317&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 1.1 Summary of steps involved in the scientific method

- The scientific method starts with an observation. This involves noticing something interesting in the chemical world. For example, a student may observe that marble chips may react more slowly with a dilute acid than with a concentrated acid.
- Arising out of this observation is the question. For example, the question might be: What is the relationship between the concentration of the acid and the rate of the reaction?
- The next step is to propose a hypothesis.

A hypothesis is a proposed explanation of why certain events take place.

A hypothesis is an 'educated guess' or a proposition or a suggestion to explain what is happening when we are carrying out a scientific investigation.

A hypothesis is like a suggested explanation that has not yet been proven. A hypothesis is always written in the form of an 'if ... then' statement. For example, the hypothesis for the reaction between the marble chips and acid could be: 'If I increase the concentration of the acid, then the rate of the reaction will increase.' Note that this prediction is very clear.

- The next step is to carry out an experiment to test the hypothesis. The student might decide to react equal masses of marble chips of similar size with HCl of different concentrations and measure the mass of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ produced over a certain period of time. In the Leaving Certificate chemistry course, we will be carrying out a wide variety of laboratory practical work. In these experiments we will be collecting data. In some cases, the data we collect will be numerical data, i.e. we will measure quantities such as mass, volume and time. This type of data is called quantitative data.

Quantitative data are numerical measurements that are made using scientific instruments. Examples of quantitative data are values of mass, temperature, volume and time.

In other experiments, we will test for the presence of certain substances in materials. For example, we will be identifying the presence of some metals in salts or testing for the presence of specific ions in solution. In these cases, we will be making observations, e.g. colour changes taking place, a solution becoming cloudy, gases being given off
or a description of the flame when a gas is burned. These types of data are called qualitative data.

Qualitative data are descriptive observations that are made by the person carrying out the experiment. Examples of qualitative data are changes in colour or observation of a gas being produced.

- The results of the experiment are collected and the data are summarised in the form of tables and graphs. The experiment is repeated a number of times to ensure that the results are reliable. A measurement is reliable if we repeat the same experiment and we get the same or similar results over and over again.
- The data analysis part of the scientific method then takes place. This is one of the most important parts of the experiment. Without collecting reliable data and analysing it carefully, we cannot draw valid conclusions.
- Having analysed the data, we then draw conclusions. These conclusions will help us to decide if the data supports or does not support the hypothesis. If the conclusions support the hypothesis, then the experiment is repeated a number of times to help to validate the results. A conclusion from the above experiment might be that the rate of reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of the acid.

If the conclusions do not support the hypothesis, then a new or modified hypothesis will have to be developed.

Note on Research Investigation: It is proposed as part of your studies in this chemistry course that you will carry out your own research investigation. Carrying out the laboratory practical work that is specified on the curriculum will be of huge help to you in acquiring the laboratory practical skills necessary to carry out the research investigation. Online resources, including details of how to carry out research investigations, types of variables and carrying out risk assessments will be available in the online resources accompanying this textbook. These online resources will help to guide you in carrying out your research investigation. These online resources will be regularly updated in the light of information received from the State Examinations Commission and exam marking schemes. Therefore, details of how to carry out research investigations will not be discussed further in this chapter.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-017.jpg?height=965&width=1863&top_left_y=367&top_left_x=319)
Figure 1.2 John Dalton's simple model of the atom had to be changed when it was discovered that subatomic particles existed.

### 1.3 How scientific ideas are modified over time

You may recall coming across the word 'theory' in your study of science at Junior Cycle level, e.g. the particle theory that was used to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases. Scientific theories are based on lots of observations and experimental results and, in general, are accepted by scientists around the world.

## A scientific theory is an explanation of observations and is based on hypotheses, laws and facts.

In this course, we will be studying theories such as atomic theory and acid-base theories. It is important to realise that scientific ideas change as new evidence is discovered and improved technology is developed to help chemists collect better quality data. For example, in Chapter 2 we will learn about the atomic theory put forward by John Dalton in 1808. The model of the atom proposed by Dalton was that atoms were like snooker balls that cannot be broken down into simple particles, Figure 1.2. However, this model had to be changed to a more modern model when it was discovered that smaller particles (called subatomic particles) existed inside the atom.

In other words, our understanding of chemistry ideas improves as new discoveries are made and new models are developed.

You may also recall meeting the idea of scientific laws in your study of science at Junior Cycle level. For example, you studied the Law of Conservation of Mass and learned that when a chemical reaction occurs, the total mass of the reactants is always equal to the total mass of the products. Antoine

Lavoisier based this law on repeated observations and experiments. He did not understand why the law was true - he just stated his observations.

## A scientific law is a description of observed occurrences.

In short, a scientific theory explains why something happens but a scientific law describes what happens. Theories can change if new evidence is found. However, laws rarely change.

### 1.4 Science as a global enterprise

The phrase 'science as a global enterprise' means that the work carried out by scientists is not just something that happens in one country or in one laboratory. On the contrary, it is a worldwide team effort where scientists all around the world work together, share their knowledge and skills, and follow the same rules and standards. This allows them to achieve beneficial and reliable results to help solve problems facing people all over the world, Figure 1.3.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-017.jpg?height=616&width=1004&top_left_y=2995&top_left_x=1666)
Figure 1.3 Scientists all over the world study similar problems such as combating diseases, climate change and developing new biodegradable plastics.

- Science relies on evidence. Scientific ideas must always be based on evidence, i.e. data gathered by means of careful observations and scientific investigations. For example, Niels Bohr put forward the idea of electrons in orbit around the nucleus as a result of evidence gathered from studying the light given out when certain elements were heated.
- Clear communication. Scientists must be able to explain their ideas and discoveries clearly so that other scientists around the world can understand and make use of these ideas and discoveries. For example, chemists throughout the world use the same symbols for the elements in the Periodic Table and the same methods of writing balanced chemical equations.
- International conventions. Scientists around the world adopt the same regulations (conventions) and systems when writing up reports of their work. For example, IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) is the organisation that sets the rules for naming elements and compounds. Similarly, chemists agree to use the SI (Système International d'Unités) system for units such as length, mass and time. This makes it easy to compare measurements made in one country with those made in other countries.
- Peer review. When scientists carry out research, their findings are usually published in scientific journals or books. However, before the research reports are published, the work is reviewed by other scientists who work in that field, Figure 1.4. These scientists are called peers, since they work in similar areas to the authors of the research articles. The editor
of the journal or book will send the research article to other scientists who have expertise in the specific area. These other scientists will check if the research work has been carried out correctly and if the conclusions are valid. This ensures that articles with mistakes or false claims are not published.
- Repeatability. If a scientist carries out an experiment and obtains a particular result, then if the method is reliable, the same results should be obtained by the same person when repeated using the same method. This process is called repeatability. In other words, repeatability means that an experiment can be done again by the same person using the same method and getting the same results. Repeatability ensures that the results are not just a one-time 'fluke'. If repeatability does not exist, then the results cannot be considered reliable.
- Reproducibility. If a scientist publishes a method for carrying out a particular experiment in the laboratory, reproducibility is a measure of how different people in different laboratories can get the same results by following the same procedure. Note the distinction between repeatability and reproducibility. Repeatability refers to the same person, carrying out their own experiment, following the same method and getting the same results. Reproducibility refers to different people following the same method in a different laboratory and getting the same results. In chemistry, reproducibility of results is particularly important in the development of new drugs. These drugs are only approved after many scientists in labs around the world obtain the same results under the same conditions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-018.jpg?height=1017&width=1886&top_left_y=2851&top_left_x=270)
Figure 1.4 The peer review process

### 1.5 Models in chemistry

Chemistry explains how and why substances change, e.g. why adding an indigestion tablet to water causes fizzing, why iron rusts, or why light and heat are given out when a firework explodes. In chemistry we have to explain what we see on a large scale (macroscopic scale) by referring to things that we cannot see, e.g. atoms, molecules, ions and electrons (microscopic scale). Therefore, we use models to help us visualise many of the concepts that we meet in chemistry. In short, models help us to translate what we observe into what is happening in terms of atoms, molecules and other similar species. (In this context, the word 'species' refers to chemical units such as atoms and molecules - it has no connection to the biological term.)

> A scientific model is a simplified representation to help us to visualise, explain and understand chemistry concepts as well as making predictions about results of physical and chemical changes.

Interpreting models helps us to improve our visualisation skills and logical reasoning skills. Models can be in the form of diagrams, animations, threedimensional models and computer simulations. You have already met models in your study of Junior Cycle chemistry. For example, when discussing the particle theory, you may recall that the model shown in Figure 1.5 was used to help you understand what happens when a liquid boils. This diagram helps you to link what you observe when a liquid boils, to the theory that explains the process of boiling.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-019.jpg?height=750&width=1453&top_left_y=1458&top_left_x=1302)
Figure 1.5 This model helps us to understand that at the boiling point of a liquid, the water molecules break away from all parts of the liquid and form a gas.

The main points about models in chemistry may be summarised as follows:

- Models may be compared to a bridge that helps us to go from the visible (macroscopic) to the invisible (microscopic). They help us to get a picture in our minds of what is happening at the microscopic level. Models help us to be good visual thinkers. Models help us to gain understanding and build pictures in our minds to help us understand many concepts in chemistry that we will meet in this textbook. In particular, we will make a lot of use of models in diagrams to help you to link observations with theory. Also, you will be using three-dimensional Molymod kits to help you understand shapes of molecules and chemical bonding. In addition, there are lots of simulations and animations online to help you visualise chemical processes in action.
- Models are simplified representations of complex systems. For example, in three-dimensional Molymod models, we represent a chemical bond by means of a length of plastic joining two atoms. This model works perfectly to help us understand chemical bonding. However, it is a simplified representation in terms of how a chemical bond is actually formed. Therefore, although models make complex ideas easier to understand, it is important to realise that models have limitations.
- Models can be modified over time. Models can evolve as more scientific knowledge becomes available. We have already seen that Dalton's simple model of the atom had to be changed when sub-atomic particles were discovered. Models may be compared to tools that help us to understand ideas in chemistry, taking into account all the information available at the present time.
- Models are very useful for making predictions. An example of this type of prediction is the use of the particle model to predict that if we decrease the volume of a gas in a container, we will increase the pressure, Figure 1.6.

At present, scientists are using mathematical models and computer simulation models to understand how the climate system of the Earth works. These models are helping to predict details of what might happen in the future in particular areas of the world as a result of global warming.

Even though we cannot see species such as atoms, molecules and ions, models help us to make sense of them. This is why chemistry is such a fantastic subject - it helps you to become a sharper and more scientific thinker. In short, the study of chemistry is good for your brain!

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-020.jpg?height=1068&width=886&top_left_y=384&top_left_x=1696)
Figure 1.6 The model of the particle theory predicts that if we decrease the volume of the container, the pressure of the gas will increase as more molecules are pushed into a smaller space.

### 1.6 Chemistry in society

Chemistry is not just a subject that you study in school. Chemistry plays an important role throughout our daily lives and in society.

- Chemistry and health. Chemistry plays an important role in the development of medicines, e.g. vaccines, antibiotics and drugs for pain relief. In addition, important drugs have been developed in the area of chemotherapy for cancer treatment as well as anaesthetics for administering to patients undergoing surgery. Chemists play a key role in designing and synthesising drugs. Millions of lives have been saved by vaccines developed by chemists, Figure 1.7. The discovery of penicillin by Alexander Fleming has revolutionised infection control in medicine. Antibiotics are now manufactured in laboratories all over the world. Without these antibiotics, simple infections could be very harmful to our health.
- Chemistry and technology. Chemists are involved in the development of lithium-ion batteries for use in items such as smartphones and laptops. In addition, chemists develop solar panels, touchscreens, silicon chips and other items that are essential for the electronics industries. Also, chemists who specialise in the area of materials chemistry are involved in developing modern materials such as touchscreens and polymers used in 3-D printing.
- Chemistry and sustainability. A lot of research is taking place in the area of developing biodegradable plastics, carbon-capture processes to remove carbon dioxide from industrial emissions, new catalysts to improve efficiency in the area of industrial chemistry and the development of biofuels from plants.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-020.jpg?height=775&width=1091&top_left_y=2881&top_left_x=1530)
Figure 1.7 This photograph shows a team of chemists working as part of a drug design team to develop new drugs to treat cancer patients.

It is worth noting that society plays an important role in influencing research in chemistry. For example the search for vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic drove research into developing an mRNA COVID vaccine. Similarly, the awareness of problems related to climate change is driving research into green energy solutions such as hydrogen fuel cells (Chapter 22).

Each of us has the responsibility to be more personally effective in addressing the impact of science and technology on society. For example, we should make more responsible personal choices such as choosing products with less packaging, using biodegradable materials where possible, and by reducing personal energy consumption with the aid of energy-efficient devices. We should also stay informed by following reliable sources of scientific information and ensure that we understand scientific issues.

In conclusion, it is clear that chemistry plays a key role in every part of our daily lives. It helps protect our health through the development of medicines. It also plays an important role in the development of modern materials used in electronic devices. It is at the heart of global research to help build a more sustainable future through the development of biodegradable plastics, cleaner energy sources and more efficient industrial processes.

It is no wonder that chemistry is often called the creative science. You are about to begin your journey of studying chemistry and we look forward to accompanying you on this journey through Chemistry Live!

The scientific method is a step-by-step approach that helps us test ideas, answer questions and discover new knowledge.

A scientific theory is an explanation of observations and is based on hypotheses, laws and facts.
A scientific law is a description of observed occurrences.
A scientific model is a simplified representation to help us to visualise, explain and understand chemistry concepts as well as making predictions about results of physical and chemical changes.

Chemistry plays an important role in our lives, especially in the areas of health, technology and susta nability.

# 2 Atomic Structure: The Nuclear Model

### 2.1 Introduction

Many observations in chemistry suggest that the materials around us are made up of small particles. The scientific name for materials is matter. Thus, the idea that materials are made up of small particles is often referred to as the particulate nature of matter.

The term particulate nature of matter refers to the idea that all substances are made up of tiny, invisible particles. These particles can be atoms, molecules or ions, depending on the substance. We will explain the precise meaning of the terms atoms, molecules and ions later in this textbook. For the moment, just think of them as small particles. They are so small that we can't see them with our eyes.

The experiment shown in Figure 2.1 provides evidence for the existence of small particles.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-023.jpg?height=408&width=1186&top_left_y=2369&top_left_x=322)
Figure 2.1 When the particles of ammonia gas meet the particles of hydrogen chloride gas, a white ring of a substance called ammonium chloride is formed.

The experiment may be explained as follows:

- Particles of the ammonia gas moving from left to right meet up with particles of hydrogen chloride gas moving from right to left. (Note that hydrochloric acid is a solution of hydrogen chloride gas in water.)
- A white, powdery substance (ammonium chloride) is formed where the particles of hydrogen chloride and ammonia meet.


## OBJECTIVES

- To help students appreciate the key discoveries that led to our understanding of the nuclear model of the atom.
- To give students an understanding of how particles inside the atom (sub-atomic particles) are arranged in the nuclear model of the atom.
- To ensure that students know the properties of the proton, neutron and electron.


### 2.2 The development of the nuclear model of the atom

In this section, we will be quoting dates of various discoveries. You do not have to remember any of these dates. They are provided simply to give you an idea of when the work took place. There are lots of good videos available online to help you understand the experiments described in this section.

## The Greek philosophers: Concept of the atom

Greek philosophers (about 400 BC ) were the first to propose that matter was composed of small particles. The Greek philosophers believed that the tiny particles (of which all matter was composed) were so small that they could not be broken down into even smaller particles, i.e. they were indivisible. The Greek word for 'indivisible' is 'atomos', which gave us the word atom in the English language. You will have met the modern definition of an atom in your study of science at Junior Cycle level.

An atom is the smallest particle of an element that still has the properties of that element.

You will learn more about elements when you study the Periodic Table of the Elements.

## Dalton's atomic theory

In 1808 an English chemist called John Dalton, Figure 2.2, wrote a book in which he put forward an Atomic Theory to explain the results of a number of experiments he had performed with gases.

The assumptions of Dalton's Atomic Theory may be summarised as follows:

1. All matter is made up of very small particles called atoms.
2. All atoms are indivisible. They cannot be broken down into simpler particles.

## John Dalton <br> (1766-1844)

Figure 2.2
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-024.jpg?height=336&width=343&top_left_y=579&top_left_x=2285)

John Dalton proposed a theory about atoms in 1808. He thought of atoms as being like tiny snooker balls that cannot be broken down into simpler particles.

Just as snooker balls are solid and can't be easily broken apart, Dalton imagined atoms as small, solid spheres that cannot be broken down. Dalton wrote a lot more about his theory but the above two key points are the essential assumptions. However, Dalton's idea of the atom began to be questioned as a result of experiments carried out towards the end of the nineteenth century.

## Discovery of cathode rays: William Crookes

In 1875 an English chemist called William Crookes, Figure 2.3, carried out experiments that involved passing an electric current through gases.

Crookes used the apparatus shown in Figure 2.4 to pass the electric current through the air at low pressure. This type of glass tube is commonly called a vacuum tube. Crookes showed that rays were coming from the negative electrode (cathode) and that these rays cast a shadow of a Maltese cross at the far end of the tube. He used the name cathode rays to describe the rays coming from the cathode. In short, Crookes discovered cathode rays.

The cathode rays themselves are invisible - but when they strike the glass, they cause it to glow (or fluoresce), Figure 2.5. The shadow is caused when these cathode rays are stopped by the Maltese cross.

Crookes did not know that cathode rays consisted of tiny charged particles. This discovery was made
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-024.jpg?height=417&width=1136&top_left_y=1894&top_left_x=188)
by another scientist called J. J. Thomson.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-024.jpg?height=827&width=1092&top_left_y=1742&top_left_x=1482)
Figure 2.4 Crookes showed that rays were coming from the negative electrode (cathode) and that these rays cast a shadow at the far end of the tube. He had discovered cathode rays.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-024.jpg?height=792&width=1180&top_left_y=2897&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 2.5 The shadow of the Maltese cross is caused by cathode rays being obstructed by the cross.

## Discovery of the electron: J. J. Thomson

In 1897 an English scientist called J.J. Thomson, Figure 2.6, working in the Cavendish Laboratory at Cambridge University, devised an experiment to investigate if the cathode rays discovered by Crookes consisted of charged particles.

Thomson's experiment may be summarised as follows:

- He produced a narrow beam of cathode rays by passing them through a small hole in the positive electrode, Figure 2.7.
- This narrow beam was passed between two parallel metal plates about halfway along the tube and then struck a fluorescent screen at the far end of the tube. This caused the fluorescent screen to glow.
- He found that when there was no charge on the parallel plates, the beam of cathode rays passed straight down the tube and struck the fluorescent screen at the position shown in Figure 2.7.
- On placing a positive charge on the top plate, the position of the spot moved upwards, as shown in Figure 2.8.
- Since the cathode rays were attracted up towards the positive plate, Thomson concluded that they consisted of negatively charged particles. (Unlike charges always attract each other.)
- The negatively charged particles are now called electrons.

We now realise that what is actually happening in the above experiment is that the high voltage is 'dragging' electrons out of the atoms of the cathode. These electrons then travel towards the positive electrode. J. J. Thomson is recognised as the person who discovered the electron.

> Cathode rays are streams of negatively charged particles called electrons.

From the results of his experiments, Thomson was able to measure the ratio of charge / mass of the electron.

In 1909 an American scientist called Robert Millikan, Figure 2.9, carried out a famous 'oil drop' experiment to determine the size of the charge on the electron. He found the value of the charge on the electron was $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulomb. (The coulomb is the unit of electric charge.)

## J.J. Thomson <br> (1856-1940)

J.J. Thomson is credited with the discovery of the electron. He received the Nobel Prize in physics in 1906 for his work on the electron.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-025.jpg?height=607&width=1134&top_left_y=940&top_left_x=1591)
Figure 2.7 J.J. Thomson's apparatus proved that the cathode rays consisted of negatively charged particles.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-025.jpg?height=782&width=1248&top_left_y=1748&top_left_x=1536)
Figure 2.8 The negative beam of electrons is attracted up towards the positive plate. In this apparatus, fluorescent paper is used to show the path of the electron beam.

## Robert Millikan <br> (1868-1953)

Figure 2.9
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-025.jpg?height=353&width=343&top_left_y=2750&top_left_x=2454)

Robert Millikan measured the size of the charge on the electron. He received the Nobel Prize in physics in 1923 for this experiment, which he carried out at the University of Chicago.

Since Thomson had measured the ratio of charge / mass of the electron, Millikan's discovery enabled the mass of the electron to be calculated as $9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$.

Therefore, by 1909 the electron had been identified as a negatively charged particle of very small mass.

### 2.3 The 'plum pudding' model of the atom: J. J. Thomson

In 1898 J.J. Thomson proposed a very simple model of the structure of the atom. His assumptions may be summarised as follows:

- An atom is like a sphere of positive charge.
- Electrons are embedded in the sphere at random.

Since Thomson's model resembled a pudding with raisins in it or bits of fruit in a cake, his model of the atom became known as the 'plum pudding' model, Figure 2.10. His model did explain why atoms were neutral but Thomson did not have any experimental evidence to back up this simple model. The results of an interesting experiment performed in 1909 showed that Thomson's simple picture of the atom was not correct. This experiment is described in the next section.

### 2.4 The nuclear model of the atom: Rutherford

In 1909 a scientist from New Zealand called Ernest Rutherford, Figure 2.11, was working at Manchester University, England. Together with two research students, Rutherford studied the scattering of particles called alpha particles by a very thin sheet of gold foil. Alpha particles are positively charged particles produced by certain radioactive substances.

A diagram of the experiment is shown in Figure 2.12 and may be summarised as follows:

- Rutherford bombarded a thin piece of gold foil with alpha particles.
- Alpha particles are positively charged and consist of groups of two neutrons and two protons stuck together, i.e. the nucleus of the helium atom. (You do not need to know any further information about alpha particles.)
- Rutherford used a phosphorescent screen to detect the alpha particles. A little flash of light appears on the screen when struck by alpha particles. The little flashes of light were observed through a microscope.

If Thomson's 'plum pudding' model of the atom were correct, then you would expect to find that some of the alpha particles would be deflected by small amounts. In other words, if the positive charge was distributed evenly throughout the atom, some of the alpha particles would suffer only slight deflections as they

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-026.jpg?height=469&width=994&top_left_y=358&top_left_x=1565)
Figure 2.10 Thomson imagined an atom as a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it at random. This model became known as the 'plum pudding' model of the atom.

## Ernest Rutherford <br> (1871-1937)

Figure 2.11
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-026.jpg?height=330&width=336&top_left_y=1158&top_left_x=2298)

Ernest Rutherford received the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1908 for his work on radioactivity. In 1909 he and his research team performed a very important experiment that led to the discovery of the nucleus.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-026.jpg?height=714&width=1121&top_left_y=1855&top_left_x=1497)
Figure 2.12 The experiment carried out by Rutherford and his research team to investigate how alpha particles were scattered by a piece of gold foil

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-026.jpg?height=590&width=812&top_left_y=2884&top_left_x=1653)
Figure 2.13 The expected result of the experiment if Thomson's model is correct. Most of the alpha particles should pass straight through the thin foil. Some alpha particles should suffer slight deflections.

passed through the atom. Most of the alpha particles should pass through undeflected, Figure 2.13.

Rutherford found that the vast majority of the alpha particles did indeed pass undeflected through the gold foil. Unexpectedly, however, some alpha particles were deflected at large angles as they passed through the gold foil. He also found that some alpha particles were deflected back along their own path. He did not expect these results, Figure 2.14.

Rutherford concluded that the positive charge and the mass of the atoms of the metal foil were concentrated in a small dense core called the nucleus of the atom, Figure 2.15. It was clear that Thomson's 'plum pudding' model was not correct.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-027.jpg?height=642&width=841&top_left_y=364&top_left_x=1132)
Figure 2.14 Rutherford did not expect the alpha particles to be deflected at large angles and for some alpha particles to be deflected back along their own paths. He described it by saying that 'it was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15 -inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you'.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-027.jpg?height=740&width=1163&top_left_y=1113&top_left_x=1155)
Figure 2.15 The large deflections can be explained if the mass and positive charge of the atom are concentrated in a small core called the nucleus.

- The positively charged alpha particles and the positively charged nucleus repelled each other.
- Some alpha particles were reflected back along their original paths after colliding head on (a direct hit) with the nucleus.
- The deflection of the alpha particles at large angles was caused by the alpha particles coming very close to the high concentration of positive charge in the nucleus and being repelled by this high concentration of positive charge.
- Only a small number of alpha particles were reflected back along their original paths because the positive charge and the mass of the atoms of the gold foil were concentrated in such a small dense core (called the nucleus).
- From careful study of the scattering angles, Rutherford and his team deduced that the nucleus of an atom had a diameter of approximately $\frac{1}{100000}$ of the size of the atom. This explains why most of the alpha particles passed straight through the foil, because they never encountered the nucleus, i.e. most of the atom is empty space. If you could increase the size of the atom to that of Croke Park, the nucleus would be the size of a marble in the centre of the stadium.

The observations and conclusions of this experiment are summarised in Table 2.1.

| Observation | Conclusion |
| :--- | :--- |
| Most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil. | Most of the atom is empty space. |
| Some alpha particles are deflected at large angles. | The alpha particles are repelled when they pass near the small positive nucleus. |
| A small number of alpha particles are reflected back along their own paths. | A small number of alpha particles collide head on with the nucleus. |

Table 2.1
Summary of some observations and conclusions from Rutherford's experiment.

There are some really good online videos that demonstrate Rutherford's experiment using modern apparatus. These videos are well worth watching.

### 2.5 Discovery of the proton

Rutherford and his research team continued bombarding various types of substances with alpha particles. They found that in the case of light atoms such as oxygen and nitrogen, small positively charged particles were given off as a result of the bombardment. Rutherford gave the name proton to these small positive particles.

This did not occur with the atoms of the heavier metals such as gold. They explained their results by saying that the alpha particles were breaking up the nuclei of the lighter atoms to release these positively charged particles. The reason that this did not occur in the case of the heavier gold atoms was because the large positive nuclear charge repelled the alpha particles before they had a chance to break up the nucleus.

### 2.6 Assumptions and limitations of Rutherford's nuclear model Assumptions of Rutherford's nuclear model

1. Atoms contain a small, dense positive core called the nucleus. Most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
2. Positive particles called protons are located in the nucleus.
3. The atom is mostly empty space.
4. Electrons are scattered around in the space surrounding the nucleus. This space is called the electron cloud. Rutherford proposed that electrons were moving around the nucleus but did not describe exactly the motion of these electrons.

The new structure of the atom proposed by Rutherford is illustrated in Figure 2.16.

Rutherford's nuclear model replaced the 'plum pudding' model and gave us a clearer understanding of the structure of the atom. The nuclear model was important, as it was the first time that scientists realised that the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in the nucleus of the atom.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-028.jpg?height=1144&width=1144&top_left_y=1484&top_left_x=1497)
Figure 2.16 The model of the atom proposed by Rutherford consisted of a nucleus containing protons, with the electrons in an electron cloud surrounding the nucleus.

## Limitation of Rutherford's nuclear model

1. Since like charges repel, why does the nucleus not fly apart due to the repulsion between the protons in the nucleus?
2. Since opposite charges attract, the model could not explain why electrons don't spiral into the nucleus. We know that this does not happen in real life as most atoms are stable.

We will discuss the explanation for these in the next chapter.

### 2.7 Discovery of the neutron

In 1932 James Chadwick, Figure 2.17, a student of Rutherford, carried out the following experiment:

- He bombarded a sample of beryllium with alpha particles, Figure 2.18.
- He discovered that some type of radiation consisting of particles with no charge came from the beryllium.
- The fact that the particles were neutral made them difficult to detect. Chadwick found that these neutral particles were penetrating enough to knock protons out of paraffin wax. This helped him to detect the neutral particles.
- He concluded that the alpha particles were knocking these neutral particles out of the nucleus of the beryllium atom.
- He found that these particles had about the same mass as the proton and, because they were neutral, he called them neutrons.
- Neutrons were discovered after electrons and protons because they were more difficult to detect since they are neutral.

After the discovery of the neutron, the nuclear model of the atom was more complete. Scientists now had a much clearer picture of the structure of the atom and the role played by neutrons. If it was only protons that existed in the nucleus, then the nucleus would fall apart because of the repulsive forces of the protons for each other (like charges repel). The neutrons help to 'cement' the positively charged protons together. After the discovery of the neutron, Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom was updated and is illustrated in Figure 2.19.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-029.jpg?height=854&width=1040&top_left_y=2750&top_left_x=325)
Figure 2.19 The updated nuclear model of the atom was an improvement on Rutherford's nuclear model, as it was now clear that the nucleus consisted of protons and neutrons.

## James Chadwick <br> (1891-1974)

Figure 2.17
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-029.jpg?height=330&width=330&top_left_y=302&top_left_x=2428)

James Chadwick received the Nobel Prize in physics in 1935 for discovering the neutron.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-029.jpg?height=440&width=1121&top_left_y=846&top_left_x=1608)
Figure 2.18 Alpha particles knocked neutrons out of the nuclei of beryllium atoms. Since neutrons have no charge, they were difficult to detect, so Chadwick used a piece of paraffin wax to detect them. The neutrons knocked protons out of the paraffin wax.

## Assumptions of the updated nuclear model of the atom

The assumptions of the updated model of the atom may be summarised as follows:

1. Atoms consist of a small, dense positive core called the nucleus. Most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
2. Positive particles called protons and neutral particles called neutrons are located in the nucleus.
3. The atom is mostly empty space.
4. Electrons are scattered around in the space surrounding the nucleus. This space is called the electron cloud. Rutherford proposed that electrons were moving around the nucleus but did not describe exactly the motion of these electrons.

## Limitation of the updated nuclear model of the atom

In the nuclear model, electrons are thought to move about in the space around the nucleus. However, since opposite charges attract, the electrons would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, i.e. the atom would collapse. We know that this does not happen in real life, as most atoms are stable.

The fact that the nuclear model cannot explain how electrons stay in motion around the nucleus without crashing into it is a major limitation of the nuclear model.

Other limitations will be discussed in Chapter 3, when we study more modern ideas about the model of the atom.

- Atoms consist of a small, dense positive core called the nucleus. Most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
- Positive particles called protons and neutral particles called neutrons are located in the nucleus.

### 2.8 Properties of the proton, neutron and electron

With the discovery of the neutron, scientists were now aware of the existence of three particles inside the atom. These three particles are often referred to as sub-atomic ('inside the atom') particles. Protons and neutrons were located inside the nucleus and the electrons were located somewhere in the space outside the nucleus. (The location of the electrons is covered in more detail in Chapter 3.)

The charge on the electron was found to be $-1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulomb, the charge on the proton was $+1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ coulomb and, as we have seen, there was no charge on the neutron. The mass of the proton was found to be the same as the mass of the neutron, i.e. $1.67 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{~kg}$. The mass of the electron was found to be much smaller at $9.1 \times 10^{-31}$ kg. You are not required to remember any of these actual values but you should know the relative values as given in Table 2.2.

|  | Relative charge | Relative mass | Location |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Proton | +1 | 1 | Nucleus |
| Neutron | 0 | 1 | Nucleus |
| Electron | -1 | $\frac{1}{1838}$ | Outside nucleus |

Table 2.2 Summary of the properties of sub-atomic particles.

## Summary What I should know

- All matter consists of small particles.

John Dalton said that all matter is made up of very small particles called atoms and that all atoms are indivisible, i.e they cannot be broken down into simpler particles.

Cathode rays are streams of electrons.
J. J. Thomson showed that electrons are negatively charged and determined the charge to mass ratio of the electron.

Robert Millikan measured the size of the charge on the electron using his 'oil drop' experiment.
J.J. Thomson incorrectly suggested the plum pudding model of the atom.

The nuclear model of the atom emerged from Daltons atomic theory and J.J. Thomsons plum pudding model of the atom.

Rutherford and his team discovered the nucleus of the atom and the existence of protons in the nucleus.

James Chadwick discovered the neutron.
Atoms contain a small, dense positive core called the nucleus. Most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

Positive particles called protons and neutral particles called neutrons are located in the nucleus.
The atom is mostly empty space. Electrons are located in the space surrounding the nucleus called the electron cloud, which surrounds the nucleus.

A limitation of the nuclear model is that it cannot explain how electrons stay in motion around the nucleus without spiralling towards the nucleus and crashing into it.

# 3 Atomic Structure: The Bohr and Orbital Models

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-033.jpg?height=466&width=2407&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=325)

### 3.1 Introduction

In the last chapter, we saw how the proton, neutron and electron were discovered. We studied how scientists found that the protons and neutrons were concentrated in the nucleus of the atom. The next question to be answered concerned the location of the electrons. Ernest Rutherford proposed that the electrons were located in some sort of electron cloud. However, he did not have a clear picture of their arrangement. It was a young Danish physicist called Niels Bohr, at the University of Copenhagen, who provided an insight into the arrangement of electrons in the atom, Figure 3.1.

### 3.2 Bohr's study of spectra

Bohr developed a theory that explained the arrangement of electrons in atoms. In order to understand how Bohr developed his theory, we first need to study a few facts about spectra.

When white light (e.g. sunlight or light from an ordinary electric light bulb) is passed through a glass prism, the white light is broken up into an array of colours. Such an array of colours is called a spectrum, Figure 3.2. This spread of colours is referred to as a continuous spectrum, i.e. there are no gaps present in the spectrum. A rainbow is a common example of this type of spectrum. A rainbow in the sky is formed when raindrops act as tiny prisms and separate sunlight into its colours.

You could repeat this using the light coming from a hydrogen discharge tube in place of white light. A hydrogen discharge tube is simply a glass tube filled with hydrogen gas at low pressure, through which an electric current is passed. Niels Bohr carried out this experiment and found that instead of seeing a continuous spectrum, he saw a series of narrow coloured lines, Figure 3.3.

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of the Bohr and orbital models of the atom.
- To provide students with the opportunity to carry out laboratory investigations to identify elements.
- To help students discuss assumptions and limitations of models of the atom.


## Niels Bohr <br> (1885-1962)

Figure 3.1
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-033.jpg?height=324&width=336&top_left_y=1692&top_left_x=2428)

Niels Bohr won the Nobel Prize in physics in 1922 for his study of the arrangement of electrons in the atom.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-033.jpg?height=509&width=1176&top_left_y=2262&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 3.2 A continuous spectrum of colours from red to violet is formed when white light is passed through a glass prism.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-033.jpg?height=547&width=1179&top_left_y=2983&top_left_x=1580)
Figure 3.3 A line spectrum is formed when the light from a hydrogen discharge tube is passed through a prism.

Since the spectrum consists of lines, it is called a line spectrum to distinguish it from a continuous spectrum. Since the light is emitted when an electric current is passed through the hydrogen, the spectrum is more accurately called an emission line
spectrum. This is also known as a line emission spectrum.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-034.jpg?height=749&width=1871&top_left_y=342&top_left_x=928)
Figure 3.4 This instrument is called a spectrometer. In this diagram, it is being used to study the emission line spectrum formed by the light coming from the neon lamp.

Spectra are usually studied using an instrument called a spectrometer, Figure 3.4.

When the light emitted by other elements (e.g. neon, sodium or mercury) was studied, it was found that these elements also produced line spectra.

Spectra are more easily studied in a darkened room. If you use a spectrometer to observe the light emitted by neon, you will see an emission line spectrum similar to that shown in Figure 3.5.

If you replace the neon lamp with a sodium lamp or a mercury lamp, you will see a different emission line spectrum for each of the elements, as shown also in Figure 3.5.

Note that each emission line spectrum is unique. These show how each element has its own unique emission line spectrum - a sort of 'fingerprint' of the element. In fact, the emission line spectrum of an element is often used by chemists to detect its presence. For example, in the analysis of steel, it is possible to detect the presence of various metals in the steel by studying the emission line spectrum obtained.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-034.jpg?height=503&width=766&top_left_y=2698&top_left_x=188)
Figure 3.6a Sodium street lamps give off a yellow light.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-034.jpg?height=642&width=460&top_left_y=2702&top_left_x=966)
Figure 3.6b Mercury vapour lamps give off a blue light.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-034.jpg?height=493&width=1144&top_left_y=1510&top_left_x=1458)
Figure 3.5 The emission line spectra of neon, sodium and mercury.

In our everyday lives, we observe the fact that different elements emit different colours when an electric current is passed through them. For example, sodium street lamps give off a yellow colour, mercury vapour lamps give off a blue colour and neon advertising signs glow red, Figure 3.6 a-c.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-034.jpg?height=499&width=841&top_left_y=2702&top_left_x=1774)
Figure 3.6c Neon signs give off a red light.

The main points of this experiment may be summarised as follows:

Flame tests may be carried out using a wooden splint soaked in water or using a platinum wire. The splint or wire is dipped into a sample of the salt and held in the blue flame of a Bunsen burner. Some examples of flame tests for salts of these metals are shown in Figure 3.8.

## Identifying elements from their line emission spectra

In addition to identifying the elements studied in Experiment 1, for your exam you are also expected to be able to identify three elements from their line emission spectra. These three elements are sodium, strontium and copper.

You can identify the elements from data collected by yourself in the school laboratory (primary data) or from copies of spectra found in textbooks or other sources (secondary data).

Study Figure 3.9 a-c carefully to ensure that you can identify the spectrum if it appears on an exam paper!

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-036.jpg?height=193&width=779&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=188)
Figure 3.9a Line emission spectrum of sodium

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-036.jpg?height=196&width=776&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=1005)
Figure 3.9b Line emission spectrum of strontium

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-036.jpg?height=193&width=776&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=1839)
Figure 3.9c Line emission spectrum of copper

1. The line emission spectrum of sodium is the simplest of the three spectra as it consists of just a 'single' yellow line. (In fact, the single yellow line consists of two yellow lines very close together.) This accounts for the strong yellow light given off in the flame test for sodium.
2. The line emission spectrum of strontium has strong red lines on the right-hand side of the spectrum. These red lines are responsible for the red colour in the emission line spectrum of strontium.
3. The line emission spectrum of copper has strong blue and green lines on the left-hand side of the spectrum. These blue and green lines are responsible for the blue-green colour observed in the flame test for copper.

So far we have been discussing spectra and you may be wondering what this has to do with the structure of the atom. In fact, it was the study of emission spectra that led Niels Bohr to an understanding of how electrons are arranged inside atoms.

### 3.3 The Bohr model of the atom

Bohr realised that any model of the atom must explain two things:

1. Why are the emission spectra of the elements line spectra rather than continuous spectra?
2. Why is the emission spectrum of each element unique to that element?

These questions were answered by Bohr's Theory of Atomic Structure in 1913.

Prior to Bohr's theory, scientists thought that electrons in an atom could have any energy value. Bohr's Theory introduced the idea of quantisation of energy, i.e. that an electron in an atom can only have a fixed amount of energy. This fixed amount of energy is called a quantum of energy. Quantisation means that the energy of an electron in an atom cannot have just any value but is restricted to having only certain specific values (or levels), Fig 3.10.

Bohr suggested a way to relate the emission line spectrum of hydrogen to the structure of an atom of hydrogen. His research work is often described as providing 'spectroscopic evidence for the existence of energy levels'.

NOTE
Quantised means that the energy of an electron comes in fixed amounts. It's like stepping up a stairs instead of walking up a smooth ramp. As you stand on each step you have a fixed amount or 'chunk' of energy. In contrast, as you move up a smooth ramp, your energy increase is continuous.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-036.jpg?height=1001&width=770&top_left_y=1829&top_left_x=1845)
Figure 3.10 Electrons can only occupy certain energy levels. Each energy level has a fixed amount of energy associated with it. The book can only occupy certain shelves. Each shelf is a fixed distance from the ground and hence the book has a certain amount of potential energy on each shelf. Bohr's mathematical calculations showed that the energy levels became closer to one another as the value of n increased.

## Assumptions of Bohr's theory

- Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed paths called orbits.
- Electrons in any one orbit have a fixed amount of energy. Orbits are also called energy levels. (Orbits are also sometimes called 'shells' but this term is now rarely used.)
- Energy levels are represented by the letter $n$. The lowest energy level is the $n=1$ level, the next highest is $n=2$, etc.
- The energy of the electron in a particular orbit or energy level is quantised, i.e. fixed at a definite value.
- As long as an electron is in any one particular energy level, it neither gains nor loses energy. This helps to explain why electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.
- Atoms normally exist in the ground state, i.e. the electrons have the lowest amount of energy possible because they occupy the lowest available energy levels. For example, in the ground state of hydrogen, its single electron is in the lowest energy state ( $n=1$ energy level), Figure 3.11.
- Electrons in the ground state have energy of fixed values, i.e. the energy of the electrons in a particular orbit or energy level is fixed or quantised.
- In the ground state, the electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels.
- When an atom in its ground state is provided with energy (by electricity or heating), a specific amount of this energy is absorbed and the electrons jump from lower energy levels to higher energy levels. The electrons are now in an excited state.
- In some atoms of hydrogen, for example, the electron may move to the second energy level; in others, it may move to the third energy level.
- The energy absorbed is equal to the difference in energy between the lower energy level (ground state) and the higher energy level (excited state).
- Electrons in the excited state are unstable and they will fall back down to lower energy levels after a short period of time.
- As an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower energy level, the excess energy is released in the form of a photon of light which has a definite or fixed amount of energy. (Sometimes the word 'discrete' is used instead of 'fixed'.)

An energy level is defined as the fixed energy value that an electron in an atom may have.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-037.jpg?height=793&width=1092&top_left_y=572&top_left_x=1666)
Figure 3.11 Bohr's Theory states that the energy of the electron in any one energy level is fixed or quantised. In the ground state of hydrogen, its single electron is in the $n=1$ energy level. When a fixed amount of energy is absorbed, the electron moves to a higher energy level. The electron is now in an excited state.

The ground state of an atom is one in which the electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels.

The excited state of an atom is one in which the electrons occupy higher energy levels than those available in the ground state.

A photon is a fixed amount or 'packet' (quantum) of light energy or other forms of electromagnetic radiation.

Electromagnetic radiation is radiation such as visible light, infrared radiation and ultraviolet radiation.

- Since an electron can only fall back to certain definite energy levels, only fixed amounts of light energy can be given off, i.e. light of a definite frequency is given off.
- The frequency of the light emitted depends on the difference in energy between the two energy levels and is given by the equation $\boldsymbol{E}_{2}-\boldsymbol{E}_{1}=\boldsymbol{h} \boldsymbol{f}$.
- $E_{2}$ represents the energy of the higher energy level, $E_{1}$ represents the energy of the lower energy level, $h$ is a number that never changes called Planck's constant and $f$ is the frequency of the light emitted.

The equation $E_{2}-E_{1}=h f$ tells us that the energy difference is proportional to the frequency of the light emitted, Figure 3.12.

- The definite amount of energy emitted (light of a definite frequency) appears as a line of a particular colour in the emission spectrum. Therefore, an emission line spectrum is formed.
- Since only definite amounts of energy are emitted, this implies that electrons can occupy only definite energy levels.
- Each definite amount of energy emitted gives rise to a line in the emission spectrum, Figure 3.13.


## EXAM TIPI

Study Figure 3.13 carefully. In past exam papers, questions were asked to relate a colour in the emission line spectrum to a particular transition. For example, be aware that the transition from $\mathrm{n}=3$ to $\mathrm{n}=2$ gives rise to a red colour.

- The series of invisible lines in the ultraviolet series (where electrons fall to the $n=1$ energy level) is called the Lyman series.
- The series of lines in the visible spectrum (where electrons fall to the $n=2$ energy level) is called the Balmer series.
- The series of invisible lines found in the infrared region (where electrons fall to the $\mathrm{n}=3$ energy level) is called the Paschen series.

These lines are named after scientists who first discovered the series of lines or studied them.

- Each element has a unique emission line spectrum because each element has a different number of electrons and has its own arrangement of these electrons in energy levels. Therefore, there will be different numbers and types of electron transitions for each element. These different electron transitions give rise to a different emission line spectrum for each element.

But is Bohr's theory correct? Bohr's work was of two kinds, both theoretical and experimental, and may be summarised as follows:

- Bohr realised that each coloured line in the emission spectrum of hydrogen has its own particular frequency.
- Firstly, he calculated mathematically the energy corresponding to each of the energy levels $n=1$, $n=2, n=3$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-038.jpg?height=505&width=985&top_left_y=384&top_left_x=1565)
Figure 3.12 Energy is given out in the form of light of a definite frequency when an electron falls back from an excited state to a lower energy state.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-038.jpg?height=330&width=1046&top_left_y=1354&top_left_x=1556)

The above equation may also be written as $E_{m}-E_{n}=h f$ where $E_{m}$ is the energy of the higher energy level and $E_{n}$ in the energy of the lower energy level.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-038.jpg?height=1039&width=1134&top_left_y=2044&top_left_x=1510)
Figure 3.13 Each electron transition results in a line of particular wavelength in the emission spectrum of hydrogen.

## EXAM TIPI

In a past exam paper, students were asked to explain why there is no yellow line in the hydrogen emission spectrum. The reason for this is because there is no electron transition in hydrogen that would give rise to an energy loss that corresponds to a yellow colour.

- Then he calculated the amounts of energy an electron would lose when falling from higher energy levels to lower energy levels.
- Finally, using the equation $E_{2}-E_{1}=h f$, he calculated the frequency and wavelength of the coloured lines corresponding to these electron transitions. (The above equation gave him the frequency and the equation velocity of light = frequency × wavelength enabled him to calculate the wavelength.)
- Bohr's experimental work involved him measuring the wavelengths of each line in the emission line spectrum of hydrogen using a spectrometer.
- He found that the wavelengths of light in the emission spectrum of the hydrogen atom calculated using his theory had exactly the same values as those measured experimentally, Figure 3.13.
- Therefore, the fact that only definite amounts of energy are emitted implies that electrons can only occupy definite energy levels, i.e. Bohr's suggestion that energy levels must exist in the atom was proven correct.
The three series of lines (Lyman, Balmer and Paschen) can all be satisfactorily explained on the basis of Bohr's theory. Bohr predicted their existence and their discovery added further credibility to his theory.

Students often ask the question: 'If the hydrogen atom has only one electron, why is it that so many electron transitions (as shown in Figure 3.13) are possible?' The reason for this is that even in a small sample of hydrogen, there are millions of atoms of hydrogen. When energy is supplied to the sample of hydrogen, not all atoms may receive exactly the same amount of energy. In some atoms, the electron may be promoted from the $n=1$ to the $n$ = 2 level, in others it may be promoted from the $n=$ 1 to the $n=3$ level, etc. Thus, when these electrons drop back down, they are coming from different energy levels and different lines will be formed in the emission spectrum since different electron transitions are involved.

Fluorescent light strips and lasers make use of electron transitions, Figure 3.14.
