## NOTE

You may be wondering about the distinction between the words spectrometer and spectroscope:

- Instruments that are used to carry out measurements on spectra are called spectrometers, e.g. the instrument shown in Figure 3.4 can be used to measure wavelengths of light.
- Instruments that are simply used to observe spectra are called spectroscopes.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-039.jpg?height=858&width=1183&top_left_y=1106&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 3.14 The light coming from this laser beam is caused by electrons falling from higher energy levels to lower energy levels.

### 3.4 Energy sublevels

As the study of spectra developed, more sophisticated spectrometers were becoming available. With these spectrometers, scientists were able to look more closely at lines formed in emission spectra.

Their work may be summarised as follows:

- In many cases, what appeared originally to be a single line actually consisted of a number of lines very close together. For example, in studying the emission spectrum of sodium, what appeared to be a single yellow line was found to be made up of two yellow lines very close together.
- These two lines could not have resulted from electrons dropping to two different energy levels as this would have given rise to lines much farther apart in the spectrum.
- To explain this observation, it was proposed that each main energy level, except the first, was made up of a number of sublevels, all of which were close in energy.
- From the analysis of spectra, it was discovered that the number of sublevels was the same as the value of $n$ for the main energy level, i.e. the $n=2$ main energy level had two sublevels, the $n=3$ main energy level had three sublevels and the $n=4$ had four sublevels, Figure 3.15.
- Scientists labelled the sublevels using the letters s, p, d and f . The sublevel of lowest energy was called the s sublevel, the one of next highest energy was called the p sublevel, the one above that the d sublevel and the one above that again was called the $\mathbf{f}$ sublevel. Note in Figure 3.15 that the 4s sublevel is in fact lower in energy than the 3d sublevel. This will be discussed in Chapter 4.
You might wonder why these particular letters were chosen to represent sublevels. Originally they were chosen from words used by scientists to describe lines in line spectra: s for 'sharp', p for 'principal', d for 'diffuse' and $f$ for 'fundamental'.


### 3.5 Developments leading to changes in Bohr's model

We have already learned that Bohr proposed his model of atomic structure in 1913. However, in 1924 a French scientist called Louis de Broglie put forward a proposal that led to Bohr's model being questioned.

- De Broglie suggested that all moving particles have a wave motion associated with them.
- His calculations suggested that for fairly large objects such as a tennis ball, this wave motion would be impossible to detect. However, for a small object such as an electron, the wave motion should be possible to detect.
- De Broglie was proved correct in 1927 when it was discovered that moving electrons had a wave motion associated with them. This idea that a particle can behave like a wave is often referred to as 'wave-particle duality'.
- The discovery that electrons have a wave motion associated with them had major implications for the Bohr theory. If the electron has a wave motion, then Bohr's idea of an electron travelling in a fixed path at a precise, constant distance from the nucleus cannot be correct, Figure 3.16.

This problem was described mathematically by a German physicist called Werner Heisenberg, Figure 3.17.

He put forward a very famous principle called
Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-040.jpg?height=926&width=915&top_left_y=432&top_left_x=1670)
Figure 3.15 This diagram shows the sublevels associated with the main energy levels. Note that the 4s sublevel has been found to be lower in energy than the 3d sublevel.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-040.jpg?height=802&width=815&top_left_y=1761&top_left_x=1705)
Figure 3.16 If the electron has a wave motion, then it cannot be travelling in a precise path at a fixed distance from the nucleus.

Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle states that it is impossible to measure at the same time both the velocity and the position of an electron.

## Werner Heisenberg <br> (1901-1976)

Figure 3.17
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-040.jpg?height=324&width=333&top_left_y=3235&top_left_x=2291)

Werner Heisenberg was a German physicist who was awarded the 1932 Nobel Prize in physics for his famous uncertainty principle.

Heisenberg reasoned as follows:

- Consider a beam of light being used to detect the presence of an electron. The beam of light is like a radar signal that bounces off an object.
- When the beam strikes the electron, the position of the electron is determined - but since the electron has such a small mass, its velocity (speed) is immediately changed by the beam of light. So the act of trying to measure the properties of something so tiny, actually changes some of its properties.
- Heisenberg suggested that the Bohr picture of the atom was not completely satisfactory. Bohr's model visualised electrons moving with a certain speed in orbits of fixed distances from the nucleus.
- Heisenberg stated that you cannot say this about the electron since, for the reasons given above, you cannot measure at the same time both its speed and its distance from the nucleus (i.e. its location).
Heisenberg actually used the word momentum (mass × velocity) instead of velocity in stating his principle. However, since the mass of the electron is a constant value, and since we are not concerned with the mathematics of his principle, the simpler term velocity will be used here.

It was clear, therefore, that the idea of an electron moving in a fixed orbit around the nucleus had to be modified. If the electron is not travelling in a fixed path, then we can only talk about the probability of finding it at a particular position inside the atom.

This idea of probability led to a new picture being developed to describe the position of electrons in atoms and the limitations of Bohr's theory became clear.

## Limitations of Bohr's model of the atom

1. Bohr's theory worked perfectly to explain the emission spectrum of hydrogen. However, when his theory was applied to atoms with more than one electron, it failed to account for many of the lines in the emission spectra of these atoms.
2. Bohr's theory did not take into account De Broglie's finding that electrons have a wave motion. Therefore, the idea of an electron travelling in a fixed path at a precise, constant distance from the nucleus cannot be true.
3. Bohr's model assumes that both the position of an electron (in an orbit) and its velocity are known precisely. However, Bohr's model is in conflict with Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle which concluded that we can only refer to the probability of finding an electron in a region in space.
4. Bohr's theory could not explain the splitting of certain lines in emission spectra and did not take into account the presence of sublevels.

For many purposes in chemistry, the Bohr picture of electrons travelling in fixed paths around the nucleus is perfectly adequate. However, in some cases where we move more deeply into the subject, it is necessary to look at some modifications or changes to the Bohr model. This does not mean that the Bohr model is 'wrong'. The Bohr model works perfectly to explain some observations in chemistry. In other cases, we need a more modern model to explain our observations. We now study this more modern model.

## SEC exam question 3.1

How did Niels Bohr modify the nuclear model of the atom? Bohr modified the nuclear model of the atom put forward by Rutherford by proposing that:

- Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed paths called orbits.
- Electrons in any one orbit have a fixed amount of energy. Orbits are also called energy levels or shells.
- Energy levels are represented by the letter $n$. The lowest energy level is the $n=1$ level, the next highest is $n=2$, etc.
- The energy of the electron in a particular orbit or energy level is quantised, i.e. fixed at a definite value.

Note: The branch of science that explains how small objects such as atoms and electrons behave is called quantum mechanics. These small objects do not behave in the same way as large objects such as footballs or cars. Therefore, the orbital model of the atom is also called the Quantum Mechanical model of the atom.

### 3.6 The orbital model of atomic structure

Imagine that you are looking at an electron in an atom of hydrogen as it revolves around the nucleus. If you could take a large number of photographs of the electron and then put all of these photographs into one photograph, you would get a picture like that shown in Figure 3.18.

Note from the diagram that the shading is heaviest near the nucleus and gets less as you move away from the nucleus. This means that there is a high probability of finding the electron near the nucleus of the atom and the probability gets less as the distance from the nucleus increases.

Although diagrams such as that in Figure 3.18 give us a picture of the probability of finding an electron, they are quite tedious to draw. Instead, chemists draw a boundary within which there is a very high probability (approximately $95 \%$ ) of finding an electron. The region within this boundary is called an orbital.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-042.jpg?height=841&width=897&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1718)
Figure 3.18 Diagrammatic representation of the position of an electron in an atom of hydrogen.

An orbital is a region in space within which there is a high probability of finding an electron.

## EXAM TIPI

When defining an orbital, make sure you use the term region rather than area. As orbitals are three-dimensional, area is incorrect and will not be awarded any marks in an exam.

- The term orbital must not be confused with the term orbit. The term orbit was used by Bohr to describe the fixed path of an electron travelling with a certain velocity at a precise, constant distance from the nucleus. As indicated above, the term orbital was introduced to describe the more realistic probability picture.
- The orbital for the electron in a hydrogen atom in the ground state is called a 1s atomic orbital and is indicated in Figure 3.19.

The Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger devised mathematical equations to work out the probability of finding an electron in any particular sublevel in an atom, Figure 3.20.

Schrödinger's equations were solved and the solutions were plotted in three dimensions to give us the shapes of the four types of orbitals, s, p, d, and f. Thus, an orbital could also be described as a pictorial representation of the solution of the Schrödinger wave equation describing a particular electron.

- All s orbitals are spherical and differ only in size, Figure 3.21. In other words, the probability of finding an electron in a particular s sublevel is identical in all directions at a fixed radius from the nucleus.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-042.jpg?height=669&width=1177&top_left_y=1692&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 3.19 An s orbital is spherical.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-042.jpg?height=1264&width=1176&top_left_y=2500&top_left_x=1445)
Figure 3.21 All s orbitals are spherical in shape.

When Schrödinger's equations were solved to describe the probability of finding an electron in a p sublevel, it was found that the resulting shapes resembled a dumbbell, i.e. p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, Figure 3.22.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-043.jpg?height=593&width=2325&top_left_y=677&top_left_x=351)
Figure 3.22 Note that p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped. Each p orbital points along one of the three main axes. Since the three axes are all at right angles to each other, it does not matter which is labelled $\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}$ or z .

- It was discovered from the splitting of lines in emission spectra that each $p$ sublevel consisted of three parts now denoted as $p_{x^{\prime}} p_{y}$ and $p_{z}$. The three corresponding $p$ orbitals are of equal energy and only differ in their orientation in space as shown in Figure 3.22.
- The letters $x, y$ and $z$ stand for the three main axes to represent direction. The three $p$ orbitals are therefore at right angles to each other. So, the probability of finding an electron in a p sublevel is represented by these dumbbell shapes.
- As one moves out from the nucleus along any of the $x, y$ or $z$ axes, the probability of finding an electron is shown by the shapes of the p orbitals. Within the boundary of the region enclosed by the dumbbell, there is a high probability of finding an electron. Outside the dumbbell, the probability of finding an electron is very low.
- Note that the 2s sublevel consists of one orbital (the 2s orbital). The 2p sublevel consists of three p orbitals all of the same energy. Thus, while the second energy level ( $n=2$ ) is divided into two sublevels ( $2 s$ and $2 p$ ), overall there are four orbitals present (one $s$ orbital and three $p$ orbitals).
We can now define a sublevel as follows:

A sublevel is a subdivision of a main energy level and consists of one or more orbitals of the same energy.

The most modern model of atomic structure is the orbital model and this model is often seen as the foundation stone of modern atomic theory.

Study Example 3.2 in the online resources.
In the next chapter, we will study how the electrons in atoms are distributed among the various orbitals.

# 4 The Periodic Table: Arrangement of Electrons

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-047.jpg?height=1098&width=1261&top_left_y=530&top_left_x=325)

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of the development of the modern Periodic Table.
- To make students familiar with some key terms associated with atoms of elements.
- To enable students to use the Periodic Table to deduce the arrangement of electrons in atoms of the first 36 elements $(\mathrm{HL})$ and the first 20


### 4.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we will study one of the most important foundation stones in chemistry - the Periodic Table of the Elements. We will begin by discussing what an element is and consider some of the early ideas about elements. We will then look at the work of some chemists in trying to put these elements into some sort of order. The Periodic Table itself will then be studied, and we will learn how this table is of enormous help to us in deducing a whole range of information. Finally, we will learn how to use the Periodic Table to deduce how electrons are arranged in atoms.

### 4.2 The Elements

Greek philosophers had the idea that the universe was made up of a few basic substances or elements. These philosophers said there were four elements - earth, air, water and fire. Believe it or not, this idea remained the basis of chemical theory for almost two thousand years! There are two scientists who made a great contribution to the modern development of our understanding of the idea of an element.

An element is a substance that cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical means. elements (OL).

## 1. Robert Boyle

The first accurate definition of an element was given by an Irish chemist called Robert Boyle, Figure 4.1. In his book The Sceptical Chemist, published in 1661, he described an element as a simple substance that cannot be broken into anything simpler - a description that was broadly similar to the modern definition of an element.

## Robert Boyle <br> (1627-1691)

Figure 4.1
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-047.jpg?height=336&width=333&top_left_y=2389&top_left_x=2435)

Robert Boyle was the first chemist to properly define the meaning of the term element. He was born in Lismore Castle, Co. Waterford.

Copper is an example of an element. The modern definition means that whatever chemical reactions copper undergoes, you cannot split the copper into any simpler chemicals.

On the other hand, water is not an element because it can be split into hydrogen and oxygen. In fact, Boyle also predicted that elements combined together in chemical reactions to form what are now called compounds.

## 2. Humphry Davy

Some of the most important discoveries in the history of the elements were made by an English chemist called Humphry Davy, Figure 4.2.

In 1807, at the age of 28 years, Davy discovered the element potassium by passing electricity through a compound of potassium.

Davy also discovered the elements sodium, calcium, barium, strontium and magnesium by passing electricity through compounds containing these elements. The discovery that an electric current could be used to obtain elements from their compounds was a turning point in the history of the discovery of the elements, Figure 4.3.

After 1807 many new elements were discovered. More than one hundred elements have been discovered to date.

### 4.3 The development of the modern Periodic Table

By 1800 approximately 35 elements had been discovered. As more and more elements were discovered, chemists were finding it difficult to understand and memorise the long lists of chemical and physical properties of these elements. They needed to find some kind of pattern or system to help simplify matters. It was the work of two chemists that eventually led to this pattern being developed. These two chemists were Dmitri Mendeleev and Henry Moseley.

## Mendeleev's Periodic Table

- In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev, Figure 4.4, professor of chemistry at the University of St Petersburg, Russia, wrote the properties of each of the 63 known elements on separate cards.
- He arranged these cards representing the elements in order of increasing atomic weight (relative atomic mass). We will study the meaning of this term later in this chapter.
- He placed elements with similar properties under each other in groups.
- He noticed a periodic repetition of properties, i.e. similar physical and chemical properties recurred at intervals. The word periodic means 'at regular interval'.
- He summarised his findings in what he called his 'Periodic Law'.

Figure 4.2

Humphry Davy
(1778-1829)
(1778-1829)
Humphry Davy discovered many elements by passing electricity through their compounds.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-048.jpg?height=1046&width=1140&top_left_y=745&top_left_x=1468)
Figure 4.3 After Davy's discovery in 1807 that elements could be extracted from their compounds using electricity, there was a marked increase in the number of elements discovered.

Mendeleev's Periodic Law: When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic weight (relative atomic mass), the properties of the elements are repeated at regular intervals in other elements.

## Dmitri Mendeleev <br> (1834-1907)

Figure 4.4
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-048.jpg?height=336&width=326&top_left_y=2441&top_left_x=2298)

Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic weight (relative atomic mass). His Periodic Table was quite similar to the modern Periodic Table.

Note: The repeating of properties at regular intervals is often referred to as a periodic system.

Mendeleev's work may be summarised as follows:
To demonstrate the regular repetition of properties, he placed all known elements with similar properties in the same vertical column in a table.

Because the properties of the elements repeated at regular intervals, or periodically, the table was called the Periodic Table of the Elements.

Mendeleev left gaps in his table. He had to do this to make all the known elements fit into the proper group (column) in terms of their properties, so that all elements with similar properties would be in the same column or group of the Periodic Table, Table 4.1. He said that the gaps represented elements that had not yet been discovered.

|  | Group I | Group II | Group III | Group IV | Group V | Group VI | Group VII | Group VIII |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Period 1 | H |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Period 2 | Li | Be | B | C | N | O | F |  |
| Period 3 | Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl |  |
| Period 4 | K | Ca | * | * | As | Se | Br |  |

Table 4.1 A section of Mendeleev's Periodic Table. The asterisks represent the gaps that Mendeleev left for undiscovered elements.

Mendeleev predicted the properties of undiscovered elements. Since he knew the properties of the other elements in a particular group, he was able to predict the properties that the undiscovered elements should have.

For example:

- He predicted that there would be an element discovered to fill the gap below silicon in Group IV of his table. He called this 'eka-silicon'. The element was discovered seventeen years later and called germanium (because it was discovered in Germany).
- He also predicted the discovery of an element to fill the gap below aluminium in Group III of his table. This element, which he called 'eka-aluminium', was discovered six years later and named gallium (because it was discovered in France - Gallia was the old Latin name for France), Figure 4.5.

When these elements were discovered, it was found that the properties predicted by Mendeleev were almost identical to the observed properties. These findings led to Mendeleev's Periodic Law being accepted.

You will notice in Table 4.1 that none of the noble gases in Group VIII are included. The reason for this is because Mendeleev did not suspect the existence of noble gases such as helium, neon and argon, as none of them had been discovered at the time.

## Mendeleev reversed the order of some elements.

- In a few cases, he had to reverse the order of elements in order to make them fall into groups of elements with similar properties.
- If you look at the modern form of the Periodic Table (inside back cover) you will observe that tellurium (element number 52) is placed before iodine (element number 53). If you look at the atomic weight of tellurium you will observe that it is 127.6 whereas the atomic weight of iodine is 126.9 .
- Since Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of atomic weight, originally he put iodine before tellurium. However, he realised that the properties were more important than the atomic weights and so he reversed the order of atomic weights for these two elements. This meant that each element would be in a group with elements of similar properties.
- By reversing the order, iodine is put in the same group as fluorine, chlorine and bromine - all of these elements have similar properties.
- Similarly, tellurium is put in the same group as oxygen, sulfur and selenium - again all of these elements have similar properties.

At last, order had been brought into the list of elements. In 1955 a newly discovered element (number 101) was named mendelevium in recognition of Mendeleev's enormous contribution to the study of the elements.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-049.jpg?height=610&width=1248&top_left_y=3001&top_left_x=1536)
Figure 4.5 Mendeleev left gaps in his Periodic Table and predicted the discovery of germanium and gallium. Gallium has a low melting point. Note that the heat from the hand is melting the gallium.

## The modern Periodic Table: Henry Moseley's contribution

We have seen that Mendeleev had to reverse the order of some elements. However, he did not understand the reason for this. It was an English scientist called Henry Moseley who provided the explanation, Figure 4.6.

Moseley studied the frequencies of the X-rays emitted by atoms of the different elements. In 1913 he found that the frequencies varied with the quantity of positive charge in the nucleus. In other words, he discovered a method of determining the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. This number is called the atomic number.

The atomic number of an atom is the number of protons in the nucleus of that atom.

## Henry Moseley

(1887-1915)

Figure 4.6
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-050.jpg?height=336&width=326&top_left_y=1074&top_left_x=1670)

Moseley developed a method of determining the atomic number of an element using X-rays. Sadly, he was killed in World War I at the age of 27.

Moseley's discovery brought about a major improvement in Mendeleev's table. His work may be summarised as follows:

- Moseley showed that if the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, it is not necessary to reverse the order of some elements as Mendeleev had to do.
- Moseley's X-ray studies showed that Mendeleev had been correct in placing tellurium (atomic number 52) before iodine (atomic number 53) in spite of the higher atomic weight of tellurium.
- Moseley showed that by arranging the elements in order of increasing atomic number the elements fall naturally into the correct groups in terms of their properties.
Moseley was the scientist who made the final step from Mendeleev's Periodic Table to the modern Periodic Table.

The modern Periodic Table is an arrangement of elements in order of increasing atomic number.

Thus, the modern version of the Periodic Law may now be stated as follows:
Modern Periodic Law: When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, the properties of the elements are repeated at regular intervals in other elements.

Although Moseley's work did not alter Mendeleev's Periodic Table to a great extent, it certainly confirmed the position of the elements.

### 4.4 The modern Periodic Table

The main differences between Mendeleev's Periodic Table and the modern form of the Periodic Table (shown inside the back cover) are:

1 In the modern Periodic Table, the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. In Mendeleev's Periodic Table, the elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic weight (relative atomic mass).
2. There are more elements in the modern Periodic Table. When Mendeleev constructed his table, some elements had not been discovered, e.g. the noble gases (group VIII or 18). There were only about 60 elements in Mendeleev's Periodic Table. There are over 100 elements in the modern Periodic Table.
3. There are no gaps in the modern Periodic Table. Mendeleev's Periodic Table contained gaps for undiscovered elements.
4. In the modern Periodic Table, the transition elements are listed in a separate
block in the middle of the table. Mendeleev did not put these elements in a separate block. He included them with the other elements. In Table 4.1 the transition elements have been left out for clarity but, in fact, Mendeleev included copper in the same box as potassium, zinc in the same box as calcium, etc.

The differences between Mendeleev's Periodic Table and the modern Periodic Table are summarised in Table 4.2.

|  | Mendeleev's Periodic Table | Modern Periodic Table |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | Elements arranged in order of increasing atomic weight (relative atomic mass) | Elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number |
| 2. | Contains gaps for undiscovered elements | No gaps present |
| 3. | Only 60 elements approximately, as not all elements had been discovered | Over 100 elements |
| 4. | Transition elements were not put in a separate block | Transition elements are in a separate block |

Table 4.2 Differences between Mendeleev's Periodic Table and the modern Periodic Table

There are some advantages of arranging the elements in order of atomic number:

- There is no need to reverse the order of some elements to force them into the correct groups.
- All of the elements are placed in groups with similar properties.
- To date, since all elements have been discovered up to element 118 , there are no gaps in the modern Periodic Table.

The Periodic Table summarises an enormous amount of information and has brought order into chemistry. As chemistry students, you will find that it greatly simplifies your study of chemistry. You are allowed the use of a Periodic Table in the Leaving Certificate exam and it is included in the Formulae and Tables booklet approved for use in the state exams. We now consider three important uses of the Periodic Table: (i) obtaining atomic numbers and mass numbers, (ii) obtaining relative atomic masses and (iii) writing electron configurations.

So let's take a close look at each of these three uses.

### 4.5 Atomic numbers and mass numbers

We have already seen that the modern Periodic Table is an arrangement of elements in order of increasing atomic number. Therefore, the number of the element in the Periodic Table tells us the number of protons in the nucleus. For example, sodium is the eleventh element in the Periodic Table and therefore it has 11 protons in its nucleus.

Since the electron has such a small mass, its mass is ignored when calculating the mass of an atom. Therefore, almost the entire mass of an atom is due to the protons and neutrons in the nucleus of the atom. This allows us to define the mass number of an element as follows:

> The mass number of an element is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom of that element

For example, sodium has 11 protons and 12 neutrons in its nucleus. Therefore, its mass number is 23 or we say that the mass of the atom is 23 atomic mass units. (Because the masses of atoms are so small, they are not normally measured in grams. A special unit is used called the atomic mass unit. The recognised symbol for atomic mass unit is $\mathbf{u}$ but in this textbook, for clarity, we shall use a.m.u. where 1 a.m.u. $=1.66 \times 10^{-24}$ gram.)

The letter Z is used to indicate the atomic number.
The letter $A$ is used to indicate the mass number.
The nuclear formula of an element is a method of summarising information about an element as shown in Figure 4.7.

Note: The nuclear formula also contains the symbol of the element. For your exam, you must know the names and symbols of the first 36 elements.

- Note that in the nuclear formula, the atomic number is given at the bottom left hand corner near the symbol. However, in each box in the Periodic Table, the atomic number is given above the symbol. To avoid getting confused, remember that the smaller number is always the atomic number.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-052.jpg?height=594&width=854&top_left_y=1718&top_left_x=1751)
Figure 4.7 The nuclear formula for an element. To calculate the number of neutrons, simply subtract the atomic number from the mass number.

- Since the mass number is simply the number of protons plus neutrons, mass numbers must always be whole numbers.
- To obtain the mass number of an element from the Periodic Table, simply round off the number under the symbol to the nearest whole number. For example, for sodium, round off the 22.99 to 23 . In fact, for most elements in the Periodic Table, you will observe the number under each symbol is not a whole number. This number is called the relative atomic mass (atomic weight) of the element. In the next section, you will learn what this number actually means.


## Example 4.1

## Question

How many (i) neutrons, (ii) electrons are in the ion ${ }_{21}^{45} \mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$ ?
[LCH]

## Answer

Number of neutrons $=45-21=24$
Number of electrons in neutral atom = number of protons = 21

Since the atom has lost three electrons (ion is $3+$ )
Number of electrons $=21-3=18$
Answer: (i) 24 neutrons, (ii) 18 electrons.

### 4.6 Relative atomic mass and isotopes

In 1919 an English chemist called Francis Aston, Figure 4.8, built an instrument called a mass spectrometer to measure the masses of atoms. Aston's work may be summarised as follows:

- He found that a sample of neon gas consisted of two varieties of neon atoms. One type of neon atom had a mass number of 20 and the other type had a mass number of 22 .
- He concluded that the neon gas consisted of atoms of neon that differed in the number of neutrons in the nucleus ${ }_{10}^{20} \mathrm{Ne}$ and ${ }_{10}^{22} \mathrm{Ne}$.
- These two varieties of neon atoms are called isotopes of neon. The first isotope, ${ }_{10}^{20} \mathrm{Ne}$ has 10 neutrons in its nucleus. The second isotope, ${ }_{10}^{22}$ Ne has 12 neutrons in its nucleus.
- Aston also identified two isotopes of chlorine: ${ }_{17}^{35} \mathrm{Cl}$ and ${ }_{17}^{37} \mathrm{Cl}$ commonly called chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.
- Carbon has been found to have three isotopes ${ }_{6}^{12} \mathrm{C},{ }_{6}^{13} \mathrm{C}$, and ${ }_{6}^{14} \mathrm{C}$ which are commonly called carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14, respectively.
- Hydrogen has been found to have three isotopes, as shown in Figure 4.9. Aston received the 1922 Nobel Prize in chemistry for his work on the discovery of isotopes.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-053.jpg?height=649&width=1156&top_left_y=2513&top_left_x=345)
Figure 4.9 Hydrogen has three isotopes called hydrogen-1 (also called protium), hydrogen-2 (also called deuterium) and hydrogen-3 (also called tritium).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-053.jpg?height=994&width=1186&top_left_y=364&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 4.8 Francis Aston built an instrument called a mass spectrometer. This instrument measures the masses of atoms. Aston was born near Birmingham, England.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (i.e. they have the same atomic number) which have different mass numbers due to the different number of neutrons in the nucleus.

Not only did Aston detect the presence of isotopes but he also determined the percentages of each of the isotopes present in a sample of the naturally occurring element. For example, in his study of chlorine gas, he found that there were approximately three times as many chlorine-35 atoms as there were chlorine-37 atoms. He was then able to work out the average mass of an atom of chlorine. His method of calculation is shown in the following example:

## Example 4.2

## Question

A sample of chlorine is found to consist of $75 \%{ }_{17}^{35} \mathrm{Cl}$ and $25 \%{ }_{17}^{35} \mathrm{Cl}$. Calculate the average mass of chlorine atoms.

## Answer

In 100 atoms of chlorine there are:
75 atoms of mass $35=75 \times 35=2625$
25 atoms of mass $37=25 \times 37=925$
Total mass of 100 atoms $\quad=3550$
Average mass of 1 atom = 35.5

From the above example, we see that the average mass of an atom of chlorine is 35.5 .
If you locate chlorine in the Periodic Table, you will find that this is the number given under the symbol for chlorine. (To be more precise, it is 35.45 because the percentages have been rounded off in the above problem.) This 'average mass' of an atom is measured relative to the mass of the carbon-12 isotope. For this reason it is called its relative atomic mass. (The old name for relative atomic mass was atomic weight.) The symbol for relative atomic mass is $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{r}}$.

## Relative atomic mass is defined as:

- The average of the mass numbers of the isotopes of the element
- As they occur naturally.
- Taking their abundances into account and
- Expressed on a scale in which the atoms of the carbon-12 isotope have a mass of exactly 12 units.

Since relative atomic mass is a ratio of two masses, it has no units (i.e. the a.m.u. units above and below the line cancel out). Thus, we say that the average mass of an atom of chlorine is 35.5 a.m.u. but its relative atomic mass is 35.5 .

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text { Relative atomic } \\
\text { mass }
\end{gathered}=\frac{\text { Mass of one atom of an element }}{\frac{1}{12} \text { mass of one atom of carbon }-12}
$$

## Example 4.3

## Question

A mass spectrometer is used to analyse a sample of boron. It is found that the boron sample contains $18.7 \%{ }_{5}^{10} \mathrm{~B}$ and $81.3 \%{ }_{5}^{11} \mathrm{~B}$ Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron.

## Answer

In 100 atoms of boron there are
18.7 atoms of mass $10=18.7 \times 10=187$
81.3 atoms of mass $11=81.3 \times 11=894.3$

Total mass of 100 atoms $\quad=1081.3$
Average mass of 1 atom = 10.813
i.e. relative atomic mass of boron $=10.813$

## Uses of the mass spectrometer

Mass spectrometers are used to:

- Identify the presence of isotopes.
- Measure the relative abundances of isotopes.
- Measure relative atomic masses and relative molecular masses.
- Identify unknown compounds, Figure 4.10.

Figure 4.10 This mass spectrometer may be used to detect banned drugs taken by athletes and to test for drugs taken by drug addicts. Drugs leave traces in the hair of the addict. As hair grows about 1 cm per month, this test can reveal when the drug was last used. Hence, the success or failure of a rehabilitation programme can be monitored.

### 4.7 Arrangement of electrons in atoms

We have already learned that Niels Bohr proposed the idea of electrons revolving around the nucleus in fixed paths called orbits or energy levels. The arrangement of electrons in an atom (i.e. the number of electrons in each main energy level) is called the electron configuration.

## The electron configuration shows the arrangement of electrons in an atom of an element.

If we use the Periodic Table, it is very straightforward to write the electron configuration of an element. There are two ways of writing electron configurations: either in terms of the simple Bohr model or in terms of energy sublevels. We now consider how this is done for both methods of writing electron configurations.

## EXAM TIPI

Students are often asked in exams to write the electron configuration for a specific element. You could also be asked to determine the number of energy levels, the number of sublevels and the number of orbitals associated with the electron configuration. The following sections will describe in detail how to write the electron configuration and determine the number of energy levels, sublevels and orbitals.

## Writing electron configurations - Bohr model

Writing the electron configuration of an element in terms of the Bohr model of the atom may easily be done using the Periodic Table. This method is shown in Example 4.4.

## Example 4.4

## Question

Write the electronic configuration for potassium showing the number of electrons in each main energy level.

## Answers

## Step 1

Find potassium in the Periodic Table. Potassium is element number 19, i.e. there are 19 protons in the nucleus and, since all atoms are neutral, there must be 19 electrons in the energy levels around the nucleus in a neutral potassium atom. We must now write down how these electrons are arranged around the nucleus.

## Step 2

Go to the beginning of the Periodic Table. Note that in the $n=1$ period, there are only two elements. This means that the $n=1$ main energy level can only hold two electrons. Of the nineteen electrons of potassium, two electrons are in the $\boldsymbol{n} \boldsymbol{=} \mathbf{1}$ main energy level.

## Step 3

Start at the second period and count along from lithium. Note that there are eight elements in the second period, i.e. there are eight electrons in the $n=2$ main energy level. Thus, we can say that potassium has eight electrons in the $\boldsymbol{n}=\mathbf{2}$ main energy level.

## Step 4

Start at the third period and count along from sodium. Note that there are eight elements in the third period, i.e. there are eight electrons in the $n=3$ main energy level. Thus, we can say that potassium has eight electrons in the $\boldsymbol{n} \mathbf{= 3}$ main energy level.

## Step 5

Start at the fourth period. Potassium is the first element you meet, i.e. potassium has one electron in the $\boldsymbol{n}=\mathbf{4}$ period.

From the above information, we can write the electronic configuration of potassium as:

$$
K=2,8,8,1
$$

The electron configurations of the first twenty elements are listed in Table 4.3.

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  | $n=1$ | $n=2$ | $n=3$ | $n=4$ |  |
| Hydrogen | 1 | 1 |  |  |  | 1 |
| Helium | 2 | 2 |  |  |  | 2 |
| Lithium | 3 | 2 | 1 |  |  | 2,1 |
| Beryllium | 4 | 2 | 2 |  |  | 2,2 |

Table 4.3 The electronic configurations of the first 20 elements given in terms of the simple Bohr picture.

For your exam, you must be able to write the electron configuration of the first 20 elements (and their ions) for Ordinary Level, and of the first 36 elements for Higher Level, in terms of the number of electrons in each main energy level. The electron configuration of transition metal ions is not required. Study Table 4.3 carefully.

- Note that the number of electrons in the outer orbit is the same as the group number in the case of a few groups, e.g. lithium (group I) has one outer electron and beryilium (group II) has two outer electrons.
- In the most recent version of the modern Periodic Table, e.g. the version on p. 79 of the Formulae and Tables booklet approved for use in the state exams, this is of limited application as the groups are numbered from 1 to 18.
- In the Periodic Table at the back inside cover of this textbook, both the traditional numbering system of eight groups (I, II, III, etc.) and the new numbering system of 18 groups are included to show the relationship between the two systems.

Note the following points when writing electron configurations:

- Since the 4 s sublevel is lower in energy than the $3 d$ sublevel, the $\mathbf{4 s}$ sublevel is always filled before the $\mathbf{3 d}$ sublevel. Using the Periodic Table will help you to write down the electron configurations of the d-block elements. Simply write down the electron configuration of calcium as shown in Example 4.6, count along the first row of the d-block (scandium, titanium, vanadium, etc.) and put the required number of electrons into the 3d sublevel. For example, since iron is the sixth element along the row, we put six electrons into the 3d sublevel, i.e. the electron configuration of iron is $1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}, 3 s^{2}, 3 p^{6}, \mathbf{4 s}^{2}, \mathbf{3 d}^{6}$.
- Note that there are ten elements in the first row of the d-block elements. This is because the $d$ sublevel can hold ten electrons. Therefore, the $n=3$ main energy level can hold a total of eighteen electrons: two electrons in the 3s sublevel, six electrons in the 3p sublevel, and ten electrons in the 3d sublevel.
- The number of electrons that any main energy level can hold may be calculated from the formula $2 \mathrm{n}^{2}$. Thus, the $n=1$ main energy level can hold two electrons, the $n=2$ main energy level can hold eight electrons, and the $n=$ 3 main energy level can hold eighteen electrons.
- If you study Table 4.5 you will see that the electron configurations of chromium and copper are not what you might expect. You might think that the electron configuration of chromium would be:
- $\mathrm{Cr}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 4 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{~d}^{4}$ rather than $\mathrm{Cr}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}$, $4 s^{1}, 3 d^{5}$ as written in Table 4.5. However, it has been found that sublevels that are exactly half filled or completely filled have extra stability.
Therefore, one of the electrons in the $4 s^{2}$ orbital 'flips over' into one of the d orbitals to give two sublevels which are exactly half filled. Therefore, the electron configuration of chromium is $1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}, 3 s^{2}, 3 p^{6}, \mathbf{4 s}^{1}, \mathbf{3 d}^{5}$.
- The situation with copper is rather similar to that of chromium. You might expect the electron configuration of copper to be:
- $\mathrm{Cu}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 4 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{~d}^{9}$ rather than $\mathrm{Cu}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 4 \mathrm{~s}^{1}$, $3 \mathrm{~d}^{10}$ as shown in Table 4.5. However, scientists explained this stability by stating that one of the electrons in the $4 s^{2}$ orbital 'flips over' to one of the $d$ orbitals. The completely filled 3d sublevel and the half-filled 4s sublevel have extra stability associated with them. Hence the electron configuration of copper is $1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}, \mathbf{4 s}^{1}, \mathbf{3 d}^{10}$.

For your exam, you are expected to know how to write the electron configurations of the first 36 elements and their ions (excluding transition metal ions) in terms of their s, p, d configurations. Therefore, Table 4.5 should be studied carefully! Also, if you are asked to write the electron configuration of either copper or chromium, alarm bells should start ringing in your head!

### 4.8 Writing electron configurations of ions

An atom that has lost or gained electrons is called an ion. Since electrons are negatively charged, an atom that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. On the other hand, an atom that loses electrons becomes positively charged. We make use of these facts when writing the electron configuration of an ion.

## Example 4.7

## Question

Write the electronic configuration (s, p) of the $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ ion. What neutral atom has the same configuration?

## Answer

## Step 1

Locate the position of aluminium in the Periodic Table. Aluminium is element number 13, i.e. an atom of aluminium has 13 electrons.

## Step 2

Work out the number of electrons in the ion. Since the aluminium ion has three positive charges, it must have lost three electrons. Thus, the $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ ion has 10 electrons, i.e. the same number of electrons as an atom of neon. Therefore, the electronic configuration of the $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ ion will be the same as an atom of neon.
$\mathrm{Al}^{3+}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}$

Study Example 4.8 in the online resources.

Study Example 4.9 in the online resources.

### 4.9 Arrangement of electrons in orbitals of equal energy

In writing electron configurations, we have not yet considered how electrons are distributed in individual orbitals of equal energy. For example, we have written the electron configuration of nitrogen as $1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{3}$. We now ask ourselves the question: How are the three electrons in the p sublevel distributed among the three p orbitals?

In 1927 Friedrich Hund, having studied the spectra of various elements, put forward an important rule in answer to this question. This rule is called Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity.

Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity states that when two or more orbitals of equal energy are available, the electrons occupy them singly before filling them in pairs.

If we apply this rule to the nitrogen atom, it simply means that of the three electrons added to the 2 p sublevel, one electron will enter the $p_{x}$ orbital, the second will enter the $p_{y}$ and the third will enter the $p_{z}$. Thus, there is the maximum number of unpaired electrons, Figure 4.13.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-060.jpg?height=440&width=467&top_left_y=1419&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 4.13 The three p electrons of nitrogen occupy the p orbitals singly to give the maximum number of unpaired electrons (Hund's Rule).

These 'electrons-in-boxes' diagrams are used to show how electrons are distributed in orbitals. The box represents the orbital and the arrow represents the electron. Arrows are used because it was discovered that as electrons revolve around the nucleus, they spin on their own axes. (This is rather like the Earth spinning on its axis as it revolves around the Sun). However, the electrons can spin in either a clockwise direction or an anti-clockwise direction.

In 1925 Wolfgang Pauli, from his study of spectra, made a very important deduction called the Pauli

## Exclusion Principle.

The Pauli Exclusion Principle states that no more than two electrons may occupy an orbital and they must have opposite spin.

The arrows are used to indicate the direction of spin of the electrons. The ↓ represents an electron spinning clockwise and ↑ represents an electron spinning anti-clockwise. The 'electrons-in-boxes' method of representing the electron arrangements in atoms is shown for the atoms of the first ten elements in Figure 4.14.

The distribution of electrons among the p orbitals may also be shown using a more detailed form of the electron configurations given in Table 4.5. For example, the electron configurations of the elements from boron to neon may also be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{B}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}^{1}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}}^{0}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{z}}^{0} \\
& \mathrm{C}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}^{1}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}}^{1}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{2}^{0} \\
& \mathrm{~N}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}^{1}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}}^{1}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{z}}^{1} \\
& \mathrm{O}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}}^{1}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{z}}^{1} \\
& \mathrm{~F}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{z}}^{1} \\
& \mathrm{Ne}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{z}}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The 'electrons-in-boxes' diagrams or the extended forms of electron configurations as written above need only be given if you are specifically asked about the distribution of electrons in the p sublevel (see Example 4.11). In all other cases, the electron configurations as given in Table 4.5 are perfectly adequate.

## Example 4.10

## Question

Write the s, p electron configuration for the potassium atom.

Hence state how many (i) energy sublevels, (ii) individual orbitals are occupied by electrons in a potassium atom.
[LCH]

## Answer

$\mathrm{K}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 4 \mathrm{~s}^{1}$
(i) There are 6 energy sublevels occupied in a potassium atom, i.e. $1 \mathrm{~s}, 2 \mathrm{~s}, 2 \mathrm{p}, 3 \mathrm{~s}, 3 \mathrm{p}$ and 4 s .
(ii) There are 10 individual orbitals occupied in a potassium atom, i.e. $1 \mathrm{~s}, 2 \mathrm{~s}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{x^{\prime}} 2 \mathrm{p}_{y^{\prime}} 2 \mathrm{p}_{z^{\prime}} 3 \mathrm{~s}$, $3 p_{x^{\prime}}, 3 p_{y^{\prime}} 3 p_{z}$ and $4 s$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-061.jpg?height=1498&width=632&top_left_y=387&top_left_x=1849)

Figure 4.14 The 'electrons-in-boxes' method of representing the electron configurations of the first ten elements.

## Example 4.11

## Question

Write the electron configuration ( $\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{p}$ ) for the sulfur atom in its ground state, showing the arrangement in atomic orbitals of the highest energy electrons.

State how many (i) energy levels, (ii) orbitals are occupied in a sulfur atom in its ground state.
[LCH]

## Answer

Sulfur $=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}{ }^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}}{ }^{1}, 3 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{z}}{ }^{1}$.
(i) There are 3 energy levels occupied in a sulfur atom in its ground state, i.e. $n=1, n=2$ and $n=3$.
(ii) There are 9 orbitals occupied in a sulfur atom in its ground state, i.e. $1 \mathrm{~s}, 2 \mathrm{~s}, 2 \mathrm{p}_{x^{\prime}} 2 \mathrm{p}_{y^{\prime}} 2 \mathrm{p}_{z^{\prime}} 3 \mathrm{~s}, 3 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}^{\prime}} 3 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{y}^{\prime}} 3 \mathrm{p}_{z^{\prime}}$.

## Summary What I should know

- An element is defined as a substance that cannot be split into simpler substances by chemical means.
- Mendeleev's Periodic Law states that when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic weight (relative atomic mass), the properties of elements with similar properties repeat at regular intervals.
- Henry Moseley used X-rays to determine the atomic number of an element, i.e. the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
- The modern Periodic Table is an arrangement of elements in order of increasing atomic number.
- The mass number of an element is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom of that element.
- Isotopes are atoms of the same element (i.e. they have the same atomic number) which have different mass numbers due to the different number of neutrons in their nuclei.
- Relative atomic mass (atomic weight) is defined as the average of the mass numbers of the isotopes of the element, as they occur naturally, taking their abundances into account and expressed on a scale in which the atoms of the carbon-12 isotope have a mass of exactly 12 units.
- The electron configuration of an element shows the arrangement of electrons in an atom of that element.
- The Aufbau Principle states that when building up the electron configuration of an atom in its ground state, the electrons occupy the lowest available energy level.

Hund's Rule of Maximum Multiplicity states that when two or more orbitals of equal energy are available the electrons occupy them singly before filling them in pairs.

The Pauli Exclusion Principle states that no more than two electrons may occupy an orbital and they must have opposite spin.

# 5 Chemical Bonding and Structure

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-064.jpg?height=486&width=1261&top_left_y=507&top_left_x=188)

### 5.1 Introduction

Most of the materials around us are made from combinations of elements. For example, water is formed when hydrogen and oxygen combine together; table salt is formed by combining sodium and chlorine; carbon dioxide is formed when carbon and oxygen combine together. Substances made by joining together two or more different elements are called compounds.

> A compound is a substance that is made up of two or more different elements combined together chemically.

When elements combine to form compounds, there are attractive forces that hold the atoms together in this new compound. These attractive forces are called chemical bonds. In this chapter, we will study the different types of chemical bonds that exist. We will see how a knowledge of chemical bonding helps us to understand chemical formulas, e.g. why the formula for water is $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ and not $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}$. We will learn how to write chemical formulas and how to name compounds.

It will become quite easy for us to understand chemical bonding if we first study an important rule called the Octet Rule.

### 5.2 The Octet Rule

Chemists have observed that the noble gases (e.g. helium, neon, argon) in Group 18 or VIII of the Periodic Table are very unreactive, i.e. they form practically no compounds. Hence, they are often called the 'inert' gases (noble gases), Figure 5.1.

All the noble gases consist of single atoms. This is explained by saying that these elements do not react because they have stable electron configurations. Since all the noble gases (except helium) have eight electrons in their outer energy level, the rule was called the octet rule (octet = eight).

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of some of the main types of chemical bonding.
- To ensure that students know how to write the chemical formulas of compounds.
- To enable students to predict the shapes of molecules.
- To provide students with the opportunity to test for the presence of anions (negative ions) in solutions of their salts.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-064.jpg?height=1482&width=1177&top_left_y=1432&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 5.1 Helium and argon are two of the noble (inert) gases. Helium is a very light gas and is safe for use in filling balloons as it is so unreactive. Argon is used in medical lasers to perform surgery.

Octet Rule: When bonding occurs, atoms tend to reach an electron arrangement with eight electrons in the outermost energy level.

Therefore, when elements react together to form compounds, their atoms tend to change their electron arrangement so that they end up with eight electrons in their outermost energy level. It is important to realise that the octet rule is more a 'rule of thumb' rather than a strict chemical law.

There are limitations in predicting bonding between atoms and one of these limitations is that there are a number of exceptions to the octet rule:

- Transition metals do not usually obey the octet rule. In many of their compounds, transition metals can have more or fewer than eight electrons in their outermost energy level.
- Helium is unreactive, as it contains a full outer energy level of two electrons. In addition, the elements near helium in the Periodic Table (hydrogen, lithium and beryllium) tend to achieve the same electron arrangement as helium, with two electrons in the outer energy level rather than the eight electrons of the other noble gases.

We will now study how the octet rule helps us to understand the two main types of chemical bonds: ionic bonds and covalent bonds.

### 5.3 Ionic bonding: Transfer of electrons

Atoms can obtain the electron configuration of a noble gas by gaining or losing electrons. When an atom gains or loses electrons, it becomes a charged atom. A charged atom is called an ion. As we shall see later, a group of atoms carrying a charge is also called an ion.

- The elements in Group I of the Periodic Table tend to lose one electron to form an ion with one positive charge.
- The elements in Group II of the Periodic Table tend to lose two electrons to form an ion with two positive charges.
- In an atom that has lost electrons, there are more protons in the nucleus than there are electrons in orbit around it. Therefore, the ion formed is positively charged.
- A positive ion is called a cation. The formation of some positive ions may be shown simply as follows:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-065.jpg?height=206&width=1141&top_left_y=2448&top_left_x=419)
- The elements in Groups VII (or 17) tend to gain one electron and the elements in Group VI (or 16) of the Periodic Table tend to gain two electrons to form negative ions. Negative ions are called anions.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-065.jpg?height=221&width=1116&top_left_y=2899&top_left_x=409)

Note that in each case, the ion formed has the electron configuration of the noble gas that is nearest to it in the Periodic Table. It is the formation of this stable electron configuration that is the 'driving force' behind the formation of the ion. Once ions are formed, they are held together in a compound by the force of attraction that exists between oppositely charged ions. This force of attraction is called an ionic bond.

Common table salt (sodium chloride) is one of the best-known examples of an ionic substance, i.e. a substance held together by ionic bonding.

An ion is a charged atom or group of atoms.

An ionic bond is the force of attraction between oppositely charged ions in a compound. Ionic bonds are always formed by the complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another.

## Using Lewis diagrams to show the formation of ionic bonding

There are two ways of showing the formation of the ionic bonding in sodium chloride: either in terms of the Bohr-type circle diagram, Figure 5.2(a), or in terms of Lewis diagrams, Figure 5.2(b). These diagrams are so called because it was Gilbert Lewis, an American chemist, Figure 5.3 who invented this system to describe chemical bonding. Lewis diagrams are also called Lewis formulas or Lewis dot-and-cross structures.

Note the following points:

- In drawing Lewis electron dot-and-cross diagrams, the outer electrons of one atom are represented by dots, with crosses used for the electrons of the other atom. The numbers under the chemical symbols show the arrangement of electrons in the energy levels.
- The transfer of electrons is shown by the arrow in the Lewis dot-and-cross diagrams.
- Unless otherwise requested, both methods of representing ionic bond formation are equally acceptable in an exam, provided the electron configuration is written as shown in Figure 5.2.
- Bohr-type circle diagrams can be timeconsuming to draw and they give more information than we need, since it is only the electrons in the outermost orbit, known as valence electrons, that are involved in bonding. Therefore, we will use Lewis dot-and-cross diagrams as much as possible in this textbook.

(a) Bohr diagram
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-066.jpg?height=733&width=1177&top_left_y=498&top_left_x=1438)

Figure 5.2 (a) The formation of the ionic bond in sodium chloride using the Bohr-type diagram. (b) The formation of the ionic bond in sodium chloride using Lewis diagrams.

## Gilbert Lewis <br> (1875-1946)

Figure 5.3
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-066.jpg?height=323&width=339&top_left_y=1575&top_left_x=2282)

Gilbert Lewis was an American chemist who introduced a simple way to represent valence (outermost) electrons using dots and crosses around symbols of elements. These help to give us a picture of how atoms and ions are bonded together. He loved teaching and was a great chemistry teacher, as evidenced by the simple dot-and-cross system that he developed to explain bonding.

## Example 5.1

## Question

Show the formation of the ionic bonds in magnesium fluoride, $\mathrm{MgF}_{2}$, by means of a suitable diagram.

## Answer

Each magnesium atom loses two electron, while each fluorine atom gains only one electron. Therefore, there must be two fluorine atoms for every one magnesium atom (Figure 5.4).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-066.jpg?height=291&width=2100&top_left_y=3141&top_left_x=319)
Figure 5.4 The formation of the ionic bond in magnesium fluoride, $\mathrm{MgF}_{2}$.

## Sodium chloride crystal structure

X-ray studies enable chemists to work out the arrangement of ions in a crystal. Sodium chloride, for example, has a cubic structure, Figure 5.5.

Note the following points about the structure of sodium chloride:

- Although Figure 5.5 shows only 27 ions, remember that the structure of sodium chloride consists of a regular three-dimensional arrangement of millions of sodium ions and chloride ions.
- The three-dimensional arrangement of ions is called a crystal lattice.
- In Figure 5.5 we see the repeating unit in the crystal lattice. This repeating unit is called the unit cell of sodium chloride and it repeats itself in all directions to build up the crystal.
- In the crystal lattice, each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions and each chloride ion is surrounded by six sodium ions. In fact, ions are so small that the tiniest crystal of sodium chloride consists of millions of ions!

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-067.jpg?height=786&width=815&top_left_y=364&top_left_x=1956)
Figure 5.5 This diagram represents the crystal structure of sodium chloride, i.e. how the ions are packed together in the crystal.

Salt is used as a food preservative and in the chemical industry to manufacture soap, sodium metal, chlorine gas, detergents, toothpaste and washing soda. Also, it is spread on roads during the winter to help melt frost and snow.

### 5.4 How to write the formulas of ionic compounds

A chemical formula is a way of representing a compound using symbols for the atoms present and numbers to show how many atoms of each element are present. We have seen in Example 5.1 that the chemical formula for magnesium fluoride is $\mathrm{MgF}_{2}$. This tells us that the compound magnesium fluoride consists of magnesium and fluorine. It also tells us that there are twice as many fluoride ions as magnesium ions in a crystal of magnesium fluoride.

The following are the key points for writing the formulas of ionic compounds:

- Ionic compounds are formed between the elements of Groups 1 and 2 (metals) and those of Groups VI (or 16) and VII (or 17) (non-metals) of the Periodic Table. In general, ionic compounds are usually formed when metals react with non-metals. (The 'steps of stairs' on the Periodic Table going from boron to astatine divide the metals on the left from the nonmetals on the right.)
- Metals have a tendency to lose electrons, and non-metals have a tendency to gain electrons. The number of electrons lost or gained depends on the group in which the elements are located.
- An ionic compound is neutral overall. Therefore, there must be the same number of positive charges as negative charges present in the compound.

Some ions of the first 36 elements (excluding the d-block metals) are shown in Figure 5.6. Studying the following examples will help you to understand how to write the formulas of ionic compounds.

| I II <br> $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ <br> $\mathrm{Be}^{2+}$ Lithum Beyllum <br> $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ <br> $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ Sodium Magnesing |  |  |  | III | IV | V | VI | VII | 0 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  |  |  |  | No ion |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | No ion | No ion | $\mathrm{N}^{3-}$ Naturide | $0^{2-}$ Oude | F Bueride | No ion |
|  |  |  |  | Al ${ }^{3+}$ Ausitari | No ion | $\mathrm{P}^{3-}$ Prosphide | $\mathrm{S}^{2}$ sande | $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ Ovioride | No ion |
| $\mathbf{K}^{+}$ Potrivian | $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ <br> Calcum |  | Charge on d-block ions cannot be predicted |  |  |  | □ |  | $\mathrm{Br}^{-}$ uenter | No ion |

## Example 5.2

## Question

Write the formula of potassium bromide.

## Answer

The potassium ion is $\mathrm{K}^{+}$. The bromide ion is $\mathrm{Br}^{-}$. The formula $\mathrm{K}^{+} \mathrm{Br}^{-}$is correct, since there is the same number of positive and negative charges.

Answer: The formula of potassium bromide is KBr .

## Example 5.3

## Question

Write the formula of calcium chloride.

## Answer

The calcium ion is $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$. The chloride ion is $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$. The formula $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+} \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$is not correct, since there are two positive charges but only one negative charge. To get two negative charges, we must have two $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ions.

Answer: The formula of calcium chloride is $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$.

## Example 5.4

## Question

Write the formula of sodium sulfide.

## Answer

The sodium ion is $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$. The sulfide ion is $\mathrm{S}^{2-}$. The formula $\mathrm{Na}^{+} \mathrm{S}^{2-}$ is not correct, since there is one positive charge but two negative charges. To get two positive charges, we must have two $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ions.

Answer: The formula of sodium sulfide is $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$.

## Example 5.5

## Question

Write the formula of aluminium oxide.

## Answer

The aluminium ion is $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$. The oxide ion is $\mathrm{O}^{2-}$. The formula $\mathrm{Al}^{3+} \mathrm{O}^{2-}$ is not correct, since there are three positive charges but only two negative charges. Bring all charges up to their lowest common denominator, i.e. 6. To get six positive charges, we need two aluminium ions. To get six negative charges, we need three oxide ions, i.e. $\left(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\right)_{2}\left(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\right)_{3}$

Answer: The formula of aluminium oxide is $\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$.

## Writing formulas of compounds with group ions

As mentioned earlier, an ion can be a charged atom or a group of atoms. There are many ionic compounds that contain group ions, e.g. the sulfate ion, the carbonate ion and the nitrate ion. For example, barium sulfate is used in X-ray examinations of internal organs, chalk is calcium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate (bread soda) is used in baking.

The group ions commonly encountered in this course are listed in Table 5.1. It is not possible to predict the formulas of group ions from the Periodic Table, so learn them off by heart!

| Name | Formula |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hydroxide ion <br> Nitrate ion <br> Hydrogencarbonate ion <br> Permanganate ion | $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ <br> $\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$ <br> $\mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{+}$ <br> $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ | $\}$ <br> One negative charge |
| Carbonate ion <br> Chromate ion <br> Dichromate ion <br> Sulfate ion <br> Sulfite ion <br> Thiosulfate ion | $\mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$ <br> $\mathrm{CrO}_{4}^{2-}$ <br> $\mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}{ }^{2-}$ <br> $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ <br> $\mathrm{SO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$ <br> $\mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-}$ | $\}$ <br> Two negative charges |
| Phosphate ion | $\mathrm{PO}_{4}{ }^{3-}$ | Three negative charges |
| Ammonium ion | $\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}$ | One positive charge |

The following examples will help you to write the formulas of ionic compounds that have group ions.

## Example 5.6

## Question

Write the formula of potassium hydroxide.

## Answer

The potassium ion is $\mathrm{K}^{+}$. The hydroxide ion is $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$. The formula $\mathrm{K}^{+} \mathrm{OH}^{-}$is correct, since there is the same number of positive and negative charges.

Answer: The formula of potassium hydroxide is KOH .

## Example 5.7

## Question

Write the formula of sodium sulfate.

## Answer

The sodium ion is $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$. The sulfate ion is $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$. The formula $\mathrm{Na}^{+} \mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ is not correct, since there is one positive charge but two negative charges. To get two positive charges, we must have two $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ions.

Answer: The formula of sodium sulfate is $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$.

## Writing formulas of compounds containing transition metals

You will see in Figure 5.6 (p.53) that we have indicated that it is not possible to predict the charges of the ions of the transition metals. In this course, we will meet a number of transition metal compounds.

Transition metals often have variable valency, Figure 5.7. The word 'valency' means 'combining power!. (A more formal definition of valency will be given in Section 5.6.)

Transition metals exhibit variable valency because there is such a small energy difference between the 4 s and 3 d sublevels. This means that the transition metals can lose different numbers of electrons from these sublevels to give metal ions with different positive charges.

The following are the main transition metals that show variable valency and their compounds that we will meet in this course:

| Iron | Iron combines with chlorine to form either $\mathrm{FeCl}_{2}$ or $\mathrm{FeCl}_{3}$. The compound $\mathrm{FeCl}_{2}$ is an ionic compound and the +2 charge on the iron atom is represented by putting the Roman numeral II in brackets. Therefore, $\mathrm{FeCl}_{2}$ is called iron(II) chloride. Similarly, the compound $\mathrm{FeCl}_{3}$ is called iron(III) chloride. |
| :--- | :--- |
| Copper | Copper combines with oxygen to form either $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ or CuO . $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ is called copper(I) oxide and CuO is called copper(II) oxide. |
| Chromium | Chromium exists as $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ ions in chromium(III) chloride, $\mathrm{CrCl}_{3}$. In $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}$ sodium dichromate, it appears that there are $\mathrm{Cr}^{6+}$ ions. (We shall clarify this in Chapter 14.) Hence sodium dichromate is also written sodium dichromate(VI). |
| Manganese | Manganese also shows variable valency. $\mathrm{MnO}_{2}$ is an ionic compound called manganese(IV) oxide - commonly called manganese dioxide. $\mathrm{MnSO}_{4}$ is called manganese(II) sulfate and $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$, is commonly called potassium permanganate - it is also called potassium manganate(VII). |


![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-069.jpg?height=773&width=1180&top_left_y=2799&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 5.7 All these solutions contain transition metal ions. All these ions have variable valency. Note also that when dissolved in water, they all form coloured solutions.

## Example 5.8

## Question

Write the formula of calcium hydrogencarbonate.

## Answer

The calcium ion is $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$. The hydrogencarbonate ion is $\mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-}$. The formula $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+} \mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-}$is not correct, since there are two positive charges but only one negative charge. To get two negative charges, we must have two $\mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-}$ ions, i.e. $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\left(\mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-}\right)_{2}$

Answer: The formula of calcium hydrogencarbonate is $\mathrm{Ca}\left(\mathrm{HCO}_{3}\right)_{2}$.

## Example 5.9

## Question

Write the formula of iron(II) carbonate.

## Answer

The Roman number (II) indicates $\mathrm{Fe}^{2 *}$. The carbonate ion is $\mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$. The formula $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$ is correct, since there are two positive charges and two negative charges.

Answer: The formula of iron(II) carbonate is $\mathrm{FeCO}_{3}$.

## Example 5.10

## Question

Name the compound $\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\left(\mathrm{SO}_{4}\right)_{3}$.

## Answer

The three sulfate ions together give a total negative charge of -6 . Since the overall charge must be zero, the two chromium atoms must carry a total charge of +6 . Therefore, each Cr atom must be $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$. Therefore, the name of the compound is chromium(III) sulfate.

Answer: Chromium(III) sulfate.

## NOTE

Do not get confused between compounds whose names end in -ide and those whose names end in -ate. A compound that contains just two elements always ends in -ide, e.g. magnesium sulfide, MgS. (Hydroxides are an exception to this rule.) Compounds whose names end in -ate contain oxygen as well as the other two elements, e.g. magnesium sulfate, $\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}$.

## 5.5 d-Block elements and transition elements

In many cases, there is no distinction made between the d-block elements and the transition elements. When referring to the $\mathrm{s}, \mathrm{p}, \mathrm{d}$ and f blocks of the Periodic Table, transition elements are regarded as those in the d-block of the table. However, if one examines the first row of the d-block from scandium to zinc, it is found that the properties of scandium and zinc are quite different from those of the other eight elements in this row. All the elements from titanium to copper inclusive are referred to as transition elements or transition metals. These show certain characteristics:

- Transition metals have variable valency.

However, scandium only forms $\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$ ions and zinc only forms $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ ions.

- Transition metals usually form coloured compounds. However, scandium and zinc only form white compounds.
- Transition metals are widely used as catalysts (Chapter 17). However, scandium and zinc show little catalytic activity.

Since scandium and zinc do not have typical transition metal properties, chemists devised a definition of transition metals that excludes these two elements but includes the elements from titanium to copper.

A transition metal is one that forms at least one ion with a partially filled d sublevel.

Neither $\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$ nor $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ has a partially filled d sublevel.
$\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}$
$\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 2 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~s}^{2}, 3 \mathrm{p}^{6}, 3 \mathrm{~d}^{10}$
In the case of $\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$ the d sublevel is completely empty. In the case of $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ the d sublevel is completely full. Since the properties of transition metals are associated with partly filled d sublevels, scandium and zinc are not considered transition metals.

In short, all of the ten elements from scandium to zinc are d-block elements but only those eight elements from titanium to copper (inclusive) are transition metals.
