### 5.6 Covalent bonding: Sharing of electrons

When studying ionic bonding, you learned that ionic compounds are usually formed when metals react with non-metals. However, there are many compounds that contain only non-metals, e.g. water, ammonia and carbon dioxide. These compounds do not contain any ions. Instead, the atoms achieve noble gas configurations by sharing electrons. A bond formed by sharing of electrons is called a covalent bond.

A covalent bond is a chemical bond that is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.

The word 'covalent' comes from the prefix 'co' meaning 'shared' and the Latin word valent meaning 'ability', i.e. the ability of an atom to combine with other atoms.

Covalent bonding results in the formation of a molecule.

A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. It is the smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently.

A molecule of hydrogen gas is written as $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ and a molecule of water is written as $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

Do not get confused between the terms molecule and compound. A compound consists of two or more different elements chemically combined, e.g. $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ is a compound as it contains two different elements. $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ also represents a molecule as it contains a group of atoms joined together. $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ represents a molecule of hydrogen. However, it is not a compound, as both atoms are of the same element.

Note: Noble gases such as helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar), naturally exist as single atoms. They are said to be monatomic (one atom). Therefore, a molecule for a monoatomic element refers to the single atom that represents the smallest particle of the element that can exist independently.

To help you understand this idea of electrons being shared, we now consider a number of examples. It is difficult to show the shapes of molecules on paper, as most molecules are threedimensional. Therefore, for each example, you will see a photograph of a model of each molecule made using a Molymod kit. It is recommended that you make these molecules yourselves and play with them to help you understand the shape!

Note: As with ionic bonding, covalent bonding also involves only the outer electrons. The shared pairs of electrons in a covalent bond are often represented simply by a dash.

The term molecule can only be used for covalent compounds. Since ionic compounds consist of giant structures of ions, it is not correct to refer to a 'molecule' of sodium chloride.

## Example 5.11

## The Hydrogen Molecule, $\mathrm{H}_{2}$

- A hydrogen atom has just one electron in its outer (and only) energy level.
- It is found that two hydrogen atoms join together to form a hydrogen molecule, $\mathrm{H}_{2}$. A cylinder of hydrogen gas consists of millions of these tiny independent units, each of which is called a molecule of hydrogen.
- A hydrogen molecule is formed when one hydrogen atom shares its single electron with another hydrogen atom.
- The second hydrogen atom shares its single electron with the first hydrogen atom.
- Two electrons are therefore shared between the two hydrogen atoms. It can be said that each hydrogen atom has a share of two electrons in its outermost energy level or orbit.
- Thus, each hydrogen atom achieves a stable electron structure like the noble gas helium (Figure 5.8).
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-071.jpg?height=242&width=512&top_left_y=2480&top_left_x=2194)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-071.jpg?height=421&width=922&top_left_y=2721&top_left_x=1712)
...or more simply

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-071.jpg?height=193&width=320&top_left_y=3294&top_left_x=2151)
Figure 5.8 Covalent bond formation in a molecule of hydrogen.

The shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond is often represented simply by a dash. Thus, $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}$ represents a molecule of hydrogen.

## Example 5.12

## The Chlorine Molecule, $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$.

- A chlorine atom has seven electrons in its outer energy level.
- To achieve a stable octet of eight electrons, two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons with each other, i.e. a covalent bond is formed between the two atoms.
- Each atom has its own seven outer electrons and a share in one of the outer electrons of the other atom.

The Lewis diagram to illustrate the formation of the covalent bond in chlorine is shown in Figure 5.9.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-072.jpg?height=324&width=798&top_left_y=1148&top_left_x=229)
Figure 5.9 In the chlorine molecule, the two atoms are held together by a covalent bond.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-072.jpg?height=203&width=522&top_left_y=1227&top_left_x=1113)
Figure 5.9 In the chlorine molecule, the two atoms are held together by a covalent bond.

## Example 5.13

## The Water Molecule, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

- An oxygen atom has six electrons in its outer energy level.
- Therefore, the oxygen atom needs two more electrons to complete its octet.
- To achieve this, the oxygen atom takes a share of one electron from each of two hydrogen atoms. Each hydrogen atom achieves the stable electron configuration of helium, i.e. they have a share of two electrons in each of their outmost orbits.
- Two covalent bonds are formed as shown in Figure 5.10. The water molecule is a V-shaped molecule. We shall understand the reason for this at a later stage.
Note that there are two pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom that are not involved in bonding. These two pairs of electrons are called 'lone pairs'. They are called 'lone pairs' because they are not bonded to another atom.

Pairs of electrons that are involved in bonding (i.e. 'tied up' in covalent bonds) are called 'bond pairs'. Thus, the oxygen atom in a water molecule has two lone pairs and two bond pairs.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-072.jpg?height=685&width=1724&top_left_y=2786&top_left_x=227)
Figure 5.10 The water molecule contains two covalent bonds and two lone pairs.

## Example 5.14

## The Ammonia Molecule, $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$

- A nitrogen atom has five electrons in its outer energy level.
- This atom needs three more electrons to complete its octet.
- To achieve this, the nitrogen atom takes a share of one electron from each of three hydrogen atoms. Thus, three covalent bonds are formed as shown in Figure 5.11.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-073.jpg?height=545&width=1085&top_left_y=1204&top_left_x=371)
Figure 5.11 The ammonia molecule contains three covalent bonds and one lone pair.

## Example 5.15

## The Methane Molecule, $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$

- A carbon atom has four electrons in its outer energy level.
- This atom needs four more electrons to complete its octet.
- To achieve this, the carbon atom takes a share of one electron from each of four hydrogen atoms.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-073.jpg?height=522&width=499&top_left_y=2874&top_left_x=377)
Figure 5.12 The methane molecule contains four covalent bonds.

- Thus, four covalent bonds are formed as shown in Figure 5.12.

From the above examples, it is clear that one can predict the number of covalent bonds formed around certain atoms:

- Hydrogen atoms form one covalent bond.
- Oxygen atoms form two covalent bonds.
- Nitrogen atoms form three covalent bonds.
- Carbon atoms form four covalent bonds.

The number of covalent bonds formed by atoms of some selected elements is given in Figure 5.13.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-073.jpg?height=519&width=1180&top_left_y=1132&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 5.13 The number of covalent bonds formed by atoms of some selected elements that you will commonly encounter on this course. Study this diagram carefully!

Since a hydrogen atom cannot combine with more than one atom of any other element, we say its valency ('combining power') is one or it is monovalent. In fact, hydrogen is used as the standard by which valency is measured.

The valency of an element is defined as the number of atoms of hydrogen or any other monovalent element with which each atom of the element combines.

- Therefore, since chlorine combines with one atom of hydrogen $(\mathrm{HCl})$, we say chlorine has a valency of one.
- Since oxygen combines with two atoms of hydrogen, oxygen has a valency of two $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)$.
- Similarly, nitrogen has a valency of three $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)$ and carbon a valency of four $\left(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\right)$.


## Double and triple bonds

In Examples 5.11-5.15, we have seen how atoms shared single pairs of electrons to form covalent bonds. Such bonds are more correctly referred to as single covalent bonds.

- A single bond is formed when one pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
- A double bond is formed when two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms. The oxygen molecule contains a double bond and the carbon dioxide molecule contains two double bonds, Figure 5.14.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-074.jpg?height=444&width=1681&top_left_y=950&top_left_x=185)
Figure 5.14 Both the oxygen molecule and the carbon dioxide molecule contain double bonds.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-074.jpg?height=525&width=675&top_left_y=996&top_left_x=1894)

- From Figure 5.14, we see that the formation of the double bonds enables each element to achieve the octet of electrons in the outer energy level.
- A triple bond is formed when three pairs of electrons are shared. The nitrogen molecule, $\mathrm{N}_{2}$, is an example of a molecule that contains a triple bond, Figure 5.15.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-074.jpg?height=346&width=1990&top_left_y=1901&top_left_x=185)
Figure 5.16
Formaldehyde solution is commonly used in preserving biological specimens.

## Sigma and Pi bonding

It is also possible to describe covalent bonding in terms of atomic orbitals.

- The formation of the $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ molecule can be described by saying that the 1s orbitals of two hydrogen atoms overlap as shown in Figure 5.18.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-075.jpg?height=287&width=1176&top_left_y=872&top_left_x=325)
Figure 5.18 The covalent bond in $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ being formed by the overlap of the 1s atomic orbitals of two hydrogen atoms

- When the two atomic orbitals overlap, they form a molecular orbital. This is rather like two soap bubbles coming together to form a larger soap bubble.
- The covalent bond formed by the head-on overlap of the two atomic orbitals is called a sigma bond. The Greek letter o (sigma) is used to indicate a sigma bond.

A sigma bond is formed by the head-on overlap of two orbitals.

- The bonding in the chlorine molecule can be explained by overlap of orbitals. If we consider the electron configuration of chlorine, we see that one of its p orbitals is half filled.

$$
\mathrm{CI}=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}, 3 s^{2}, 3 p_{x}^{2}, 3 p_{y}^{2}, 3 p_{z}^{1}
$$

- The covalent bond in $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ is formed when two half-filled $p_{z}$ atomic orbitals (one from each atom) overlap head on to form a sigma bond, Figure 5.19.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-075.jpg?height=283&width=1178&top_left_y=2890&top_left_x=328)
Figure 5.19 The covalent bond in $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ being formed by the head-on overlap of two p orbitals.

- There is very little difference between the orbital approach to single-bond formation and the simple 'shared electron pair' approach as already discussed in Examples 5.11-5.16.
- Both approaches describe the same occurrence, i.e. all single bonds can also be called sigma bonds.
- The two types of description of sigma and pi bonding differ from each other when we look at the formation of double and triple bonds.
- Consider how the double bond in the $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ molecule is formed.

$$
O=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p_{x}^{2}, 2 p_{y}^{1}, 2 p_{z}^{1}
$$

- There are two half-filled p orbitals in the oxygen atom. Imagine two oxygen atoms approaching each other so that the two $2 p_{y}$ orbitals overlap head on to form a sigma bond, Figure 5.20. However, the two $p_{z}$ orbitals overlap sideways to form what is called a pi $(\pi)$ bond.
- Therefore, the double bond in oxygen consists of one sigma and one pi bond. This is true of all double bonds.

A pi bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-075.jpg?height=538&width=1147&top_left_y=1748&top_left_x=1604)
Figure 5.20 The double bond in oxygen consists of one sigma and one pi bond.

Consider how the triple bond in the nitrogen molecule, $\mathrm{N}_{2}$, is formed.

$$
N=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p_{x}^{1}, 2 p_{y}^{1}, 2 p_{z}^{1}
$$

There are three half-filled $p$ orbitals in the nitrogen atom. Imagine two nitrogen atoms approaching each other so that the two $2 \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{x}}$ orbitals overlap head on to form a sigma bond, Figure 5.21.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-075.jpg?height=577&width=1042&top_left_y=3167&top_left_x=1634)
Figure 5.21 The triple bond in nitrogen consists of one sigma and two pi bonds.

- The two $2 p_{y}$ orbitals overlap sideways to form a pi bond.
- A second pi bond is formed from the sideways overlap of the two $2 p_{2}$ orbitals.
- Therefore, the triple bond in nitrogen consists of one sigma and two pi bonds. This is true of all triple bonds.
- In a double bond, one of the bonds is a sigma and one is a pi bond, Figure 5.22.
- Sigma bonds are stronger than pi bonds as there is more overlapping of orbitals in sigma bonds. Therefore, an $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ double bond is not twice as strong as an O-O single bond, since pi bonds are not as strong as sigma bonds.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-076.jpg?height=382&width=1822&top_left_y=1178&top_left_x=188)

Some differences between sigma and pi bonds are summarised in Table 5.2.

| Sigma | Pi |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1. Formed by head-on overlap of two orbitals | 1. Formed by sideways overlap of orbitals |
| 2. Involves any type of orbital (s, p, d, etc.) | 2. Involves p orbitals (or d orbitals) - cannot involve s orbitals |
| 3. Involves more overlap of orbitals | 3. Involves less overlap of orbitals |
| 4. Stronger bond which is not easily broken | 4. Weaker bond which is more easily broken |
| 5. Associated with single covalent bonds | 5. Associated with double and triple covalent bonds |
| 6. In a multiple bond, formed first and can exist on its own | 6. Only formed after sigma bond is formed and cannot exist on its own |

Table 5.2 Comparing sigma and pi bonding

The orbital theory gives us a detailed picture of the formation of double and triple bonds. This is the only use we will make of this theory in our study of chemistry for the Leaving Certificate. For all other cases of bond description, the simpler description of shared pairs of electrons (the 'shared-pair theory') is perfectly adequate.

### 5.7 Shapes of covalent molecules

We have already learned that ionic compounds consist of giant crystal lattices, whereas covalent compounds consist of separate molecules. The molecules of covalent compounds have particular shapes. In 1940, Nevil Sidgwick and Herbert Powell, two English chemists, proposed a theory to account for the shapes of molecules. Their theory is known as the Valence Shell Electron
Pair Repulsion Theory or VSEPR Theory for short. The term valence shell simply means 'outer energy level'.

The VSEPR Theory states the shape of a molecule depends on the number of pairs of electrons around the central atom. Since electrons are negatively charged, the electron pairs repel each other and arrange themselves in space so that they are as far apart as possible.

## Example 5.20

## Question

Use the VSEPR theory to deduce the shape of the ammonia molecule, $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$.

## Answer

## Step 1

Locate nitrogen in the Periodic Table. It is in Group V (or 15). It has five electrons in its outer energy level.

## Step 2

Work out the number of electrons contributed by the three hydrogen atoms to the bonds around the central atom. Since each hydrogen atom contributes one electron, the three hydrogen atoms will contribute a total number of three electrons, Figure 5.26(a).

## Step 3

Work out the total number of electron pairs around the central atom.

$$
\begin{aligned}
N & =5 \text { electrons } \\
3 \mathrm{H}=3 \times 1 & =3 \text { electrons } \\
\hline \text { Total } & =8 \text { electrons } \\
& =\text { four pairs of electrons } \\
& \Rightarrow \text { tetrahedral shape. }
\end{aligned}
$$

We would therefore predict that ammonia has a regular tetrahedral shape.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-079.jpg?height=512&width=649&top_left_y=1621&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 5.26 (a) Ammonia has the shape of a pyramid.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-079.jpg?height=395&width=473&top_left_y=1686&top_left_x=2233)
Figure 5.26 (b) Model of ammonia molecule.

- By experiment, it is found that the bond angle in the ammonia molecule is $107^{\circ}$.
- It is less than the regular tetrahedral bond angle of $109.5^{\circ}$ due to the presence of the lone pair of electrons.
- The ammonia molecule has one lone pair and three bond pairs of electrons.
- The increased repulsion caused by the presence of the lone pair causes the bond angle to decrease by about $2.5^{\circ}$ to $107^{\circ}$, Figure 5.26(a).
- Thus, the shape of the ammonia molecule is pyramidal, Figure 5.26(b).


## Exampte 5.21

## Question

Use the VSEPR theory to deduce the shape of the water molecule.

Proceeding as in Example 5.20.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 & =6 \text { electrons } \\
2 \mathrm{H}=2 \times 1 & =2 \text { electrons } \\
\hline \text { Total } & =8 \text { electrons } \\
& =\text { four pairs of electrons } \\
& \Rightarrow \text { tetrahedral shape }
\end{aligned}
$$

- We would predict that the water molecule has a regular tetrahedral shape.
- By experiment, it is found that the bond angle is $104.5^{\circ}$.
- It is less than the regular tetrahedral bond angle of $109.5^{\circ}$ because of the presence of the two lone pairs of electrons.
- The water molecule has two lone pairs and two bond pairs of electrons.
- The increased repulsion caused by the presence of the two lone pairs results in the bond angle being decreased by about $5^{\circ}$ from $109.5^{\circ}$ to $104.5^{\circ}$ (Figure 5.27).
- Thus, the shape of the water molecule is V-shaped, Figure 5.27.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-079.jpg?height=454&width=1062&top_left_y=3235&top_left_x=1644)
Figure 5.27 The water molecule is V-shaped.

### 5.8 Tests for anions in aqueous solution

We have already seen in Chapter 3 that the presence of positive metal ions in a substance may be detected by means of flame tests. Positive ions are called cations.

A cation is a positive ion.
Examples of positive ions that we met in Chapter 3 were $\mathrm{Na}^{+}, \mathrm{K}^{+}, \mathrm{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$.

We will now carry out tests to detect the presence of certain negative ions dissolved in water. A solution made by dissolving a substance in water is called an aqueous solution (from the Latin word aqua for water). In all the following experiments, the negative ions will be dissolved in water. A negative ion is also called an anion.

An anion is a negative ion.
The ions we will investigate in this course are:

1. The chloride ion, $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$.
2. The sulfate ion, $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ and the sulfite ion, $\mathrm{SO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$,
3. The carbonate ion, $\mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$ and the hydrogencarbonate ion, $\mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-}$. The old name for the hydrogencarbonate ion was the 'bicarbonate ion'.

You are not required to write fully balanced equations for all of the following tests. In most cases, simple equations involving ions (called ionic equations) are perfectly acceptable. You will study the balancing of equations in more detail in Chapter 8.

Note: The type of analysis where we detect the presence of certain substances is known as qualitative analysis, i.e. we are determining the presence of a particular substance rather than determining how much of the substance is present.

Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 2 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

When you are carrying out laboratory practical work, please ensure that you follow the detailed instructions, including all safety precautions, given in the Student Laboratory Notebook. The points given in Student Experiment 2 summarise the key areas but must not be taken as a substitute for detailed instructions.
4. The nitrate ion, $\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$.
5. The phosphate ion, $\mathrm{PO}_{4}{ }^{3-}$.

## Student Experiment No. 2

Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 2 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

This Student Experiment is made up of the following five individual experiments:
(i) Experiment 5.1A: To detect the presence of chloride ions in aqueous solution.
(ii) Experiment 5.1B: To detect the presence of sulfate ions $\left(\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}\right)$ and sulfite ions $\left(\mathrm{SO}_{3}{ }^{2-}\right)$ in aqueous solution.

### 5.1A Experiment

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 2 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

## Student Experiment No. 2

## To detect the presence of chloride ions in aqueous solution

## Key steps in procedure

- The chloride salt is dissolved in deionised water.
- A clear solution is obtained.
- A few drops of silver nitrate solution are added to the chloride salt solution.


## Observation

- The clear solution turns cloudy.
- A white solid material settles out of solution, Figure 5.30.

This is an example of a precipitation reaction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-081.jpg?height=818&width=1232&top_left_y=1406&top_left_x=452)
Figure 5.30 A white precipitate of silver chloride is formed when silver nitrate solution is added to a solution containing chloride ions. is added to a solion contaning chorde ions.

A precipitation reaction is a reaction in which an insoluble substance is produced from soluble substances in solution. The insoluble substance formed in a precipitation reaction is called the precipitate.

## Explanation

- In this experiment, the precipitate formed is called silver chloride. It is formed when the silver ions from the silver nitrate combine with the chloride ions from the chloride salt that are dissolved in the water.

$$
\mathrm{Ag}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl} \downarrow
$$

- The arrow pointing down as shown indicates a precipitate is formed.
- The cloudiness is observed because the silver chloride formed does not dissolve in water.


## Confirmatory test <br> \section*{Conirmatory test}

- To confirm that the white precipitate is silver chloride, dilute ammonia solution is added to the cloudy solution.


## Observation <br> Observation

- The cloudiness disappears.


## \section*{Explanation <br> <br> Explanation}

- Silver chloride is soluble in dilute ammonia solution.$$

- The cloudiness disappears.
- Silver chloride is soluble in dilute ammonia solution.


## \section*{Conclusion <br> <br> Conclusion}

- Chloride ions were present in solution.

Note: In chemistry, the substances which cause a chemical reaction to take place are referred to as reagents, e.g. in the above reaction, silver nitrate is a reagent. Full details of all the reagents needed for each experiment are given in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

### 5.1C Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 2

## To detect the presence of carbonate ions ( $\mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$ ) and hydrogencarbonate ions $\left(\mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-}\right)$in aqueous solution

## Key steps in procedure

- The carbonate salt is placed in a boiling tube.
- A one-holed rubber stopper is inserted into the boiling tube.
- The apparatus shown in Figure 5.32 is set up.
- The one-holed rubber stopper is removed and dilute hydrochloric acid is added to the carbonate salt in the boiling tube.
- The one-holed rubber stopper is replaced.


## Observation

- A brisk effervescence (fizzing) is observed as the acid comes in contact with the carbonate.
- The gas given off is seen bubbling through the limewater.
- The limewater turns a milky colour.


## Explanation

The fizzing is caused by the carbonate ions reacting with the acid to give off a gas:

$$
\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}+2 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

- The fact that the limewater turns milky shows that the gas is carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form chalk (limestone). The chemical name for chalk is calcium carbonate.

$$
\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}+\mathrm{CO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \downarrow+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

limewater
chalk
(limestone)
Note: If you continue to bubble carbon dioxide through the limewater, the milky colour disappears. This is because the insoluble calcium carbonate eventually reacts with the carbon dioxide to form soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate.

$$
\underset{\text { insoluble }}{\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}+\mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca}\left(\mathrm{HCO}_{3}\right)_{2}} \text { soluble }
$$

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 2 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-083.jpg?height=1423&width=1147&top_left_y=628&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 5.32 Carbon dioxide is given off when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a carbonate or a hydrogencarbonate compound. The carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

- If the experiment is repeated using a hydrogencarbonate salt instead of the carbonate salt, the same results are obtained. As in the case of the carbonate, the hydrogencarbonate reacts with the acid to liberate carbon dioxide.

$$
\mathrm{HCO}_{3}^{-}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

## Conclusion

- Both carbonate ions and hydrogencarbonate ions react with dilute hydrochloric acid to give off carbon dioxide gas.

This effervescence is also observed when you add substances such as Alka-Seltzer to water. These are substances that contain sodium hydrogencarbonate and citric acid. When dissolved in water, the citric acid reacts with the hydrogencarbonate to give off carbon dioxide. This causes the fizzing to occur.

### 5.1C Experiment

## To distinguish between carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ions

- Magnesium sulfate $\left(\mathrm{MgSO}_{4}\right)$ solution is added to solutions of the carbonate salt and the hydrogencarbonate salt in separate testtubes.
- A white precipitate is formed in the solution containing the carbonate.
- No precipitate is formed in the solution containing the hydrogencarbonate, Figure 5.33.


## Explanation

- In the solution of the carbonate, a white precipitate of insoluble magnesium carbonate is formed.
$\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}+\mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCO}_{3} \downarrow$
Insoluble
- In the solution of the hydrogencarbonate salt, no precipitate is formed, as magnesium hydrogencarbonate is soluble in water.
$\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg}\left(\mathrm{HCO}_{3}\right)_{2}$
Soluble
- If the clear solution of magnesium hydrogencarbonate is boiled, a white precipitate of magnesium carbonate appears.
$\mathrm{Mg}\left(\mathrm{HCO}_{3}\right)_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCO}_{3} \downarrow+\mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Soluble Insoluble


## Conclusion

- Carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ions are distinguished from each other using magnesium sulfate solution.
- Magnesium sulfate solution added to a solution containing carbonate ions gives a white precipitate. Magnesium sulfate

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-084.jpg?height=2172&width=1125&top_left_y=690&top_left_x=1451)
Figure 5.33 A solution of magnesium sulfate is used to distinguish between carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ions.

solution added to a solution containing hydrogencarbonate ions gives a clear solution.

- Magnesium carbonate is insoluble in water but magnesium hydrogencarbonate is soluble.


## Student Experiment No. 2

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 2 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

## To detect the presence of nitrate ions $\left(\mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{-}\right)$in aqueous solution

Since all nitrate salts are soluble in water, it is not possible to detect the presence of the nitrate ion by a precipitation reaction. A special test called the Brown Ring Test is used to detect the presence of the nitrate ion.

## Key steps in procedure

- A nitrate salt is dissolved in deionised water in a test-tube.
- Freshly prepared iron(II) sulfate solution, $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$, is added to the solution in the testtube.
- Using a dropper, concentrated sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$, is added down the inside of the test-tube. The test-tube is slanted slightly as shown in Figure 5.34. Since the concentrated sulfuric acid is so dense, it settles at the bottom of the test-tube and forms a layer underneath the mixture.


## Observation

- A brown ring is formed at the junction of the two layers, Figure 5.35.


## Explanation

- The brown ring is formed as a result of nitrate ions being present, and hence is the confirmatory test for the presence of the nitrate ion.
- The brown colour is due to the formation of the substance $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{NO}$.
- When describing this experiment, it is important that you use the phrase concentrated sulfuric acid as this experiment does not work with dilute sulfuric acid.


## Conclusion

- Nitrate ions are present in the solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-085.jpg?height=682&width=798&top_left_y=963&top_left_x=1712)
Figure 5.34 Adding concentrated sulfuric acid to the mixture of nitrate ion solution and iron(II) sulfate solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-085.jpg?height=1222&width=1141&top_left_y=1933&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 5.35 A brown ring is formed at the junction between the concentrated sulfuric acid at the bottom and the mixture of the nitrate ion solution and iron(II) sulfate solution on top.

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 2 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

## Student Experiment No. 2

## To detect the presence of phosphate ions in aqueous solution

## Key steps in procedure

- A phosphate salt is dissolved in deionised water in a test-tube.
- Ammonium molybdate solution is added. Ammonium molybdate is a compound of molybdenum (element number 42 in the Periodic Table). The chemical formula for ammonium molybdate is $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{MoO}_{4}$.
- Using a dropper, a few drops of concentrated nitric acid are added to the test-tube.
- The test-tube is placed in warm water.


## Observation

- A yellow precipitate is formed, Figure 5.36.


## Explanation

- The yellow precipitate is a substance called ammonium phosphomolybdate.


## Conclusion

- Phosphate ions are present in solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-086.jpg?height=1596&width=1020&top_left_y=638&top_left_x=1477)
Figure 5.36 A yellow precipitate is obtained when concentrated nitric acid is added to a solution containing phosphate ions and ammonium molybdate.

## Summary What I should know

- The octet rule states that when bonding occurs, atoms tend to reach an electron arrangement, with eight electrons in the outermost energy level.
- Ionic bonding involves the complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another.

Covalent bonding involves the sharing of electrons.

- A transition metal is one that forms at least one ion with a partially filled $d$ sublevel.
- A sigma bond is formed by the head-on overlap of two orbitals. A pi bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals.
- The VSEPR theory can be used to predict the shapes of molecules.
- The chloride ion is detected using silver nitrate solution. The confirmatory test is that the cloudy precipitate dissolves in dilute ammonia solution.
- Sulfate and sulfite ions are detected using barium chloride solution. In the case of the sulfate ion the cloudy precipitate is insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid. In the case of the sulfite ion the cloudy precipitate is soluble in dilute hydrochloric acid.
- Carbonate and hydrogencarbonate compounds give off carbon dioxide when dilute acid is added. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. The carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ions are distinguished from each other using magnesium sulfate. A precipitate is formed with the carbonate, but not with the hydrogencarbonate.
- The presence of the nitrate ion is confirmed using the brown ring test. The brown ring is formed when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to a solution containing the nitrate compound and freshly prepared iron(II) sulfate.
- The phosphate ion is detected using ammonium molybdate solution and concentrated nitric acid. A yellow precipitate is obtained.
