# 6 Electronegativity and the Continuum of Chemical Bonding

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-090.jpg?height=1080&width=1356&top_left_y=552&top_left_x=179)

### 6.1 Introduction

In the last chapter, we studied ionic and covalent bonding. In this chapter, we will complete our study of bonding by looking at ionic and covalent bonding as part of a continuum or spectrum of bonding. We will see that ionic and covalent bonding are at different ends of this spectrum.

In order to understand this continuum of chemical bonding, we will first study an important concept in chemistry called electronegativity.

### 6.2 Electronegativity: 'Tug-of-war' for electrons

In a covalent bond between identical atoms (e.g. in $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ or $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ ), the pair of electrons is shared equally between the two atoms in the molecule. However, chemists have found that in bonds between different atoms, the pair of electrons is often more attracted to one of the atoms than to the other.

- In hydrogen chloride, HCl , it is found that the two electrons in the covalent bond are more attracted to the chlorine than to the hydrogen.
- As the two electrons spend more of their time nearer to the chlorine atom, this gives the chlorine atom a slight negative charge and leaves the hydrogen atom with a slight positive charge.
- This small amount of charge is indicated by the Greek letter $\delta$ (delta), Figure 6.1.

$$
H_{x-C} \underset{. \ddot{C}:}{ }
$$

Figure 6.1 In the single covalent bond in HCl , the two electrons are more attracted to the Cl atom than to the H atom. This gives the chlorine atom a slight negative charge and the H atom a slight positive charge. This small amount of charge is indicated by the Greek letter $\delta$ (delta).

The ability of an atom in a covalent bond to attract the electrons in the bond to itself is given a special name and is called the electronegativity of the atom.

Electronegativity is the relative attraction that an atom in a molecule has for the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond.

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of the concept of electronegativity.
- To provide students with the opportunity to make use of electronegativity values to discuss bonding in various compounds.
- To ensure that students know how to interpret the continuum of chemical bonding.
- To make students familiar with a range of intermolecular forces.
- To give students an understanding of the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.

Some important points about electronegativity may be summarised as follows:

- Since the 'electron pulling power' of chlorine is greater than that of hydrogen in HCl , we say that chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen.
- A famous American chemist called Linus Pauling, Figure 6.2, studied the amounts of energy needed to break certain bonds. From his results, he set up a scale of relative values of electronegativity.

For example, he found that fluorine had four times the 'electron pulling power' of calcium. Therefore, he assigned an electronegativity value of 4.0 to fluorine and 1.0 to calcium. A table of electronegativity values is shown in Figure 6.3.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-091.jpg?height=763&width=1180&top_left_y=364&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 6.2 In 1939 the American chemist, Linus Pauling, made an enormous contribution to our understanding of chemical bonding in his famous book The Nature of the Chemical Bond. In 1954 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in chemistry and he was awarded the Nobel Prize for peace in 1962.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-091.jpg?height=1004&width=1929&top_left_y=1565&top_left_x=559)
Figure 6.3 Electronegativity values of the elements

- Note from Figure 6.3 that the more electronegative elements are the very reactive non-metals such as fluorine and chlorine. The least electronegative elements are the very reactive metals such as potassium and sodium.
- Elements with low electronegativity values are said to be electropositive.
- Since chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, it is more correct to refer to the bond in $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{Cl}$ as a polar covalent bond.

A polar covalent bond is a bond in which there is unequal sharing of the pair (or pairs) of electrons. This causes one end of the bond to be slightly positive ( $\delta+$ ) and the other end slightly negative ( $\delta-$ ).

Some examples of polar covalent bonds are shown in Figure 6.4.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-091.jpg?height=390&width=1179&top_left_y=2713&top_left_x=1580)
Figure 6.4 Some examples of polar covalent bonds

## Pure covalent

The term pure covalent is often used to refer to a covalent bond where there is equal sharing of the two electrons in the bond.

A pure covalent bond is a bond in which there is equal sharing of the pair (or pairs) of electrons. This occurs because the atoms bonded together have identical or very similar electronegativity values, i.e. neither atom exerts a significantly stronger pull on the shared pair or pairs of electrons.

Some examples of pure covalent bonds are shown in Figure 6.5. Note that in the compound $\mathrm{PH}_{3}$, the P-H bond is considered pure covalent, since the electronegativity values of $P$ and $H$ are virtually identical (2.19 and 2.20 respectively).

$$
\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H} \quad \mathrm{Cl}-\mathrm{Cl}, \mathrm{P}-\mathrm{H}
$$

Figure 6.5 Some examples of pure covalent bonds

## Uses of electronegativity values

There are two main uses of electronegativity values:

1. To predict the polarity of covalent bonds.
2. To predict the type of bonding in a compound.

We now explain both of these uses.

## To predict polarity of covalent bonds

By referring to the table of electronegativity values, we can tell if the bonds in a molecule are pure covalent or polar covalent. The greater the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond, Figure 6.6.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-092.jpg?height=404&width=1177&top_left_y=2995&top_left_x=188)
Figure 6.6 The electronegativity difference between the elements in a covalent bond tells us whether the bond is polar covalent or pure covalent.

## Polar covalent bonds in polar molecules

In most molecules that have polar covalent bonds, the molecules themselves are also polar.

A polar molecule is a molecule that has an uneven distribution of electrical charges. This means that the molecule has regions (poles) with partial positive and partial negative charges separated by a distance.

Polarity in a molecule occurs due to differences in electronegativity between the atoms in the molecule, and also the shape of the molecule, which prevents the charges from cancelling out.

For a molecule to be polar, the following two conditions must be fulfilled:

1. One or more bonds must be polar covalent, i.e. there must be a significant electronegativity difference between the atoms in the molecule.
2. The centres of partial positive and partial negative charges in the molecule must be separated by a distance. This usually occurs when the molecule is asymmetric or lacks uniformity in the balance of charges. In other words, the polar bonds do not cancel each other out.

Examples of polar molecules are hydrogen fluoride $(\mathrm{HF})$, water $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)$ and ammonia $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)$, Figure 6.7.
<img class="imgSvg" id = "mincxtf7szri68ew60g" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>

Figure 6.7 Hydrogen fluoride, water and ammonia have polar covalent bonds. Overall, each of these molecules is a polar molecule since the positive and negative poles are separated by a distance. Note that since each molecule is neutral overall, the sum of all the partial charges must add up to zero.

If you examine the shapes of models of each of these three molecules, you will see that the centres of partial positive and partial negative charges (also called positive and negative poles) are separated by a distance.

Note that when representing polar molecules, the sums of all the positive and negative charges must add up to zero.

## Polar covalent bonds in non-polar molecules

There are some molecules which, even though they have polar covalent bonds, are not polar molecules.

- It is found that if the shape of the molecule is symmetrical or uniform, the charges cancel each other out. In doing so, the molecule overall is considered to be non-polar. Studying Figure 6.8 will help you to understand this.
- Note that all the molecules in Figure 6.8 are symmetrical. These shapes cause the centre of all the partial positive charges and partial negative charges to coincide and cancel each other out.
- Examining models of these molecules will help you to understand that they are symmetrical. This is explained in more detail in the online videos accompanying this textbook.

The fact that water is a polar molecule gave chemists an indication of the shape of the molecule. If water were linear rather than V-shaped, then it would not be a polar molecule, Figure 6.9.

Note: If there are no polar covalent bonds in a molecule, then the molecule must be non-polar. For example, $\mathrm{H}_{2}, \mathrm{~N}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ are all non-polar molecules.

A non-polar molecule is a molecule that has an even distribution of electrical charges due to the symmetry of the molecule. This means that the molecule has regions (poles) with partial positive and partial negative charges that are not separated by a distance but coincide with each other.
<img class="imgSvg" id = "mincxtfkpegd2pfq7hg" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>

Figure 6.8 In each molecule, the centre of the partial negative charges coincides with that of the partial positive charges. Therefore, none of these molecules are polar molecules.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-093.jpg?height=261&width=965&top_left_y=1940&top_left_x=1692)
Figure 6.9 If the water molecule were linear, it would not be a polar molecule. The fact that water is V -shaped means that the partial positive and negative charges do not cancel out, and hence water is a polar molecule.

## To demonstrate whether a liquid is polar or non-polar

A simple way of demonstrating whether a liquid is polar or non-polar is to study the effect of a negatively charged plastic rod on a stream of liquid from a burette, Figure 6.10.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-094.jpg?height=1182&width=792&top_left_y=638&top_left_x=188)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-094.jpg?height=1182&width=844&top_left_y=638&top_left_x=976)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-094.jpg?height=1186&width=818&top_left_y=634&top_left_x=1829)

Figure 6.10 A polar liquid (e.g. water) is attracted to the charged rod. The type of charge on the rod does not make any difference to the result of the experiment. A non-polar liquid (e.g. cyclohexane) is not affected by the charged rod.

- If the liquid is a polar liquid (e.g. water), the stream of liquid is attracted to the rod as shown.
- The positive poles of the water molecules are attracted towards the negatively charged rod.
- It does not matter if the negatively charged rod is replaced with a positively charged one. The water will still be attracted to the rod, as the water molecules will turn so that the negative poles of the molecules are attracted to the positively charged rod.
- If the experiment is repeated with a non-polar liquid (e.g. cyclohexane), no attraction is observed, since there are no polar molecules in the liquid.

Note: The fact that water is a polar molecule is the reason why microwave ovens can cook food. These ovens produce electromagnetic waves which change direction millions of times per second. The polar water molecules continuously try to line up with the changing direction of the waves. This causes a lot of friction between the molecules and generates a lot of heat to cook the food., Figure 6.11.

The second use of electronegativity values is to predict the type of bonding in a compound. This will be studied in the next section.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-094.jpg?height=788&width=1151&top_left_y=2842&top_left_x=1464)
Figure 6.11 The fact that the water molecule is polar helps microwave ovens to cook food.

There is a useful 'rule of thumb' that summarises the continuum of bonding. A rule of thumb means that this is a method that is a rough guideline but is not a scientific law. This rule of thumb assists us in predicting whether a compound is ionic or covalent, and also the degree of polarity in a covalent bond.

An electronegativity difference greater than $\mathbf{1 . 7}$ indicates ionic bonding in a compound.
An electronegativity difference less than or equal to 1.7 indicates covalent bonding in a compound.
An electronegativity difference greater than 0.4 and less than 1.7 indicates that the covalent bond is polar covalent.
An electronegativity difference greater than zero but less than or equal to 0.4 indicates that the covalent bond is slightly polar which, in practice, may be considered nonpolar.
An electronegativity difference of zero indicates that the bond is pure covalent and, therefore, also nonpolar.

For example, consider the electronegativity differences of the elements in potassium fluoride and methane, Figure 6.13.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-096.jpg?height=411&width=1033&top_left_y=1640&top_left_x=572)
Figure 6.13 Electronegativity differences may be used to predict ionic and covalent bonding.

It is important to remember that the above is not a definite law but simply a rule of thumb, which is useful for predicting the type of bonding that might be expected in a given compound. There are some exceptions to the above rule of thumb.

- The main exceptions are lithium hydride (LiH), sodium hydride (NaH), potassium hydride $(\mathrm{KH})$ and calcium hydride $\left(\mathrm{CaH}_{2}\right)$. All these compounds are ionic and contain the hydride ion, $\mathrm{H}^{-}$. The above rule of thumb would indicate incorrectly that the bonding is covalent.
- The compound HF is also an exception. The electronegativity difference in the $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{F}$ bond is 1.78 . Therefore, the rule of thumb would suggest that the bonding is ionic. However, HF is a covalent compound.
- Another exception is the covalent compound $\mathrm{BF}_{3}$. The electronegativity difference in the B - F bond is 1.94 . Therefore, the rule of thumb would suggest that the bonding is ionic. However, $\mathrm{BF}_{3}$ is a covalent compound.

TEST YOURSELF: Attempt Questions 6.1 and W6.1-W6.2.

Study SEC exam question 6.1 and model answer in the online resources.

## NOTE

Similar to the octet rule, this rule-ofthumb for predicting bonding is another example of a limitation in predicting bonding between atoms.

### 6.4 Intermolecular forces

So far we have studied the two main types of bonding: ionic bonding and covalent bonding. Since these types of bonds hold atoms together inside or within the molecule, this type of bonding is often referred to as intramolecular bonding (Latin: intra = inside or within). Think of the phrase INTRAvenous injection, i.e. where the drug is injected INSIDE the vein, Figure 6.14.

There are other types of bonds that exist between one molecule and another. These types of bonding are referred to as intermolecular forces (Latin: inter = between). Think of the word INTERnet which allows communication BETWEEN people.

Studying Figure 6.15 may help you to understand the difference between intramolecular bonding and intermolecular forces. (Remember that intermolecular forces do not apply to ionic compounds, as ionic compounds consist of ions in a crystal lattice rather than individual molecules.)

Note in Figure 6.15 that intermolecular forces are represented using dashes. (Do not use dots, as these are used to represent electrons). Intramolecular forces in covalent bonds are much stronger than intermolecular forces between molecules. These intermolecular forces of attraction are commonly called van der Waals forces, after the Dutch scientist Johannes van der Waals who discovered them, Figure 6.16. In 1910 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in physics for his work on these forces.

Van der Waals forces are weak, intermolecular forces of attraction that exist between all molecules.

Characteristics of van der Waals forces:

- Van der Waals forces are weaker than covalent or ionic bonds.
- They occur between all molecules regardless of the individual characteristics of the molecules (e.g. polar or non-polar).
- The strength of van der Waals forces decreases greatly as the distances between molecules increases.

Although van der Waals forces are weak compared to covalent or ionic bonds, they are present in large numbers. Therefore, they play an important role in determining the physical properties of substances such as boiling points, melting points, and solubility.

Intramolecular bonding is bonding that takes place within a molecule, i.e. the bond that holds the atoms together. Covalent bonding and polar covalent bonding are examples of intramolecular bonding.

Intermolecular forces are the forces of attraction that exist between molecules.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-097.jpg?height=720&width=1183&top_left_y=885&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 6.14 An intravenous injection is so called because the drug is being injected inside the vein. Intramolecular bonding is bonding that occurs inside the molecule, i.e. it holds the molecule together.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-097.jpg?height=320&width=1117&top_left_y=1937&top_left_x=1608)
Figure 6.15 Intramolecular bonding is bonding within a molecule. Intermolecular forces are forces of attraction between molecules.

There are three main types of van der Waals forces which we will study on this course:

Figure 6.16 Johannes van der Waals discovered that there were weak attractive forces between molecules.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-097.jpg?height=707&width=499&top_left_y=2539&top_left_x=2252)

1. London dispersion forces.
2. Permanent dipole-dipole forces, including a special type of dipole-dipole force called hydrogen bonding.
3. Ion-dipole forces.

We will now discuss these types of intermolecular forces.

## 1. London dispersion forces

Imagine what happens to a molecule of hydrogen when another molecule of hydrogen comes near it, Figure 6.17.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-098.jpg?height=300&width=1072&top_left_y=732&top_left_x=250)
Figure 6.17 London dispersion forces are weak attractive forces between temporary dipoles.

From our previous studies of bonding, we know that there are two electrons moving inside a molecule of hydrogen. As the two electrons move inside the molecule, it may happen that, at any one instant, both electrons may be closer to one end of the molecule than the other, i.e. one side of the molecule may be slightly negative leaving the other side of the molecule slightly positive.

- The picture may be compared to taking a series of random photographs. At a given instant in some photos, one part of the molecule may have slightly more electron density than another part. This means that a temporary dipole is set up in the molecule, i.e. two poles with one $\delta+$ and the other $\delta-$. It is temporary because it only exists for a short time. This is in contrast to the permanent dipole in a molecule of HCl . This temporary dipole is often called an instantaneous dipole, as it is only set up for a short time.
- This temporary dipole could cause a similar dipole to be set up in a nearby molecule. This process of setting up the dipole in a nearby molecule is called induction.
- There is then an attraction between the opposite charges as shown in Figure 6.17. This attraction is called a London dispersion force after the German-American scientist, Fritz London, who studied this particular type of van der Waals force in great detail, Figure 6.18. The word 'dispersion' refers to the fact that there is a temporary redistribution or dispersion of charge in the electron clouds. This temporary redistribution causes temporary dipoles to be set up.

London dispersion forces are weak forces of attraction between molecules resulting from the formation of temporary dipoles. They are the only forces of attraction between non-polar molecules.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-098.jpg?height=1401&width=1180&top_left_y=367&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 6.18 Fritz London studied the intermolecular forces between non-polar molecules.

- Since the electrons are moving about at high speed, the attraction between any two molecules only exists for an instant. These London dispersion forces are very weak. It has been estimated that this type of force is only about one-thousandth as strong as the covalent bond holding the atoms together in the molecule.
- London dispersion forces are the only forces of attraction that exist between non-polar molecules, e.g. $\mathrm{H}_{2}, \mathrm{O}_{2}, \mathrm{~N}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$.
- London dispersion forces occur between all atoms and molecules, regardless of whether the molecule is polar or non-polar. The reason for this is because electrons are in constant movement. As they move within the molecule, the motion leads to changes in the distribution of electron charge in the molecule. Therefore, at any given instant, the charge may be unevenly distributed. This gives rise to temporary dipoles as described above.
- London dispersion forces also exist between single atoms, e.g. the noble gases helium, neon and argon exist as single atoms, and London dispersion forces exist between all of the atoms. (Note that even though these elements exist as individual atoms, the London dispersion forces between the atoms are still referred to as 'intermolecular'.)


## The effect of London dispersion forces on physical properties

- It has been found that the strength of London dispersion forces increases as the molecules get larger in size. This is because the increase in the number of electrons means bigger electron clouds, allowing the temporary dipoles to form more easily. The bigger atoms are said to have a higher polarisability. The greater the polarisability, the greater is the strength of the dispersion forces.
- For example, at room temperature, $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ is a gas, $\mathrm{Br}_{2}$ is a liquid and $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ is a solid. This progression in boiling point is due to the increasing strength of the London dispersion forces. The strength of these forces increases because, as the relative molecular masses increase, the numbers of electrons increases, and the size of the electron clouds in the molecules increases. To convert a liquid to a gas, the particles of the liquid must be 'freed' from each other. Therefore, the forces of attraction between these particles must be broken. The boiling point reflects the energy required to overcome the intermolecular forces.

Study the data summarised in Table 6.2, as you could be given similar data in an exam and asked to explain the reason for the trend.

| Molecule | Boiling point of <br> element $\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ |
| :---: | :---: |
| $\mathrm{F}_{2}$ | -188 |
| $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ | -34 |
| $\mathrm{Br}_{2}$ | 59 |
| $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ | 184 |

Table 6.2 Note the increase in boiling point as the size of the molecules increases. The increase in boiling point is due to the increasing strength of the London dispersion forces.

- Similarly, $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ has a boiling point of $-253^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ but $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ does not boil until $-183^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The higher boiling point of oxygen is due to the fact that the London dispersion forces in oxygen are stronger than in hydrogen, since the oxygen atom is bigger than the hydrogen atom, i.e. it contains more electrons than hydrogen and more temporary dipoles are formed. Therefore, more heat is required to break the stronger London dispersion forces formed between the bigger molecules of oxygen.
- London dispersion forces also exist in the case of the noble gases - all of which consist of atoms. The boiling points of these gases increase with the size of the atoms because of the increasing strength of the London dispersion forces, Figure 6.19. As you go down the group, the atoms increase in size and the greater number of electrons in the larger electron clouds allow the temporary dipoles to form more easily. (The boiling points are given on the Kelvin scale. We will study this scale in Chapter 9.)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-099.jpg?height=1265&width=1177&top_left_y=2011&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 6.19 The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing atomic number because the strength of the London dispersion forces increases as the atoms get bigger.

- London dispersion forces are also used to explain the difference in the boiling points of compounds such as propane, $\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8}\left(-42^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$, and butane, $\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{10}\left(-1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$. The molecules of both of these compounds are non-polar. Butane has a higher boiling point because it is a bigger molecule than propane and has more electrons and a bigger electron cloud than propane. Therefore, temporary dipoles are more easily formed in butane, causing greater numbers of London dispersion forces. Therefore, more heat must be supplied to boil butane than propane.
- London dispersion forces are used to explain why butane, $\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{10}$ is a gas at room temperature but hexane, $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{14^{\prime}}$ is a liquid. The molecules of both of these compounds are non-polar. Hexane is a larger molecule with more electrons and a bigger electron cloud. Therefore, temporary dipoles are more easily formed, i.e. the London dispersion forces are strong enough to hold the molecules together as a liquid.
- London dispersion forces are used to explain why carbon dioxide is more easily liquefied than helium. Both gases are non-polar but the London dispersion forces are stronger in carbon dioxide than the London dispersion forces in helium because carbon dioxide is a larger molecule with more electrons and a bigger electron cloud. Therefore, temporary dipoles are more easily formed.


## Example 6.2

## Question

The boiling points of hydrogen and oxygen are 20.0 K and 90.2 K respectively.
Account for the higher boiling point of oxygen.

## Answer

Since both of these molecules are non-polar, the only intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces.

The strength of London dispersion forces increases as the molecules get bigger. Oxygen is a bigger molecule than hydrogen. Therefore, the London dispersion forces are stronger between oxygen molecules than between hydrogen molecules.

Therefore, it takes more energy to break the London dispersion forces in oxygen than in hydrogen, i.e. oxygen has a higher boiling point, Figure 6.20.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-100.jpg?height=629&width=1085&top_left_y=2161&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 6.20 The boiling point of oxygen is higher than that of hydrogen because the London dispersion forces in oxygen are stronger than those in hydrogen. This is because the oxygen atom is bigger than the hydrogen atom and contains more electrons and a bigger electron cloud than hydrogen, i.e. more temporary dipoles are formed in the oxygen molecule than in the hydrogen molecule.

## 2. Dipole-dipole forces

In the previous section, we saw how temporary dipoles can lead to an attraction between one non-polar molecule and another. However, in compounds whose molecules are polar, forces called dipole-dipole forces exist permanently.

For example, since hydrogen chloride is a polar molecule, dipole-dipole forces exist between the molecules of HCl , Figure 6.21.

The main points about dipole-dipole forces may be summarised as follows:

- Dipole-dipole forces are caused by the partially negative end of one polar molecule attracting the partially positive end of a neighbouring polar molecule.
- Since dipole-dipole forces are between partial electric charges ( $\delta-$ and $\delta+$ ), these forces are much weaker than the ionic bonds holding ionic compounds together.
- Dipole-dipole forces only exist between molecules with a permanent dipole in the molecule. These forces are stronger than the temporary dipoles that cause London dispersion forces.
- Note in Figure 6.21 that the molecules align themselves so that oppositely charged ends of dipoles face each other - unlike charges attract each other.
- Similar to London dispersion forces, dipoledipole forces decrease with increasing distance between the molecules.
- The dipole-dipole forces between the molecules give rise to higher boiling points than those of similar non-polar molecules. For example, the boiling point of $\mathrm{HCl}\left(-85^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ is much higher than that of $\mathrm{H}_{2}\left(-253^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ as more heat must be supplied to overcome the greater strength of the dipole-dipole forces in HCl .
- Similarly, the boiling point of a substance called methanal (formaldehyde), HCHO , is much higher ( $-21^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ) than that of ethene, $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{4^{\prime}} \left(-104^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$. Dipole-dipole forces exist between the polar methanal (formaldehyde) molecules but only weaker London dispersion forces exist between ethene molecules since they are nonpolar molecules, Figure 6.22.

Dipole-dipole forces are forces of attraction between the negative pole of one polar molecule and the positive pole of another polar molecule.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-101.jpg?height=805&width=1176&top_left_y=618&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 6.21 Dipole-dipole forces exist between polar molecules. Two examples are shown here: HCl and propanone (also called acetone), $\left(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\right)_{2} \mathrm{CO}$, used in nail varnish remover. For the sake of clarity, only three molecules are shown in the diagram. Remember that these forces act in all directions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-101.jpg?height=900&width=1180&top_left_y=1855&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 6.22 The dipole-dipole attractions between the molecules in methanal (formaldehyde) give it a much higher boiling point than that of ethene. There are no permanent dipole-dipole forces in ethene since it is a non-polar molecule. Only weak London dispersion forces exist between the ethene molecules.

Study Example 6.3 in the online resources.

## Hydrogen bonding: a special type of dipole-dipole force

When chemists studied the boiling points of water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride, they found that the boiling points of these substances were far higher than expected. (These compounds are often referred to as hydrides, i.e. compounds of hydrogen and one other element.)

- $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ has a boiling point of $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ but $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$ has a much lower boiling point of only $-61^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Both oxygen and sulfur are in the same group of the Periodic Table. Why the big difference in boiling points?
- Similarly $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ has a boiling point of $-33^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ but $\mathrm{PH}_{3}$ has a far lower boiling point of only $-88^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
- Finally, HF has a boiling point of $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ but HCl has a boiling point of only $-85^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
- The fact that the boiling points of water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride are remarkably high is very obvious when one studies the boiling points of various hydrides, Figure 6.24.
- Note the bottom line (Group IV or 14) where the boiling points of the compounds $\mathrm{CH}_{4}, \mathrm{SiH}_{4}$, $\mathrm{GeH}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{SnH}_{4}$ increase regularly. The reason for this is because these molecules only have intermolecular forces that consist of weak London dispersion forces. This regular increase is what we expect because London dispersion forces increase as the number of electrons increase with the increasing size of each molecule. We might expect this regular increase to be repeated in the other three series shown in the graph.
- However, it is clear in Figure 6.24 that the regular increase is not observed for the nitrogen group (Group V or 15), the oxygen group (Group VI or 16) or the fluorine group (Group VII or 17).
- Therefore, the molecules of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{NH}_{3}$ and HF must have stronger intermolecular forces pulling them together than if there were just London dispersion or simple dipole-dipole forces present as discussed in the previous section. This type of strong dipole-dipole attraction is given the special name of hydrogen bond.

The main points about hydrogen bonding are:

- Hydrogen bonding arises when an atom of hydrogen is bonded to an atom of fluorine or oxygen or nitrogen, i.e. with the three most electronegative elements in the Periodic Table. The hydrogen bonds in the compounds $\mathrm{HF}, \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ are shown in Figure 6.25.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-102.jpg?height=1694&width=1098&top_left_y=540&top_left_x=1513)
Figure 6.24 The high boiling points of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{HF}$ and $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ are evidence for the existence of hydrogen bonding in these three compounds. Note how much higher the boiling points of these compounds are compared with the boiling points of the hydrogen compounds of the other elements in the same group.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-102.jpg?height=1052&width=1170&top_left_y=2689&top_left_x=1471)
Figure 6.25 Hydrogen bonding occurs in hydrogen fluoride, water and ammonia.

- As is the case with other intermolecular forces, hydrogen bonds are shown by dashed lines. Note from Figure 6.25 that the hydrogen atoms form a sort of 'bridge' between the two molecules, i.e. the hydrogen atom is bonded to one atom by a covalent bond and to the other atom by a hydrogen bond.
- The hydrogen atom in each of the three compounds $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{HF}$ and $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ has a fairly strong partial positive charge because, in each case, it is bonded to a very electronegative element. This causes a strong polarity in the molecules and they line up in molecular chains or groups that hold the molecules together quite strongly. (To help you remember the three elements - nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine - involved in hydrogen bonding, think of 'NOF'.)
- The high boiling points in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{NH}_{3}$ and HF are caused by the fact that considerable energy must be supplied to break the hydrogen bonds so that the molecules can be separated from each other and escape from the liquid.
- Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than either London dispersion forces or dipole-dipole forces. However, they are much weaker than ordinary covalent bonds. It has been calculated that the strength of a hydrogen bond is about 10\% of that of a covalent bond.
- Despite the fact that hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds, the effect of hydrogen bonding is significant because so many hydrogen bonds are present.
- Note in Figure 6.24 that the boiling point of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\left(100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ is higher than that of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}\left(-33^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$. The reason for this is because the electronegativity of oxygen is higher than that of nitrogen. Therefore the hydrogen bonding in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ is stronger than that in $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$, since the $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}$ bond is more polar than the $\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}$ bond. Therefore, more energy is required to break the hydrogen bonds in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ and to separate the molecules of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ from each other so that they can escape from the liquid.
- Note in Figure 6.25 that the boiling point of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\left(100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ is higher than that, of $\mathrm{HF}\left(19.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$. This is because there are twice as many hydrogen bonds for each molecule of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ than there are for each molecule of HF - even though the individual hydrogen bonds between HF molecules are stronger, as fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen. Therefore, it takes more energy to break the hydrogen bonds in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ and to separate the molecules of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ from each other so that they can escape from the liquid.
- The strength of hydrogen bonds is approximately ten times as strong as other dipole-dipole forces. It is only about ten times weaker than a covalent bond.

Hydrogen bonds are formed by a particular type of dipole-dipole attractions between molecules in which hydrogen atoms are bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine. The hydrogen atom carries a partial positive charge and is attracted to the electronegative atom in another molecule. Thus, the hydrogen bond acts as a bridge between two electronegative atoms in separate molecules.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-104.jpg?height=1574&width=2436&top_left_y=364&top_left_x=185)

Hydrogen bonding is very important in our everyday lives. If hydrogen bonding did not exist in water, then water would be a gas at room temperature and life, as we know it, could not exist on Earth. Hydrogen bonding is also very important in synthetic clothing. Kevlar is a type of fibre developed by the DuPont company, Figure 6.26. It is fire-resistant, extremely strong and flexible. Kevlar is strong because long chains of molecules line up parallel to each other and are held together strongly by hydrogen bonding. This makes Kevlar an ideal material for making bullet-proof vests, jackets for fencers and protective suits for professional motorcyclists.

Hydrogen bonding also helps fibres absorb water. Wool contains chains of substances called proteins that contain many oxygen and nitrogen atoms. These atoms can form hydrogen bonds with water. This means that wool can absorb water and does not feel clammy to wear.

Hydrogen bonding explains many of the properties of water:

- Boiling and melting points: Water has a much higher boiling point ( $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ) and melting point ( $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ) than other molecules of similar size, such as methane ( $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ ). This is because extra energy is needed to overcome the hydrogen bonding.
- Excellent solvent: The polarity of water molecules, combined with hydrogen bonding, allows water to dissolve ionic compounds (such as salt) and polar molecules (such as HCl). Water is often called the 'universal solvent' because so many substances dissolve in it. We will discuss this in more detail later.
- High surface tension: At the surface of water, hydrogen bonds pull the water molecules together. This effect is known as surface tension and it forms a type of 'skin' on water. This allows some insects to walk on its surface.


## Example 6.4

## Question

Use your knowledge of intermolecular forces to explain why methane has a very low boiling point (bp $=-164^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ).

The relative molecular mass of methane is only slightly lower than that of water but the boiling point of water is much higher ( $\mathrm{bp}=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ). Suggest a reason for this.
[LCH]

## Answer

Methane is non-polar and so the forces of attraction that exist between its molecules are weak London dispersion forces. Therefore, little energy is needed to separate methane molecules from each other, i.e. methane has a low boiling point.

Water is a polar molecule and hydrogen bonds exist between its molecules. The boiling point of water is much higher than that of methane because of the much stronger hydrogen bonds between the water molecules. Hydrogen bonding does not exist in methane.

## Solubility in water and hydrogen bonding

Since water is a polar covalent solvent, many compounds which are also polar covalent tend to dissolve in it ('like dissolves like'). Ammonia is an example of a polar covalent compound that is extremely soluble in water. The high solubility of ammonia in water may be shown by the 'Fountain Experiment', Figure 6.27.

The reason for the high solubility of ammonia in water may be understood by studying what happens when ammonia dissolves in water, Figure 6.28.

- Note the formation of hydrogen bonds between the slightly negative nitrogen atoms ( $\mathrm{N}^{53-}$ ) of ammonia with the slightly positive hydrogen atoms $\left(\mathrm{H}^{\delta^{+}}\right)$of water.
- Note the formation of hydrogen bonds between the slightly positive hydrogen atoms $\left(\mathrm{H}^{\delta+}\right)$ of ammonia and the slightly negative oxygen atoms ( $\mathrm{O}^{\delta 2-}$ ) of water.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-105.jpg?height=792&width=1222&top_left_y=1549&top_left_x=1536)
Figure 6.27 The round-bottomed flask is filled with ammonia gas. As soon as water enters the flask, the first drop of water dissolves the entire flask of ammonia. This causes a fall in pressure inside the flask and the water 'fountains' into the flask. Some phenolphthalein has been added to the water so that it turns pink when it comes in contact with the ammonia.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-105.jpg?height=574&width=1111&top_left_y=2835&top_left_x=1621)
Figure $6.28 \mathrm{NH}_{3}$ is very soluble in water, as hydrogen bonds are formed between the slightly negative N atoms ( $\mathrm{N}^{\delta 3-}$ ) of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ and the slightly positive H atoms ( $\mathrm{H}^{\delta+}$ ) of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$, and also between the slightly positive hydrogen atoms of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}\left(\mathrm{H}^{\delta+}\right)$ and the slightly negative O atoms $\left(\mathrm{O}^{62-}\right)$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$, as shown in the diagram. For clarity, only two hydrogen bonds are shown.

In short, ammonia is very soluble in water due to the fact that the ammonia molecule forms hydrogen bonds with the water molecule. This helps the ammonia to form a perfect mixture with the water, i.e. it readily dissolves.

- The general rule 'like dissolves like' summarises a lot about solubility.
- Polar substances such as HCl readily dissolve in a polar solvent such as water.
- In the case of ammonia, even if we knew nothing about hydrogen bonding, we would expect it to dissolve in water, since it is a polar substance.
- Non-polar substances such as methane, oil and most plastics do not dissolve in water. This is because non-polar substances have no charged ions or partially charged molecules. Therefore, the positive and negative ends of the water molecules are not attracted to these molecules. Therefore, oil and water do not mix.
- Similarly, iodine crystals (non-polar) will not dissolve in water, Figure 6.29 , but will dissolve in a non-polar solvent such as hexane $\left(\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{14}\right)$. This is due to the existence of London dispersion forces between the molecules of the iodine and those of the hexane.
- A gas called phosphine, $\mathrm{PH}_{3}$, is virtually insoluble in water since phosphine is non-polar (electronegativity values of P and $\mathrm{H}=2.19$ and 2.20 respectively almost identical). However, it will dissolve in hexane due to the existence of London dispersion forces between the molecules of the phosphine and those of the hexane.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-106.jpg?height=981&width=1756&top_left_y=1904&top_left_x=273)
Figure 6.29 'Like dissolves like.' Iodine is non-polar. Therefore, iodine crystals do not dissolve in water (polar) but will dissolve in hexane (non-polar).

## Example 6.5

## Question

Hydrogen sulfide has a boiling point of 212.3 K and water has a boiling point of 373 K .
Account for the difference in the boiling points of these substances.
[LCH]

## Answer

Hydrogen bonding exists in water as there is a large electronegativity difference (1.24) between O and H . Hydrogen bonding does not exist in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$, as the electronegativity difference between S and H is smaller ( 0.38 ) than between O and H . Therefore, the dipole-dipole intermolecular forces in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$ are weaker than the hydrogen bonding intermolecular forces in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$ has a lower boiling point than water.

## 3. Ion-dipole forces

One of the most important properties of water is the fact that it is an excellent solvent. This property depends on the fact that water is a polar molecule. It is found that most ionic substances and most polar-covalent substances dissolve in water. An ionic substance such as sodium chloride dissolves in water because the ionic bonding in NaCl is overcome by the strong attraction between the ions and the polar water molecules, Figure 6.30. These ions are dragged away from the crystal lattice and become surrounded by water molecules i.e. the salt dissolves.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-107.jpg?height=1098&width=1180&top_left_y=970&top_left_x=328)
Figure 6.30 Sodium chloride dissolves readily in water. Note how the polar water molecules line up around the ions and draw them into solution.

An ion-dipole force is the force of attraction between an ion and a polar molecule.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-107.jpg?height=662&width=1186&top_left_y=1341&top_left_x=1565)
Figure 6.31 Ion-dipole forces exist between (a) positive ions and the negative pole of the water molecules, and (b) between negative ions and the positive poles of the water molecule.

Note from Figure 6.30 that the negative end of the water molecule is attracted to the positive sodium ion. Also, the positive end of the water molecule is attracted to the negative chloride ion. This is true of all ion-dipole forces.

These ion-dipole forces are shown in Figure 6.31.

## Evidence for existence of intermolecular forces

We have now concluded our study of all the intermolecular forces on our course. The following points summarise some evidence that intermolecular forces exist:

1. Trends in physical properties can only be explained if intermolecular forces are present.
2. In many cases, experimental evidence can only be explained by the presence of intermolecular forces. For example, non-polar gases such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, helium and neon, can condense into liquids at low temperature. This demonstrates that there are weak attractive forces between the atoms or molecules holding them in the liquid state.
3. Some non-polar substances such as iodine exist as solids at room temperature. The solid state implies that the intermolecular forces are strong enough to hold the molecules together in a crystal lattice.
4. Calculations involving the behaviour of very small particles such as electrons (i.e. quantum mechanics) predict the presence of intermolecular forces.

### 6.5 Physical properties of ionic and covalent compounds

We have seen that ionic compounds usually consist of a network of ions, whereas covalent compounds generally consist of individual molecules. Many of the properties of ionic and covalent compounds can be understood if we keep these facts in mind. These properties are summarised in Figure 6.32.

## (a) State of matter at room temperature

- Most ionic compounds are solid at room temperature. This is because they consist of crystal lattice structures. The strong forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions mean that a lot of energy would be required to break the bonds. Therefore, they are solid at room temperature.
- Examples: Sodium chloride ( NaCl ) and limestone ( $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ ) are solid at room temperature.
- Most covalent substances are either liquids or gases at room temperature. This is because the forces between one molecule and another are weaker than those found in ionic compounds.
- Examples: Oxygen $\left(\mathrm{O}_{2}\right)$ and carbon dioxide $\left(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\right)$ are gases and water $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)$ is a liquid.


## (b) Melting and boiling points

- In ionic compounds, the ions can only vibrate about fixed positions. When heat is supplied, the ions gain energy and vibrate more and more. Eventually, the ions vibrate so much that they break away from their fixed positions in the crystal. When this happens, the crystal structure breaks down and we observe the substance melting. However, because the forces of attraction between the ions are so strong, most ionic substances have high melting points and high boiling points.
- Example: The melting point of sodium chloride is $801^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and its boiling point is $1413^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
- In covalent substances, there are only weak forces between the molecules. Therefore, the melting points and boiling points are much lower than ionic compounds.
- Example: The melting point of iodine is $114^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and its boiling point is $184^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Other covalent substances have even lower melting and boiling points, e.g. water (m.p. $=0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, b.p. $=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), ammonia (m.p. $=-77^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, b.p. $=-33^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), methane (m.p. $= -182^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, b.p. $=-164^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ). Therefore, as mentioned above, at room temperature, most covalent compounds are usually either liquids or gases.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-108.jpg?height=1489&width=2436&top_left_y=2291&top_left_x=185)

## (c) Electrical conductivity

- Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity in the solid state. The reason for this is because the ions are locked in fixed positions and cannot carry the electric current through the crystal. However, if the ionic substance is melted or dissolved in water, the ions are now free to move. The electricity can now pass through the solution or molten salt as the ions carry the current. Therefore, molten ionic compounds and ionic compounds in solution conduct an electric current. The fact that the bulb lights (Figure 6.32) indicates that there are ions in solution. It does not necessarily mean that the substance that was originally dissolved in the water is ionic. For example: Hydrogen chloride is a covalent substance that dissolves in water to give ions:

$$
\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}
$$

- Covalent compounds do not usually conduct electricity. The reason for this is because they do not contain ions to carry the electric current.


## (d) Solubility in water

Ionic compounds are usually soluble in water. The ions in ionic compounds are attracted to the polar water molecules through ion-dipole interactions. The water molecules surround the ions and dissolve the compound.

The solubility of covalent compounds depends on whether the molecules are polar or non-polar. Polar covalent compounds such as HCl and $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ are highly soluble in water due to dipole-dipole interactions. However, non-polar covalent substances such as $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ are only sparingly soluble in water. For example, only 9.2 mg of oxygen will dissolve in a litre of water at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. However, the fact that a small amount of oxygen dissolves is very important for the survival of fish. Some compounds such as oils and fats are classified as insoluble in water.

- Covalent compounds do not usually conduct electricity as solids, liquids or gases, or when dissolved in water. The reason for this is because covalent substances do not contain ions to carry the electric current. The properties of ionic and covalent compounds are summarised in Table 6.3.

| Ionic | Covalent |
| :--- | :--- |
| Contain a network of ions in the crystal | Contain individual molecules |
| Usually hard and brittle | Usually soft |
| Have high melting points and boiling points | Have low melting and boiling points |
| Usually solid at room temperature | Usually liquids, gases or soft solids at room temperature |
| Conduct electricity in molten state or when dissolved in water | Do not conduct electricity |
| Usually soluble in water | Solubility depends if polar covalent (soluble) or <br> Non-polar (insoluble or sparingly soluble) |

Table 6.3 The properties of ionic and covalent substances.

## Summary What I should know

- Electronegativity is the relative attraction that an atom in a molecule has for the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
- A polar covalent bond is a bond in which there is unequal sharing of the pair of electrons. This causes one end of the bond to be slightly positive ( $\delta+$ ) and the other end to be slightly negative ( $\delta-$ ).

Electronegativity values may be used to predict the polarity of covalent bonds and also to predict which compounds are ionic and which are covalent.

A polar molecule is a molecule that has an uneven distribution of electrical charges. This means that the molecule has regions (poles) with partial positive and partial negative charges separated by a distance.

- A non-polar molecule is a molecule that has an even distribution of electrical charges. This means that the molecule has regions (poles) with partial positive and partial negative charges that are not separated by a distance but coincide with each other.
- Intermolecular forces are the forces of attraction that exist between molecules. Examples of intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole forces, hydrogen bonding and ion-dipole forces.
- Van der Waals forces are weak, intermolecular forces of attraction that exist between all molecules.
- London dispersion forces are weak forces of attraction between molecules resulting from the formation of temporary dipoles. They are the only forces of attraction between non-polar molecules.

Dipole-dipole forces are forces of attraction between the negative pole of one polar molecule and the positive pole of another polar molecule.

- Hydrogen bonds are particular types of dipole-dipole attractions between molecules in which hydrogen atoms are bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.

An ion-dipole force is the force of attraction between an ion and a polar molecule.
