# 7 Families and Trends in the Periodic Table

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-112.jpg?height=1078&width=1274&top_left_y=553&top_left_x=182)

### 7.1 Introduction

In Chapter 4, we studied the development and overall structure of the modern Periodic Table. We learned that when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, the properties of the elements recur periodically. In other words, the properties displayed by an element are repeated in other elements within the same group or family in the Periodic Table. In this chapter, we will begin by studying some general trends in the Periodic Table and then focus on four specific groups (families) of elements. We will discuss how properties of the elements repeat within each group of elements. We will then discuss how the trends in repetition of properties may be explained and predicted using our knowledge of general trends in the Periodic Table.

### 7.2 Trends in atomic radii

You might think that the atomic radius of an atom is the distance from the nucleus of the atom to the outermost electrons. However, since the position of an electron cannot be precisely located (Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle), it is not possible for chemists to measure exactly where the electron cloud of an atom ends. It is possible, however, for chemists to measure experimentally the distance between the nuclei of atoms, Figure 7.1. This distance is known as the bond length and may be measured by methods known as 'X-ray diffraction' and 'electron diffraction'.

## OBJECTIVES

- To make students familiar with trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity in the Periodic Table.
- To give students an understanding of the properties of Group 1 (Alkali Metals), Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals), Group 17 (Halogens) and Group 18 (Noble Gases) of the Periodic Table.
- To ensure that students know how to explain and predict properties of the elements in Groups 1, 2, 17 and 18, using their knowledge of the above trends.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-112.jpg?height=723&width=766&top_left_y=2321&top_left_x=1647)
Figure 7.1 The atomic radius (covalent radius) is half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms of the same element that are joined together by a single covalent bond.

This atomic radius is also called the covalent radius and is defined as follows:

The atomic radius (covalent radius) of an atom is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms of the same element that are joined together by a single covalent bond.

## The values of the atomic radius increase down the groups in the Periodic Table for two reasons:

## 1. New energy level

- As you move down a group in the Periodic Table, the additional electrons are going into a new energy level (orbit) which is further from the nucleus, e.g. in lithium the electrons are being added to the $n=2$ energy level, and in sodium they are being added to the $n=3$ energy level.
- With each extra energy level (orbit) the outer electrons are becoming further away from the nucleus, i.e. the atomic radius increases.


## 2. Screening effect of inner electrons

- You might expect that since the nuclear charge increases down a group, there would be an increased attractive force on the outer electrons, causing the atomic radius to get smaller.
- However, even though the nuclear charge increases going from, say, lithium to sodium to potassium, the influence of the increase in the nuclear charge is lessened because of what is called a screening effect.
- In an atom with one electron, that electron experiences the full attractive force of the positive nucleus.
- However, in an atom with many electrons, the electrons in the inner energy level or levels help to screen or shield the outer electrons from the positive charge in the nucleus, Figure 7.5.
- Thus, some of the attractive force of the positive charges in the nucleus is lessened by the inner energy levels of electrons.
- Therefore, even though the nuclear charge increases, the increase is counteracted by the increase in the shielding effect of the inner energy levels of electrons.
- Therefore, the atomic radius increases for the reason given in point 1 (above).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-114.jpg?height=2531&width=864&top_left_y=442&top_left_x=1653)
Figure 7.5 The increase in the nuclear charge is counteracted by the increase in the screening effect of the inner electrons.

The values of the atomic radius decrease across a period in the Periodic Table for two reasons:

1. Increase in effective nuclear charge

- The number of protons in the nucleus increases from left to right across any one period in the Periodic Table.
- This means that there is a greater attractive force on the outer electrons.
- The increased nuclear charge tends to draw the energy levels closer to the nucleus.
- As this attractive force increases from left to right across the Periodic Table, the nucleus pulls the outer electrons closer to it.
- Therefore, the atoms become smaller, i.e. the atomic radius decreases.

2. No increase in the screening effect

- In moving from left to right across any one period in the Periodic Table, the extra electrons being added are going into the same outer energy level as the previous electron.
- Therefore, there is no increase in the screening effect caused by the electrons in the inner energy levels. (For the $n=1$ energy level, there is no screening effect at all by inner electrons. Beyond the $n=1$ energy level, there is a screening effect but there is no increase in it along any one period.) For example, as we move across period 2, all electrons are being added to the same $n=2$ energy level (orbit or shell). Since electrons are being added to the same energy level, there is no increase in the number of inner energy levels to cause additional shielding.
- As there is no additional energy level of electrons being added to counteract the increasing attractive force of the nucleus, the size of the atom shrinks, i.e. the atomic radius decreases.

In short, the atomic radius decreases across a period since there is an increasing number of protons but no increase in the screening effect. Therefore, there is an increase in the effective nuclear charge. This increase in the effective nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus and reduces the overall size of the atom.

Note that in the above explanation, we have used the phrase increase in effective nuclear charge. This phrase refers to the net positive charge pulling the electrons towards the nucleus. The effective nuclear charge is obtained by subtracting the effect of the screening electrons from the effect of the positive charge of the nucleus. When the number of protons in the nucleus is increasing without any increase in the screening effect of the electrons in the inner energy levels, we say that there is an increase in the effective nuclear charge. Remember this phrase!

### 7.3 Trends in ionisation energy

We now need to study a topic that helps us to understand why some elements are highly reactive and others are very unreactive. For example, sodium and potassium are very reactive and have to be stored under oil to prevent them from reacting with the air. The reason that they are so reactive is because they lose their outer electrons very easily. On the other hand, silver and gold have very little tendency to lose their outer electrons and hence are very unreactive.

In order to measure the tendency of an atom to lose an electron, chemists define a term called the first ionisation energy.

We could represent the first ionisation energy of sodium by the equation:

$$
\mathrm{Na}_{(\mathrm{g})}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{2+}{ }_{(\mathrm{g})}+\mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

For example, the first ionisation energy of sodium is $496 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. The symbol $\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ reads 'per mole' and can also be written as $\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$. This means that it

The first ionisation energy of an atom is the minimum energy required to completely remove the most loosely bound electron from a neutral gaseous atom in its ground state. takes 496 kilojoules of energy to remove the most loosely bound electron from a certain number of atoms of sodium. We will explain the meaning of the chemistry term mole in the next chapter. In chemistry, it refers to a certain number of atoms - it has nothing to do with the furry animal!

The symbol (g) indicates the gaseous state.
A table of first ionisation energy values is given in Figure 7.6. Note that the term first ionisation energy is only being discussed here. We shall discuss other categories of ionisation energy later in this chapter.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-116.jpg?height=1004&width=2150&top_left_y=2164&top_left_x=240)
Figure 7.6 The first ionisation energies of the elements (in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ). Note that ionisation energy values decrease down the groups and increase along the periods.

Ionisation energy values are obtained from the emission spectra of atoms. If you examine the values of the ionisation energies in Figure 7.6, a definite pattern emerges. In general, ionisation energy values decrease down the groups and increase along the periods in the Periodic Table. In an exam, if you cannot remember this trend, simply look up the table of ionisation energies in the Formulae and Tables booklet of the State Examinations Commission.

## Exceptions to the general trend across a period

If a graph of first ionisation energy versus atomic number is plotted for the first 37 elements, Figure 7.8, it is clear that within any one period some elements do not follow the trend of a smooth increase.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-118.jpg?height=1270&width=2273&top_left_y=716&top_left_x=247)
Figure 7.8 Plot of first ionisation energy versus atomic number. Note that in the $n=2$ period, beryllium and nitrogen have higher values than expected. Also in the $n=3$ period, magnesium and phosphorus have higher values than expected.

- In the $n=2$ period, beryllium and nitrogen have higher values than expected.
- The value for beryllium might be expected to lie on the dotted line between that of lithium and boron.
- Similarly, the value for nitrogen might be expected to lie on the dotted line between that of carbon and oxygen.
- It is clear from Figure 7.8 and from the values given in Figure 7.6 that the values for the first ionisation energies of beryllium and nitrogen are much higher than expected.
- Note also that in the $n=3$ period, the values for the first ionisation energies of magnesium and phosphorus are much higher than expected.
- These irregularities in first ionisation energy trends are explained by the fact that any sublevel that is completely filled (as is the case with beryllium and magnesium) or exactly half filled (as is the case with nitrogen and phosphorus) has extra stability.


## Completely filled sublevel

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Be}=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2} \\
& \mathrm{Mg}=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}, 3 s^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

In beryllium, the 2s sublevel is completely filled. In magnesium, the 3 s sublevel is completely filled.

- Completely filled s sublevels give a stable electron configuration.
- Therefore, removing an electron from a stable s sublevel requires more energy.
- Therefore, the ionisation energy is higher.


## Half-filled sublevel

$$
\begin{aligned}
& N=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{3} \\
& P=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}, 3 s^{2}, 3 p^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

- In nitrogen, the $2 p$ sublevel is exactly half filled. In phosphorus, the $3 p$ sublevel is exactly half filled.
- Half-filled sublevels have extra stability.
- Therefore, removing an electron from a sublevel that is exactly half filled requires more energy.
- Therefore, the ionisation energy is higher.


## Further evidence for the existence of energy levels: successive ionisation energies

So far we have only discussed first ionisation energy. The term first ionisation is so called because it involves the removal of only one electron. However, it is also possible to have second, third, fourth, etc. ionisation energies. The second ionisation energy of an element refers to the removal of a second electron from the positive ion formed after the first electron has been removed. For example, the second ionisation energy of sodium may be represented by the equation:

$$
\mathrm{Na}_{(\mathrm{g})}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{2+}{ }_{(\mathrm{g})}+\mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

In Chapter 3, we discussed the spectroscopic evidence for the existence of energy levels. We will now look at additional evidence for the existence of energy levels.

- Evidence for the fact that electrons are arranged in energy levels of different energies is also provided by studying the values of a number of ionisation energies of any one particular element.
- Suppose we measure the first, second and third - up to the nineteenth - ionisation energy of potassium, Figure 7.9.
- Note that the ionisation energy values become so large that it is necessary to take the log of the values to condense the graph into a smaller space.
- To help explain the meaning of this graph, we have labelled the parts of the graph with the letters A-G.
- It will help us to understand the graph if we keep the electron configuration of potassium in mind.

$$
K=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}, 3 s^{2}, 3 p^{6}, 4 s^{1}
$$

Two things are apparent from the graph. Firstly, with each electron removed, the ionisation energy increases. Secondly, the graph is not smooth, as there are peaks in it. The evidence for the existence of energy levels may be summarised as follows:

At A , the one electron in the $n=4$ energy level has been removed from potassium. The energy required to do this is the first ionisation energy. This has the lowest ionisation energy value, since the electron in

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-119.jpg?height=1316&width=1173&top_left_y=1611&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 7.9 Plot of log of ionisation energy versus number of electrons removed from an atom of potassium. This graph provides very good evidence for the existence of energy levels.

Moving from A to B on the graph, note the following:

- The second electron is much more difficult to remove for two reasons:

1. The electron is being removed from the $n=3$ energy level of the $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ion, which is closer to the nucleus :

$$
K^{+}=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}, 3 s^{2}, 3 p^{6}
$$

- The values steadily increase as we remove the eight electrons from the $n=3$ energy level.
- After removing the eight electrons in the $n=3$ energy level, (point C on the graph) there is another very large jump in the value of the ionisation energy for the next electron.
- This implies that the electron at D is being removed from an energy level that is closer to the nucleus i.e. the $n=2$ energy level. (This increase is actually much larger than it appears from the graph. Due to the logarithmic scale, the jump is actually greater by a factor of ten.)
- Since an electron is being removed from the filled $2 p^{6}$ sublevel, a lot of energy is needed as this full sublevel has extra stability.
- This ion (C on graph) has the same electron configuration as neon.

$$
K^{9+}=1 s^{2}, 2 s^{2}, 2 p^{6}
$$

Moving from D to E on the graph, note the following:

- From D to E, we are removing the eight electrons in the $n=2$ energy level.
- At E there is again a very large jump, as we remove electrons from an energy level that is closer to the nucleus, i.e. the $n=1$ energy level.
- The ion at E has the same electron configuration as helium. Since the $1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}$ sublevel is filled, it has extra stability and more energy is needed to remove the electron.
- At G we have removed all 19 electrons.

Two general points emerge from this study:

1. There is a steady increase in ionisation energy values as electrons are removed from an atom. There are two reasons for this steady increase;
(a) For each electron that is removed, the size of the positive charge on the ion that is left behind increases by one. Therefore, there is a greater attraction between the positive nucleus and the remaining electrons.
(b) It is found that a positive ion is smaller than the neutral atom from which it has been formed. Therefore, the electrons remaining behind in the positive ion are closer to the nucleus and thus more strongly attracted to the nucleus. With the removal of each successive electron, the size of the positive charge on the ion increases and the next electron to be removed will be closer to the nucleus.
2. There is a large increase in ionisation energy whenever an electron is removed from a new energy level and a reasonably substantial increase in the case of an electron being removed from a new sublevel. This is because filled sublevels have extra stability, i.e. it requires more energy to remove electrons from a filled sublevel.

## Example 7.1

## Question

The first four ionisation energies of the element of atomic number 5 are shown in Table 7.2.
(a) Explain why the second ionisation energy is greater than the first.
(b) Explain why the increase in ionisation energy is relatively small for the third

| Electron removed | Ionisation energy $\left(\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}\right)$ |
| :---: | :---: |
| 1st | 799 |
| 2nd | 2421 |
| 3rd | 3650 |
| 4th | 24962 |

electron but very large for the fourth electron.
[LCH]

## Answer

(a) An atomic number of 5 (boron) indicates that the atom has five electrons.

- The second ionisation energy is always greater than the first because the second electron is being removed from a positively charged ion.
- The electrons are held more firmly in a positively charged ion than in the corresponding neutral atom, because a positive ion is smaller than the neutral atom from which it is formed.
- Since the electrons are closer to the nucleus, more energy is required to remove them.
- Therefore, the second ionisation energy is greater than the first ionisation energy.
(b)
- The third electron, like the second electron, is being removed from the $n=2$ energy level.
- Therefore, the increase in ionisation energy is fairly small.
- However, the fourth electron is being removed from the $n=1$ energy level.
- Since the $n=1$ energy level is nearer the nucleus than the $n=2$ energy level, it requires a lot more energy to remove the electron from the $n=1$ energy level.
- Also, the fourth electron is being removed from the filled $n=1$ energy level ( $1 s^{2}$ electron configuration) which is very stable. This ion has the same electron configuration as helium

$$
\mathrm{B}^{3+}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}
$$

- Therefore, extra energy will have to be supplied to remove this electron.
- Therefore, the increase in ionisation energy is very large for the fourth electron.


### 7.4 Trends in electronegativity

In Chapter 6, we discussed electronegativity and learned that electronegativity is the relative attraction that an atom in a molecule has for the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond. From studying the table of electronegativity values (Figure 6.3, p.77) we saw that elements such as fluorine and chlorine on the right-hand side of the Periodic Table have high electronegativity values. On the other hand, elements such as potassium and sodium on the left-hand side of the Periodic Table have low electronegativity values.

We now examine the trends in electronegativity values in the Periodic Table and explain the reasons for these trends. In general, electronegativity values decrease down the groups and increase along the periods, Figure 7.10.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-123.jpg?height=1010&width=2146&top_left_y=374&top_left_x=351)
Figure 7.10 Electronegativity values decrease down the groups and increase along the periods.

The values of electronegativity decrease down the groups in the Periodic Table for two reasons:

## 1. Increasing atomic radius.

- As already discussed, the atomic radius increases as you move down any one group.
- Therefore, the outermost electrons are becoming further and further away from the attractive force of the nucleus.
- Therefore, there is a smaller attraction between the nucleus and the shared pair of electrons.
- Therefore, the electronegativity decreases.


## 2. Screening effect of inner electrons.

- Although the nuclear charge increases down a group, this increase in nuclear charge is essentially cancelled out by the increase in screening effect of the added intervening energy levels of electrons.
- Therefore, the outermost electrons are somewhat shielded from the attractive force of the positively charged nucleus.
- Since it is these outermost electrons that are involved in bonding, the attraction of the nucleus for these electrons decreases going down the group.
- Therefore, the electronegativity decreases.

The values of electronegativity increase across the periods in the Periodic Table for two reasons:

## 1. Increasing effective nuclear charge.

- Moving from left to right across the Periodic Table, the number of protons in the nucleus (nuclear charge) increases. Also, there is no increase in the screening effect.
- Therefore, the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons is steadily increasing.
- Therefore, the electrons involved in bonding are being more strongly attracted to the nucleus.
- Therefore, the electronegativity increases.


## 2. Decreasing atomic radius.

- As already discussed, within any period in the Periodic Table, the atomic radius decreases from left to right.
- Therefore, the electrons in the outermost level are becoming closer to the nucleus.
- Therefore, there is a greater attraction between the nucleus and these outer electrons.
- Therefore, the electronegativity increases.

Note that the trends in electronegativity generally follow the same pattern as those of ionisation energy. Electronegativity values are not assigned to the noble gases, as these elements have no tendency to form bonds and so the definition of electronegativity does not apply to them. The trends in electronegativity may easily be deduced from the tables shown in the Formulae and Tables booklet available to you in state exams.

So far we have seen that there is a definite repeating pattern or periodicity associated with atomic radii, ionisation energies and electronegativities of the elements. We now consider how the chemical properties of certain groups of elements are affected by these trends.

The trends in electronegativity are clearly seen in a graph of electronegativity versus atomic number, Figure 7.11.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-124.jpg?height=851&width=1186&top_left_y=364&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 7.11 Plot of electronegativity values versus atomic number for the first 35 elements. Note the increase along any one period, e.g. lithium to fluorine, sodium to chlorine, or potassium to bromine. Note also the decrease down the groups, e.g. fluorine to chlorine to bromine, and lithium to sodium to potassium.

### 7.5 Properties of four groups in the Periodic Table

In our study of chemical bonding in Chapter 5, we have seen how bonds are formed when chemical reactions occur. In the case of ionic bond formation, the bonds are formed by the transfer of an electron (or electrons) from the outermost energy level of one atom to that of another atom. In the case of covalent bond formation, the bonds are formed by the sharing of electrons between outermost energy levels of adjacent atoms.

The chemical properties of elements are largely determined by the number of electrons in the outermost energy level. For example, all of the elements in Group 1 (the alkali metals) have one electron in their outermost energy level. As a result of this, all of these elements have similar chemical properties. Similarly, all of the elements in Group 17 (or VII) have seven electrons in their outermost energy level. As a result of this, all of these elements also have similar chemical properties.

To illustrate this similarity of elements in the same group (family), we now consider some of the properties of four groups (families) of elements: the alkali metals (Group 1), the alkaline earth metals (Group 2), the halogens (Group 17) and the noble gases (Group 18). These are the four groups that are specified in the Leaving Certificate chemistry curriculum - so study these groups carefully!

### 7.5.1 Group 1: The alkali metals

The alkali metals are located in Group 1 of the Periodic Table. They are called 'alkali' metals because they form alkaline or basic solutions when added to water. The three alkali metals on your course are lithium, sodium and potassium, Figure 7.12. As they are all very reactive, they have to be stored under oil to prevent them coming in contact with oxygen in the air and with water. The main properties of the alkali metals are

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-124.jpg?height=500&width=1212&top_left_y=2929&top_left_x=1406)
Figure 7.12 (a) Lithium metal. Note that lithium has a very low density and floats on oil. (b) Sodium metal is a soft metal and can be cut with a knife. After cutting, the shiny metal is quickly covered with a white coating of sodium oxide. (c) Potassium metal is shiny when cut, but very quickly reacts with oxygen in the air to form potassium oxide.

summarised in Table 7.4

The properties of the alkali metals may be summarised as follows:

- All of the alkali metals are very reactive elements because they all have low first ionisation energy values, i.e. they readily lose the single electron in the outer energy level.
- They are so reactive that none of them occurs free in nature as the uncombined metal itself. The alkali metals in your school laboratory have been extracted from their compounds.
- Since the alkali metals have low first ionisation energies and low electronegativity values, they readily form ionic compounds by losing their single outer electron.
- By losing the single outer electron, potassium obtains the stable arrangement of eight electrons in its outer energy level. In other words, the octet rule is satisfied since potassium now has the electron configuration of the noble (inert) gas argon.
- The tendency to lose an electron is observed in all of the chemical reactions of the alkali metals.
- The reaction of the alkali metals with water illustrates very nicely the trend of increasing reactivity down the group. As shown in Table 7.4, all of the alkali metals react with water
- Lithium reacts quite vigorously with water, sodium more vigorously and potassium even more vigorously. In fact, the reaction is so vigorous in the case of potassium that the heat generated by the reaction causes the hydrogen gas given off in the reaction to catch fire.
- This increase in reactivity reflects the decrease in ionisation energy values down the group.

Rubidium and caesium react so violently with water that their reactions are too dangerous to demonstrate. Professor Martyn Poliakoff, has made videos about every element in the Periodic Table and these are worth viewing online. Even though you will not have rubidium and caesium in your school laboratory, you can watch the very violent reactions online.

Note: The reaction of the alkali metals with dilute acids is so dangerous that it must never be attempted. So much hydrogen is released in such a short time that an explosion occurs.

### 7.5.2 Group 2: The alkaline earth metals

The alkaline earth metals are located in Group 2 of the Periodic Table. They are called 'alkaline' earth metals because they form alkaline or basic solutions when added to water. They are called 'earth' metals because many of their compounds are found in the earth. For example, MgO (magnesium oxide) is found in the earth and is commonly called magnesia - hence the name Milk of Magnesia used in indigestion remedies. Calcium oxide, CaO , is also found in the earth and is commonly called lime.

The three alkaline earth metals on your course are beryllium, magnesium and calcium, Figure 7.13.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-126.jpg?height=366&width=1190&top_left_y=504&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 7.13 The alkaline earth metals (from left) beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium and barium.

Beryllium, magnesium and calcium are all shiny, silvery-looking metals. You will not have beryllium in your school laboratory, as it is a very toxic substance.

The main properties of the alkaline earth metals are summarised in Table 7.5.

The properties of the alkaline earth metals may be summarised as follows:

- All the alkaline earth metals are reactive elements because they have low first ionisation energy values, i.e. they readily lose the two electrons in their outermost energy level.
- They are less reactive than the alkali metals but still too reactive to occur freely in nature as pure metals. Instead, they are found in stable compounds such as magnesium oxide and calcium carbonate $\left(\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}\right)$, which is commonly called limestone.

Table 7.6 Summary of properties of Group 17 elements (the Halogens).

The properties of the halogens may be summarised as follows:

- The halogens contain some highly electronegative elements.
- Since the electronegativity values decrease down the group, this means that fluorine is the most electronegative element of the halogens. In fact, fluorine is the most electronegative element in the Periodic Table.
- Since the halogens have such a great attraction for electrons, they are very reactive.
- The halogens do not exist free in nature, e.g. chlorine gas has to be extracted from one of its compounds such as sodium chloride.
- Fluorine is the most reactive of all the halogens because of its high electronegativity. It is far too reactive to be kept in school laboratories. Most chemists have never seen the element fluorine, as it is so highly reactive.
- Since the halogens are non-metals, they are poor conductors of electricity.
- Note that in Table 7.6, the reaction of each halogen with sodium is the example given, as this is the one most commonly observed, Figure 7.16. However, similar reactions occur with all the other alkali metals and alkaline earth metals.
- An unusual property of iodine is that it does not melt to a liquid when heated. Instead, it changes directly from a solid to a gas. This process is called sublimation. The purple vapour of iodine is easy to see, Figure 7.17.

Sublimation is the changing of a solid directly to a gas on heating without going through the liquid phase.

## Why does the reactivity of the halogens increase up the group?

As shown in Table 7.6, the trend in reactivity of the halogens is in the opposite direction to that of the alkali metals. The reactivity of the halogens increases up the group because:

- The atomic radius decreases as you go up the group.
- There is a decrease in the screening effect, as there are fewer inner energy levels as you go up the group.
- The above two factors cause the first ionisation energy to increase up the group.
- Therefore, the electrons in the outermost energy levels are more tightly held as you go up the group. For example, fluorine is the most electronegative element in the Periodic Table. Figure 7.18.
- Therefore, the reactivity increases up the group.

Because of their high electronegativities, the halogens remove electrons easily from other substances. This makes them very reactive. Examples of a halogen taking electrons from a less electronegative halogen may be shown as follows:

- If chlorine gas is bubbled through a solution containing bromide ions, the chlorine takes electrons from the bromide ions, converting them into bromine:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-129.jpg?height=297&width=1326&top_left_y=2422&top_left_x=579)

This shows that the electronegativity of the chlorine atom (E.N. = 3.16) is greater than that of the bromine atom (E.N. = 2.96), as the chlorine atom takes an electron from the bromide ion. This reaction is shown happening in one of the videos accompanying this textbook. The colourless solution of bromide ions turns red due to the formation of the red bromine.

If a solution of bromine in water ('bromine water') is added to a solution containing iodide ions, iodine is displaced from the solution. The more electronegative bromine atoms (E.N. = 2.96) take electrons from the less electronegative iodide ions (E.N. = 2.66) as shown in the following equation:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-129.jpg?height=303&width=1371&top_left_y=3405&top_left_x=553)

Note that in each case the more reactive halogen displaces the less reactive halogen from the solution of its ions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-129.jpg?height=609&width=551&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=2233)

### 7.5.4 Group 18: The noble (inert) gases

When it comes to studying the chemistry of the noble (inert) gases, you can sit back and relax! The reason for this is that, since they are so unreactive, there is little to study about their chemistry. The noble gases are located in Group 18 of the Periodic Table. With the exception of helium, they all have eight electrons in their outer energy level. Therefore, they are all very stable. Helium has a full outer energy level ( $\mathrm{He}=1 \mathrm{~s}^{2}$ ) and is also very stable.

One of the popular uses of noble gases is in plasma balls, Figure 7.19.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-130.jpg?height=981&width=1437&top_left_y=1002&top_left_x=188)
Figure 7.19 Plasma balls usually contain a mixture of the noble gases neon, argon and xenon.

Noble gases are used in plasma balls, as these gases are very unreactive. Therefore, when a high voltage current is passed through the gases, no unwanted side reactions take place. In addition, different colours are given off when electricity is passed through these gases. Helium is probably the best-known noble gas, as it is commonly used to fill balloons.

The properties of the noble gases are summarised in Table 7.7.

| Helium | Gas | Poor | Unreactive |
| Neon | Gas | Poor | Unreactive |
| Argon | Gas | Poor | Unreactive |
| Krypton | Gas | Poor | Unreactive |


Table 7.7 Summary of properties of Group 18 elements (the noble gases)

You may remember in Chapter 6 that we learned that the boiling points of the noble gases increase down the group from helium to radon (Figure 6.19, p.85). We explained that this increase is related to the size of the atoms. The increase in atomic radius means that the electron clouds are getting bigger and so, temporary dipoles are more easily formed, giving rise to stronger London dispersion forces. These stronger forces are more difficult to break. This means that more energy is required to separate the atoms from each other and this causes the increase in boiling points.

## Summary What I should know

- The atomic radius of an atom is defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms of the same element, which are joined together by a single covalent bond.

Atomic radius values increase down any one group in the periodic table because the electrons are going into a new energy level that is further from the nucleus and there is an increase in the screening effect by inner electrons.

Atomic radius values decrease from left to right across a period because of increasing effective nuclear charge and no increase in the screening effect.

- The first ionisation energy of an atom is the minimum energy required to completely remove the most loosely bound electron from a neutral gaseous atom in its ground state.

Ionisation energy values decrease down the groups because of increasing atomic radius and an increase in the screening effect of inner electrons.

Ionisation energy values increase along the periods because of increasing effective nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius.

Second ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an ion with one positive charge in the gaseous state, i.e the energy required to carry out the following:

$$
\mathrm{X}_{1 \mathrm{~g}}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{X}^{2+}{ }_{1 \mathrm{~g}}+\mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

Electronegativity values decrease down a group because of increasing atomic radius and an increase in the screening effect of inner electrons.

Electronegativity values increase along the periods because of increasing effective nuclear charge and decreasing atomic radius.

The chemical properties of an element are determined by the number of electrons in the outermost energy level.

Within the alkali metals alkaline earth metals and halogen groups of the Periodic Table, there are definite trends in the chemical and physical properties of the elements.

# 8 The Mole: The Chemist's Counting Unit

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-134.jpg?height=1101&width=1267&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=185)

### 8.1 Introduction

In our everyday lives, we use various counting units, e.g. a pair (2) of gloves, a dozen (12) of eggs, a ream of writing paper (500 sheets) and a millennium (1,000 years), Figure 8.1. When studying chemistry, we deal with very tiny particles such as atoms, molecules and ions. It would not be possible to count these individually because even a small sample of a substance contains very large numbers of these tiny particles. Therefore, to help us count these tiny particles, which are invisible to the naked eye, chemists have invented a special counting unit called the mole.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-134.jpg?height=854&width=1179&top_left_y=2630&top_left_x=192)
Figure 8.1 Some examples of counting units. The mole is the counting unit used by chemists.

Just as the kilogram is the SI unit of mass, the mole is the SI unit of amount of substance. The symbol for the mole is $\mathbf{~ m o l}$.

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of the development of the mole concept in chemistry.
- To give students experience in carrying out calculations involving the mole.
- To make students familiar with the applications of the mole concept in chemistry.

In 2018 the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) defined a mole as follows;

One mole of a substance contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ elementary entities of the substance.

- The word 'entity' simply means something that exists as its own single and separate unit. Examples of 'elementary entities' in chemistry are atoms, molecules and ions.
- When referring to a mole of anything, the elementary unit should always be specified. For example, the phrase 'one mole of chlorine' should never be used. We should specify the elementary unit, e.g. one mole of chlorine atoms, or one mole of chlorine molecules, or one mole of chloride ions.
- The number $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ is called the Avogadro constant. The symbol for the Avogadro constant is $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}$.
- The Avogadro constant is named in honour of a famous Italian chemist called Amedeo Avogadro, who devised a method for chemists to count atoms and molecules, Figure 8.2. The Avogadro constant is determined by experiment using X-rays and also by passing fixed quantities of electrical charges through chemical solutions. The value is known precisely and is defined by IUPAC as $6.02214076 \times 10^{23}$. When using this number in calculations, we usually use $6.02 \times 10^{23}$.
- It is found by experiment that 12 grams of the carbon-12 isotope contain $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms of carbon. This is shown diagrammatically in Figure 8.3.

NOTE
The number $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ is an enormous number and is difficult to comprehend because it is beyond our everyday experiences. It is greater than the entire population of the Earth and greater than the number of grains of sand on the Earth.

Avogadro's ideas may be summarised as follows:

- We know from our study of the Periodic Table that an atom of magnesium is twice as heavy as an atom of carbon: relative atomic mass $\left(A_{r}\right)$ of $\mathrm{Mg}=$ 24 , relative atomic mass of $C=12$, Figure 8.4
- Since one atom of magnesium is twice as heavy as one atom of carbon, then one hundred magnesium atoms are twice as heavy as one hundred carbon atoms. Similarly, a million magnesium atoms are twice as heavy as a million carbon atoms.
- Therefore, if we have a piece of magnesium that has twice the mass of a piece of carbon, the two amounts must contain equal numbers of atoms. Think carefully about this. For example, 2 grams of magnesium and 1 gram of carbon contain the same number of atoms. Similarly, 20 kilograms of magnesium and 10 kilograms of carbon contain the same number of atoms.
- Let's look at carbon and hydrogen as a further example. Since an atom of carbon ( $A_{r}=12$ ) has a mass 12 times that of an atom of hydrogen ( $A_{r}=1$ ), 1 gram of hydrogen atoms and 12 grams of carbon atoms both contain the same number of atoms.
- Similarly, if we look at silver and carbon, a silver atom ( $A_{r}=108$ ) has nine times the mass of a carbon atom ( $A_{r}=12$ ). Therefore, if we have 12 g of carbon, this will contain a certain number of atoms. To calculate the mass of silver which will contain the same number of atoms of carbon, it is $9 \times 12=108 \mathrm{~g}$.
In short, if we weigh out elements in the same proportions as their relative atomic masses ( $A_{r}$ ), we will always have the same number of atoms of these elements. Therefore, a chemist can 'count the number of atoms by weighing'. This is similar to the way that a bank cashier can count the number of coins in a bag by weighing the bag.


## Amedeo Avogadro <br> (1776-1856)

Figure 8.2
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-135.jpg?height=336&width=336&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=2474)

Amedeo Avogadro was an Italian chemist who set up a system to enable chemists to count atoms and molecules.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-135.jpg?height=945&width=1163&top_left_y=963&top_left_x=1621)
Figure 8.3 It is found that 12 grams of the carbon-12 isotope contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms of carbon. In other words, a mole of carbon is 12 grams.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-135.jpg?height=812&width=1182&top_left_y=2174&top_left_x=1621)
Figure 8.4 An atom of magnesium is twice as heavy as an atom of carbon.

Suppose we take the relative atomic mass in grams of a number of elements, Table 8.1.

| Element | Mass |
| :--- | :--- |
| Carbon | 12 g |
| Magnesium | 24 g |
| Aluminium | 27 g |
| Calcium | 40 g |
| Iron | 56 g |
| Copper | 63.5 g |
| Silver | 108 g |

Table 8.1 All these different masses of elements contain the same number of atoms.

Table 8.1 is illustrated in Figure 8.5.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-136.jpg?height=874&width=1177&top_left_y=1702&top_left_x=188)

Figure 8.5 The amount of each element (1 mole) contains the same number ( $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ ) atoms.

All the amounts of each element listed in Table 8.1 contain the same number of atoms, i.e. $6.02 \times 10^{23}$. The Avogadro constant is also called Avogadro's number. The 'old' definition of the mole was that it is the number of atoms of carbon in 12 g of the carbon-12 isotope. However, the new definition given above was agreed by IUPAC in 2018 in order to put the emphasis on the Avogadro constant.

The word 'mole' comes from the Latin word moles meaning 'a heap or pile'. It draws attention to the particle nature of matter - a heap or pile of particles containing the Avogadro constant number of particles.

Q. What face cream did Avogadro invent?
A. Oil of Molay.
Q. What element do moles love to study in chemistry?
A. Molybdenum.
Q. How did Avogadro help his team win the match?
A. He scored the winning Mole.
Q. What did Avogadro have on his pancakes?
A. Molasses.
Q. What did the chemistry teacher say when she saw all of her students in the lab at 6:02 a.m.?
A. 'Holy Moley, there's a Mole-titude of students here!'
Q. How do you contact a mole?
A. Call Avogadro's number.

## National Mole Day $\mathbf{6 . 0 2} \boldsymbol{\times} \mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{2 3}}$

Thus, when you weigh out 12 g of carbon, this amount of carbon contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms of carbon. We say that this amount of carbon is one mole ( 1 mol ) of carbon atoms. Similarly, 48 g of magnesium is two moles $(2 \mathrm{~mol})$ of magnesium atoms. We say that the amount of magnesium is two moles $(2 \mathrm{~mol})$. The mole concept is a very useful one for chemists, as it enables them to calculate the number of atoms (or molecules or ions) that are in a particular amount of a substance that they have weighed out.

## We will now learn how to carry out various calculations involving the mole. These calculations are:

1. How to convert moles to grams.
2. How to convert grams to moles.
3. How to perform calculations involving the Avogadro Constant.
4. How to perform miscellaneous calculations from past exam papers.

### 8.2 How to convert moles to grams

Hopefully, it is clear from Section 8.1 that the mass of one mole of any element is simply the relative atomic mass expressed in grams.

Mass of one mole of an element
= Relative Atomic Mass in grams.

Table 8.2 lists the relative atomic masses of some common elements.
| Element | Symbol | Relative Atomic Mass |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hydrogen | H | 1.008 |
| Carbon | C | 12.01 |
| Nitrogen | N | 14.01 |
| Oxygen | O | 16.00 |
| Sodium | Na | 22.99 |
| Chlorine | Cl | 35.45 |


Table 8.2 The relative atomic masses of some common elements

From Table 8.2, it is clear that one mole of $\mathrm{Na}=22.99$ grams, one mole of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ (oxygen molecules) $=32.00$ grams, etc.

For all calculations involving the mole concept, you will need to refer to a list of relative atomic masses of elements. A list of the relative atomic mass values needed for calculations is included in Formulae and Tables booklet published by the State Examinations Commission. Read carefully the instructions on exam papers, as you may be told to round off the relative atomic masses.

## Example 8.1

## Question

Aluminium metal is very useful in construction, Figure 8.7. What is the mass of three moles of aluminium atoms?

Answer

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \text { mole of } \mathrm{Al} & =26.98 \mathrm{~g} \\
3 \text { moles of } \mathrm{Al} & =26.98 \times 3 \\
& =80.94 \mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-137.jpg?height=564&width=877&top_left_y=2324&top_left_x=1878)

If we add up the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a molecule of a compound, we obtain what is called the relative molecular mass ( $\boldsymbol{M}_{\mathbf{r}}$ ) of the compound. The relative molecular mass of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in a molecule of the compound.

The definition of relative molecular mass that you should use in exams is:
Relative molecular mass is sometimes referred to as relative formula mass. This is because some compounds (e.g. NaCl) consist of ions rather than molecules. However, in this textbook, we will use the term relative molecular mass, as this term is more widely used and is the term specified on the syllabus.

The method of calculating the relative molecular mass of a compound is shown in Example 8.2.

The relative molecular mass of a compound is the average mass of one molecule of that compound compared with one-twelfth of the mass of one atom of the carbon-12 isotope.

## Example 8.2

## Question

What is the relative molecular mass of water, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ ?

## Answer

Rel. atomic mass of $2 \mathrm{H}=2 \times 1.008=2.016$
Rel. atomic mass of $1 \mathrm{O}=1 \times 16.00=16.00$
Relative molecular mass $\quad=18.016$
Thus, we may conclude that one mole of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=18.016$ grams.
In this amount of water there are $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ molecules of water.
Answer: 18.016

From this example it is clear that:
Mass of one mole of a compound = Relative Molecular Mass in grams.
In Chapter 4, we saw that the mass spectrometer may be used to measure relative atomic masses and abundances of isotopes. A second important use of the mass spectrometer is to measure relative molecular masses. The molecule is broken up into ions in the mass spectrometer and, from a study of the fragments that are formed, chemists can determine the relative molecular mass of the substance.

## Molar mass

The mass of one mole of a substance is often referred to as the molar mass, e.g. the molar mass of carbon is $12 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. Thus, the molar mass of an element is the relative atomic mass expressed in grams per mole.

The molar mass is the atomic mass or the molecular mass of the substance expressed in grams. Some examples of molar masses are listed in Table 8.3.

The molar mass is the mass of one mole of any substance (element or compound) expressed in grams per mole ( $\mathrm{g} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ).

| Substance (element or compound) | Molar mass $\boldsymbol{(} \mathbf{g} \mathbf{~ m o l}^{-1} \boldsymbol{)}$ | Number of particles | Type of particles |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Na | 22.99 | $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ | Atoms |
| $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ | 32.00 | $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ | Molecules |
| $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ | 18.02 | $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ | Molecules |
| NaCl | 58.44 | $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ | Formula units |

Table 8.3 Some examples of molar masses

Molar masses of some compounds are shown in Figure 8.8.
Note also that molar mass has units of grams per mole $\left(\mathrm{g} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}\right)$. Since 1 mole of water has a mass of 18.02 grams , this means that the molar mass of water is $18.02 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. However, the relative molecular mass of water is simply written as 18.02 . There are no units since relative molecular mass (and relative atomic mass) compare masses relative to one-twelfth of the mass of the carbon-12 isotope. Therefore, the units cancel out.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-138.jpg?height=561&width=998&top_left_y=3040&top_left_x=1617)
Figure 8.8 The amount of each compound ( 1 mole) is called the molar mass and contains the same number ( $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ ) of entities (atoms, molecules or formula units).

## Example 8.3

## Question

Aluminium sulfate contains sulfate ions, Figure 8.9. What is the mass of one mole of sulfate ions, $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ ?

## Answer

$1 \mathrm{~S}=1 \times 32.07 \quad=32.07$
$4 \mathrm{O}=4 \times 16.00 \quad=64.00$
Rel. Molecular Mass = 96.07
i.e. one mole of sulfate ions $=96.07$ grams
Answer: 96.07 g

The negative charges make no difference to the calculations (since electrons have negligible mass).

## Example 8.4

## Question

Copper(II) sulfate is commonly used to control fungal diseases in trees, Figure 8.10.
What is the mass of one mole of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4} .5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ ?

## Answer

| Cu | $=63.5$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| S | $=32.07$ |
| $4 \mathrm{O}=4 \times 16.00$ | $=64.00$ |
| $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=5 \times 18.016$ | $=90.08$ |
| Rel. Molecular Mass | $=249.65$ |

Figure 8.10 Copper sulfate is being used to control fungal growth on this apple tree.

Figure 8.10 Copper sulfate is being used to control fungal growth on this apple tree.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-139.jpg?height=584&width=876&top_left_y=1930&top_left_x=1810)

i.e. one mole of $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=249.65$ grams.
$\mathrm{CuSO}_{4} .5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ has a relative molecular mass of 249.65 .
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-139.jpg?height=502&width=1039&top_left_y=667&top_left_x=1686)

### 8.3 How to convert grams to moles

In the previous section, we learned how to convert moles to grams. In the second type of calculation, we will learn how to do the reverse, i.e. convert grams to moles.

## Example 8.6

## Question

The 'lead' in pencils consists of a pure form of carbon called graphite, Figure 8.11.
How many moles are there in 36.02 g of the element carbon?

Answer
12.01 g carbon = 1 mole

Therefore, 1 g carbon $\quad=\frac{1}{12.01}$ mole
Therefore, 36.02 g carbon $=\frac{36.02}{12.01}$ mole

$$
=2.999 \text { moles } .
$$

Answer: 2.999 moles

Figure 8.11
Graphite is a form of the element carbon that is found in pencils.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-140.jpg?height=591&width=880&top_left_y=1054&top_left_x=1696)

From the above example, it is clear that:
No. of moles of an element $=\frac{\text { Mass of element }}{\text { relative atomic mass }}$
In the case of elements that consist of two atoms (e.g. $\mathrm{H}_{2}, \mathrm{O}_{2}, \mathrm{~N}_{2}$ ), use the relative molecular mass instead of relative atomic mass when performing calculations using the above equation.

Similarly, if one is dealing with a compound, the relationship becomes:

$$
\text { No. of moles of a compound }=\frac{\text { Mass of compound }}{\text { relative molecular mass }}
$$

This type of calculation is shown in Example 8.7.

## Example 8.7

## Question

How many moles of water molecules are there in 117 g of water?

## Answer

First calculate the relative molecular mass of water
$\mathrm{O} \quad=16.00$
$2 \mathrm{H}=2 \times 1.008=2.016$
Rel. Molecular Mass $=18.016$
Number of moles of water $=\frac{\text { Mass of water }}{\text { Rel. molecular mass of water }}=\frac{117}{18.016}=6.49$ moles

Answer: 6.49 moles

We can summarise the above two relationships in the following general relationship:

$$
\text { Number of moles of a substance }=\frac{\text { Mass of the substance }}{\text { Mass of one mole of the substance }}
$$

## Example 8.8

## Question

How many moles of sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$, are there in 12.25 g of sulfuric acid?

## Answer

First calculate the relative molecular mass of sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$
$2 \mathrm{H}=2 \times 1.008=2.016$
$1 \mathrm{~S}=1 \times 32.07=32.07$
$4 \mathrm{O}=4 \times 16.00 \quad=64.00$
Rel. Molecular Mass $=98.086$
No. of moles of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$
$=\frac{\text { Mass of } \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}}{\text { Mass of one mole of } \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}}=\frac{12.25}{98.086}=0.125 \mathrm{~mole}$
Answer: 0.125 mol

In solving problems involves mass, number of moles and relative molecular mass, some students may find it helpful to use the 'mole triangle' that relates the above three variables, as shown in Figure 8.12. Place your thumb over the variable that you wish to calculate and you will see what must be done with the other two variables in order to solve the problem.

### 8.4 How to perform calculations involving the Avogadro constant

Calculations involving Avogadro's number may be divided into four types. All calculations are based on the following fact:

One mole of a substance contains $\mathbf{6 . 0 2} \boldsymbol{\times} \mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{2 3}}$ particles of that substance.
The following examples indicate the type of calculations involved.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-141.jpg?height=760&width=847&top_left_y=1497&top_left_x=1956)
Figure 8.12 The mole triangle helps to relate the number of moles, the mass (in grams) and the mass of one mole (molar mass or relative molecular mass).

## (a) Converting moles to number of atoms or molecules

TEST YOURSELF: Attempt Questions 8.4-8.5 and W8.4W8.5.

## Example 8.9

## Question

How many atoms of sodium are present in 0.25 mole of this metal, Figure 8.13?

## Answer

1 mole of sodium contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms.
$\therefore 0.25$ mole of sodium contains $0.25 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms
$=1.505 \times 10^{23}$ atoms
Answer: $1.505 \times 10^{23}$ atoms

Figure 8.13
Calculating the number of atoms of sodium present
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-141.jpg?height=557&width=883&top_left_y=3125&top_left_x=1842)

Study Example 8.10 in the online resources.

## (b) Converting grams to number of atoms or molecules

## Example 8.11

## Question

How many atoms are there in 28.75 g of sodium?

## Answer

1 mole of sodium contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms,
i.e. 22.99 g sodium contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms
Therefore, 1 g sodium contains $\frac{6.02 \times 10^{23}}{22.99}$
Therefore, 28.75 g sodium contains $\frac{28.75 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}}{22.99}$ atoms $=7.528 \times 10^{23}$ atoms
Answer: $7.528 \times 10^{23}$ atoms

## Example 8.12

## Question

Carbon dioxide is commonly used in fire extinguishers, Figure 8.15. How many molecules of carbon dioxide are there in a fire extinguisher which contains 150 g of carbon dioxide?

## Answer

First calculate the relative molecular mass of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$
$1 \mathrm{C}=1 \times 12.01 \quad=12.01$
$2 \mathrm{O}=2 \times 16.00=32.00$
Rel. Molecular Mass = 44.01
1 mole of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ molecules i.e. $44.01 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CO}_{2}$ contain $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ molecules
$1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CO}_{2}$ contains $\frac{6.02 \times 10^{23}}{44.01}$ molecules
$150 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CO}_{2}$ contains $\frac{150 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}}{44.01}$ molecules

$$
=2.05 \times 10^{24} \text { molecules }
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-142.jpg?height=705&width=1141&top_left_y=1858&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 8.15 Calculate the number of carbon dioxide molecules that was in the fire extinguisher.

Answer: $2.05 \times 10^{24}$ molecules

## (c) Converting numbers of atoms or molecules to moles

## Example 8.13

## Question

How many moles of aluminium atoms are there in $9 \times 10^{22}$ atoms of aluminium?

## Answer

$6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms of AI = 1 mole
1 atom of $\mathrm{Al}=\frac{1}{6.02 \times 10^{23}}$ mole

$$
\begin{aligned}
9 \times 10^{22} \text { atoms of Al } & =\frac{9 \times 10^{22}}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \text { mole } \\
& =0.15 \text { mole }
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: 0.15 mol

## (d) Converting numbers of atoms or molecules to grams

## Example 8.14

## Question

How many grams of zinc are present in $3 \times 10^{20}$ atoms of zinc?

## Answer

1 mole of Zn has a mass of 65.41 grams,
i.e. $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms of zinc have a mass of 65.41 g
1 atom of zinc has a mass of $\frac{65.41}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \mathrm{~g}$
$3 \times 10^{20}$ atoms have a mass of $\frac{3 \times 10^{20} \times 65.41}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \mathrm{~g}$

$$
=0.0326 \mathrm{~g}
$$

Answer: 0.0326 g

## Example 8.15

## Question

What is the mass (in grams) of $3 \times 10^{22}$ molecules of ethanol, $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}$ ?

## Answer

First calculate the relative molecular mass of ethanol

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
2 \mathrm{C}=2 \times 12.01 & =24.02 \\
5 \mathrm{H}=5 \times 1.008 & =5.04 \\
1 \mathrm{O}=1 \times 16.00 & =16.00 \\
1 \mathrm{H}=1 \times 1.008 & =1.008 \\
\hline \text { Rel. Molecular Mass } & =46.068
\end{array}
$$

i.e. 1 mole of $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}=46.068 \mathrm{~g}$

$$
\therefore 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text { molecules of } \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}=46.068 \mathrm{~g}
$$

1 molecule of $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}=\frac{46.068}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \mathrm{~g}$
$3 \times 10^{22}$ molecules of $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{3 \times 10^{22} \times 46.068}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} \\
& =2.296 \mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 8.5 Miscellaneous questions

In the Leaving Certificate exam paper, there may be some short questions on the mole concept.
Study Examples 8.16-8.18 in the online resources.

### 8.6 Some concluding points

It is very important that you have a good understanding of the mole. It is one of the key concepts in chemistry and you will be meeting it frequently in subsequent chapters. As you will have seen from the above examples, many questions on the mole can be answered if you remember two important facts.

$$
\text { Number of moles }=\frac{\text { Mass in grams }}{\text { Relative molecular mass }}
$$

One mole of any substance contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ entities.

# 9 Kinetic Theory of Matter and Behaviour of Gases 

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-146.jpg?height=444&width=1270&top_left_y=556&top_left_x=182)

### 9.1 Introduction

You may recall in Chapter 2 that we learned that the word 'matter' is simply a scientific term for substances or materials. A more formal definition of matter is as follows:

> Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.

We also learned that the fact that materials are made up of small particles is often referred to as the particulate nature of matter. By 'particles' we mean tiny entities that are invisible to the naked eye, e.g. atoms, molecules and ions. In pure substances (elements and compounds) all the particles in any one particular element or compound are the same. Figure 9.1 (a) and (b).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-146.jpg?height=1079&width=1133&top_left_y=2239&top_left_x=192)
Figure 9.1 Particles in pure substances: (a) elements and (b) compounds.

In a mixture of substances (e.g. oxygen gas and hydrogen gas), then the particles in the mixture will not be the same. In a mixture, different particles are mingled together (in this case, a mixture of oxygen molecules and hydrogen molecules).

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of the evidence for the Kinetic Theory of Matter.
- To ensure that students appreciate the relationships between pressure, volume and temperature of gases.
- To provide students with the opportunity to carry out an experiment to determine the relative molecular mass of a gas in the school laboratory.
- To ensure that students know how to solve problems involving the behaviour of gases.

In Chapter 2, we studied one property of a gas, i.e. its ability to spread throughout all the available space. We saw that ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas spread from opposite ends of a glass tube and formed a white ring where they met, Figure 2.1 (p.9). It is found that a gas will spread throughout any container in which it is placed. This spreading of gases is called diffusion. For example, if a small amount of a gaseous air freshener is released into a room, it will be detected in all parts of the room after a short time. Similarly, smoke can quickly spread throughout a building due to diffusion.

If some crystals of iodine are heated, they change directly from a solid to a gas (sublimation), Figure 9.2 Note that the gaseous iodine fills the entire container.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-146.jpg?height=730&width=1183&top_left_y=2692&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 9.2 When iodine crystals are warmed, the iodine gas that is formed fills the entire flask.

In this chapter, we will study the laws that gases obey and we will learn why they obey these laws. Before we study these laws, we first study a theory which helps us to understand the behaviour of gases.

### 9.2 The Kinetic Theory of Matter

Many of the ideas about the behaviour of atoms, molecules and ions in solids, liquids and gases are summarised in a theory called the Kinetic Theory of Matter. The word 'kinetic' comes from a Greek word meaning 'movement'. You may recall that at Junior Cycle, this theory was called the 'particle theory'. As we are going to study this theory in more detail, the term Kinetic Theory will be used.

The main points of the Kinetic Theory of Matter can be summarised in a number of assumptions.

## Assumptions of the Kinetic Theory of Matter

1. All matter is made up of tiny particles that are invisible to the naked eye. In this course, the tiny particles that we will be studying will be mainly atoms and molecules.
2. The tiny particles are always in motion.

The degree of motion depends on whether the substance is a solid, liquid or gas. These three are often referred to as the three states of matter.

- In solids, the particles are packed closely together. They do not have as much energy as particles in the liquid and gaseous states. The particles can only vibrate about fixed positions, Figure 9.3(a) in Table 9.1.
- In liquids, the particles are also packed closely together but are not in fixed positions as they are in solids. Evidence for this is the fact that liquids cannot be compressed, Figure 9.3(b).
- In gases, the particles are more widely separated and have larger amounts of energy than the particles in solids and liquids. The energy of gas particles is sufficient to spread out and fill the container, Figure 9.3(c). Gas particles move very fast in a random and haphazard way. The particles of a gas have more freedom of movement than the particles of a solid or a liquid.

| Solid | Liquid | Gas |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| ![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-147.jpg?height=552&width=546&top_left_y=2002&top_left_x=482) | Figure 9.3(b) The arrangement of particles in a liquid <br> - The particles have more freedom of movement than in a solid. <br> - The particles are very close together. <br> - The particles in the liquid can slide over each other. <br> - The forces between the particles are not as strong as in a solid. | Figure 9.3(c) The arrangement of particles in a gas <br> - The particles in a gas are farther apart than in a solid or liquid. <br> - The particles are continuously moving very fast around in all the space available. <br> - The movement is random and haphazard. The particles collide with each other and with the walls of the container. <br> - There are weak forces between the particles. |

Table 9.1 Summary of some key points in the Kinetic Theory of Matter

## 3. Temperature affects the movement of particles.

- An increase in temperature causes an increase in the kinetic energy of the particles, i.e. the particles move faster. Kinetic energy is energy due to movement.
- A decrease in temperature (reduced energy) causes a decrease in the kinetic energy of the particles, i.e. the particles move more slowly.


## 4. Temperature can cause a change in state.

When a solid is heated, the heat energy causes the vibration of the particles to increase. As heating continues, the particles vibrate faster and faster. The more heat that is supplied, the more the particles vibrate. Eventually, the particles break free and begin to slide over each other. The solid has now melted to form a liquid. We say that a change of state has occurred.

A small number of solids change directly from a solid to a gas when heated. This occurrence is known as sublimation. Solid carbon dioxide ('dry ice') and iodine are examples of substances that sublime. Dry ice is often used in special effects, Figure 9.4.

You may have noticed that puddles on the road dry up quickly on a warm, sunny day. This is because heat from the Sun gives some particles near the surface of the liquid extra energy. These particles now have enough energy to escape from the liquid into the air. We say that some of the liquid has evaporated to form a gas.

When a liquid is heated, the particles obtain more energy and move faster and faster. Eventually, the particles break away from the liquid state and form a gas. When a certain temperature is reached, particles of gas form throughout the liquid and not just at the surface. The liquid is now boiling.

When a liquid is boiling, the particles are escaping from all parts of the liquid very quickly.

Bubbles of gas are seen forming throughout the liquid. In the case of water, these bubbles of gas are made up of water vapour. The boiling point of the liquid has then been reached, Figure 9.5.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-148.jpg?height=784&width=1807&top_left_y=2697&top_left_x=187)
Figure 9.5 At the boiling point of a liquid, the particles break away from all parts of the liquid and form a gas.

The melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-148.jpg?height=635&width=882&top_left_y=1250&top_left_x=2063)
Figure 9.4 Solid carbon dioxide changes directly from a solid to a gas. This process is called sublimation and is used in special effects.

Evaporation is the changing of a liquid to a gas at the surface of the liquid.

The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas throughout the liquid.

Note that when evaporation takes place, no bubbles are formed in the liquid. However, when boiling takes place, bubbles are formed throughout the liquid.

When a gas is cooled, the particles slow down and a liquid is formed. Condensation is often seen in a kitchen when steam (gas) meets the much colder glass in a window. It may also be seen on a cold day when the warm water vapour that you are breathing out condenses.

When condensation occurs, the particles lose energy as the gas changes to a liquid.

The various changes of state are summarised in Figure 9.6.
Note from Figure 9.6 that a liquid can be changed into a solid by cooling the liquid, e.g. water freezes to ice. The temperature at which this occurs is called the freezing point.

As in the case of condensation, the particles lose energy when a liquid changes to a solid.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-149.jpg?height=863&width=1808&top_left_y=1517&top_left_x=325)
Figure 9.6 The state of a substance can be changed by heating or cooling.

## 5. Forces between particles

We have already discussed the forces between particles (Chapter 6). We saw that, in solids, the particles are held tightly together by strong forces and this gives solids a definite shape. The forces in liquids are weaker and these weaker forces allow the particles to slide over each other. Therefore, liquids flow. In gases, the forces are very weak and gases can diffuse to fill all the available space.

## 6. Pressure in gases

The Kinetic Theory of Matter explains how gases exert a pressure. This pressure is caused by the gas particles colliding with each other and with the walls of the container. As the temperature is raised, the particles gain more energy and this additional energy increases the pressure. We will study the relationship between temperature and pressure in more detail later in this chapter.

The ability of a gas to diffuse is often used to define what a gas is.
If you study Figure 2.1 (p.9), you will notice that the white ring is closer to one end (the hydrogen chloride end) of the tube. This shows that the lighter ammonia molecules diffused more quickly than the heavier hydrogen chloride molecules.

Condensation is the changing of a gas to a liquid.

The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes to a solid.

A gas is a substance that has no welldefined boundaries but diffuses rapidly to fill any container in which it is placed.

### 9.3 Evidence for the Kinetic Theory of Matter

Two observations provide evidence for the Kinetic Theory of Matter.

## 1. Brownian motion

This type of motion is named after Robert Brown (Figure 9.7). In his work as a botanist, he spent a lot of time using microscopes to help classify plants. In 1827 he was viewing a suspension of pollen in water under the microscope. To his surprise, he noticed that the individual grains of pollen were moving about in an irregular way. He also observed this type of erratic motion in dye particles. Brown noted his observations but could not explain what was happening. This type of motion was called 'Brownian motion'.

Brown observed the tiny pollen grains moving in a random, zig-zag, irregular fashion because the pollen grains were involved in collisions with the water molecules in the suspension being viewed under the microscope. The kinetic energy possessed by these water molecules causes them to be continuously moving and colliding with the pollen grains. Since the collisions are random, the movement of the pollen grains is also random, irregular and unpredictable. Therefore, Brownian movement provides evidence for the Kinetic Theory of Matter, since this theory proposes that the molecules of water are continuously in motion.

A diagrammatic representation of Brownian motion is shown in Figure 9.8. This observed movement is used to define Brownian motion.

## Robert Brown <br> (1773-1858)

Figure 9.7
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-150.jpg?height=333&width=346&top_left_y=296&top_left_x=2278)

Robert Brown was a Scottish botanist who spent some time in Ireland collecting plants. He also spent some time in Australia and returned to Scotland with over four thousand species of plants. In 1827, as he was viewing a suspension of pollen in water under the microscope, he noted that the individual grains were moving about irregularly.

Brownian motion is the random, irregular, zig-zag and continuous movement of tiny particles (such as pollen grains or smoke particles) suspended in a liquid or gas. The movement results from the collisions of these tiny particles with the molecules of the liquid or gas.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-150.jpg?height=772&width=1164&top_left_y=1582&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 9.8 This diagram represents Brownian motion observed under the microscope.

Brownian motion provides physical evidence for the Kinetic Theory of Matter. As well as supporting the Kinetic Theory of Matter, it also provides evidence for the existence of atoms and molecules.
