Brownian motion may be demonstrated in the laboratory by observing smoke particles trapped in a small 'smoke cell', Figure 9.9

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-150.jpg?height=626&width=727&top_left_y=3193&top_left_x=1263)
Figure 9.9 Using a microscope, the tiny smoke particles suspended in air may be observed moving about in an irregular way. The smoke particles are continuously colliding with the molecules of the gases in the air.

The Kinetic Theory of Matter states that all matter is made up of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are in constant random motion.
Both Brownian motion and diffusion of gases provide observable evidence for this theory.

## How does Brownian motion provide evidence for the Kinetic Theory of Matter?

The random, zig-gag, irregular movement of the visible particles (pollen or smoke particles) is observed because they are constantly being bombarded by much smaller, invisible molecules of water or gases in the air. Since Brownian motion is continuously taking place, the smaller molecules must be continuously in motion.

## 2. Diffusion of gases

We have already discussed the concept of diffusion in Chapter 2 and in the introduction to this chapter.

Diffusion is the process by which small particles (atoms, molecules or ions) move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

- Diffusion is a normal process and does not require any external energy to be applied. It occurs due to the natural kinetic energy of the small particles.
- Diffusion can occur in gases, liquids and solids. Diffusion in a liquid may be seen if a large crystal of copper sulfate is placed at the bottom of a large graduated cylinder filled with water. After a few hours, the blue colour will have spread throughout the water. The $\mathrm{Cu}^{2 *}$ and $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ ions have diffused throughout the water. Diffusion can also occur between two solids that are in contact with each other, but the rate of diffusion is usually much slower than in gases and liquids.


## How does diffusion provide evidence for the Kinetic Theory of Matter?

The observable evidence of diffusion demonstrates that particles must be in constant motion, colliding with each other and spreading out to occupy all the available space as stated in the assumptions of the Kinetic Theory of Matter. The only way to explain the results of the experiment shown in Figure 9.10 is in terms of the Kinetic Theory of Matter.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-151.jpg?height=825&width=2136&top_left_y=2057&top_left_x=475)
Figure 9.10 The molecules of ammonia gas diffuse from left to right. The molecules of hydrogen chloride gas diffuse from right to left. A white ring of ammonium chloride is formed when the ammonia and hydrogen chloride react with each other. Note that the white ring is closer to one end (the hydrogen chloride end) of the tube. This shows that the lighter ammonia molecules diffused more quickly than the heavier hydrogen chloride molecules.

The equation that describes what happens when the two gases meet to form the solid ammonium chloride may be written as:

In short, both Brownian motion and diffusion of gases provide us with strong, observable evidence that tiny particles are in constant, random motion. This evidence is in keeping with the Kinetic Theory of Matter.

### 9.4 Relationships between volume, pressure and temperature of gases

We have seen that the particles in a gas have greater freedom of movement than those in a solid or liquid.

Gases also differ from solids and liquids because gases do not have a fixed volume - they expand to fill the container in which they are placed. The volume of the gas is the volume of the container. Since a gas can be either compressed or allowed to expand, the volume of a sample of gas depends on temperature and pressure, Figure 9.11.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-152.jpg?height=416&width=1383&top_left_y=620&top_left_x=1239)
Figure 9.11 The volume occupied by the fixed amount of air in the balloon depends on the pressure that the gas in the balloon exerts on the balloon. As the pressure outside the balloon is decreased by pumping air out of the bell jar, the air inside the balloon now occupies a greater volume.

We will study the relationship between volume and pressure in more detail later on in this chapter.

Before studying some of the laws that gases obey, it is important that we understand how to measure the three main properties of a fixed amount of gas: volume, pressure and temperature. Let us first discuss what these terms mean and the units in which they are measured.

## Volume

- The volume of a sample of gas is the same as the volume of the container in which the sample is held.
- The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre $\left(\mathrm{m}^{3}\right)$. However, this unit is too large for ordinary laboratory work.
- In the laboratory, we normally measure volume in cubic centimetres ( $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ ) or litres (L). In this textbook we shall use the symbol L to represent litres rather than the small letter I which can easily be confused with the number 1.
- A litre is also called a cubic decimetre ( $\mathrm{dm}^{3}$ ). A cubic decimetre is exactly the same volume as a litre. (A decimetre is one tenth of a metre, i.e. 10 cm . If you make a cube of length 10 cm , the volume of the cube will be $10 \mathrm{~cm} \times 10 \mathrm{~cm} \times 10 \mathrm{~cm} =1000 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, i.e. one litre or one cubic decimetre.)

1 cubic metre $=1$ metre × 1 metre $\times 1$ metre

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =100 \mathrm{~cm} \times 100 \mathrm{~cm} \times 100 \mathrm{~cm} \\
& =10^{6} \mathrm{~cm}^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

(i.e. $1000000 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ or 1 million $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ )
i.e. $1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}=10^{6} \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.
If you were asked to fit sugar lumps of volume $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ into a cubic metre, you could fit in a million of them, Figure 9.12. Think about this.

1 litre $=1000 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=1$ cubic decimetre $\left(\mathrm{dm}^{3}\right)$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-152.jpg?height=1092&width=1189&top_left_y=2317&top_left_x=1432)
Figure 9.12 A volume of $1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ is equal to $10^{6} \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.

## EXAM TIPI

Remember that $1 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$ is equal to $1 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, as you will need this information for calculations in exams.

## Temperature

The main points about temperature may be summarised as follows.

- Temperature is a measure of the degree of hotness of an object.
- There are two scales of temperature used in science: the Celsius scale (also called the centigrade scale) and the Kelvin scale (also called the absolute scale).
- The Celsius scale is named after Anders Celsius who proposed it in 1742, Figure 9.13. This scale takes the freezing point of water as $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the boiling point of water as $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. These two points are called the two fixed points of the Celsius scale. Since the scale is divided into 100 degrees, it is also called the centigrade ('one hundred steps') scale.
- The Kelvin scale is named after Lord Kelvin who was born William Thomson in Belfast in 1824, Figure 9.14. In 1848 he proposed that the energy of molecules of a gas should reach zero at $-273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
- Kelvin proposed that the temperature of $-273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ should be considered the lowest possible temperature (absolute zero).
- He set up a new scale of temperature with the zero mark at absolute zero and each degree rise was the same as a degree rise on the Celsius scale.
- The temperature scale proposed by him is called the Kelvin scale and is also called the absolute scale.
- In theory, at the zero mark of the Kelvin scale, a gas would occupy zero volume if it could be cooled indefinitely without becoming a liquid or a solid.
- A temperature of absolute zero or zero kelvin is given the symbol 0 K . Note that the unit does not have the ${ }^{\circ}$ degree symbol.
- The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (symbol K).

The relationship between the Celsius scale and the Kelvin scale is illustrated in Figure 9.15.

## William Thomson <br> (1824-1907)

William Thomson, also known as Lord Kelvin, was born in Belfast. He was a child prodigy (genius) and attended his father's lectures in mathematics at the age of eight. He proposed a new scale of temperature with its zero mark at absolute zero $\left(-273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$.

## Anders Celsius <br> (1701-1744)

Figure 9.13
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-153.jpg?height=327&width=336&top_left_y=302&top_left_x=2428)

Anders Celsius was a Swedish scientist who set up a scale of temperature in which he divided the difference between the freezing point of water and the boiling point of water into 100 degrees.

Figure 9.14
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-153.jpg?height=342&width=314&top_left_y=944&top_left_x=2441)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-153.jpg?height=577&width=1430&top_left_y=2858&top_left_x=364)
Figure 9.15 The relationship between the Celsius and Kelvin scales of temperature.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=0+273=273 \mathrm{~K} \\
& 50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=50+273=323 \mathrm{~K} \\
& 100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=100+273=373 \mathrm{~K} \\
& -273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=-273+273=0 \mathrm{~K}
\end{aligned}
$$

Temperature can be converted from the Celsius scale to the Kelvin scale by adding 273 to the Celsius scale.

Note that a difference in temperature is the same for both scales as the size of a degree on the Celsius scale is the same as that on the Kelvin scale. For example, a rise in temperature of $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is the same as a rise in temperature of 10 K . In the SI system, the unit of temperature is the kelvin.

## Pressure

- The pressure of a gas is the force that the gas exerts on a unit area (e.g. one square metre) of its container.
- In the SI system, pressure is measured in newtons per metre squared, $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^{-2}$. This is also called the pascal (Pa).
- Normal atmospheric pressure is approximately $1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m}^{-2}$ also written as $1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$ or 100000 Pa .
- As the pascal is a small unit of pressure, the kilopascal, symbol kPa, is also used ( $1 \mathrm{kPa}=1000 \mathrm{~Pa}$ )
- Weather forecasters often use hectopascals ( $1 \mathrm{hPa}=100 \mathrm{~Pa}$ ). Thus, normal atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa (or 1000 hPa ). If you find it difficult to remember prefixes such as 'kilo' and 'hecto', their meanings are given in the SEC Formulae and Tables booklet.

Normal atmospheric pressure $=1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}=100 \mathrm{kPa}$

## Standard temperature and pressure (s.t.p.)

The volume of a gas varies with temperature and pressure. Therefore, to compare volumes of gases, the temperature and pressure at which they are measured must be known. Thus, when comparing volumes occupied by gases, it is normal to measure all volumes at the same temperature and pressure. For this reason, chemists decided to measure volumes of gases at standard temperature and pressure (s.t.p.). The standards that have been chosen are:

Standard temperature $=273 \mathrm{~K}$ (i.e. $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the freezing point of water)

Standard pressure $=1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}=100 \mathrm{kPa}$
To be more precise, standard pressure is actually $1.01325 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$. However, for all calculations in this course, we may use the approximate value of $1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$ or 100 kPa . If you are told on an exam paper to use the value of standard pressure in the SEC Formulae and Tables booklet, then use $\mathbf{1 . 0 1 3 2 5} \boldsymbol{\times} \mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{5}} \mathrm{Pa}$.

If you study a wide variety of gases, you will find that they differ from each other in many ways, e.g. some are flammable, some are coloured, some are vital to maintain life and others are poisonous. However, scientists have found that even though gases have different physical and chemical properties, all gases obey certain laws.

We now consider the five main laws that determine the behaviour of gases.

## 1. Boyle's Law

In 1662 the Irish chemist Robert Boyle (also referred to in Chapter 4, as he was the first person to give an accurate definition of an element) built an air pump in order to study the properties of gases, Figure 9.16 . He used this pump to investigate how the volume of a fixed mass of gas, kept at constant temperature, varied with changes in pressure.

Imagine a sample of gas trapped in a container with a movable piston, similar to what you have in a bicycle pump, Figure 9.17.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-155.jpg?height=616&width=1300&top_left_y=1504&top_left_x=390)
Figure 9.17 As the pressure is increased, the volume is decreased.

Boyle found that as the pressure of a gas increased, the volume decreased. In other words, volume is inversely proportional to the pressure, Figure 9.18(a). To check that this was correct, Boyle plotted the values of pressure against the inverse of volume as shown in Figure 9.18(b). The straight-line graph passing through the origin that he obtained showed that the pressure and volume of the gas were inversely proportional.

Boyle found that this relationship was true for all the gases he studied, regardless of their different properties. In 1662 he summarised his results in a statement that is now known as Boyle's Law.

A modern method of verifying Boyle's Law is shown in Figure 9.19.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-155.jpg?height=815&width=1258&top_left_y=3043&top_left_x=328)
Figure 9.19 A modern method of verifying Boyle's Law. The pressure is increased on the air in the plastic syringe.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-155.jpg?height=929&width=597&top_left_y=367&top_left_x=2164)
Figure 9.16 Robert Boyle built this air pump to study the relationship between the volume and pressure of a gas.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-155.jpg?height=1010&width=564&top_left_y=1676&top_left_x=2181)
Figure 9.18 (a) As the pressure increases, the volume decreases. (b) Pressure is inversely proportional to volume.

Boyle's Law states that, at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

This pressure is measured by means of a pressure sensor and the data are recorded on the computer. For each pressure value, the corresponding value of the volume of the gas is read off.
The computer plots a graph of Pressure vs $\frac{1}{\text { Volume }}$.

## How do we explain Boyle's Law?

Boyle's Law may be explained using the Kinetic Theory of Matter.

- A gas is made up of particles (atoms or molecules) which are continuously in motion. If you look back at Figure 9.17, if you push down on the plunger, the volume of the container is decreased.
- Therefore, the molecules are now moving within a smaller space.
- Therefore, they collide more frequently with each other and with the walls of the container.
- The increased number of collisions causes an increase in the pressure.

The reverse of the above happens if you pull the plunger up. The molecules of the gas have more space to spread out. Therefore, the molecules collide less often with each other and with the walls of the container. Therefore, the pressure decreases.

Boyle's Law can be expressed mathematically as:

$$
V \propto \frac{1}{p}
$$

The symbol $\propto$ stands for 'is proportional to'.
Therefore, $V=k \frac{1}{p}$ where k is a constant of proportionality.
This is another way of proving Boyle's Law, i.e. you only need to show that the pressure of a fixed mass of the gas multiplied by its volume is always a constant value. This is shown in Table 9.2.

| Pressure (p) (kPa) | Volume (V) (L) | Pressure × volume $p \times V$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 40 | 0.100 | 4.0 |
| 67 | 0.060 | 4.0 |
| 80 | 0.050 | 4.0 |
| 100 | 0.040 | 4.0 |
| 120 | 0.033 | 4.0 |
| 160 | 0.025 | 4.0 |

Table 9.2 Data obtained from compressing a sample of air at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-156.jpg?height=832&width=896&top_left_y=2457&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 9.20 A plot of $p V$ against $p$ is a straight line.

Therefore, since $p V$ is always a constant value, if $p V$ is plotted against $p$, a graph similar to that shown in Figure 9.20 will result, i.e. at different values of $p$, the value of $p V$ will always be the same.

## 2. Charles' Law

We have seen that Robert Boyle studied the relationship between the volume and pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature. A French scientist, Jacques Charles, also studied gases and, in 1783, he constructed the first hydrogen balloon, Figure 9.21. He noticed that, as the balloon went higher, the temperature decreased and the volume of the gas in the balloon also decreased.

On returning to his laboratory, he investigated the relationship between the volume and temperature of a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure. He carried out an experiment similar to that shown in Figure 9.23. Imagine a fixed mass of gas trapped by a thin thread of concentrated sulfuric acid in a long glass tube as shown in Figure 9.22. The tube is sealed at the bottom and open at the top. As the water is heated, the volume of trapped air increases and the concentrated sulfuric acid is pushed up the tube.

Charles summarised the results of his experiments on a graph similar to that shown in Figure 9.23.

You will observe that the straight line in Figure 9.23 does not pass through the origin. Therefore, one cannot say that the volume of the gas is directly proportional to the temperature measured in ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. However, if the line is continued backwards, it cuts the X axis at $-273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, Figure 9.24.

As already stated, this temperature of $-273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is taken as the starting point for the Kelvin or absolute scale of temperature. As shown in Figure 9.24, using this scale of temperature there is now a direct relationship between volume and temperature. This relationship is stated in Charles' Law:

Charles' Law states that, at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its temperature measured on the Kelvin scale.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-157.jpg?height=551&width=1144&top_left_y=3115&top_left_x=338)
Figure 9.24 Volume is directly proportional to temperature on the Kelvin scale.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-157.jpg?height=903&width=616&top_left_y=312&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 9.21 This drawing shows Jacques Charles and his colleague MarieNoel Robert in the first hydrogen balloon flight in 1783. They ascended to an approximate height of 1.6 km over Paris.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-157.jpg?height=1078&width=1059&top_left_y=1250&top_left_x=1588)
Figure 9.22 Apparatus to investigate Charles' Law. As the temperature of the trapped air increases, its volume also increases and this pushes the concentrated sulfuric acid upwards.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-157.jpg?height=1001&width=971&top_left_y=2685&top_left_x=1679)
Figure 9.23 The volume of the gas increases as the temperature is increased.

## How do we explain Charles' Law?

Charles' Law may be explained using the Kinetic Theory of Matter. A gas is made up of particles (atoms or molecules) which are continuously in motion. Consider Figure 9.25.

- If the temperature of the container is increased, the molecules are now moving more quickly due to the extra kinetic energy they obtain from the heat supplied.
- This means that the molecules collide more frequently and more forcefully with each other and with the walls of the container.
- In order to prevent an increase in pressure, it is necessary to give the molecules more room in which to move around.
- Therefore, the volume of the container increases.

The reverse happens if you cool the gas. Cooling the gas slows down the molecules, as they now have less kinetic energy.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-158.jpg?height=863&width=799&top_left_y=410&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 9.25 In order to keep the pressure constant as the container is heated, the volume of the container must increase.

Therefore, they collide with each other and with the walls of the container less often and less forcefully. In order to prevent a decrease in pressure, it is necessary to give the molecules less room in which to move around. Therefore, the volume of the container decreases.

Mathematically, Charles' Law may be stated as:
$V \propto T$ provided $T$ is measured on the Kelvin scale.
$V=k T$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality.

$$
\frac{V}{T}=k
$$

This is another way of proving Charles' Law, i.e. dividing the volume of the gas by its temperature (measured on the Kelvin scale) always gives a constant value. This is shown in Table 9.3.

| Volume ( $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ ) | $T\left({ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ | $T(\mathrm{~K})$ | $\frac{V}{T}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 75 | -173 | 100 | 0.75 |
| 150 | -73 | 200 | 0.75 |
| 225 | 27 | 300 | 0.75 |
| 300 | 127 | 400 | 0.75 |
| 375 | 227 | 500 | 0.75 |

Table 9.3 Data obtained by heating a sample of hydrogen at atmospheric pressure.

Therefore, since $\frac{V}{T}$ is always a constant value, if $\frac{V}{T}$ is plotted against $T$, a straight-line graph as shown in Figure 9.26 should result, i.e. at different values of $T, \frac{V}{T}$ always has the same value.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-158.jpg?height=663&width=824&top_left_y=2268&top_left_x=1553)
Figure 9.26 A plot of $\frac{V}{T}$ against $T$ is a straight line.

## 3. The Combined Gas Law

We have seen from Boyle's Law that $p V=k$.
Therefore, if the volume of a gas is allowed to change from $V_{1}$ to $V_{2}$ and its pressure changes from an initial value of $p_{1}$ to a final value of $p_{2}$ (keeping the temperature constant), then we can say:

$$
p_{1} V_{1}=p_{2} V_{2}
$$

(This may also be seen from Table 9.2: Any particular value of pressure multiplied by its corresponding volume is equal to any other value of pressure multiplied by its corresponding volume.)
Similarly, from Charles' Law: $\frac{V_{1}}{T_{1}}=\frac{V_{2}}{T_{2}}$

Combining Boyle's Law and Charles' Law, the following equation is obtained:

$$
\frac{p_{1} V_{1}}{T_{1}}=\frac{p_{2} V_{2}}{T_{2}}
$$

This is called the Combined Gas Law. (It is also called the General Gas Law but, since the term Combined Gas Law is used more widely, we will use it in this textbook.) Always remember that pressure, volume, and temperature of gases are always linked. The Combined Gas Law is very useful for converting between these three variables under one set of conditions ( $p_{1}, V_{1}, T_{1}$ ) to what they would be under a different set of conditions $\left(p_{2}, V_{2}, T_{2}\right)$. This type of calculation is illustrated in Example 9.1.

## Example 9.1

## Question

A sample of nitrogen gas has a volume of $75 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ at a temperature of $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and a pressure of 95 kPa . Find the volume that the gas would have at s.t.p.

## Answer

Summarise the data given as shown in Table 9.4.

| Given | s.t.p. |
| :--- | :--- |
| $V_{1}=75 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ | $V_{2}=?$ |
| $p_{1}=95 \mathrm{kPa}$ | $p_{2}=100 \mathrm{kPa}$ |
| $T_{1}=27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}+273=300 \mathrm{~K}$ | $T_{2}=0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}+273=273 \mathrm{~K}$ |

Table 9.4

## EXAM TIPI

Since the Combined Gas Law is derived from Charles' Law, do not forget to convert all temperatures to the Kelvin scale.
Remember that Charles' Law is only true when temperature is measured on the Kelvin scale.

Substitute into:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{p_{1} V_{1}}{T_{1}} & =\frac{p_{2} V_{2}}{T_{2}} \\
\frac{95 \times 75}{300} & =\frac{100 \times V_{2}}{273} \\
V_{2} & =\frac{95 \times 75 \times 273}{300 \times 100} \\
& =64.84 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $64.84 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$

## EXAM TIPI

The units on either side of the equation must be consistent. The question gives pressure in kilopascals. These units are used for pressure on the left-hand side of the equation. Therefore, standard pressure must be written in kilopascals on the right-hand side of the equation. This also applies to the units for volume. In the question, the volume is given in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$. Therefore, the volume in the answer will also be in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$.

## 4. Gay-Lussac's Law of combining volumes

Joseph Gay-Lussac (Figure 9.27) was a French chemist who was interested in what happens when gases react with each other. In 1805 he was studying the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen.

He confirmed that when hydrogen reacts with oxygen, two volumes of hydrogen always react with one volume of oxygen to form two volumes of steam (all volumes being measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure).

i.e. hydrogen $\quad+\underset{\text { 2 volume }}{\text { oxygen }} \rightarrow \underset{\text { 2 volumes }}{\text { steam }}$

Note the simple ratio 2:1:2.
This led him to study the reactions of other gases to see whether they reacted in simple ratios also. Some of the reactions which he studied were:
hydrogen + chlorine → hydrogen chloride

1 volume 1 volume 2 volumes (simple ratio 1:1:2)
nitrogen monoxide + oxygen → nitrogen dioxide

$\mathbf{2}$ volumes $\mathbf{1}$ volume $\mathbf{2}$ volumes (simple ratio: $\mathbf{2}: \mathbf{1 : 2}$ )

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-160.jpg?height=828&width=695&top_left_y=367&top_left_x=1959)
Figure 9.27 Joseph GayLussac (on the left) and his colleague Jean-Baptiste Biot were French scientists who were interested in gases. The drawing shows a balloon flight that they made in 1804 to study the composition of air at high altitudes.

In 1808 Gay-Lussac summarised the results of his work in his Law of Combining Volumes.

Gay-Lussac's Law of Combining Volumes states that, in a reaction between gases, the volumes of the reacting gases and the volumes of any gaseous products are in the ratio of small whole numbers, provided the volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

Gay-Lussac's law is very helpful as it allows you to predict how much gas you need or how much gas will be produced in a reaction involving gases when all volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

Special types of syringes made of glass called gas syringes are used to study the volumes of gases that react with each other, Figure 9.28.

The results of experiment to study the volume of nitrogen monoxide that reacts with oxygen may be summarised as follows:

- The results of the experiment are plotted on a graph as shown in Figure 9.29.

Tell us that the reaction is complete when approximately $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of oxygen has been added to the $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of nitrogen monoxide, proving that one volume of oxygen reacts with two volumes of nitrogen monoxide.

$$
2 \mathrm{NO} \quad+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \quad 2 \mathrm{NO}_{2}
$$

nitrogen monoxide + oxygen → nitrogen dioxide

| 2 volumes | 1 volumes | 2 volumes |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $\left(50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}\right)$ | $\left(25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}\right)$ | $\left(50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}\right)$ |


![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-160.jpg?height=363&width=1169&top_left_y=1872&top_left_x=1486)
Figure 9.28 Apparatus to investigate the volume of nitrogen monoxide that reacts with oxygen

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-160.jpg?height=1017&width=1137&top_left_y=2438&top_left_x=1510)
Figure 9.29 The reaction is complete when $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of oxygen is added to $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of nitrogen monoxide to give $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of nitrogen dioxide. The total volume at the end of the experiment is $75 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, since a volume of $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the original $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of oxygen has not reacted.

This assumption that Avogadro made is now called Avogadro's Law (also called Avogadro's Theory or Avogadro's Hypothesis) and is stated as follows:

> Avogadro's Law states that equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.

This law is illustrated in Figure 9.32.
Avogadro's Law is an important law in chemistry, as it explains the relationship between the volume of a gas and the number of molecules present. Avogadro's Law was not accepted for nearly 50 years after he proposed it. This was because Dalton's Theory did not allow for the existence of molecules. Avogadro was the first to distinguish between atoms and molecules and introduced the word 'molecule' into the language of chemistry. Using his theory, he also proposed that the water molecule contained two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom. His explanation of Gay-Lussac's results for the reaction of oxygen and hydrogen is summarised in Figure 9.33.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-162.jpg?height=1092&width=1170&top_left_y=406&top_left_x=1445)
Figure 9.32 Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules under the same conditions of temperature and pressure. In the case of one mole of the gas, the volume occupied is 22.4 L at standard temperature and pressure.

Figure 9.32 Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules under the same conditions of temperature and pressure. In the case of one mole of the gas, the volume occupied is 22.4 L at standard temperature and pressure.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-162.jpg?height=681&width=1727&top_left_y=1953&top_left_x=188)

By experiment it is found that a mole of oxygen gas (i.e. $32 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{O}_{2}$ ) occupies a volume of 22.4 litres at s.t.p. Since one mole of any gas contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ molecules, then by Avogadro's Law, one mole of any gas should occupy 22.4 litres at s.t.p.

At s.t.p. one mole of any gas occupies a volume of 22.4 litres.
Note the following:

- The volume occupied by one mole of any gas is called its molar volume. Thus, the molar volume of all gases at s.t.p. is $\mathbf{2 2 . 4}$ litres. This value is given in the SEC Formula and Tables booklet.
- For some calculations, you need to use the molar volume at room temperature and pressure. The value of this quantity is 24.0 litres. Thus, the molar volume at room temperature and pressure is $\mathbf{2 4 . 0}$ litres. This value will be given to you if it is required for calculations.

Figure 9.33 Avogadro's Law explains why two volumes of hydrogen react with one volume of oxygen to produce two volumes of steam.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-162.jpg?height=698&width=561&top_left_y=2669&top_left_x=2060)

## How is Avogadro's Law explained by the Kinetic Theory of Matter?

- In a container, equal numbers of gas particles (atoms or molecules) exert equal pressure under the same conditions of temperature and volume.
- Pressure and volume depend on the number of collisions.
- If two gases are at the same temperature, their molecules will have the same average kinetic energy, regardless of the type of molecule.
- The number of collisions is independent of the type of gas.
- It is the number of molecules that determines the pressure and volume not the type of molecules.
- Therefore, under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases must contain equal numbers of molecules.

Since one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at s.t.p, the density of a gas is easily calculated. This is illustrated in Example 9.2.

## Example 9.2

## Question

Calculate the density of carbon dioxide at s.t.p.

## Answer

Relative molecular mass
$\mathrm{CO}_{2}=12.01+2(16)=44.01$
i.e. 1 mole $\mathrm{CO}_{2}=44.01 \mathrm{~g}$
i.e. $44.01 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CO}_{2}$ occupy 22.4 L at s.t.p.
Density $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Volume }}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{44.01 \mathrm{~g}}{22.4 \mathrm{~L}} \\
& =1.96 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $1.96 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$

## Example 9.3

## Question

Calculate the volume occupied by 20 g of sulfur dioxide gas at s.t.p.

## Answer

Relative molecular mass of $\mathrm{SO}_{2}=32.07+2(16)$

$$
=64.07
$$

1 mole of sulfur dioxide occupies 22.4 L at s.t.p. i.e. $64.07 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{SO}_{2}$ occupy 22.4 L
$1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{SO}_{2}$ occupies $\frac{22.4}{64.07} \mathrm{~L}$
Therefore, $20 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{SO}_{2}$ occupy $=\frac{20 \times 22.4}{64.07} \mathrm{~L}$

$$
=6.99 \mathrm{~L}
$$

Answer: 6.99 L

## Example 9.4

## Question

$200 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of a certain gas at s.t.p. have a mass of 0.25 g . Calculate the relative molecular mass of the gas.

## Answer

$200 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ have a mass of 0.25 g
$1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ has a mass of $\frac{0.25}{200} \mathrm{~g}$
$22400 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ have a mass of $\frac{22400 \times 0.25}{200} \mathrm{~g}=28 \mathrm{~g}$
i.e. 22.4 L of the gas have a mass of 28 g
Therefore, relative molecular mass of gas $=28$
Answer: 28

### 9.5 The Kinetic Theory of Matter applied to gases

We now take a closer look at the Kinetic Theory of Matter as it applies to gases. In order to help us understand the behaviour of gases, a number of assumptions were developed.

## Assumptions of the Kinetic Theory of Matter as applied to gases

1. Gases are made up of particles (molecules or atoms) that are in continuous rapid, random motion, colliding with each other and with the walls of the container.
2. There are no attractive or repulsive forces between the molecules of a gas, i.e. the molecules are independent of each other.
3. The gas molecules are so small and so widely separated that the actual volume of all the molecules is negligible compared with the space they occupy. This can be used to explain why equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles when measured under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.
4. When molecules collide, the collisions are perfectly elastic, i.e. there is no loss of kinetic energy in these collisions, although there may be a transfer of energy between the colliding particles, Figure 9.34. This means that, if one molecule loses energy in a collision, its partner in the collision gains this energy. (If they stuck together after the collision, the collision would be called an inelastic collision.) You can study some interactive elastic collisions on the PhET University of Colorado website.
5. The average kinetic energy of the molecules in a sample of gas is proportional to the temperature measured on the Kelvin (absolute) scale.

## Limitations to the Kinetic theory of Matter as applied to gases

If we examine these assumptions, we see that there are certain limitations to the kinetic theory of gases:

- Contrary to Assumption 2, all real gases actually do have tiny attractive or repulsive forces between the molecules of the gas. As discussed in Chapter 6, gas molecules that are polar (e.g. $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ and HCl ) will have attractive intermolecular forces because the partially negative end of one molecule will be attracted to the partially positive end of another molecule. For example, in the case of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$, these intermolecular forces are hydrogen bonds. In the case of HCl , the intermolecular forces are dipole-dipole forces. Similarly, there are weak London dispersion forces between nonpolar molecules (e.g. $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}, \mathrm{O}_{2}$ ).
- Contrary to Assumption 3, it is not valid to say that the volume of the molecules of a gas is always negligible compared with the space that they occupy. Under very high pressure, when molecules are crowded closer together, it is clear that their volume is not negligible compared with the distances between them.

Therefore, it is true to say that all of the assumptions of the kinetic theory do not hold for real gases but only hold for what is called an ideal gas.

An ideal gas is one that perfectly obeys all the assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases under all conditions of temperature and pressure.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-164.jpg?height=984&width=1958&top_left_y=2881&top_left_x=185)
Figure 9.34 The collisions between molecules are similar to the collisions between snooker balls. The collisions between the balls are elastic collisions as they bounce off each other.

## Ideal gases do not exist! However, real gases do come very close to ideal gas behaviour under two conditions:

- At low pressure, when the molecules are widely spaced.
- At high temperatures, when the molecules are moving rapidly, preventing the forces between molecules from exerting an influence.
At very high pressures, gas molecules are forced much closer together. This means that we can no longer assume that the volume of the molecules can be ignored compared with the volume in which they move.

At high pressures and low temperatures, because the molecules are close together and moving slowly, the attractive forces between the molecules can be significant under these conditions.

However, under normal conditions (e.g. atmospheric pressure and a temperature of $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ) the behaviour of real gases comes very close to that of an ideal gas and, under these conditions, it is reasonable to take the

Real gases differ from ideal gases because:
(i) forces of attraction and repulsion do exist between the molecules.
(ii) the volume of the molecules is not negligible. assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases as validly applying to real gases.

In terms of the gas laws, an ideal gas may be described as one that obeys the gas laws exactly, e.g. an ideal gas would have zero volume at $-273^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (see Figure 9.25). This never occurs as real gases become liquids long before they reach this temperature. It should be noted that under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, non-polar molecules come closer to ideal behaviour than polar molecules, since the attractive forces are less in the case of non-polar molecules.

Boyle's Law, Charles' Law, Gay-Lussac's Law of Combining Volumes, and Avogadro's Law may all be explained in terms of the kinetic theory of gases.

## Example 9.5

## Question

Give two reasons why real gases depart from ideal behaviour. Under what conditions of temperature and pressure do real gases come closest to ideal behaviour?

## Answer

Real gases depart from ideal behaviour because:
(i) In an ideal gas, it is assumed that there are no forces of attraction between the molecules. In real gases, attractive forces exist between the molecules.
(ii) In an ideal gas, it is assumed that the molecules occupy negligible space. However, in real gases, the molecules occupy a small but definite space, which is not negligible at high pressure.

Real gases come closest to ideal behaviour at high temperature and low pressure.

### 9.6 The Ideal Gas Equation

Boyle's Law, Charles' Law and Avogadro's Law may be combined to give a mathematical relationship between the volume $(V)$, pressure $(p)$, temperature $(T)$ and number of moles $(n)$ of a gas.

Boyle's Law: $V \propto \frac{1}{p}$ at constant temperature.
Charles' Law: $V \propto T$ at constant pressure.
Avogadro's Law: $V \propto n$ at constant temperature and pressure.
Combining the above three relationships:

$$
V \propto\left(\frac{1}{p}\right) T n
$$

i.e. $V=R \frac{1}{\rho} T n$ where $R$ is a constant of proportionality called the Universal Gas Constant.
Rearranging the above equation gives: $\boldsymbol{p V}=\boldsymbol{n R T}$
This equation is called the Ideal Gas Equation or the Equation of State for an Ideal Gas. It is called the Equation of State because it tells us how, in going from one set of conditions in the gaseous state to another, the four variables $V, P, T$ and $n$ change.

The numerical value for $R$ can be found by substituting experimental values into the equation. For example, we know that at s.t.p. one mole of any gas occupies a volume of 22.4 litres.

At s.t.p.
$T=273 \mathrm{~K}$
$p=1.013 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$ (normal atmospheric pressure)
$n=1$ (for 1 mole of gas)
$V=22.4 \mathrm{~L}=\frac{22.4}{1000}=0.0224 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$
Note: We must convert litres to cubic metres. (There are 1000 litres in a cubic metre.) This is because we use metres in the units for pressure and we must, therefore, measure volume in cubic metres to keep the units consistent.

$$
\begin{aligned}
p V & =n R T \\
R & =\frac{p V}{n T} \\
& =\frac{1.013 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{Nm}^{-2} \times 0.0224 \mathrm{~m}^{3}}{1 \mathrm{~mole}^{3} \times 273 \mathrm{~K}} \\
& =8.31 \mathrm{~N} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since a newton metre is also called a joule (symbol J), the above is often written as

$$
R=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}
$$

| $\boldsymbol{P} \boldsymbol{V}=\boldsymbol{n} \boldsymbol{R} \boldsymbol{T}$ | $\boldsymbol{V}: \mathrm{m}^{3}$ | $\boldsymbol{R}: \mathrm{J} \mathrm{mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ (always given to you) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\boldsymbol{P}: \mathrm{Pa}$ | $\boldsymbol{n}: \mathrm{mol}$ | $\boldsymbol{T}: \mathrm{K}$ |

When substituting into the equation $P V=n R T$, always ensure that the units of pressure are pascals, the units of volume are cubic metres and the units of temperature are kelvins.

## Example 9.6

## Question

Calculate the volume occupied by 10 g of oxygen gas at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and a pressure of 200 kPa .
$\left[\mathrm{R}=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right]$

## Answer

$p=200 \mathrm{kPa}=200 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~Pa}$
$V=$ ?
$n=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Rel. Molecular Mass }}=\frac{10}{32}=0.31$ mole

$$
\begin{aligned}
& R=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \\
& T=25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}+273=298 \mathrm{~K} \\
& p V=n R T \\
& \begin{aligned}
V & =\frac{n R T}{p} \\
& =\frac{0.31 \times 8.31 \times 298}{200 \times 10^{3}} \\
& =0.0038 \mathrm{~m}^{3} \\
& =0.0038 \times 1000 \text { litres } \\
& =3.8 \mathrm{~L}
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Alternative Method

This problem could also be solved using the Combined Gas Law.

| Given | s.t.p. |
| :--- | :--- |
| $V_{1}=?$ | $V_{2}=22.4 \mathrm{~L}$ |
| $p_{1}=200 \mathrm{kPa}$ | $p_{2}=100 \mathrm{kPa}$ |
| $T_{1}=25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}+273=298 \mathrm{~K}$ | $T_{2}=0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}+273=273 \mathrm{~K}$ |

Substitute into $\frac{p_{1} V_{1}}{T_{1}}=\frac{p_{2} V_{2}}{T_{2}}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{200 \times V_{1}}{298} & =\frac{100 \times 22.4}{273} \\
V_{1} & =\frac{100 \times 22.4 \times 298}{273 \times 200}=12.23 \mathrm{~L}
\end{aligned}
$$

1 mole of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ occupies 12.23 L under the above conditions,
i.e. $32 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{O}_{2}$ occupies 12.23 L

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{O}_{2} \text { occupies } \frac{12.23}{32} \mathrm{~L} \\
& 10 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{O}_{2} \text { occupies } \frac{12.23 \times 10}{32}=3.8 \mathrm{~L}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answers: 3.8 L

## Example 9.7

## Question

A volatile liquid is one with a low boiling point. Calculate the relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid $(X)$ from the following information: 0.20 g of $X$ on vaporisation gave $40 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of vapour measured at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and a pressure of $100 \mathrm{kPa} .\left[\mathrm{R}=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}\right]$

## Answer

$p=100 \mathrm{kPa}=100 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$
$V=40 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=40 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{3}$
$n=$ ?
$R=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$
$T=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}+273=373 \mathrm{~K}$
$\mathrm{pV}=\mathrm{nRT}$
$n=\frac{p V}{R T}$
$n=\frac{100 \times 10^{3} \times 40 \times 10^{-6}}{8.31 \times 373}=0.0013$ moles
i.e. 0.0013 mole $=0.20$ gram

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \text { mole } & =\frac{0.2}{0.0013} \text { grams } \\
& =153.85 \text { grams }
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. Relative molecular mass $=153.85$
Answer: 153.85

## EXAM TIPI

A common error among students when substituting into the equation $p V=n R T$ is to forget to convert volumes to $\mathrm{m}^{3}$. As already explained, if you are given the volume in litres, you must divide by 1000 (i.e. × $10^{-3}$ ) to convert to $\mathrm{m}^{3}$. If you are given the volume in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$, you must divide by a million (i.e. $\times 10^{-6}$ ) since there are a million cubic centimetres in a cubic metre.

Volume in cubic metres = volume in litres × $10^{-3}$
Volume in cubic metres = volume in $\mathrm{cm}^{3} \times 10^{-6}$

Study Examples 9.8 and 9.9 in the online resources.

### 9.1 Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 3

Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 3 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To measure the relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid using a conical flask

## Introduction

The relative molecular mass of a compound may be found to a very high degree of accuracy with the aid of a mass spectrometer (Chapter 4). Using a mass spectrometer is the most accurate method of measuring the relative molecular masses of substances (solid, liquid or gas). However, mass spectrometers are not usually available in school laboratories. Therefore, we shall use a method first developed by a German chemist called Victor Meyer to measure the relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid. As previously mentioned, a volatile liquid is one with a low boiling point. This method is restricted to liquids that are volatile, as we will be using boiling water to vaporise the liquid and so the boiling point of the liquid must be below that of water.

In this method, we will fill a flask with the vapour of a volatile liquid at a known temperature. We will then find the mass of this vapour and, by calculation we will find the volume that this vapour would occupy at s.t.p. We will then calculate what the mass of $22400 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of this vapour would be at s.t.p. This is the relative molecular mass of the liquid.

## Key steps in procedure

The overall procedure may be divided into four stages.
1 A flask is filled with the vapour of the volatile liquid at the temperature of boiling water and at atmospheric pressure.

## Procedure

- The mass of a clean, dry conical flask, a rubber band and a piece of aluminium foil are found using a laboratory balance.
- Approximately $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the volatile liquid (e.g. propanone or cyclohexane) are poured into the conical flask.
- The aluminium foil is placed over the mouth of the flask and held in place using the rubber band.
- A very small pinhole is made in the aluminium foil cap.
- The flask is clamped in a large beaker of boiling water until all the volatile liquid has vaporised, Figure 9.35.
- The temperature of the boiling water is measured

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-168.jpg?height=1163&width=906&top_left_y=1764&top_left_x=1670)
Figure 9.35 Apparatus to measure the relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid.

using a thermometer.

- The atmospheric pressure is measured using a barometer, Figure 9.36.

Figure 9.36 This datalogger is an easy way to measure the pressure of the atmosphere. The reading here is 101.5 kPa .
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-168.jpg?height=606&width=906&top_left_y=3190&top_left_x=1670)

## Observation

- After heating the conical flask for a while, all of the volatile liquid in the flask will have vaporised. No liquid will then be visible in the flask.


## Explanation

- The purpose of the boiling water is to convert the volatile liquid to a vapour.
- The flask is left in the boiling water for about 8 minutes to ensure that all the liquid has vaporised.
- Although it appears that the flask is empty, it is now full of the vapour of the volatile liquid at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (the temperature of the boiling water). The temperature of the vapour is obtained by reading the temperature of the boiling water.
- The pinhole allows the air to be expelled from the flask, which is filled at this point with the vapour of the liquid.
- Any excess vapour escapes from the flask through the pinhole.
- The pressure of the vapour in the conical flask is the same as atmospheric pressure because the pinhole allows the vapour in the conical flask to be in contact with the air outside the conical flask, i.e. the conical flask is open to the atmosphere. The volume of volatile liquid added at the start of the experiment does not need to be accurately known since, when the liquid boils, the vapour of the liquid fills the flask and any excess vapour escapes through the pinhole.

2 The mass of the vapour of the volatile liquid that filled the flask is found.

## Procedure

- The flask is removed from the boiling water and allowed to cool to room temperature.
- The outside of the flask and foil are dried.
- The flask, foil and rubber band are re-weighed.


## Observation

- As the flask cools, droplets of liquid are seen forming inside the conical flask.


## Explanation

- The vapour of the volatile liquid condenses back to a liquid as the flask is cooled.
- Air returns to fill the flask.
- The mass of the liquid whose vapour has filled the flask is calculated by subtracting the initial mass of the flask, foil and rubber band from the final mass of flask, foil, rubber band and condensed volatile liquid.

3 The volume occupied by the vapour of the volatile liquid is found. Its volume is the same as that of the flask, which it had filled completely.

- The volume of the conical flask is found by filling it completely with water and pouring the water (in portions) into a $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ graduated cylinder. As the volume of the water will exceed the capacity of the graduated cylinder, this will have to be repeated a number of times.

4 The results are recorded under the headings shown in your Laboratory Notebook. Using these results, you can now calculate the relative molecular mass of the volatile liquid. To assist you with calculations, some specimen results are shown in Example 9.10.

## Example 9.10

## Question

Some students carried out an experiment to measure the relative molecular mass of a volatile liquid. They filled a conical flask with the vapour of the liquid by placing the conical flask in boiling water at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. They obtained the following data:

| Mass of empty flask, foil and rubber band | $=105.21 \mathrm{~g}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mass of flask, foil, band and condensed liquid | $=106.30 \mathrm{~g}$ |
| Volume of conical flask | $=326 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ |
| Atmospheric pressure | $=98.5 \mathrm{kPa}$ |

Calculate the relative molecular mass of the volatile liquid.

## Answer

| Mass of empty flask, foil and rubber band | $=105.21 \mathrm{~g}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mass of flask, foil, band and condensed liquid | $=106.30 \mathrm{~g}$ |
| Therefore, mass of condensed liquid | $=106.30-105.21=1.09 \mathrm{~g}$ |
| Volume of flask = volume of vapour | $=326 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ |
| Atmospheric pressure | $=98.5 \mathrm{kPa}$ |
| Temperature of vapour in flask | $=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}+273=373 \mathrm{~K}$ |

## Calculations

Given:
$p=98.5 \mathrm{kPa}=98.5 \times 10^{3} \mathrm{~Pa}$
$V=326 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=326 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{3}$
$R=8.3 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$
$T=100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=100+273=373 \mathrm{~K}$

## Step 1

Calculate the number of moles of vapour present

$$
\begin{aligned}
p V & =n R T \\
n & =\frac{p V}{R T} \\
& =\frac{98.5 \times 10^{3} \times 326 \times 10^{-6}}{8.3 \times 373} \\
& =0.01
\end{aligned}
$$

No of moles = 0.01

## Step 2

Calculate the relative molecular mass
No of moles $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Rel Molecular Mass }}$
Rel Molecular Mass $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { No of moles }} \quad=\frac{1.09}{0.01} \quad=109$
Answer: Rel molecular mass = 109

Note: Do not be disappointed if you do not get exactly the right answer, as there are a number of possible sources of experimental error in this experiment:

- The laboratory balance may only read to an accuracy of one or two decimal places.
- A measuring instrument that is more accurate than the graduated cylinder could be used to measure the volume of the conical flask, e.g. a burette.
- It is very difficult to cover the entire flask with boiling water, so the vapour in the space near the top of the conical flask may not be at the temperature of the boiling water.
- The outside of the conical flask and foil may not be completely dry when carrying out the second weighing.


### 9.2 Teacher Demonstration Experiment

## Teacher Demonstration Experiment 9.2

## To verify the Ideal Gas Equation

To verify the Ideal Gas Equation, $p V=n R T$, you could use the same datalogging apparatus as was used to verify Boyle's Law.

1. Find the mass of an empty gas syringe.
2. Place a known volume of oxygen gas in the syringe.
3. By subtraction, find the mass of oxygen gas in the syringe.
4. Note the room temperature.
5. Attach the gas syringe to a pressure sensor, Figure 9.37.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-171.jpg?height=577&width=799&top_left_y=1510&top_left_x=1907)
Figure 9.37 Verifying the Ideal Gas Equation using a fixed quantity of oxygen gas in a gas syringe attached to a pressure sensor.

6. Vary the volume of the gas by pushing down on the plunger. In each case, read the pressure corresponding to each volume.
7. Calculate the average value of pV .
8. Substitute the average value of $p V$ into the left-hand side of the equation $p V=n R T$.
9. Now calculate the right hand side of the equation $p V=n R T$ by substituting in the measured value of $n$ (number of moles of oxygen in the syringe), the value of $T$ (room temperature) and the value of $R$.
10. Compare both sides of the equation. They should be equal!

If the two sides of the equation are not exactly equal, this may be due to:

- Experimental error: The measurements that you have taken of pressure, volume, temperature and mass may be slightly inaccurate.
- Non-ideal gas behaviour: The Ideal Gas Equation hold for ideal gases. However, you are dealing with a real gas which can deviate from idea gas behaviour under condition of high pressure.
- The Kinetic Theory of Matter contains a number of assumptions about how substances behave under various conditions such as temperature, pressure and volume.
- Boyle's Law states that, at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

Charles' Law states that, at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its temperature measured on the Kelvin scale.

- The Combined Gas Law (or General Gas Law) states that:
$\frac{p_{1} V}{T_{1}}=\frac{p_{2} V_{2}}{T_{2}}$
- Avogadros Law states that equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules, under the same conditions of temperature and pressure.

An ideal gas is one that perfectly obeys all the assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases under all conditions of temperature and pressure.

The equation $p V=n R T$ is called the Ideal Gas Equation or the Equation of State for an Ideal Gas.

# 10 Law of Conservation of Mass: Introducing Stoichiometry

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-174.jpg?height=464&width=1190&top_left_y=536&top_left_x=182)

### 10.1 Introduction

The story of our next chemistry topic begins in France. It was here, in his laboratory in Paris, that Antoine Lavoisier (1743-1794) carried out chemistry experiments in which he was interested in taking accurate measurements. He convinced other chemists of the importance of taking accurate measurements when carrying out chemistry experiments. Lavoisier is considered to be one of the founders of modern quantitative chemistry, i.e. that branch of chemistry that focuses on amounts or quantities of substances that react together, Figure 10.1. He had hundreds of different measuring instruments in his laboratory.

Figure 10.1 Antoine Lavoisier took very accurate measurements of the masses and volumes of chemicals that take part in chemical reactions. This drawing shows him carrying a container of mercury for use in one of his most important experiments.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-174.jpg?height=760&width=538&top_left_y=2135&top_left_x=735)

Many of his experiments involved gases and, by carefully measuring the masses of reactants and products, he made many important discoveries. For example, he discovered that air was made up of approximately 20\% of oxygen gas. His careful measurements allowed him to work out the precise ratios in which substances react with each other. In particular, his experiments gave chemists a clear understanding of what happens when substances burn and this helped to debunk old theories about the process of burning.

We will now study one of the most important discoveries of Antoine Lavoisier.

## OBJECTIVES

- To make students familiar with the work of Antoine Lavoisier and the Law of Conservation of Mass.
- To give students an understanding of the relationship between the amounts of reactants and products.
- To provide students with the opportunity to solve problems in the area of quantitative chemistry.


### 10.2 Law of Conservation of Mass

In 1774 Lavoisier heated a known mass of mercury in a sealed glass container that had a limited supply of air. He observed that on heating the silvery mercury, it changed into a red powder called mercuric oxide $(\mathrm{HgO})$, Figure 10.2.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-174.jpg?height=691&width=1056&top_left_y=1959&top_left_x=1425)
Figure 10.2 Diagrammatic representation of the experiment carried out by Lavoisier. He heated mercury in a sealed container and carefully measured the masses of reactants and products.

He carefully measured the mass of the container and its contents before and after heating it. He found that, even though the mercuric oxide looked different to the mercury, the mass of the entire container was the same before and after heating. He also noted that the mercuric oxide formed was heavier than the mercury.

The mass of the mercury had increased because it gained oxygen from the air:

$\underset{\substack{\mathrm{Hg} \\ \text { mercury } \\ 100 \mathrm{~g}}}{ }+\underset{\text { oxygen }}{1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{\text { mercuric oxide }}{\mathrm{HgO}}$

However, Lavoisier also found that the loss in mass of the oxygen in the container was exactly equal to the gain in mass of the mercury when it changed to mercuric oxide. In short, he discovered that there was no change in the total mass of reactants and products. Although the substances themselves had changes as a result of the reaction, the number of each type of atom remained the same and, therefore, there was no overall change in mass. In other words, he discovered that mass is conserved or kept the same in the chemical reaction. He repeated his experiment by heating various other elements (such as phosphorous, sulfur, tin and lead) in sealed containers of air. In all cases, he found that the total mass of the
products was equal to the total mass of the reactants. He summarised his findings in the Law of Conservation of Mass.

The Law of Conservation of Mass states that when a chemical reaction occurs, the total mass of the reactants is always equal to the total mass of the products.
Total mass of reactants = Total mass of products
For example, if 12 grams of carbon combine with 32 grams of oxygen it is found that 44 grams of carbon dioxide are formed. Thus, atoms cannot simply 'disappear', i.e. all atoms present in the reactants must also be present in the products.

## To Verify the Law of Conservation of Mass

You may recall that you carried out some experiments to verify the Law of Conservation of Mass at Junior Cycle level. We now study two experiments to verify this law. The Law of Conservation of Mass may be verified by carrying out the reaction between silver nitrate and chloride ions. We have already met this reaction in Chapter 5 when testing for the presence of chloride ions in aqueous solution.

$$
\mathrm{Ag}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl} \downarrow
$$

This experiment is shown in Figure 10.3. Full details of how to carry out this experiment are given in the Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-175.jpg?height=720&width=1092&top_left_y=2448&top_left_x=442)
Figure 10.3a Before reaction, the total mass of the reactants and containers is 197.0 g .

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-175.jpg?height=717&width=1082&top_left_y=2451&top_left_x=1614)
Figure 10.3b After mixing the reactants, silver chloride is formed. The total mass is still 197.0 g .

Note that experiments to verify the Law of Conservation of Mass must be carried out in such a way that nothing can enter or escape when the reaction is taking place. This is often called a closed system. An example of a closed system is a flask with a tightly-fitting rubber stopper. The sealed container ensures that gases cannot escape or that materials cannot enter the flask to give false results.

The Law of Conservation of Mass may also be verified by studying the reaction that takes place when Alka-Seltzer tablets are added to water. The citric acid in the tablets reacts with the sodium hydrogencarbonate (also in the tablets) to produce carbon dioxide. We have also met this reaction in Chapter 5 when testing for the presence of hydrogencarbonate ions in aqueous solution:

$$
\mathrm{HCO}_{3}^{-}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

This experiment is shown in Figure 10.4. Full details of how to carry out this experiment are given in the Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

### 10.3 Physical and chemical changes: Law of Conservation of Mass

The Law of Conservation of Mass applies to all physical and chemical changes. You may recall at Junior Cycle that you studied both physical and chemical changes. To ensure that you are clear on the meaning of these terms, we now summarise some key points.

An example of a physical change is the melting of ice (solid to liquid) or the boiling of water (liquid to gas). In each case, no new substance is formed. Ice, water and steam are the same substance, i.e, they have the same chemical formula $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)$. Some more examples of physical changes are shown in Figure 10.5. The Law of Conservation of Mass applies to all of these physical changes.

A physical change is a change that does not result in the formation of any new substance. For example, this may easily be shown by placing some ice cubes in a sealed container and finding the mass of the container and ice cubes. The same mass is observed when the ice cubes have melted.

Physical change may be compared to physical appearance. Physical appearance means how you look. You may change your physical appearance such as hair style or the clothes that you wear. Even though you look different,

Physical properties are properties that can be observed without changing the substance into another substance. you are still the same person. Similarly, ice, water and steam all look different but they are still the same substance.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-176.jpg?height=883&width=1730&top_left_y=3001&top_left_x=185)
Figure 10.5 These changes are examples of physical changes because no new substance is formed. We are just changing the appearance of the substances.

> Examples of physical properties are mass, shape, volume, density, melting point, and boiling point.

In Chapter 5, when testing for the presence of various anions in aqueous solution, you carried out many chemical changes.

A chemical change is a change that results in the formation of one or more new substances.

- When a chemical change has taken place, we could also say that a chemical reaction has taken place. One of the most spectacular types of chemical reaction that take place is during a fireworks display. In this chemical reaction, a lot of heat, light and sound are produced. These are signs that a chemical reaction is taking place. The Law of Conservation of Mass applies to all these chemical changes.
- Other signs that a chemical reaction is taking place are that there may be a colour change, cloudiness may be observed, a smell may be detected or bubbles of gas may be formed, Figure 10.6.

Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts with other substances in a chemical reaction to form a new substance.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-177.jpg?height=473&width=629&top_left_y=1406&top_left_x=358)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-177.jpg?height=499&width=259&top_left_y=1959&top_left_x=520)
