Figure 10.6 All of these are examples of chemical changes because new substances are formed.

We have already studied examples of chemical properties in Chapter 7, where we studied the reactions of groups of elements with water and oxygen.

The main differences between physical changes and chemical changes are summarised in Table 10.1. Many physical changes are easy to reverse, e.g. an ice cube that has melted can be frozen again. However, it would be very difficult to reverse the chemical reaction when Alka-Seltzer is added to water.

| Physical change | Chemical change |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1. No new substance is formed. | 1. New substance is formed. |
| 2. Usually no energy changes take place. | 2. Energy changes take place: heat, light or sound are produced. |
| 3. Easy to reverse. | 3. Difficult to reverse. |

Table 10.1 The differences between physical changes and chemical changes

### 10.4 Law of Conservation of Mass and balancing chemical equations

The Law of Conservation of Mass provides the reason why chemical equations must always be balanced. You may recall learning about balanced chemical equations in your study of science at Junior Cycle level.

If a chemical equation is not balanced, this would have to mean that some atoms have vanished or appeared out of nowhere - this, of course, does not

A balanced chemical equation has equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides of the equation. happen. The Law of Conservation of Mass implies that there must be equal number of each type of atom on both sides of the equation. All that takes place when a chemical reaction occurs is that there is a rearrangement of atoms to form new substances.

Is the equation $2 \mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ balanced?
There are four hydrogen atoms on the left and four hydrogen atoms on the right of the equation. Also, there are two oxygen atoms on the left and two oxygen atoms on the right. Therefore, the equation is balanced. This may also be seen using Molymod models to illustrate the balanced equation, Figure 10.7.

Let's look at another example to help you to understand the procedure involved in balancing an equation.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-178.jpg?height=470&width=1183&top_left_y=1383&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 10.7 This equation is balanced, as the same number of each type of atom is present on both sides of the equation.

## Example 10.1

## Question

Balance the equation $\mathrm{CH}_{4}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

## Answer

## Step 1

Count the number of atoms of each element.

| Left-hand side | Right-hand side |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1 C atom | 1 C atom |
| 4 H atoms | 2 H atoms |
| 2 O atoms | 3 O atoms |

## Step 2

Adjust the numbers in front of the formulas to ensure that equal numbers of each type of atom are on both sides of the chemical equation.

To get four H atoms on the right-hand side of the equation, put a '2' before the $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ :
$\mathrm{CH}_{4}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
The '2' before the $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ tells us that there are two water molecules, consisting of four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms. Thus, there are now four H atoms on the right-hand side. Therefore, the H atoms are balanced. Now check for the balancing of oxygen atoms.

### 10.5 Applying the mole concept to balanced chemical equations

Consider the reaction between hydrogen gas and oxygen gas to form water. As already discussed, this reaction may be represented by the following balanced equation:

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

We can interpret this equation in a number of ways. Firstly, it tells us that two hydrogen molecules react with one oxygen molecule to form two molecules of water.

$$
\underset{2 \text { molecules }}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2}}+\underset{1 \text { molecule }}{\mathrm{O}_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{2 \text { molecules }}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

Secondly, we can interpret it in terms of the Avogadro number of molecules that react. If we multiply the number of molecules in the above balanced equation by the Avogadro constant, we now have:

$$
\underset{2 \times 6 \times 10^{23}}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2}}+\underset{\substack{1 \times 6 \times 10^{23} \\ \text { molecules }}}{\mathrm{O}_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{2 \times 6 \times 10^{23}}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

We have already seen that the amount of a substance that contains the Avogadro constant number of particles is called a mole of that substance. Therefore, the above equation may also be written as:

$$
\underset{2 \text { moles }}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2}}+\underset{1 \text { mole }}{\mathrm{O}_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{2 \text { moles }}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

By converting moles to grams, we can also tell the masses of these substances that react and the amount of water that is formed.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-180.jpg?height=353&width=1274&top_left_y=2708&top_left_x=494)

This branch of chemistry is called stoichiometry.
Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry that tells us the relationship between the amounts of reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation.

The word 'stoichiometry' comes from the Greek stoicheoin meaning 'element' and metron meaning 'measure'. Chemists need to have knowledge of stoichiometry because it enables them to decide on the quantities of reactants required to form a certain amount of product.

### 10.6 To calculate the percentage of each element in a compound

Very often it is important to be able to calculate the percentage of an element in a compound. For example, a farmer may wish to know the percentage of nitrogen in a particular fertiliser, Figure 10.9. A chemical engineer may need to calculate the percentage of a metal in an ore. The method of performing this type of calculation is shown in the examples that follow.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-181.jpg?height=727&width=929&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1829)

## Example 10.2

## Question

Ammonium nitrate, $\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{NO}_{3}$, is often used in fertilisers to supply nitrogen to the soil.
What is the percentage of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate? ( $\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{~N}=14, \mathrm{O}=16$ )

## Answer

## Step 1

## Calculate the relative molecular mass of ammonium nitrate.

Note that in one molecule of ammonium nitrate, there are two atoms of nitrogen, four atoms of hydrogen and three atoms of oxygen:

| $2 \mathrm{~N}=2 \times 14$ | $=28$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $4 \mathrm{H}=4 \times 1$ | $=4$ |
| $3 \mathrm{O}=3 \times 16$ | $=48$ |

Rel. Molecular Mass $=80$

## Step 2

## Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in $\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{NO}_{3}$.

Percentage of $\mathrm{N}=\frac{28}{80} \times 100=35 \%$
The percentage of nitrogen is 35\%.

## NOTE

In Example 10.2, we have given the values of relative atomic masses as rounded-off numbers. This will enable you to concentrate on the methods of solving problems in stoichiometry rather than being distracted by constantly referring to the SEC Tables and Formulae booklet. However, as previously mentioned, ensure you follow the instructions on the Leaving Certificate exam paper regarding the actual values of relative atomic masses to be used in solving problems.

## Example 10.3

## Question

Calcium oxide, CaO , is commonly called lime or quicklime. Calculate the percentage composition by mass of each element in calcium oxide, $\mathrm{CaO} .(0=16, \mathrm{Ca}=40)$

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the relative molecular mass of CaO .
Ca $=40$
$\mathrm{O} \quad=16$
Rel. Molecular Mass $=56$

TEST YOURSELF: Attempt Questions
10.3-10.4 and W10.3-W10.4

## Step 2

Calculate the percentage of both calcium and oxygen in CaO .
Percentage of $\mathrm{Ca}=\frac{40}{56} \times 100=71.43 \%$
Percentage of $\mathrm{O}=\frac{16}{56} \times 100=28.57 \%$
The percentage composition of CaO by mass is 71.43\% Ca and 28.57\% O.

### 10.7 To calculate the empirical formula of a compound given the percentage composition

We have already seen that a compound is represented by a chemical formula, e.g. a molecule of water is represented by the formula $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. This is called the molecular formula of the compound. It tells us that a molecule of water consists of two atoms of hydrogen and one atom of oxygen, i.e. the molecular formula tells us the actual number of atoms of each element present.

There is another type of formula called the empirical formula.
For example, the molecular formula of ethene is $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{4}$ but the empirical formula is $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$. Some other examples of empirical and molecular formulas are shown in Table 10.2.

| Compound | Molecular formula | Empirical formula |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Water | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ |
| Methane | $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ | $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ |
| Hydrogen peroxide | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}$ | HO |
| Acetylene | $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2}$ | CH |
| Butane | $\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{10}$ | $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5}$ |
| Benzene | $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{6}$ | CH |

Table 10.2 Examples of molecular and empirical formulas

Note that the molecular formula is a simple multiple of the empirical formula. Note also that in some cases, the molecular formula and the empirical formula are the same.

## Example 10.5

## Question

Glucose is the name of the sugar found in blood. The empirical formula of glucose is $\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. When the relative molecular mass of glucose is measured by a mass spectrometer, it is found to be 180 . What is the molecular formula of glucose?

## Answer

## Step 1

Apply the formula relating molecular formula and empirical formula to determine $\mathbf{n}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Molecular formula }=\text { empirical formula } \text { × } n \\
& \qquad \begin{aligned}
& =\left(\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right) \times n \\
\text { i.e. } 180 & =(12+2+16) \times n \\
180 & =30 \times n \\
n & =6
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

The molecular formula of a compound is a formula which shows the number and type of each atom present in a molecule of that compound.

The empirical formula of a compound is the formula showing the simplest wholenumber ratio of the numbers of different atoms present in the molecule.

## Step 2

## Multiply empirical formula by $\mathbf{n}$.

Therefore, molecular formula $=\left(\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right) \times 6$

$$
=\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_{6}
$$

Answer: $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_{6}$

Chemists involved in quality control often need to have compounds analysed. One of the methods of doing this is to measure in the laboratory the percentage by mass of each of the elements present in the compound. Using this information, it is possible to work out the empirical formula of the compound, Figure 10.12. The method of calculation is illustrated in Example 10.6.

## Example 10.6

## Question

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-183.jpg?height=379&width=642&top_left_y=276&top_left_x=2116)
Figure 10.12 This apparatus is used to determine the empirical formula of a compound.

A compound containing only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen was found on analysis to contain $52.17 \%$ carbon, $13.04 \%$ hydrogen and $34.79 \%$ oxygen. What is the empirical formula of the compound? Using a mass spectrometer, it was found that the relative molecular mass of the compound was 92. What is the molecular formula? [ $\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{C}=12,0=16$ ]

The basic idea behind solving this problem is to realise that if we have 100 grams of the compound, 52.17 grams will be due to carbon atoms, 13.04 grams will be due to hydrogen atoms, and 34.79 grams will be due to oxygen atoms.

## Step 1

Convert each of these masses to moles of atoms by dividing by the appropriate relative atomic mass. This will lead us to the mole ratio.

## Step 2

Divide by the smallest number of moles to obtain the simplest whole number ratio, i.e. the empirical formula. Lay out your work in the form of a table as follows:

| Element | Percentage | Percentage Rel. atomic mass | Simplest ratio (divide by 2.17) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Carbon | 52.17 | $\frac{52.17}{12}=4.35$ | $\frac{4.35}{2.17}=2$ |
| Hydrogen | 13.04 | $\frac{13.04}{1}=1304$ | $\frac{13.04}{2.17}=6$ |
| Oxygen | 34.79 | $\frac{3479}{16}=2.17$ | $\frac{2.17}{2.17}=1$ |
| i.e. empirical formula $=\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{6} \mathrm{O}$ <br> smallest number |  |  |  |

## Step 3

Apply the equation relating molecular formula and empirical formula.
Molecular formula $=$ empirical formula × $n$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 92=\left(\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{6} \mathrm{O}\right) \times n \\
& 92=[2(12)+6(1)+1(16)] \times n \\
& 92=46 n \\
& \frac{92}{46}=n \\
& n=2
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, molecular formula $=\left(\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{6} \mathrm{O}\right) \times 2=\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_{2}$
Answer: $\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_{2}$

Note: In some cases, dividing by the smallest number obtained in the third column of the above table may not give whole numbers in the fourth column. To get whole numbers, it may be necessary to multiply by a certain factor. This is illustrated in Example 10.7.

### 10.8 To calculate the empirical formula of a compound given the masses of reactants and products

In many cases, it is possible to calculate the formula of a compound by carefully measuring the masses of the substances involved in the reaction. Analysis that is based on the masses of compounds that react is usually referred to as gravimetric analysis. Some examples of this type of calculation now follow.

## Example 10.8

## Question

A student heated 1.02 g of copper powder in air and noted that that the brown copper powder turned black, Figure 10.13. It was found that the mass of black powder formed was 1.28 g . Assuming that the black powder is an oxide of copper, calculate the empirical formula of this oxide. ( $\mathrm{Cu}=63.5,0=16$ )

## Answer

## Step 1

Write out the word equation and insert the given masses.
copper + oxygen → copper oxide
1.02 g 1.28 g

## Step 2

Apply the Law of Conservation of Mass to calculate the unknown mass.
> mass of copper $=1.02 \mathrm{~g}$
> mass of copper oxide formed $=1.28 \mathrm{~g}$

∴ mass of oxygen in copper oxide $=1.28-1.02=0.26 \mathrm{~g}$

## Step 3

Calculate the number of moles of copper atoms and oxygen atoms.
No. of moles of copper atoms in copper oxide $=\frac{1.02}{63.5}=0.016$ and no. of moles of oxygen atoms in copper oxide $=\frac{0.26}{16}=0.016$

## Step 4

Divide by the smallest number of moles to obtain the simplest whole number ratio.
In this case, the mole ratios are the same.
Ratio of $\mathrm{Cu}: \mathrm{O}=0.016: 0.016=1: 1$
Therefore, empirical formula of copper oxide is CuO .
Thus, the following reaction has occurred:
$\mathrm{Cu}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuO}$
Answer: CuO

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-184.jpg?height=632&width=948&top_left_y=1149&top_left_x=1549)
Figure 10.13 The brown copper powder turns black when heated. Copper is being converted into an oxide of copper. By measuring the mass of the copper metal and the mass of the oxide of copper that is formed, we can work out the empirical formula of the oxide of copper.

## Example 10.9

## Question

In an experiment to determine the formula of an oxide of copper, hydrogen gas was passed over the heated oxide. It was found that 5.4 g of the oxide gave 4.8 g of copper. Calculate the empirical formula of the oxide. $(\mathrm{Cu}=63.5, \mathrm{O}=16)$

## Answer

## Step 1

Write out the word equation and insert the given masses.
copper oxide + hydrogen → copper
5.4 g
4.8 g

## Step 2

Apply the Law of Conservation of Mass to calculate the unknown mass.

| mass of copper oxide | $=5.4 \mathrm{~g}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| mass of copper in copper oxide | $=4.8 \mathrm{~g}$ |

Therefore, mass of oxygen in copper oxide $=5.4-4.8=0.6 \mathrm{~g}$

## Step 3

## Calculate the number of moles of copper atoms and oxygen atoms.

No. of moles of copper atoms in copper oxide $=\frac{4.8}{63.5}=0.076$ moles
No. of moles of oxygen atoms in copper oxide $=\frac{0.6}{16}=0.038$ moles

## Step 4

## Divide by the smallest number of moles to obtain the simplest whole number ratio.

Ratio of $\mathrm{Cu}: \mathrm{O}=0.076: 0.038$

$$
\text { = } 2: 1
$$

Therefore, the empirical formula of copper oxide is $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.
Thus, the following reaction has occurred:
$\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Cu}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Answer: $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Note that there are two oxides of copper, Figure 10.14. CuO is called copper(II) oxide. $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ is called copper(I) oxide.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-185.jpg?height=873&width=1095&top_left_y=2588&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 10.14 The formula of the black copper(II) oxide is CuO . The formula of the red copper(I) oxide is $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

## Example 10.10

## Question

Sodium sulfate is commonly called Glauber's salt and is used as a laxative in many medicines, Figure 10.15. A student heated 1.61 g of hydrated sodium sulfate crystals, $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \times \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$, in a crucible over a Bunsen burner until no further loss in mass occurred. It was found that 0.71 g of the anhydrous salt was obtained. Calculate the formula of the hydrated salt. $(H=1, O=16, N a=23, S=32)$.

## Answer

## Step 1

Write out the equation and insert the given masses.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-186.jpg?height=597&width=1005&top_left_y=481&top_left_x=1593)
Figure 10.15 Sodium sulfate is commonly called Glauber's salt after the pharmacist who discovered it.

Heating the crystals converts the hydrated sodium sulfate to anhydrous sodium sulfate.

$$
\begin{array}{cl}
\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot x \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} & \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}+x \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \\
1.61 \mathrm{~g} & 0.71 \mathrm{~g}
\end{array}
$$

## Step 2

## Apply the Law of Conservation of Mass to calculate the unknown mass.

Mass of hydrated crystals $=1.61 \mathrm{~g}$
Mass of anhydrous salt $\quad=0.71 \mathrm{~g}$
Therefore, mass of water $\quad=1.61-0.71=0.90 \mathrm{~g}$

## Step 3

## Calculate the number of moles of $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ and water.

Rel. Molecular Mass $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}=2(23)+32+4(16)=142$
No. of moles of $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \quad=\frac{0.71}{142}=0.005$
No. of moles of water

$$
=\frac{0.90}{18}=0.05
$$

## Step 4

## Divide by the smallest number of moles to obtain the simplest whole number ratio.

Therefore, ratio $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}: \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=0.005: 0.05$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =1: 10 \\
\text { i.e. } x & =10
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. formula of hydrated salt is $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot 10 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Answer: $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot 10 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

### 10.9 Calculating masses of reactants and products from balanced chemical equations

We have already seen that a balanced equation tells us the amounts of substances that react together and the amounts of products formed. This type of information is very useful for chemists and enables them to perform calculations to determine the amounts of reactants needed to produce a certain amount of product. We now consider some of these types of calculations.

## Example 10.12

## Question

Magnesium reacts with oxygen to produce magnesium oxide, Figure 10.16, according to the equation:
$2 \mathrm{Mg}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{MgO}$
If a student burns 9 g of magnesium in excess oxygen (i.e. there is plenty of oxygen present to ensure that all of the magnesium reacts), what mass of magnesium oxide will be formed? $(M g=24,0=16)$

## Answer

## Step 1

Write down the given equation and circle what we know and what we want to know.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-187.jpg?height=740&width=1010&top_left_y=1009&top_left_x=1722)
Figure 10.16 The reaction of magnesium with oxygen in the air is one of the reactions that take place when sparklers are lit.

$$
2 \mathrm{Mg}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{MgO}
$$

## Step 2

Make a shortened version of the equation and put in the amounts.

| 2 Mg | $\rightarrow 2 \mathrm{MgO}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| 2 moles | $\rightarrow 2$ moles |
| $2(24) \mathrm{g}$ | $\rightarrow 2(24+16) \mathrm{g}$ |
| i.e. 48 g Mg | $\rightarrow 80 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{MgO}$ |

## Step 3

## Determine the mass of MgO formed.

Therefore, $1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{Mg} \rightarrow \frac{80}{48} \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{MgO}$
Therefore, $9 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{Mg} \rightarrow \frac{9 \times 80}{48} \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{MgO}$

$$
=15 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{MgO}
$$

Answer: 15 g of magnesium oxide will be formed from 9 g of Mg .

## Example 10.13

## Question

Lime (calcium oxide) is manufactured in a lime kiln, Figure 10.17, by heating limestone (calcium carbonate) to bring about the following reaction:

$$
\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO}+\mathrm{CO}_{2}
$$

Calculate the amount of lime that could theoretically be obtained by heating 5 kg of limestone.

$$
(C=12, C a=40, O=16)
$$

## Answer

## Step 1

## Convert kilograms to grams.

This problem is fairly straightforward if one remembers

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-188.jpg?height=721&width=1003&top_left_y=481&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 10.17 Limestone is converted into lime by heating the limestone in this lime kiln. The lime produced will be used to make cement.

to convert kilograms to grams.
$5 \mathrm{~kg}=5000 \mathrm{~g}$

## Step 2

Write down the given equation and circle what we know and what we want to know.

$$
\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO}+\mathrm{CO}_{2}
$$

## Step 3

Make a shortened version of the equation and put in the amounts.
$\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO}$
1 mole $\quad \rightarrow 1$ mole
$[40+12+3(16)] \mathrm{g} \rightarrow[40+16] \mathrm{g}$
i.e. $100 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \rightarrow 56 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CaO}$

## Step 4

Calculate the mass of CaO obtained.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CaCO}_{3} & \rightarrow \frac{56}{100} \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CaO} \\
\therefore 5000 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CaCO}_{3} & \rightarrow \frac{5000 \times 56}{100} \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CaO} \\
& =2800 \mathrm{~g} \\
& =2.8 \mathrm{~kg}
\end{array}
$$

Answer: 2.8 kg of lime will be obtained from 5 kg limestone.

## NOTE

## Unit analysis

In solving problems in stoichiometry, it is important that you pay close attention to the units. This is commonly called unit analysis. For instance, in Example 10.14 we had to convert kilograms to grams by multiplying by 1000 (or

## TEST YOURSELF:

Attempt Questions 10.13-10.15 and W10.11-W10.12. $1 \times 10^{3}$ ). Similarly, if the problem was given in tonnes, we would have to convert tonnes to grams by multiplying by $1 \times 10^{6}$. Other examples of unit analysis are where we convert number of grams to number of moles, and where we convert number of moles to number of molecules, as shown in the above examples.

### 10.10 Calculating volumes of gases from balanced chemical equations

When performing calculations on balanced equations which involve gases, chemists usually measure the volume of a gas rather than just its mass. We have already learned that one mole of any gas occupies a volume of 22.4 litres at s.t.p. We use this fact to calculate the volumes of gases used up or formed in chemical reactions. In calculating volumes of gases from balanced chemical equations, we follow the same procedure as shown in the following examples.

## Example 10.14

## Question

Carbon dioxide is formed when carbon is burned in oxygen, Figure 10.18, according to the equation:

$$
\mathrm{C}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}
$$

What volume of carbon dioxide (at s.t.p.) is formed when 30 g of carbon are burned in excess oxygen?

## Answer

## Step 1

Write down the given equation and circle what we know and what we want to know.

$$
\text { (C) }+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}
$$

## Step 2

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-189.jpg?height=730&width=1000&top_left_y=1162&top_left_x=1725)
Figure 10.18 The burning of large carbon electrodes plays an important role in the manufacture of steel in the electric arc furnace.

Make a shortened version of the equation and put in the amounts.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{C} & \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2} \\
1 \text { mole } & \rightarrow 1 \text { mole } \\
30 \mathrm{~g} & \rightarrow ?
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 3

Calculate the volume of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ obtained.
$\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2}$
1 mole $\rightarrow 1$ mole
$12 \mathrm{gC} \rightarrow 22.4 \mathrm{~L}$ of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ at s.t.p.
$1 \mathrm{gC} \rightarrow \frac{22.4}{12} \mathrm{~L}_{\text {of } \mathrm{CO}_{2}}$
$30 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \frac{30 \times 22.4}{12} \mathrm{~L}$ of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$
$=56 \mathrm{~L}$ of carbon dioxide.
Answer: 56 litres.

## SEC exam question 10.16

Nitric acid may be used to produce calcium ammonium nitrate $\left(5 \mathrm{Ca}\left(\mathrm{NO}_{3}\right)_{2} \cdot \mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{NO}_{3} \cdot 10 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)$.

This compound is used as a fertiliser and is commonly known as CAN.
When dissolved in water, CAN dissociates into the calcium ion ( $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ ), the ammonium ion ( $\mathrm{NH}_{4}{ }^{*}$ ), and the nitrate ion ( $\mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{-}$).

Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in calcium ammonium nitrate.
Calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN) is an unusual salt but do not worry as you do not need to know anything about the salt itself. You just need to be able to perform the required calculation.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-190.jpg?height=773&width=499&top_left_y=533&top_left_x=1992)

This type of salt is often called a double salt, as its crystals actually contain two salts. One salt is calcium nitrate $\left[\mathrm{Ca}\left(\mathrm{NO}_{3}\right)_{2}\right]$ and the other salt is ammonium nitrate $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{NO}_{3}\right)$. The ' 5 ' at the beginning of the formula tells you that for every one mole of ammonium nitrate in the crystal, there are five moles of calcium nitrate in the crystal.

## Step 1.

Work out the relative molecular mass of calcium ammonium nitrate
$5 \mathrm{Ca}\left(\mathrm{NO}_{3}\right)_{2} \cdot \mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{NO}_{3} \cdot 10 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$5 \mathrm{Ca}=5 \times 40.08=200.40$
$12 \mathrm{~N}=12 \times 14.01=168.12$
$430=43 \times 16.00=688.00$
$24 \mathrm{H}=24 \times 1.008=24.192$

$$
M_{r}=1080.712
$$

## Step 2.

Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in calcium ammonium nitrate
Percentage of $\mathrm{N}=\frac{168.12}{1080.712} \times 100=15.56 \%$
Answer 15.56\%

## Summary What I should know

- The Law of Conservation of Mass states that when a chemical reaction occurs the total mass of the reactants is always equal to the total mass of the products.
- A physical change is a change that does not result in the formation of any new substance.
- A chemical change is a change that results in the formation of one or more new substances.
- A balanced chemical equation has equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides of the equation.
- Balanced chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of molecules, moles, grams and volumes of gases.

Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry that tells us the relationship between the amounts of reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation.

The molecular formula of a compound is a formula which shows the number and type of each atom present in a molecule of that compound.

The empirical formula of a compound is the formula showing the simplest whole-number ratio of the numbers of different atoms present in the molecule.

Molecular formula $=$ empirical formula × $n$ (where $n=a$ whole number).

- The empirical formula of a compound can be calculated from the percentage composition and also from the masses of reactants and products in the reaction to form the compound.

Masses of reactants and products as well as volumes of gases can be calculated from balanced chemical equations.

# 11 Acids and Bases

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-194.jpg?height=473&width=2391&top_left_y=520&top_left_x=185)

### 11.1 Introduction

You may recall that we met the word 'acid' at Junior Cycle science level. We learned that the word 'acid' comes from the Latin word acidus meaning 'sour'. If you study Figure 11.1 you will recognise many substances with a sour or sharp taste. For example, fizzy drinks contain an acid called carbonic acid. Vinegar contains an acid called acetic acid (also called ethanoic acid).

Many people think of acids as dangerous substances. It is true that some acids can be dangerous and must be handled with care (e.g. the sulfuric acid in a car battery). However, as is clear from Figure 11.1, many other acids are part of our diet. For example, we find acetic acid (ethanoic acid) in vinegar, citric acid in oranges and lemons, and carbonic acid in fizzy drinks. Rainwater also contains carbonic acid and, therefore, is slightly acidic. Also, some acids are necessary to keep us healthy: vitamin C is an acid called ascorbic acid, soap contains the salt of an acid called stearic acid, and benzoic acid is used as a food preservative.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-194.jpg?height=1078&width=1177&top_left_y=2630&top_left_x=188)
Figure 11.1 Examples of everyday substances that contain acids

## OBJECTIVES

- To introduce students to commonly used substances classified as acids or bases.
- To give students an understanding of two important theories of acids and bases.
- To ensure that students know the main types of chemical reactions involving acids and bases.
- To give students experience of predicting products of reactions involving acids and bases and balancing chemical equations.

You may also remember that we met the word 'base' in studying chemistry at Junior Cycle level. A base is often called the 'chemical opposite' of an acid.

Some examples of common bases are shown in Figure 11.2.

One of the reasons why bases are called the 'chemical opposites' of acids is because they have the opposite effect to acids on litmus paper. While acids turn blue litmus paper red, bases turn red litmus paper blue, Figure 11.3.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-194.jpg?height=1078&width=1177&top_left_y=2630&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 11.2 Examples of everyday substances containing bases

- Bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis. Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda), NaOH , is an example of an alkali. It dissolves in water and is very corrosive - especially to skin!
- You may have some caustic soda at home as it is used to clear blocked drains. It works by breaking down the material blocking the drain. Always wear safety glasses and gloves when handling sodium hydroxide as it is highly corrosive.
- Bases are often used in products that remove grease. This is because they react with fats to form soap.
- Many household cleaners (e.g. oven cleaners and window cleaners) contain soluble bases to help remove grease. They convert oil and grease into soluble soaps, which are easily washed away.
- Another example of a base is magnesium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$, found in Milk of Magnesia and Maalox.
- Calcium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$, commonly called lime or slaked lime, produces 'limewater' when dissolved in water; limewater is used to

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-195.jpg?height=871&width=642&top_left_y=367&top_left_x=2116)
Figure 11.3 (a) Acids turn blue litmus paper red.
(b) Bases turn red litmus paper blue.

detect the presence of carbon dioxide.

We will be studying the reactions of acids and bases in more detail in this chapter and subsequent chapters. However, let us now go to Sweden where the first major attempt was made to accurately define the terms acid and base.

### 11.2 Arrhenius theory of acids and bases

In 1884 a young Swedish student called Svante Arrhenius submitted his PhD thesis at the University of Uppsala, Sweden, Figure 11.4. In his thesis, he put forward a theory that acid and bases when added to water dissociate (break up) into ions. Unfortunately, the examiners of his thesis were not impressed by his work, and he was awarded the lowest possible grade to pass the exam!

However, Arrhenius was not discouraged and moved to Stockholm University where his outstanding work was recognised. In 1903 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in chemistry for the thesis that was awarded such a low grade by his examiners. So if you ever feel disappointed that your chemistry teacher does not recognise that you are a genius, just think of Arrhenius!

Arrhenius defined an acid as follows:
Arrhenius definition: An acid is a substance that dissociates in water to produce

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-195.jpg?height=721&width=642&top_left_y=1894&top_left_x=2116)
Figure 11.4 The Swedish chemist Arrhenius put forward one of the first definitions of acids and bases.

$\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions.

For example, when hydrogen chloride is added to water, it dissociates, or breaks up, into $\mathrm{H}^{*}$ ions and $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ions:
$\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$

Similarly, the dissociation of nitric acid and sulfuric acid may be represented as:
$\mathrm{HNO}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$
$\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$

- A solution of hydrogen chloride gas in water is commonly called hydrochloric acid. Acids such as hydrochloric acid and nitric acid, molecules of which dissociate to give one $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion in aqueous solution, are called monobasic (or monoprotic) acids.

$$
\text { Monobasic: } \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}
$$

- Acids such as sulfuric acid, a molecule of which can dissociate to give $\mathbf{t w o} \mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in aqueous solution are called dibasic (or diprotic) acids.

$$
\text { Dibasic: } \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}
$$

- An acid such as phosphoric acid, $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{PO}_{4}$, a molecule of which can dissociate to give three $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in aqueous solution, is called a tribasic (or triprotic) acid.

$$
\text { Tribasic: } \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{PO}_{4} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{PO}_{4}^{3-}
$$

Acids such as hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid and nitric acid are described as strong acids since they fully dissociate in water, i.e. almost every molecule breaks up to give $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions.

On the contrary, acids such as ethanoic acid (acetic acid) and methanoic acid (formic acid) are described as weak acids since they dissociate only to a slight extent in water.

- As knowledge about atomic structure developed, chemists realised that a $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion (a hydrogen atom that had lost an electron) is simply a bare proton.
- Arrhenius did not realise that it was not possible for a bare proton to exist independently in solution.
- In fact, it was discovered that the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion actually reacts with a water molecule to form the $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$ion. The formation of this ion is shown in Figure 11.5.

Note in this diagram that one of the lone pairs on the oxygen atom forms a covalent bond with the proton. Both electrons in this bond come from the same atom (the oxygen atom). Such a bond is often called a dative covalent bond or a coordinate covalent bond. (The word 'dative' is a Latin word meaning 'giving' since the same atom gives

Arrhenius definition: A strong acid is a substance that almost completely dissociates in water to give hydrogen ions.

Arrhenius definition: A weak acid is a substance that only slightly dissociates in water to give hydrogen ions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-196.jpg?height=369&width=734&top_left_y=2246&top_left_x=1881)
Figure 11.5 The $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion reacts with a water molecule to form the $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$ion, which is called the hydronium ion (or oxonium ion).

both of the shared pair of electrons in the bond.)

The $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$ion is called the 'hydronium ion', the 'hydroxonium ion' and occasionally the 'oxonium ion'. In this textbook we use the term hydronium ion, since this term is the most widely used. The hydronium ion is a very common ion - it is present in every acidic solution.

Since aqueous solutions of acids contain $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$ions - and not $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions - it is more accurate to represent the dissociation of acids in water as:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{HA}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}+\mathrm{A}^{-} \\
\text {e.g. } \mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}
\end{gathered}
$$

For the sake of simplicity, many chemists use the term hydrogen ion when talking about acidic solutions - even though hydrogen ions do not exist in solution. The above equation recognises the essential role of the water molecules in the dissociation of acids. If substances such as pure ethanoic acid (acetic acid) or pure hydrogen chloride are added to solvents such as benzene or methylbenzene, no $\mathrm{H}^{+}$or $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$ions are found to be present. A piece of dry blue litmus paper added to these solutions does not show any colour change. Thus, substances such as ethanoic acid and hydrogen chloride only show acidic properties when dissolved in water.

## EXAM TIPI

If 'hydrogen chloride' or ' HCl ' is required as an answer in an exam, 'hydrochloric acid' will not be accepted as a correct answer. So read the question carefully!

In his study of bases, Arrhenius proposed the idea that bases dissociate into ions when added to water. He defined a base as follows:

Arrhenius definition: A base is a substance that dissociates in water to produce $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions.

The $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ion is commonly called the hydroxide ion. For example, when sodium hydroxide is added to water, it dissociates or breaks up into $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ions and $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions:
$\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-}$

Similarly, the dissociation of magnesium hydroxide and calcium hydroxide may be represented as:
$\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
$\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
Since sodium hydroxide dissociates almost completely in water to give $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions, it is referred to as a strong base, Figure 11.6.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-197.jpg?height=1010&width=1183&top_left_y=1136&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 11.6 Sodium hydroxide, NaOH , and calcium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$, are strong bases. However, magnesium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$, and aluminium hydroxide $\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{OH})_{3}$, are weak bases.

Arrhenius definition: A strong base is a substance that almost completely dissociates in water to give hydroxide (hydroxyl) ions.

The solubility of calcium hydroxide in water is low. However, the dissolved portion dissociates completely. Therefore, calcium hydroxide is classified as a strong base. On the other hand, magnesium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ and aluminium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{OH})_{3}$, dissociate only to a slight extent in water and hence are referred to as weak bases.

Arrhenius definition: A weak base is a substance that only slightly dissociates in water to give hydroxide ions.

## Shortcomings of the Arrhenius theory

Although the theory of acids and bases put forward by Arrhenius is a reasonably adequate one, it does have a number of shortcomings:

1. Hydronium ions. As already stated, it is hydronium ions, $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$, rather than the bare $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions suggested by Arrhenius, that exist in solution.
2. Aqueous solutions. Arrhenius restricted his definitions to aqueous solutions, i.e. reactions occurring in water. Solvents such as liquid ammonia, benzene and methylbenzene (toluene) are excluded from his definitions.
3. Dissolving in water. Not all acid-base reactions require water. For example, in Chapter 2 we learned that, when ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas come in contact with each other, white fumes of ammonium chloride are formed, Figure 11.7.

$$
\underset{\text { base }}{\mathrm{NH}_{3}}+\underset{\text { acid }}{\mathrm{HCl}} \rightarrow \underset{\text { ammonium chloride }}{\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{Cl}}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-198.jpg?height=890&width=1180&top_left_y=2031&top_left_x=188)
Figure 11.7 The reaction between HCl gas and $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ gas to form white fumes of $\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{Cl}$ is an acid-base reaction. However, since water is not involved, this would not be classified as an acid-base reaction using the Arrhenius theory

However, the Arrhenius definitions of acids and bases would not allow us to classify the above reaction as an acid-base reaction, since there is no water present.

In view of the limitations of the Arrhenius definitions, we now consider a more modern theory of acids and bases.

### 11.3 Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases

In 1923 Johannes Brønsted, a Danish chemist, and Thomas Lowry, an English chemist, independently of each other proposed new definitions of an acid and of a base, Figure 11.8.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-198.jpg?height=666&width=1186&top_left_y=891&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 11.8 Johannes Brønsted (right) and Thomas Lowry independently developed the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases.

Since the properties of acids and bases were, in many respects, opposed to each other, they believed it would make more sense to have definitions that were opposed to each other. These definitions are:

Brønsted-Lowry definition:
An acid is a proton donor.

## Brønsted-Lowry definition: <br> A base is a proton acceptor.

Let us now consider these definitions in a little more detail. When hydrogen chloride is added to water, we have already learned that the following reaction occurs:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-198.jpg?height=330&width=1105&top_left_y=2858&top_left_x=1438)

In this reaction we see that a molecule of HCl donates a proton to a molecule of water. Since HCl is a proton donor, it is classified as an acid. Since the molecule of water accepts a proton, it is classified as a base.

## Comparing the Arrhenius theory and the Brønsted-Lowry theory

1. The Arrhenius theory is limited to reactions in water (aqueous solutions). The Bronsted-Lowry theory is more general and not limited to reactions in water but also applies to reactions in the gaseous state and in solvents other than water. For example, in the above reaction between HCl and $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ in liquid ammonia or in the gaseous state, the hydrogen chloride molecule acts as an acid by donating a proton to the ammonia molecule. No water molecules are present.
2. The Arrhenius theory is limited to bases that produce hydroxide ions in water but not all bases produce hydroxide ions, e.g. there are no oxygen atoms in $\mathrm{NH}_{3} \mathrm{so}$ it is impossible for $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ to produce $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions.
3. Substances that would not be classified as acids or bases in the Arrhenius theory are classified as acids or bases in the Brønsted-Lowry theory, i.e. the Brønsted-Lowry definitions broaden the range of species that can be defined as acids and bases. For example, in reactions, both carbonate $\left(\mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-}\right)$ and hydrogencarbonate ions ( $\mathrm{HCO}_{3}{ }^{-}$) can accept $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions. Therefore, they are classified as bases by the Brønsted-Lowry theory but not by the Arrhenius theory.
4. The Arrhenius theory does not take the existence of hydronium ions into account but the BrønstedLowry theory does.
5. The Arrhenius theory cannot explain how a substance can act as both an acid and a base (i.e. an amphoteric substance) but the Brønsted-Lowry theory explains this in terms of proton transfer.

These points are summarised in Table 11.1.

| Feature | Arrhenius theory | Bronsted-Lowry theory |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Role of water | Limited to reactions in water. | Not limited to reactions in water. Can apply to reactions between gases and in solvents other than in water. |
| 2. Hydroxide ions | Limited to substances that produce hydroxide $\left(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right)$ions. | Applies to any substance that can accept a proton, e.g. the $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ molecule does not produce $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ ions. |
| 3. Classification as acids or bases | Only substances with $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions are classified as bases. Therefore, substances such as carbonate ions and hydrogencarbonate ions are not classified as bases by the Arrhenius theory. | Has a more general classification. Since carbonate and hydrogencarbonate ions can accept protons, these are classified as bases by the Brønsted-Lowry theory. |
| 4. Hydronium ion | Does not take the existence of hydronium ion into account. | Explains the existence of the hydronium ion. |
| 5. Amphoteric substances | Does not explain how a substance can act as both an acid and a base. | Explains amphoteric substances in terms of proton loss and proton gain. |

Table 11.1 Comparing the Arrhenius Theory and Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases

In short, the two theories are not in conflict with each other. The Brønsted-Lowry theory adds to the Arrhenius theory and improves our understanding of reactions involving acids and bases.

### 11.4 Conjugate acid-base pairs

Ethanoic acid (acetic acid), $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$, is the acid found in vinegar. When pure ethanoic acid is added to water, the following reaction occurs:

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}
$$

It is found that this reaction also takes place in the reverse direction, i.e. the following reaction also takes place:

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

We use the symbol like ⇌ to indicate that a reaction takes place in both directions:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH} & +\underset{2}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+} \\
\text {donates } & \text { accepts } \\
\text { a proton } & \text { a proton } \\
\therefore \mathrm{B} / \mathrm{L} \text { acid } & \therefore \mathrm{B} / \mathrm{L} \text { base }
\end{array}
$$

Consider the reaction in the forward direction. In this reaction, the $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ molecule donates a proton to the $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ molecule, i.e. the $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ molecule is behaving as an acid and the $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ molecule is behaving as a base. In the reverse direction, the $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$ion accepts a proton from the $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$ion, i.e. the $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$ion is behaving as a base and the $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$ion is behaving as an acid.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-201.jpg?height=264&width=1046&top_left_y=2552&top_left_x=351)

Note from the above equations that $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ changes into $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$by donating a proton. Also, $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$changes into $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ by accepting a proton. We say that $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$is the conjugate base of $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$.

An acid changes into its conjugate base when it donates a proton.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-201.jpg?height=147&width=1020&top_left_y=3480&top_left_x=358)
$\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ is said to be the conjugate acid of $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$.

A base changes into its conjugate acid when it accepts a proton.

$$
\underset{\text { base }}{\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \underset{\text { conjugate acid }}{\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}}
$$

Every acid has a conjugate base and every base has a conjugate acid.

Since $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ and $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$only differ by a proton, we refer to this pair as a conjugate acidbase pair or simply a conjugate pair.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-201.jpg?height=346&width=1066&top_left_y=1409&top_left_x=1601)

Similarly, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$are a conjugate acid-base pair, since they differ only by one proton.

A conjugate acid-base pair (conjugate pair) is any pair consisting of an acid and a base that differ by one proton.

Note from the definition that there is only a single (one) proton difference between the conjugate acid-base pair. Sometimes chemists use the formula HA to represent an acid. Its conjugate base is represented as $\mathrm{A}^{-}$and the equation relating them is then written as follows:
$\mathrm{HA} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A}^{-}+\mathrm{H}^{+}$

## EXAM TIPI

Since the definitions of a conjugate acid, conjugate base and conjugate acid-base pair all specify a single proton, it follows that the conjugate base of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ is $\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}$and not $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$.

## Example 11.1

## Question

What is (i) the conjugate acid, (ii) the conjugate base of $\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-}$?
[LCH]

## Answer

(i) A base changes into its conjugate acid by accepting a proton. Therefore, if $\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}{ }^{-}$is to change into its conjugate acid it must accept a proton, i.e. the following reaction must occur:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-}+\mathrm{H}^{+} & \rightarrow \underset{\text { conjugate acid }}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}} \\
\text { base } & \text { conjugate }
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the conjugate acid is $\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{2}} \mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{2}} \mathbf{O}_{\mathbf{4}}$.
(ii) An acid changes into its conjugate base by donating a proton. Therefore, if $\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-}$is to change into its conjugate base it must donate a proton, i.e. the following reaction must occur:

$$
\underset{\text { acid }}{\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{+}+\underset{2}{+} \mathrm{C}_{4}^{2-} ~ \text { conjugate base }
$$

Therefore, the conjugate base is $\mathbf{C}_{2} \mathbf{O}_{4}{ }^{2-}$.

## Example 11.2

## Question

Indicate which species are acting as acids and which are acting as bases:
$\mathrm{HNO}_{3}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~F}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{+}+\mathrm{HF}_{2}{ }^{-}$Also indicate the conjugate acid-base pairs.

## Answer

Working from left to right, we see that $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ accepts a proton from $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~F}_{2}$ i.e. $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ is acting as a base. The $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ changes into $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{+}$(the conjugate acid). $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~F}_{2}$ is acting as an acid since it donates a proton to $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$.

Working from right to left, we see that $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{+}$donates a proton to $\mathrm{HF}_{2}{ }^{-}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{+}$ is acting as an acid and $\mathrm{HF}_{2}{ }^{-}$is acting as a base.

We indicate the conjugate acid-base pairs by linking up the species that differ by a proton.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-202.jpg?height=340&width=1225&top_left_y=2656&top_left_x=208)

## EXAM TIPI

In an exam, it is very important that you clearly indicate the pairing as shown.

## Example 11.3

## Question

Explain, by giving a balanced equation for its dissociation in water, that the conjugate base of sulfuric acid is itself an acid.
[LCH]

## Answer

The conjugate base of sulfuric acid is $\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}$.
The balanced equation for its dissociation in water is:

$\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}+\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$
The $\mathrm{HSO}_{4}{ }^{-}$ion donates a proton to the water molecule, i.e. $\mathrm{HSO}_{4}{ }^{-}$is acting as an acid.

### 11.5 Types of reactions involving acids and bases

There are three types of reactions involving acids and bases on your course:

1. Acid-base neutralisation
2. Reactions between acids and carbonates
3. Reactions between acids and metals.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-203.jpg?height=317&width=1209&top_left_y=615&top_left_x=1510)

### 11.5.1 Neutralisation

When acids and bases react with each other in the right proportions, it is found that they 'cancel' each other out and both the acid and the base lose their characteristic properties. Since the solution formed has no effect on litmus (i.e. the solution is neutral), the process is called neutralisation.

Consider the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, Figure 11.10.

$$
\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-203.jpg?height=319&width=1724&top_left_y=1602&top_left_x=328)
Figure 11.10 The reaction between an acid and a base produces a salt.

Note that the reaction between the acid and the base produces a salt - in this case, sodium chloride or common table salt. The word 'salt' is a general term and is defined as follows:

A salt is the substance formed when the hydrogen ion from an acid is replaced by a metal or by an ammonium ion.

Thus, when the hydrogen ion from hydrochloric acid HCl is replaced by a

Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water.

The process of neutralisation may be defined as: sodium ion, the salt sodium chloride, NaCl is formed. When the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion in $\mathrm{HCl}_{(a a)}$ is replaced by $\mathrm{NH}_{4}{ }^{+}$, the salt ammonium chloride, $\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{Cl}$, is formed. $\left[\mathrm{HCl}_{(\mathrm{aq})}\right.$ is hydrochloric acid]

It is worth remembering the following, if you are ever asked to write a chemical equation for a neutralisation reaction.

In order to understand what is happening in a neutralisation reaction, consider the ions that are present in solution.

$$
\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

i.e. in solution: $\mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}+\mathrm{Na}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
If we ignore the ions that are present on both sides of the equation ('spectator ions'), the above equation becomes:

$$
\mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Thus, neutralisation occurs because the hydrogen ions (or more precisely the hydronium ions) from the acid react with the hydroxide ions from the base to form water. Some examples of neutralisation reactions are given in Table 11.2.

|  | acid | + | base | → | salt |  | + water |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ sulfuric acid | + | 2 NaOH sodium hydroxide | → | $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ sodium sulfate |  | $+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ water |
| 2. | HCI hydrochloric acid | + | KOH potassium hydroxide | → | KCl potassium chloride |  | $+ \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ water |
| 3. | 2 HCl hydrochloric acid | $+$ | $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ magnesium hydroxide | → | $\mathrm{MgCl}_{2}$ magnesium chloride |  | $+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ water |
| 4. | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ sulfuric acid | $+$ | $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ calcium hydroxide | → | $\mathrm{CaSO}_{4}$ calcium sulfate |  | $+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ water |
| 5. | $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ nitric acid | + | NaOH sodium hydroxide | → | $\mathrm{NaNO}_{3}$ sodium nitrate |  | $+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ water |
| 6. | $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{PO}_{4}$ phosphoric acid | $+$ | 3 KOH potassium hydroxide | → | $\mathrm{K}_{3} \mathrm{PO}_{4}$ potassium phosphate |  | $+ 3 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ water |

Table 11.2 Some examples of balanced chemical equations for the reaction of acids and bases

## Examples of neutralisation in our everyday lives

1. Medicine. Hydrochloric acid is produced by the stomach to help digest food. Sometimes the stomach produces too much HCl as a result of for example overeating or stress. If this condition persists, the lining of the stomach may be damaged and this may give rise to ulcers. Relief from excess HCl may be obtained by taking an antacid preparation that contains a base to neutralise the excess HCl , Figure 11.11.

For example, Alka-Seltzer and Bisodol contain sodium hydrogencarbonate, which reduces the acidity in the stomach by the following neutralisation reaction:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-204.jpg?height=711&width=1027&top_left_y=1744&top_left_x=1588)
Figure 11.11 Some indigestion remedies that are used to neutralise excess acid in the stomach

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\mathrm{HCl} & +\mathrm{NaHCO}_{3} & \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{CO}_{2} \\
\begin{array}{l}
\text { hydrochloric } \\
\text { acid }
\end{array} & \underset{\text { hydrogencarbonate }}{\text { sodium }} \rightarrow \begin{array}{c}
\text { sodium } \\
\text { chloride }
\end{array}+\text { water }+\begin{array}{l}
\text { carbon } \\
\text { dioxide }
\end{array}
\end{array}
$$

Similarly, Milk of Magnesia, and Maalox contain magnesium hydroxide, which reacts with the hydrochloric acid as follows:

```
2HCl}+\textrm{Mg(OH)}\mp@subsup{)}{2}{}->\mp@subsup{\textrm{MgCl}}{2}{}+2\mp@subsup{\textrm{H}}{2}{}\textrm{O
hydrochloric + magnesium → magnesium + water
acid hydroxide chloride
```

2. Agriculture. If soil is too acidic, the yield of crops tends to be low, e.g. wheat and barley grow best in soils which are approximately neutral or slightly basic. Therefore, farmers often spread lime on soil to neutralise the acidity in the soil, Figure 11.12. Lime is calcium oxide, CaO , also known as quicklime. The calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$, commonly called slaked lime. (Ground limestone (calcium carbonate, $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ ), may also be used.)

$$
\underset{\substack{\text { calcium } \\
\text { oxide }}}{\mathrm{CaO}}+\underset{\text { water }}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}} \rightarrow \quad \rightarrow \quad \begin{gathered}
\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2} \\
\text { calcium } \\
\text { hydroxide }
\end{gathered}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-205.jpg?height=714&width=1066&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1692)
Figure 11.12 Lime had been spread on these fields to neutralise the acidity in the soil.

Calcium hydroxide neutralises the acidity in the soil as follows:

$$
\underset{\substack{\text { sulfuric } \\ \text { acid }}}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}}+\underset{\substack{\text { calcium } \\ \text { hydroxide }}}{\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{\substack{\text { calcium } \\ \text { sulfate }}}{\mathrm{CaSO}_{4}}+\underset{\text { water }}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

3. Environmental protection. In areas that suffer from acid rain, limestone is often added to lakes to neutralise the acidity.

$$
\underset{\substack{\text { sulfuric } \\ \text { acid }}}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}}+\underset{\text { limestone }}{\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}} \rightarrow \underset{\substack{\text { calcium } \\ \text { sulfate }}}{\mathrm{CaSO}_{4}}+\underset{\text { water }}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}+\underset{\substack{\text { carbon } \\ \text { dioxide }}}{\mathrm{CO}_{2}}
$$

Limestone is often used in the tall chimneys of coal-burning power plants. The limestone neutralises the acidic substances formed as a result of burning coal.
4. Miscellaneous. Toothpaste is slightly basic to neutralise the acids in the foods that cause tooth decay. Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) is used to neutralise the acidic sting of bees. Vinegar is used to neutralise the alkaline sting of wasps. Shampoo is slightly basic and this can cause the scales that coat the surface of each hair to open out. Hair conditioner is slightly acidic to neutralise the base in shampoo. This causes the scales on each hair to close down and leaves the hair more manageable and shiny, Figure 11.13.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-205.jpg?height=1036&width=1670&top_left_y=2835&top_left_x=323)
Figure 11.13 The reaction between hair conditioner and shampoo is an example of a neutralisation reaction.

### 11.5.2 Reactions between acids and carbonates

In the previous section, we studied neutralisation reactions. You will have noticed that in some cases, we took the reaction between acids and carbonates as examples of neutralisation reactions. Carbonates are good examples of bases because the carbonate ion is a proton acceptor. The general reaction between an acid and carbonate may be summarised as follows:
Acid + Carbonate → Salt + Water + Carbon Dioxide

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-206.jpg?height=636&width=1137&top_left_y=299&top_left_x=1500)
Figure 11.14 The reaction between hydrochloric acid and marble chips forms calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. Note the bubbles of carbon dioxide being produced.

One of the best-known examples of this type of reaction is used in the preparation of carbon dioxide gas. Note the fizzing that takes place when hydrochloric acid is added to calcium carbonate (also called limestone or marble).

$\underset{\substack{\text { hydrochloric } \\ \text { acid }}}{2 \mathrm{HCl}}+\underset{\substack{\text { calcium } \\ \text { carbonate }}}{\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}} \rightarrow \underset{\substack{\text { calcium } \\ \text { chloride }}}{\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}}+\underset{\text { water }}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}+\underset{\substack{\text { carbon } \\ \text { dioxide }}}{\mathrm{CO}_{2}}$

Note the bubbles of carbon dioxide formed in the above reaction, Figure 11.14.
The above reaction is responsible for the damage caused to limestone buildings and statues by acid rain, Figure 11.15.

Some further examples of acid-carbonate reactions are given in Table 11.3. You don't have to learn these off, but note the reaction that is common to all of them.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-206.jpg?height=655&width=630&top_left_y=1224&top_left_x=2011)
Figure 11.15 This limestone statue has been worn away by the reaction between acid rain and calcium carbonate.

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ sulfuric acid | + | $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ calcium carbonate | → | $\mathrm{CaSO}_{4}$ calcium sulfate | + | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ water |  |
| 2. | 2 HCl hydrochloric acid | + | $\mathrm{MgCO}_{3}$ magnesium carbonate | → | $\mathrm{MgCl}_{2}$ magnesium chloride | $+$ | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+$ water | $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ carbon dioxide |
| 3. | 2 HCl hydrochloric acid | $+$ | $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ sodium carbonate | → | 2 NaCl sodium chloride | + | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+$ water | $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ carbon dioxide |
| 4. | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ sulfuric acid | $+$ | $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ sodium carbonate | → | $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ sodium sulfate | $+$ | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+$ water | $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ carbon dioxide |
| 5. | $2 \mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ nitric acid | + | $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ sodium carbonate | → | $2 \mathrm{NaNO}_{3}$ sodium nitrate | $+$ | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+$ water | $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ carbon dioxide |

| 8. | $2 \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{PO}_{4}$ phosphoric acid | $+$ | $3 \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ sodium carbonate | → | $2 \mathrm{Na}_{3} \mathrm{PO}_{4}$ sodium phosphate | $+$ | $3 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+$ water | $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ carbon dioxide |

## Summary What I should know

- There are many everyday substances that contain acids or bases.
- The Arrhenius definition of an acid is that it is a substance that dissociates in water to produce $\mathrm{H}^{\prime}$ ions.
- The Arrhenius definition of a base is that it is a substance that dissociates in water to produce $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions.
- Arrhenius definitions: A strong acid is a substance that almost completely dissociates in water to give hydrogen ions. A weak acid is a substance that only slightly dissociates in water to give hydrogen ions. A strong base is a substance that almost completely dissociates in water to give hydroxide ions. A weak base is a substance that only slightly dissociates in water to give hydroxide ions.
- The Brønsted-Lowry definition of an acid is that an acid is a proton donor.
- The Brønsted-Lowry definition of a base is that a base is a proton acceptor.
- Brønsted-Lowry definitions: A strong acid is a good proton donor. A weak acid is a poor proton donor. A strong base is a good proton acceptor. A weak base is a poor proton acceptor.

A substance that can act both as an acid and as a base is said to be amphoteric or amphiprotic.
An acid changes into its conjugate base when it donates a proton.
A base changes into its conjugate acid when it accepts a proton.
A conjugate acid-base pair (conjugate pair) is defined as any pair consisting of an acid and a base that differ by one proton.

Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water.
Acid + Carbonate → Salt + Water + Carbon Dioxide
Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen gas
