# 12 Volumetric Analysis: Acid-Base

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-210.jpg?height=470&width=1264&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=188)

### 12.1 Introduction

In Chapter 11, we studied how the composition of substances could be determined by careful weighing. We called this method of analysis gravimetric analysis. Gravimetric analysis is one of the branches of quantitative analysis, i.e. finding the quantities or amounts of materials present. (Do not confuse this with qualitative analysis, where we simply identify the presence of substances without finding the quantities present, e.g. testing for anions in Experiment 5.1 is an example of qualitative analysis.) The other main branch of quantitative analysis is volumetric analysis. As the name suggests, this method of analysis involves reacting volumes of solutions with each other.

Volumetric analysis has many applications not only in the school laboratory but also in industry and in research, Figure 12.1. For example, in this chapter, we will use volumetric analysis to find the amount of ethanoic acid (acetic acid) in a sample of vinegar. Before learning the techniques of volumetric analysis, we must first study how chemists express the concentrations of solutions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-210.jpg?height=909&width=1180&top_left_y=2689&top_left_x=188)
Figure 12.1 Volumetric analysis is being used by this laboratory technician in Inniscarra Water Quality Laboratory, Co. Cork, to measure the hardness of water.

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an introduction to chemical solutions and concepts associated with chemical solutions.
- To make students familiar with the units for expressing concentrations of solutions.
- To provide students with the opportunity to determine the concentrations of substances being analysed in volumetric analysis.


### 12.2 Expressing the concentrations of solutions

You may recall at Junior Cycle that we dissolved copper sulfate in water when making crystals of copper sulfate. The substance that dissolves in the water is called the solute. In this case, the solute is copper sulfate. The substance that dissolves the solute is called the solvent. In this case, the solvent is water. The solute and solvent together form a perfect mixture which is called a solution.

A solution is a completely perfect mixture of a solute and a solvent. In a solution, the particles of the solute are uniformly distributed throughout the solvent, i.e. the mixture is homogeneous.

Note that when a solution is formed, it is no longer possible to distinguish between the particles of the solute and the particles of the solvent, Figure 12.2. The word used in the English language to describe this is homogeneous (from the Greek 'of the same type') to emphasise that the solution looks the same throughout the flask.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-210.jpg?height=897&width=617&top_left_y=2955&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 12.2 All of these solutions of coloured salts in water are perfect mixtures. Note that solutions are always clear. You can no longer see the individual solute and solvent used to make up the solution.

Solutions are always clear, as you can no longer see the individual solute and solvent.

- Solute: The substance that dissolves in a solvent to form a solution. It is usually present in a smaller amount. For example, in saltwater, salt (NaCl) is the solute because it dissolves in the water.
- Solvent: The substance that dissolves the solute, forming a solution. It is usually present in a larger amount. For example, in saltwater, water ( $\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{2}} \mathbf{O}$ ) is the solvent because it dissolves the salt.
- Solution: A homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent, where the particles are evenly distributed. For example, saltwater is a solution because salt (the solute) is completely dissolved in water (the solvent), forming a uniform mixture.

Since there is no boundary between the particles (salt ions and water molecules) in a salt water solution, we say that they are in the same phase or homogeneous. Although the most common type of solution is where the solute is a solid and the solvent is a liquid, solutes and solvents can be solids, liquids or gases.

- If there is a large amount of solute relative to the quantity of solvent, the solution is said to be concentrated.
- If there is only a small amount of solute relative to the quantity of solvent, the solution is said to be dilute.
- Chemists often need to know the exact amount of solute present in a certain volume of solution. A chemist who is analysing polluted water, for example, must very accurately measure the quantity of oxygen dissolved in the water.

The precise amount of solute in a given amount of solution is referred to as the concentration of the solution.

There are a number of different ways of expressing the concentration of a solution.

The concentration of a solution is the amount of solute that is dissolved in a given volume of solution.

### 12.2.1 Percentage of solute

This method of expressing concentration is used for many household solutions as well as in the areas of biochemistry and medicine, Figure 12.3.

There are three ways in which the percentage of solute in a solution is expressed:

## 1. Weight per weight ( $\mathrm{w} / \mathrm{w}$ )

- A solution labelled $10 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{w} \mathrm{NaCl}$ means that there are 10 g of sodium chloride per 100 g of solution.
- This solution is made up by weighing out 10 g of the salt, dissolving it in water, and then adding more water until the total mass of the solution is 100 grams.
This can also be summarised by the formula:
$\frac{\text { Mass of NaCl }}{\text { Total mass of solution }} \times 100=\frac{10 \mathrm{~g}}{100 \mathrm{~g}}=10 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{w}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-211.jpg?height=893&width=864&top_left_y=2516&top_left_x=1894)
Figure 12.3 Note that the concentration of the active ingredient in this medicine is given as \% $\mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$.

## 2 Weight per volume (w/v)

- A solution labelled $10 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v} \mathrm{NaCl}$ means that there are 10 g of sodium chloride per $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution.
- This solution is made up by weighing out 10 g of the salt, dissolving it in water, and then adding more water until the total volume of the solution is $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.
- The concentration of glucose solution is usually stated as \% w/v, Figure 12.4.

This can also be summarised by the formula:

$$
\frac{\text { Mass of NaCl }}{\text { Total volume of solution }} \times 100=\frac{10 \mathrm{~g}}{100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}}=10 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}
$$

## 3. Volume per volume (v/v)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-212.jpg?height=792&width=1095&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1523)
Figure 12.4 Patients are often fed glucose intravenously. The glucose solution is normally about $4 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$ concentration.

- This method of expressing concentration involves a liquid solute dissolved in a liquid solvent, i.e. the solution is made from two liquids.
- A solution of ethanol marked $10 \% \mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}$ has $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of ethanol per 100 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of solution.
- This solution is made up by measuring out $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of ethanol, adding it to water, and then adding more water until the volume of the solution is $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.

This can also be summarised by the formula:

$$
\frac{\text { Volume of alcohol }}{\text { Total volume of solution }} \times 100=\frac{10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}}{100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}}=10 \% \mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}
$$

- The amount of alcohol in alcoholic drinks is usually given in terms of percentage ( $\mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}$ ), e.g. beer and cider are about $4-5 \% \mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}$, wine is $10- 12 \% \mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}$, sherry is $20 \% \mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}$, and spirits (whiskey, gin and vodka) have an alcohol content of $40 \% \mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}$, Figure 12.5. The high concentration of alcohol in spirits explains why drinking spirits is particularly harmful to your health. Alcohol is a toxic substance, and when consumed, it must be broken down in the liver and removed from the body. However, the liver can only metabolise a limited amount per hour, so excessive drinking can harm your health in many ways, including liver damage, impaired brain function, and long-term health risks such as liver cirrhosis and addiction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-212.jpg?height=913&width=303&top_left_y=1435&top_left_x=2116)
Figure 12.5 Due to the high $\% \mathrm{v} / \mathrm{v}$ of alcohol in spirits, drinking spirits is particularly harmful to your health.

## Example 12.1

## Question

Some illnesses can upset the salt balance in the body and it may be necessary for a doctor or nurse to administer salt intravenously. The solution of salt that is injected is marked $0.85 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$. What mass of sodium chloride is needed to make up $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of this solution?

## Answer

$0.85 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$ means that there are 0.85 g NaCl per $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ solution.
Therefore, there are $0.85 \times 2.5=2.125 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{NaCl}$ per $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ solution.
Answer: 2.125 g NaCl

## Example 12.2

## Question

65 g of a solution contains 8 g of solute. Express the concentration of this solution as $\% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{w}$.

## Answer

$$
\% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{w}=\frac{\text { Mass of solute }}{\text { Total mass of solution }} \times 100=\frac{8 \mathrm{~g}}{65 \mathrm{~g}} \times 100=12.31 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{w}
$$

### 12.2.2 Parts per million (ppm)

This method of expressing the concentration of a solution is only used for very dilute solutions. It is particularly useful in water analysis, where you are dealing with very low concentrations of certain substances, perhaps only a few milligrams of a substance in a litre of water, Figure 12.6.

1 mg per litre $=1$ mg per 1000 grams of water (the density of water is $1 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$ )

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =1 \mathrm{mg} \text { per } 1000 \times 1000 \mathrm{mg} \text { of water } \\
& =1 \mathrm{mg} \text { per million } \mathrm{mg} \\
& =1 \mathrm{ppm}
\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, $\mathbf{1 ~ p p m}=\mathbf{1 ~ m g} / \mathbf{L}$
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-213.jpg?height=941&width=945&top_left_y=957&top_left_x=1813)

For example, a chemist may report that the concentration of chlorine in water is 2 ppm . This means that there are two milligrams of chlorine per litre of water.

## Example 12.3

## Question

On analysing a sample of water, a chemist found that $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of it contain 0.005 g of calcium carbonate. What is the concentration of calcium carbonate in ppm?

## Answer

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.005 \mathrm{~g} \text { per } 100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} & =0.005 \times 10 \mathrm{~g} \text { per litre } \\
& =0.05 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L} \\
& =0.05 \times 1000 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L} \\
& =50 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L} \\
& =50 \mathrm{ppm}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: 50 ppm

### 12.2.3 Moles of solute per litre of solution (molarity)

The most important method of expressing the concentration of a solution is in terms of moles of solute per litre of solution. This is called the molarity of the solution.

The molarity of a solution is the number of moles of solute per litre of solution.

- The symbol for molarity is $\mathbf{M}$ or $\mathbf{~ m o l} \mathbf{/ L}$ (moles per litre).
- It is more usual to use the symbol M instead of $\mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{L}$. Therefore, if a solution contains 1 mole of solute per litre of solution, we say that the concentration of the solution is 1 M or $1 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$.
- In the S.I. system of units, the symbol $\mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{L}$ is recommended rather than M. However, since the term molarity and its symbol M are used so widely in industry and at third level, it is important for students to realise that the two terms are identical, i.e. $\mathbf{1} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{~ N a O H}=\mathbf{1} \mathbf{~ m o l} / \mathbf{L} \mathbf{~ N a O H}$.
- Whenever the symbol M is used, always make sure that it is used in conjunction with a chemical formula, e.g. a 1 M NaOH solution means a sodium hydroxide solution that has a concentration of 1 mole per litre. Thus a $1 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$ solution of sodium hydroxide contains 40 grams of sodium hydroxide ( $\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{r}}$ of $\mathrm{NaOH}=40$ ) per litre of solution. Since it is important in volumetric analysis to have solutions whose concentrations are accurately known, we usually use a flask called a volumetric flask when making up solutions, Figure 12.7. The correct procedure for using a volumetric flask to prepare a definite volume of solution will be studied at a later stage.
- Suppose that two moles of sodium hydroxide ( 80 g ) are dissolved in water and the solution is made up to the graduation mark in a 1 litre flask. The concentration of this solution is $2 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$ or 2 M .
- Similarly, a solution which is marked $0.5 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$ or 0.5 M will contain only half a mole of sodium hydroxide ( 20 g ) per litre of solution.
- A solution that contains one-tenth of a mole per litre is often said to be decimolar ( 0.1 M ), e.g. a decimolar solution of sodium hydroxide contains 4 g (one-tenth of a mole) per litre of solution.


### 12.3 Converting moles per litre to grams per litre

Chemists often find it necessary when carrying out volumetric analysis to convert from concentrations expressed in moles per litre to concentrations expressed in grams per litre. The method of carrying out this conversion is shown in the following examples.

## Example 12.4

A 1 M (one molar) solution is one that contains one mole of the solute dissolved in one litre of solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-214.jpg?height=863&width=486&top_left_y=755&top_left_x=2103)
Figure 12.7 If one mole of a substance is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to the litre mark, we have a $1 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$ (1 molar $=1 \mathrm{M})$ solution.

## Question

How many grams of NaCl per litre are present in a solution marked 0.25 MNaCl ? (Na=23, Cl=35.5)

## Answer

Rel. Molecular Mass of NaCl $=23+35.5=58.5$
A 1 M NaCl solution contains 58.5 grams per litre.
∴ a 0.25 M NaCl solution contains $58.5 \times 0.25=14.625 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$
Answer: 14.625 grams NaCl per litre.

## Example 12.5

## Question

Calculate the concentration in grams per litre of bench dilute sulfuric acid whose concentration is $1.5 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L} .(\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{O}=16, \mathrm{~S}=32)$

## Answer

Rel. Molecular Mass of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}=2(1)+32+4(16)=98$
A $1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ solution contains 98 grams per litre.
∴ a $1.5 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ solution contains $98 \times 1.5=147 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$
Answer: 147 grams $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ per litre.

### 12.4 Converting grams per litre to moles per litre (molarity)

This type of calculation is met very often in volumetric analysis. Study the following examples carefully.

## Example 12.6

## Question

What is the molarity of a solution that contains 3.68 g of NaOH per litre of solution? ( $\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{O}=16, \mathrm{Na}=23$ )

## Answer

Rel. Molecular Mass of NaOH $=23+16+1=40$
40 g in 1 L solution $\rightarrow 1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaOH}$ solution
1 g in 1 L solution $\rightarrow \frac{1}{40} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaOH}$ solution
3.68 g in 1 L solution $\rightarrow \frac{3.68}{40} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaOH}$ solution
$=0.092 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaOH}$ solution
Answer: 0.092 M NaOH .

## Example 12.7

## Question

Calculate the concentration in moles per litre of a solution containing 45 grams of sulfuric acid per $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution. ( $\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{O}=16, \mathrm{~S}=32$ )

## Answer

Rel. Molecular Mass of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}=2(1)+32+4(16)=98$
$98 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ in 1L solution $\quad \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{M}$ solution
$1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ in 1 L solution $\quad \rightarrow \frac{1}{98} \mathrm{M}$ solution
$45 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ in 1 L solution $\quad \rightarrow \frac{45}{98} \mathrm{M}$ solution
$45 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ in $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ solution $\rightarrow \frac{4 \times 45}{98}$ M solution

$$
=1.84 \mathrm{M}
$$

Answer: The concentration of the solution is 1.84 M .

Study the last step of Example 12.7 carefully.

- Since the sulfuric acid is actually dissolved in only $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution, the concentration of the solution is four times higher than it would be if it were dissolved in a litre.
- If you find this difficult to understand, studying the dissolving of copper sulfate in water may help, Figure 12.8.
- As the concentration increases the intensity of the colour also increases.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-215.jpg?height=786&width=333&top_left_y=2942&top_left_x=1305)
1 mole/L

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-215.jpg?height=746&width=271&top_left_y=3086&top_left_x=1627)
Figure 12.8 If the same mass of solute is dissolved in different quantities of water, the smaller the volume of water, the higher the concentration.

Figure 12.8 If the same mass of solute is dissolved in different quantities of water, the smaller the volume of water, the higher the concentration.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-215.jpg?height=604&width=558&top_left_y=3235&top_left_x=1920)

### 12.5 Using (i) first principles and (ii) a formula to calculate the number of moles given the volume and the molarity of a solution

In all examples studied so far in this chapter, we have worked out the answers from first principles. This means that we solved all the problems using the basic definitions without have to use any formulas. In the next example, we will first solve the problem using first principles and then derive a general formula to help in this type of calculation.

Chemists, having prepared a solution in a volumetric flask, usually take a smaller quantity (e.g. $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ ) of the solution out of the volumetric flask in order to perform various experiments in volumetric analysis. When using this smaller volume, it is necessary to be able to answer questions like that given in Example 12.8.

## Example 12.8

## Question

How many moles of NaOH are present in $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.55 M NaOH ?

## Answer

By definition:
1 litre of 0.55 M NaOH contains 0.55 moles NaOH .
i.e. $1000 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.55 M NaOH contains 0.55 moles NaOH
$\therefore 1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.55 M NaOH contains moles $\frac{0.55}{1000}$ moles NaOH
$\therefore 25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.55 M NaOH contains $\frac{25 \times 0.55}{1000}$ moles NaOH
$=0.014$ moles NaOH .
Answer: 0.014 moles
In general, if the volume is given in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ and the concentration in molarity (moles per litre), the number of moles may be calculated from the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Number of moles }=\frac{\text { volume } * \times \text { molarity }}{1000} \\
& \left({ }^{*} \text { in } \mathrm{cm}^{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a very useful expression and is worth learning off.

## Example 12.9

## Question

How many moles of hydrochloric acid are present in $30 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.2 M HCl ?

## Answer

$$
\text { Number of moles of } \begin{aligned}
\mathrm{HCl} & =\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000} \\
& =\frac{30 \times 0.2}{1000} \\
& =0.006 \text { moles }
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: 0.006 mol

## Example 12.10

## Question

What mass of sodium hydroxide is contained in $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of a 0.75 M solution of sodium hydroxide? $(\mathrm{H}=1,0=16, \mathrm{Na}=23)$

Answer

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Number of moles } & =\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000} \\
& =\frac{25 \times 0.75}{1000} \\
& =0.019 \text { moles } \\
& =0.019 \times 40 \mathrm{~g}\left(M_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{NaOH}=40\right) \\
& =0.76 \mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: 0.76 g

## Example 12.11

## Question

What volume of 0.15 M sodium hydroxide solution will contain 5 grams of sodium hydroxide?
( $\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{O}=16, \mathrm{Na}=23$ )

## Answer

First convert 5 grams to moles.
Calculate the volume using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { No. of moles of NaOH } & =\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Rel. Molecular Mass }} \\
& =\frac{5}{40} \\
& =0.125 \text { moles }
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { No. of moles } & =\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000} \\
\qquad 0.125 & =\frac{\text { volume } \times 0.15}{1000} \\
\frac{0.125 \times 1000}{0.15} & =\text { volume } \\
\text { i.e. volume } & =833.33 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \\
\text { Answer } & =833.33 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

TEST YOURSELF: Attempt Questions 12.3-12.4 and W12.3-W12.5.

### 12.6 Reaction between a solution and a solid

In a number of chemical reactions, solids react with solutions, e.g. as discussed in Chapter 11, many metals react with acidic solutions. Examples 12.12 and 12.13 (online) show how we can calculate the mass of a solid that reacts with a given volume of solution.

## Example 12.12

## Question

What mass of magnesium will react with $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of $0.5 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ ? The balanced equation for the reaction is:
$\mathrm{Mg}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgSO}_{4}+\mathrm{H}_{2}$

## Answer

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { No. of moles of acid } & =\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000} \\
& =\frac{50 \times 0.5}{1000} \\
& =0.025 \text { moles }
\end{aligned}
$$

From the balanced equation, one mole of sulfuric acid reacts with one mole of magnesium.
Therefore, moles of magnesium which react:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =0.025 \\
& =0.025 \times 24 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{Mg} \\
& =0.6 \mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: 0.6 g magnesium.

### 12.7 Dilution of solutions

Many common laboratory reagents are purchased as solutions of high concentration, e.g. the concentration of sulfuric acid supplied to laboratories is 18 M . Some of the common laboratory reagents and their concentrations as supplied are given in Table 12.2.

| Substance | Concentration |
| :--- | :---: |
| Sulfuric acid | 18 M |
| Nitric acid | 16 M |
| Hydrochloric acid | 12 M |
| Ammonia | 16 M |
| Ethanoic acid (acetic acid) | 17 M |

Table 12.2 The concentrations of common reagents as supplied to laboratories.

- For most laboratory experiments, these reagents must be used in their diluted state, e.g. the concentration of 'bench' dilute hydrochloric acid and 'bench' dilute ammonia is only 3 M approx.
- When a solution is diluted, more solvent is added but the quantity of solute is unchanged.
- Since the volume of the solution increases and the same number of moles is present, then the concentration of the solution must decrease, Figure 12.9.


## Example 12.14

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-218.jpg?height=997&width=1180&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 12.9 Adding water does not affect the amount of solute present but does reduce the concentration of the solution.

In order to dilute a concentrated solution to give a dilute solution of known concentration, it is important to remember that the number of moles of solute in the diluted solution is the same as the number of moles of solute in the concentrated solution.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-218.jpg?height=392&width=1134&top_left_y=2011&top_left_x=1438)

We use this relationship to solve problems on dilution as shown in Examples 12.14 and 12.15 (online).

Note: It does not matter what units are used to express the concentration, as long as the same units are used on each side of the equation.

## Question

What volume of 12 M HCl solution is required to make up $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 3 M HCl solution?

## Answer

No. of moles of solute in diluted solution = No. of moles of solute in concentrated solution
i.e. $\frac{\mathrm{Vol}_{\text {dil }} \times \mathrm{M}_{\text {dil }}}{1000}=\frac{\mathrm{Vol}_{\text {conc }} \times \mathrm{M}_{\text {conc }}}{1000}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
500 \times 3 & =\mathrm{Vol}_{c o n c} \times 12 \\
\mathrm{Vol}_{c o n c} & =\frac{500 \times 3}{12} \\
\mathrm{Vol}_{c o n c} & =125 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $125 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the concentrated acid would have to be diluted to $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.

## Example 12.17

## Question

A solution containing $150 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$ is diluted twice by $1: 10$ and once by $1: 5$. What is the final concentration of the solution in grams per litre?

## Answer

## Step 1

After one dilution 1:10 the concentration will be $15 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$.

## Step 2

After the second dilution of 1:10 the concentration will be $1.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$.

## Step 3

After the third dilution of $1: 5$ the concentration will be $0.3 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$.

### 12.1 Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 5

Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 5 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To prepare a series of 1:10 serial dilutions of a stock potassium permanganate, $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$, solution and investigate how the concentration decreases at each step

Note that potassium permanganate is also called potassium manganate(VII).
We will explain the origin of this name in Chapter 14.

## Introduction

In this experiment, we will investigate how to perform a number of simple dilutions to produce a range of solutions of different concentrations. We will use a dilution factor of 1:10. In other words, the concentration of each diluted solution is one-tenth of the concentration of the solution from which it has been made. The source of solution to be diluted comes from the diluted solution of the previous step. The key steps involved in a serial dilution are summarised in Figure 12.12.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-220.jpg?height=851&width=343&top_left_y=2633&top_left_x=429)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-220.jpg?height=775&width=1088&top_left_y=2728&top_left_x=1038)
Figure 12.12 In a serial dilution, the concentration of each diluted solution is a fraction of the concentration of the solution from which it has been made. In the example shown, the dilution factor is $1: 10$.

Stock solution of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$

## Key steps in procedure

1．Using a graduated dropper（also called a graduated Pasteur pipette），a volume of $9 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of deionised water is placed in each of five test－tubes．The graduated Pasteur pipettes are usually graduated up to $3 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ ．
2．Each test－tube is labelled 1 to 5 ．Some of the stock solution is poured into a small beaker． A graduated dropper is used to transfer $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the stock $0.05 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution from the beaker into test tube 1．（Dilution 1）．

3．Test－tube 1 is gently shaken to ensure a homogeneous mixture．
4．A clean graduated dropper is used to transfer $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the dilute $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution from test－tube 1 to test－tube 2．（Dilution 2）．
5．Test－tube 2 is gently shaken to ensure a homogeneous mixture．
6．A clean graduated dropper is used to transfer $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the dilute $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution from test－tube 2 to test－tube 3．（Dilution 3）．
7．Test－tube 3 is gently shaken to ensure a homogeneous mixture．
8．A clean graduated dropper is used to transfer $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the dilute $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution from test－tube 3 to test－tube 4．（Dilution 4）．
9．Test－tube 4 is shaken to ensure a homogeneous mixture．
10．A clean graduated dropper is used to transfer $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the dilute $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution from test－tube 4 to test－tube 5．（Dilution 5）．
11．Test－tube 5 is shaken to ensure a homogeneous mixture．

## Observation

－The colour of the diluted solution in each test－tube is a lighter shade of purple compared to the solution from which it has been made．

## Conclusion

－Since we started with a 0.05 M solution，we have made a series of solutions of concentration 0.005 M （in test－tube 1）， 0.0005 M （in test－tube 2）， 0.00005 M （in test－tube 3）， 0.000005 M （in test－tube 4）and 0.0000005 M （in test－tube 5）．This is illustrated in Figure 12．12．

In Experiment 12．1，we used a $1: 10$ dilution．If for example，the dilution is $1: 2$ ，then we would add $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution to $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of water in each test－tube．Therefore，if you started with，say， a 1 M solution，the resulting concentrations would be $0.5 \mathrm{M}, 0.25 \mathrm{M}, 0.125 \mathrm{M}$ and 0.0625 M ．

### 12.8 Standard solutions

When carrying out laboratory practical work, we often have to use solutions of exactly known concentrations. Such solutions are called standard solutions, e.g. a solution containing 4.65 grams of sodium chloride per litre is a standard solution.

A standard solution is prepared by dissolving a definite, precisely known mass of solute in a suitable solvent (usually deionised water) to give a definite, precisely known volume of solution.

- The concentration of a solution may be determined either by preparing the solution ourselves or by finding the concentration of the solution by analysis.
- Since many substances cannot be obtained in a high degree of purity, it is not possible for chemists to make up a wide range of standard solutions by simply dissolving a weighed amount of solute and making the solution up to a precise volume. For example, it is not possible to weigh out a precise quantity of sulfuric acid because sulfuric acid absorbs moisture from the air. Similarly, an accurately known quantity of iodine cannot be weighed out because iodine tends to sublime (change to a vapour) at room temperature.

In order to make up standard solutions, chemists need substances with several characteristics. Ideally, they should be very pure, stable in air, soluble in water to give stable solutions, and, if possible, have high relative molecular masses in order to minimise percentage error. Such substances are called primary standards.

A primary standard is a substance that meets the criteria summarised in Table 12.3.

A standard solution is a solution whose concentration is accurately known.

|  | Criteria for primary standard |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1. | It must be available in a highly pure state. |
| 2. | It must be stable in air, e.g. it should not lose water of crystallisation to the air (efflorescence) or absorb water from the air (be deliquescent or hygroscopic). |
| 3. | It must dissolve easily in water. |
| 4. | It should have a fairly high relative molecular mass (so that the precision in weighing out a known mass is as high as possible). |
| 5. | When used in volumetric analysis, it should undergo complete and rapid reaction. |
| 6. | If possible, it should not be hydrated, i.e. it must be anhydrous (have no water of crystallisation). |

Table 12.3 A primary standard must meet the criteria specified in this table.

Therefore, a primary standard may be defined as follows:
A primary standard is a substance that can be obtained in a stable, pure and soluble solid form so that it can be weighed out and dissolved in water to give a solution of accurately known concentration.

Many common chemicals cannot be considered as primary standards, Table 12.4.

| Substance | Why is it not a primary standard? |
| :--- | :--- |
| Sulfuric acid | It is hygroscopic, i.e. it absorbs water from the air. |
| Hydrochloric acid | HCl is a gas at room temperature and difficult to weigh out accurately. |
| Sodium hydroxide | It is deliquescent, i.e. it absorbs enough water from the air to form a solution. |
| Hydrated sodium carbonate | It effloresces, i.e. it loses water of crystallisation to the air. |
| Iodine | It sublimes at close to room temperature. |
| Potassium permanganate | It is not available in a pure state and it is not stable, e.g. its solutions deteriorate if exposed to light. |

Table 12.4 Many common chemicals do not match the requirements for primary standards.

Only a small number of common substances satisfy the above criteria and are classed as primary standards, e.g. anhydrous sodium carbonate, $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ and sodium chloride, NaCl . Standard solutions are widely used in industry and in research, and so it is important to be able to prepare them. So let's get started on preparing a standard solution!

### 12.2 Experiment

Student Experiment No. 6

> Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 6 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To prepare a standard solution of sodium carbonate

## Introduction

In this experiment, an accurately known amount of anhydrous sodium carbonate is weighed, dissolved in water and then the solution is made up to a known volume. Since anhydrous sodium carbonate is a primary standard, the concentration of the solution will be known precisely, i.e. we are using a primary standard to make up a standard solution.

## Key steps in procedure

- A known mass of anhydrous sodium carbonate is accurately weighed out on a clock glass using the laboratory balance.
- The anhydrous sodium carbonate is added to a beaker containing deionised water.
- A wash bottle of deionised water is used to wash all traces of the sodium carbonate from the clock glass into the beaker.
- The mixture is stirred with a clean glass rod until the solid dissolves completely.
- The solution is transferred to a clean $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask using a funnel and glass rod, Figure 12.13.
- All traces of the solution are washed from the beaker, rod and funnel into the volumetric flask using deionised water. The funnel is removed.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-224.jpg?height=718&width=1088&top_left_y=406&top_left_x=286)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-224.jpg?height=512&width=558&top_left_y=403&top_left_x=1406)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-224.jpg?height=1202&width=542&top_left_y=410&top_left_x=1998)
Figure 12.13
Stages involved in making up a standard solution of sodium carbonate. Sodium carbonate is an example of a primary standard.

- Deionised water is added to the volumetric flask until the bottom of the meniscus of the liquid is exactly level with the graduation mark, Figure 12.14. Towards the end, the water is added slowly using a dropper. The volumetric flask must be placed on a level surface. The bottom of the meniscus must be viewed at eye-level.
- The mark on the neck of the flask should be viewed at eye-level to ensure that the bottom of the meniscus of the liquid coincides with it.
- The stoppered flask is inverted about 20 times to mix the contents thoroughly (homogeneous mixture).

The concentration (in moles per litre) of the solution is then calculated. The calculation involved is similar to that in Example 12.7.

We now have a solution whose concentration is known precisely, i.e. a standard solution of sodium carbonate.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-224.jpg?height=1065&width=789&top_left_y=2487&top_left_x=1748)
Figure 12.14 The bottom of the meniscus must be brought up to the graduation mark using a dropper.

## EXAM TIPI

When answering exam questions on the procedure for making up standard solutions, pay particular attention to giving precise details:

1. Do not forget to mention that you used deionised water. Ordinary tap water contains many dissolved substances that could interfere with the solution and affect the results of the experiment.
2. Always mention that deionised water is added until the bottom of the meniscus is on the graduation mark of the volumetric flask and the reading taken at eye-level.
3. It is important that you use the term inverted (not 'shaken') as merely shaking the volumetric flask would not mix the contents sufficiently.

## Example 12.18

## Question

5.28 grams of anhydrous sodium carbonate, $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$, were weighed out and made up to $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution. Calculate the molarity of the solution.

## Answer

We can solve this from first principles using the basic definition of a 1 M solution.
1 mole $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ in 1 litre of solution $\rightarrow 1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ solution
i.e. $106 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ in 1 litre of solution $\rightarrow 1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ solution $\left(M_{r} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}=106\right)$
1g $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ in 1 litre of solution $\rightarrow \frac{1}{106} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ solution
$5.28 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ in 1 litre of solution $\rightarrow \frac{1 \times 5.28}{106} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ solution
$5.28 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ in $\mathbf{2 5 0} \mathbf{~ c m}^{\mathbf{3}}$ of solution $\rightarrow \frac{4 \times 5.28}{106} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}$ solution

$$
=0.199 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3} \text { solution }
$$

Answer: 0.199 M
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-225.jpg?height=213&width=734&top_left_y=2187&top_left_x=1972)

### 12.9 Volumetric analysis apparatus

- Volumetric analysis involves reacting together volumes of solutions.
- In volumetric analysis, the concentration of a solution is determined by reacting that solution with another solution of known concentration (standard solution).
- A definite volume (usually $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ ) of one of the solutions is taken and the other solution is added slowly until the two solutions have reacted completely.
- This procedure is known as a titration.
- The stage when the two solutions just react completely with each other is called the equivalence point of the titration.
- When the equivalence point is shown by an indicator it is called the end point of the titration.

In chemistry, the chemical which is being analysed in an experiment is called the analyte.

A titration is a laboratory procedure where a measured volume of one solution is added to a known volume of another solution until the reaction is complete.

The analyte is the chemical species being analysed to determine its concentration, identity or properties.

For example, in a titration of vinegar against a solution of known concentration, the ethanoic acid (acetic acid) in the vinegar is the analyte. In the photograph shown at the beginning of this chapter where the hardness of water is being measured, the analyte is calcium and magnesium ions. In measuring the amount of salt in a saline solution, the analyte is sodium chloride.

In volumetric analysis, titrations are performed to determine the concentration of analytes in solution. These concentrations are determined by titration using primary standard solutions or solutions that have been standardised using primary standards.

Before studying the correct procedure for performing a titration, we shall study the apparatus that is used in volumetric analysis. One of the advantages of volumetric analysis is that the apparatus required is fairly simple. The main apparatus used in volumetric analysis consists of (i) the beaker, (ii) the graduated cylinder, (iii) the volumetric flask, (iv) the pipette, (v) the burette and (vi) the conical flask.

Graduation marks on these instruments may be written in cubic centimetres ( $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ ) or in millilitres ( ml ). $\mathrm{A} \mathrm{cm}^{3}$ is exactly the same as a ml .

A detailed description of each item of apparatus is given in the Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

### 12.10 Procedure in carrying out a titration

Because of the importance of volumetric analysis, it is vital that you master the technique involved in carrying out a titration accurately. This technique is described in detail in Student Experiment 12.3 in your Laboratory Notebook along with some important precautions to take. The main stages in carrying out a titration will now be outlined.

### 12.3 Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 7

Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 7 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To use the standard solution of sodium carbonate solution prepared in the previous experiment to standardise a given hydrochloric acid solution

## Introduction

Sodium carbonate is a base that reacts with hydrochloric acid according to the equation:

$$
\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}+2 \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{CO}_{2}
$$

Essentially, what is happening is that the carbonate ion is accepting two protons from the hydrochloric acid to form carbon dioxide and water:

$$
\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}+2 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{CO}_{2}
$$

By titrating the given hydrochloric acid solution against a known volume of sodium carbonate solution whose concentration is accurately known, we can determine the concentration of the hydrochloric acid solution. An indicator (methyl orange in this case) is used to find the end point of the titration.

Note: In acid-base titrations, the acid is usually placed in the burette and the base in the conical flask ('Acid Above, Base Below'). One of the main reasons for this is that some common bases (e.g. sodium hydroxide), if placed in a burette would cause the tap to stick. Sodium hydroxide solution attacks glass, especially the ground glass surfaces in some burette taps. Also, it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and forms a crust of sodium carbonate around the tap - this happens even with the modern plastic taps. Both of these actions cause the burette taps to seize up.

## Key steps in procedure

- The pipette, burette and conical flask are washed with deionised water.
- The pipette is rinsed with sodium carbonate solution.
- The burette is rinsed with hydrochloric acid solution.
- $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the sodium carbonate solution are pipetted from a beaker into the conical flask, Figure 12.15. The beaker should have been perfectly dry before pouring the sodium carbonate solution into it from the volumetric flask.
- A few drops of methyl orange indicator are added to the sodium carbonate solution in the conical flask.


## Observation

The methyl orange indicator in the conical flask is a yellow colour as it is in a basic (alkaline) solution.

Step 1
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-227.jpg?height=1105&width=541&top_left_y=1207&top_left_x=351)

Step 5
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-227.jpg?height=672&width=477&top_left_y=2710&top_left_x=348)

## (5) Carry out one rough and

two accurate titrations

Figure 12.15 The main steps in carrying out a titration
Figure 12.15 The main steps carrying out a titration

Step 6
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-227.jpg?height=877&width=620&top_left_y=2708&top_left_x=865)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-227.jpg?height=1397&width=1294&top_left_y=1077&top_left_x=1431)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-227.jpg?height=1280&width=1186&top_left_y=2490&top_left_x=1513)
(7) When the indicator has just changed colour, stop the titration and note the volume of acid added

## Procedure (continued)

- The burette is clamped vertically using the retort stand (or burette stand) and is filled through a funnel with the dilute hydrochloric acid solution to above the zero mark.
- The funnel is removed from the burette.
- The tap of the burette is opened to fill the tap and the space below the tap with the solution.
- The level of hydrochloric acid solution is adjusted until the bottom of the meniscus is level with the zero graduation mark, taking the reading at eye level.
- A white tile is placed on the base of the retort stand and the conical flask is placed on the white tile.
- Using the thumb and first two fingers of the left hand, the tap of the burette is opened. The acid is allowed to run fairly quickly into the conical flask.
- The conical flask is continuously swirled with the right hand.
- The titration is stopped from time to time and the sides of the conical flask are washed down with deionised water from the wash bottle.


## Explanation

- Only a small volume of indicator should be added. This is because acid-base indictors are either weak acids or weak bases themselves, and if too much is added it could lead to a significant inaccuracy in the result of the titration.
- Methyl orange is suitable because we are titrating a strong acid against a weak base. This will be explained in more detail in Chapter 19.
- The purpose of the white tile is to enable us to detect colour changes more clearly.
- Washing down the side of the flask ensures that no drops of acid are stuck to the side of the flask. It is important that all of the acid added from the burette reacts with the sodium carbonate.
- Deionised water may be added to the conical flask at any stage of the titration. It does not affect the amount of sodium carbonate in the conical flask. A volume of $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the sodium carbonate solution has been pipetted into the conical flask. This volume of sodium carbonate contains a certain number of moles of sodium carbonate. Whether we now add $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ or 100 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of deionised water to the conical flask, this will not affect the number of moles of sodium carbonate present in the conical flask.
- Note the distinction between washing out the pipette and burette with the solutions which they contain and not washing out the conical flask with the solution it is about to contain. In the case of adding water to the conical flask during the titration, the dilution occurs after the required amount of sodium carbonate solution has already been measured and so will not bring about a change in the end point.


## Procedure (continued)

- The titration is stopped when the colour of the indicator changes from yellow to red (pink).
- The volume of acid added is noted. Two further accurate titrations are carried out. The hydrochloric acid solution is added drop by drop as the end point is approached.
- At the end point, one drop of acid turns the solution in the conical flask a faint red (pink) colour.
- The results of these two accurate titrations should agree to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. If they do not agree, a further titration must be carried out until agreement to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ is obtained.
- The titration result (also called the titre) for the experiment is taken as the average of the two readings which agree to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.


## Explanation

- The indicator changes from yellow to red (pink) because the solution in the conical flask becomes acidic.
- The rough titration reading is an indication of the approximate end point. It gives you an idea of where the accurate end point is located, i.e. it helps you to locate the accurate end point more precisely. It also saves time as it allows rapid addition from the burette until the end point is close rather than adding the solution drop-by-drop during the entire titration.
- In calculations, the rough titration figure should be neglected. For example, if the three titration readings are $22.9 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}, 22.4 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ and $22.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, the titration figure to be used in calculations is the average of 22.4 and 22.5 , i.e. $22.45 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.


## Calculations

The method of calculating the concentration of the hydrochloric acid solution is shown in Example 12.19 in the next section.

## Introduction

Since sodium hydroxide is deliquescent（i．e．it absorbs so much water vapour from the air that it becomes a solution），we cannot weigh out a fixed amount of it and make up a solution of exact concentration．In this experiment，we will make up an approximate 0.1 M solution of sodium hydroxide and standardise it by titrating it against a hydrochloric acid solution of known concentration．The equation for the reaction is：

## Student Experiment No. 9

Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 9 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To determine the concentration of a solution of ammonia using a standardised HCl solution (strong acid-weak base titration)

## Introduction

In Experiment 12.3, we used a standard solution of sodium carbonate to determine the exact concentration of a hydrochloric acid solution. This hydrochloric acid solution may now be used to standardise (find the exact concentration of) other solutions, e.g. a solution of ammonia. Ammonia is supplied to laboratories as a highly concentrated solution of ammonia (usually about $16 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NH}_{3}$ ). Therefore, your teacher will supply you with a more dilute solution of ammonia to use.

The equation for the reaction is:

$$
\mathrm{HCl}_{(a q)}+\mathrm{NH}_{3(a q)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{Cl}_{(a q)}
$$

Recall that the 'aq' (aqueous) indicates that everything is dissolved in solution. A solution of ammonia in water is also called ammonium hydroxide as $\mathrm{NH}_{4}{ }^{+}$ions and $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions (from water) are present in solution.

## Key steps in procedure

- A pipette is rinsed with deionised water and with some of the ammonia solution.
- A burette is rinsed out with deionised water and with some of the hydrochloric acid solution.
- A volume of $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the ammonia solution is pipetted into a conical flask that has been previously rinsed with deionised water.
- A few drops of methyl orange indicator are added to the ammonia solution in the conical flask.
- The burette is filled with the dilute hydrochloric solution, the bottom of the meniscus is adjusted to the zero graduation mark, and the apparatus is set up for titration, Figure 12.17.
- A white tile is placed on the base of the retort stand and the ammonia solution is titrated against the standard solution of hydrochloric acid. One rough and two accurate titrations agreeing to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ are carried out.


## Observation

- The methyl orange indicator changes from yellow to red (pink).


## Explanation

- The methyl orange changes colour from yellow to red (pink) because the solution in the conical flask becomes acidic.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-233.jpg?height=1401&width=942&top_left_y=2044&top_left_x=1777)
Figure 12.17

## Calculations

- From the results of your titration, work out the exact concentration of the ammonia solution. Express the concentration of the ammonia solution (a) in moles per litre and (b) in grams per litre. A sample calculation is given in Example 12.22.


## Example 12.22

## Question

Hydrochloric acid and ammonia solution react according to the equation:
$\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{Cl}$
$25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of an ammonia solution were titrated against a 0.15 M HCl solution. The average titration figure was $22.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Calculate the concentration of the ammonia solution in (a) moles per litre and (b) grams per litre. ( $\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{~N}=14$ )

## Answer

From the balanced equation, we see that one mole of acid reacts with one mole of base, i.e. $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{a}}=1$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{b}}=1$.

## $\mathrm{HCl} \mathrm{NH}_{3}$

Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}=22.5$
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{a}}=0.15$
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{a}}=1$
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{b}}=25$
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{b}}=$ ?
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{b}}=1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{V_{a} \times M_{a}}{n_{a}} & =\frac{V_{b} \times M_{b}}{n_{b}} \\
\frac{22.5 \times 0.15}{1} & =\frac{25 \times M_{b}}{1} \\
M_{b} & =\frac{22.5 \times 0.15}{25} \\
& =0.135 \text { moles per litre. } \\
& =0.135 \times 17 \text { grams per litre }\left(M_{r}, N H_{3}=17\right) \\
& =2.295 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: Concentration of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ solution is (a) 0.135 M , (b) $2.295 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$.

### 12.6 Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 10

Full step-by-step details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 10 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To determine the concentration of ethanoic acid (acetic acid) in vinegar (weak acid-strong base titration)

## Introduction

Vinegar is a dilute solution of an acid called ethanoic acid, $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$, the old name of which is acetic acid. The amount of ethanoic acid in vinegar can be determined by titrating the vinegar against a standard sodium hydroxide solution. The equation for the reaction is:

$$
\underset{\text { ethanoic acid }}{\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}}+\underset{\text { sodium hydroxide }}{\mathrm{NaOH}} \rightarrow \underset{\text { sodium ethanoate }}{\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

To detect the end point, we use an indicator called phenolphthalein. Phenolphthalein is colourless in an acid and pink in a base. (Phenolphthalein is suitable because we are titrating a weak acid against a strong base. This will be explained in more detail in Chapter 19.)

As the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution being used is quite small ( 0.1 M approx.), it is necessary to dilute the vinegar to avoid having to use a large volume of sodium hydroxide solution to neutralise it. Alternatively you could say that, since the vinegar is much more concentrated than the sodium hydroxide solution, a very small amount of vinegar would be needed to neutralise the base and this would be likely to contribute to a higher percentage error in the experiment.

## Key steps in procedure

- Two $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ samples of vinegar are added to a $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask, Figure 12.18. Deionised water is added until the bottom of the meniscus is level with the graduation mark. Note that the sample of vinegar has been diluted by a factor of five (from $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ to $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ ) in the volumetric flask.
- The pipette is washed with deionised water and with the standard sodium hydroxide solution.
- Use the pipette to transfer $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the standard sodium hydroxide solution to a conical flask that has been previously rinsed with deionised water.
- About three drops of phenolphthalein indicator are added to the sodium hydroxide solution in the conical flask.


## Observation

- The phenolphthalein is a pink colour in the sodium hydroxide solution.


## Explanation

- Phenolphthalein indicator is pink in a basic (alkaline) solution.


## Procedure (continued)

- The burette is rinsed with water and with some of the diluted vinegar.
- Using a small funnel, the burette is filled with the diluted vinegar. The funnel is removed and the bottom of the meniscus adjusted to the zero graduation mark. A white tile is placed on the base of the retort stand, Figure 12.19.
- The diluted vinegar is titrated against the sodium hydroxide solution. One rough and two accurate titrations, agreeing to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, are carried out.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-235.jpg?height=1297&width=427&top_left_y=416&top_left_x=2220)
Figure 12.18 The vinegar is diluted by a factor of five by pipetting two $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ samples of vinegar into a $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask and making the solution up to the graduation mark with deionised water

## Observation

- At the end point, the phenolphthalein changes from pink to colourless.


## Calculations

- From the results of the titration, work out the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar (a) in moles per litre, (b) in grams per litre and (c) in \% w/v. A sample calculation is given in Example 12.23.

Figure 12.19 Finding the percentage of ethanoic acid in vinegar by titrating it against a standard sodium hydroxide solution.

The green colour is used in Figure 12.26 to distinguish the vinegar from the sodium hydroxide solution (blue) and the colour of the sodium hydroxide and phenolphthalein in the conical flask (pink). ## Example 12.23

## Question

A $20 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ sample of vinegar was diluted to $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ in a volumetric flask. This diluted solution was then titrated against $20 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.12 M NaOH solution. The balanced equation for the reaction is:
$\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
The average titration figure was $14.2 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Calculate the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar in (a) mol/L, (b) g/L and (c) \% w/v. (H = 1, $\mathrm{C}=12, \mathrm{O}=16$ )

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate concentration of ethanoic acid in diluted solution.
From the balanced equation, we see that one mole of acid reacts with one mole of base, i.e. $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{a}}=1$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{b}}=1$.

## $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ (NaOH

Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}=14.2$
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{a}}=$ ?
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{a}}=1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{V_{a} \times M_{a}}{n_{a}} & =\frac{V_{b} \times M_{b}}{n_{b}} \\
\frac{14.2 \times M_{a}}{1} & =\frac{20 \times 0.12}{1} \\
M_{a} & =\frac{20 \times 0.2}{14.2} \\
& =0.169 \text { moles per litre. }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 1

Calculate concentation of ethanoic acid in original vinegar.
Since the solution was diluted by a factor of five, concentration of ethanoic acid in original vinegar
$=0.169 \times 5$ moles per litre
$=0.845 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$
(a)
$=0.845 \times 60 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}\left(M_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}=60\right)$

$$
\begin{equation*}
=50.7 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L} \tag{b}
\end{equation*}
$$

Since there are 50.7 g of ethanoic acid in a litre of vinegar, there are 5.07 g of ethanoic acid in $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of vinegar.

Therefore, $\% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}=5.07 \%$
(c)

Answer: Concentration of ethanoic acid in vinegar is (a) 0.845 M (b) $50.7 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$ (c) $5.07 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$.

## Summary What I should know

- The concentration of a solution is the amount of solute that is dissolved in a given volume of solution. Concentration may be expressed in terms of percentage of solute or in parts per million or in moles per litre (molarity).

A 1 M solution is one that contains one mole of the solute dissolved in one litre of solution.
Serial dilution is a step-by-step dilution process where a solution is diluted multiple times in a systematic way

To calculate the number of moles, when the volume and the molarity of the solution are given, use the formula:
number of moles $=\frac{\text { volume }{ }^{*} \times \text { molarity }}{1000} \quad\left(* \mathrm{in} \mathrm{cm}^{3}\right)$

- For calculations involving dilution of solutions, use the formula:
$\frac{\mathrm{Vol}_{\text {di }}{ }^{*} \times \mathrm{M}_{\text {dil }}}{1000}=\frac{\mathrm{Vol}_{\text {conc }}{ }^{*} \times \mathrm{M}_{\text {conc }}}{1000} \quad\left({ }^{*}\right.$ in $\left.\mathrm{cm}^{3}\right)$
A standard solution is a solution of precisely known concentration.
A primary standard is a substance that can be obtained in a stable, pure and soluble solid form so that it can be weighed out and dissolved in water to give a solution of accurately known concentration.

A titration is a laboratory procedure where a measured volume of one solution is added to a known volume of another solution until the reaction is complete.

Many volumetric problems may be solved using the formula:
$\frac{V_{a} \times M_{a}}{n_{a}}=\frac{V_{b} \times M_{b}}{n_{b}}$
The analyte is the chemical species being analysed to determine its concentration, identity or properties.

Titration data may be used to calculate the unknown concentration of a solution.
