# 13 Acid-Base Volumetric Exam-Style Questions

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-239.jpg?height=1091&width=1241&top_left_y=540&top_left_x=325)

### 13.1 Introduction

In Chapter 12 we studied how many problems in volumetric analysis can be solved from first principles. Thus, in Examples 12.1-12.7 we saw how all the problems could be solved starting with some basic definitions without the need to use any formulas. We also saw how the molarity of the standard solution of sodium carbonate that was made up by you, could be calculated by starting with the basic definition of a 1 M solution. In addition, we learned in Example 12.19 that this problem could be solved using both first principles and also by means of a general formula for calculating unknown concentrations given the results of titration data, Figure 13.1.

Learning to solve problems from first principles is very helpful in giving you an understanding of key concepts in volumetric analysis. However, it can be time-consuming to do this for every volumetric problem. Therefore, in this chapter, we will introduce you to some key formulas to help you solve volumetric problems when you are under time pressure in exams. When solving a problem in an exam paper from first principles or using formulas, always remember that it is very important to show all your work.

## OBJECTIVES

- To introduce students to a range of different types of questions in volumetric analysis.
- To give students practice in solving volumetric problems from first principles and also by using some key formulas.
- To ensure that students know the importance of accuracy and precision in volumetric analysis practical work.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-239.jpg?height=1404&width=1147&top_left_y=1966&top_left_x=1572)
Figure 13.1 The first principles method of solving problems is a good starting point as it ensures that you understand what you are doing. However, in examinations the use of key formulas is faster and very effective as long as you show all your calculations.

### 13.2 Key formulas for solving volumetric problems

In this section, we will summarise some of the key formulas that we have met so far in stoichiometry and volumetric analysis, Table 13.1. We will then show how these key formulas can be used in solving some volumetric problems in exam-style questions.

| Formula |  | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | Number of moles $=\frac{\text { Mass (in grams) }}{\text { Relative Molecular Mass }}$ | This is a very useful formula (Chapter 8) for calculating the number of moles of a substance when we know the relative molecular mass. It can also be manipulated to: <br> (i) Calculate the mass if we know the number of moles and relative molecular mass <br> or <br> (ii) Calculate the relative molecular mass if we know the mass and number of moles. |
| 2. | Number of moles $=\frac{\text { volume } \mathbf{e}^{*} \times \text { molarity }}{1000}$ <br> (*in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ ) | This is a very useful formula (Chapter 12) for calculating the number of moles when given a volume of solution and the molarity of the solution. |
| 3. | $\frac{V_{a} \times M_{a}}{n_{a}}=\frac{V_{b} \times M_{b}}{n_{b}}$ | This is a very useful formula (Chapter 12) for calculating the unknown concentration of a solution from titration data. |
| 4. | Density $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Volume }}$ | You have met this formula when studying Junior Cycle science. It is very useful if we are given the density of a liquid and its volume and we need to calculate the mass of the liquid. |

Table 13.1 Some key formulas in volumetric analysis

### 13.3 Solving exam-style problems

We will now study some examples of exam-style questions to show you how the above formulas can be used. So far, we have been using values of relative atomic masses which have been rounded off. This was done to enable you to concentrate on acquiring basic skills of calculations without being distracted by consulting the Formulae and Tables booklet of the SEC every time you wished to find out the exact relative atomic mass of an element.

However, in keeping with the style of sample exam papers published by the State Examinations Commission, instead of rounding off relative atomic masses, we will now use the values given in the SEC booklet.

The relative atomic masses most commonly encountered in acidbase volumetric analysis are given in Table 13.2.

| Element | Relative atomic mass |
| :--- | :--- |
| H | 1.008 |
| C | 12.01 |
| N | 14.01 |
| O | 16.00 |
| Na | 22.99 |
| Mg | 24.31 |
| S | 32.07 |
| Cl | 35.45 |

Table 13.2 Relative atomic masses of elements commonly encountered in acid-base volumetric problems

## Example 13.1

## Question

To determine the concentration of ethanoic acid in a sample of vinegar, Figure 13.2, $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the vinegar were diluted to $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ and then the diluted vinegar was titrated with a previously standardised solution which contained 1.20 g of sodium hydroxide in $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution.

On average, $18.75 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the diluted vinegar were required to neutralise $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of this sodium hydroxide solution.
The equation for the titration reaction is:

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

(a) Calculate:
(i) the number of moles of sodium hydroxide in each $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion
(ii) the number of moles of ethanoic acid per $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of diluted

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-241.jpg?height=538&width=837&top_left_y=787&top_left_x=1875)
Figure 13.2 Vinegar contains an acid called ethanoic acid (acetic acid).

vinegar.
(b) Find the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar:
(i) in terms of moles per litre.
(ii) as a percentage ( $\mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$ ).
(Given $\mathrm{H}=1.008, \mathrm{C}=12.01, \mathrm{O}=16, \mathrm{Na}=22.99$ )
[LCH]

## Answer

(a) (i) First calculate the molarity of 1.2 g sodium hydroxide solution in $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ solution. We can do this using first principles or using the formula.

## Step 1

Calculate the molarity of the NaOH solution.
Relative molecular mass NaOH $=22.99+16+1.008=39.998$
Using formula 1, no. of moles NaOH $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Relative Molecular Mass }}=\frac{1.20}{39.998}=0.03$ moles
0.03 mole of NaOH in $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ solution $=0.06$ mole $\mathrm{NaOH} / \mathrm{L}=0.06 \mathrm{M}$ solution

## Step 2

Calculate the number of moles of NaOH in $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the 0.06 M solution.
Using formula 2, no. of moles $\mathrm{NaOH}=\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000}=\frac{25 \times 0.06}{1000}=0.0015$ moles
Answer: There is 0.0015 mole NaOH in each $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion.
(a) (ii) Calculate the number of moles of ethanoic acid per $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of diluted vinegar.

## Step 1

Calculate the molarity of the diluted ethanoic acid (vinegar) solution.

## $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$

Using formula 3: $\frac{V_{a} \times M_{a}}{n_{a}}=\frac{V_{b} \times M_{b}}{n_{b}}$

## Step 2

Substitute in the values: $\frac{18.75 \times \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{a}}}{1}=\frac{25 \times 0.06}{1}$

## Given

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{a}}=18.75 & \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{b}}=25 \\
\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{a}}=? & \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{b}}=0.06 \\
\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{a}}=1 & \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{b}}=1
\end{array}
$$

## Step 3

Solve for the unknown (molarity of acid):
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{25 \times 0.06}{18.75}=0.08$ mole $/ \mathrm{L}$ (diluted vinegar)

## Step 4

Calculate the number of moles of ethanoic acid per $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of diluted vinegar.
From Step 3 above, we see that there is 0.08 mole in one litre $\left(1000 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}\right)$ of solution.
Therefore, there are $\frac{0.08}{1000}=0.0008$ mole per $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of diluted vinegar.
Answer: Number of moles of ethanoic acid per $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of diluted vinegar $=0.0008$
(b) (i) Find the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar in terms of moles per litre.

Concentration of ethanoic acid in diluted vinegar $=0.08 \mathrm{M}$
Since $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the vinegar were diluted to $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, dilution factor $=10$
Therefore, concentration of ethanoic acid in original vinegar $=0.08 \times 10=0.8 \mathrm{M}$
Answer: Concentration of ethanoic acid in original vinegar is 0.8 M
(b) (ii) Find the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar as a percentage (w/v)

## Step 1

Calculate the relative molecular mass of $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ as follows:
$\mathrm{C}=2 \times 12.01=24.02$
$\mathrm{O}=2 \times 16=32$
$\frac{\mathrm{H}=4 \times 1.008=4.032}{M_{r}=60.052}$

## Step 2

Convert molarity of $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ to grams per litre:
A 1 M solution of $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ contains $60.052 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$
A 0.8 M solution of $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ contains $60.052 \times 0.8 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}=48.0416 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$

## Step 3

Convert grams per litre to $\mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$.
$48.0416 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}=4.80416 \mathrm{~g} / 100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=4.80 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$
Answer: Concentration of ethanoic acid in original vinegar $=4.80 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$

## Example 13.2

## Question

A student carried out an experiment to determine the concentration of ethanoic acid in vinegar, Figure 13.3. A $10.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion of the vinegar was first diluted to exactly $50.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. The diluted vinegar solution was titrated against a 0.09 M sodium hydroxide solution in a conical flask. On average, $12.4 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the diluted vinegar were required to neutralise $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the NaOH solution.

The titration reaction is described by the following balanced chemical equation:

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

[LCH]

## Question

(a) (i) Name the piece of apparatus used to measure accurately the $10.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion of the original vinegar.

## Answer

A pipette is used (or a burette is also acceptable).

## Question

(ii) Describe how this piece of apparatus was rinsed before use.

## Answer

The pipette is first rinsed with deionised water and then with the solution (vinegar) that it is to contain.

## Question

(iii) Describe a suitable method to dilute the $10.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion of the original vinegar to exactly $50.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.

## Answer

1. Using a pipette place $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of vinegar in a $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask.
2. Add deionised water.
3. Ensure that the bottom of the meniscus is level with the graduation mark.

## Question

(b) (i) Calculate the volume of undiluted vinegar which would be required to neutralise $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the 0.09 M NaOH solution.

## Answer

## Step 1

Note that $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ vinegar were diluted to $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Therefore, the dilution factor $=5$.

## Step 2

We are told in the question that $12.4 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the diluted vinegar neutralised $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the NaOH solution.

## Step 3

Therefore, only $\frac{12.4}{5}=2.48 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the undiluted vinegar would be required to neutralise $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the 0.09 M NaOH solution.

## Question

(ii) Outline an advantage of diluting the vinegar before carrying out the titration.

## Answer

If the vinegar was not diluted, a much smaller volume of this more concentrated solution of ethanoic acid would be required to neutralise the dilute sodium hydroxide solution. (This small volume was calculated in (b)(i) above as only $2.48 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.) Smaller volumes have a higher percentage error, because even a slight misreading of the volume will have a greater impact on the accuracy of the results. Diluting the vinegar increases the volume needed for neutralisation, which in turn makes the percentage error smaller, leading to a more accurate titration figure. (We will be discussing errors in volumetric analysis in more detail in Chapter 16.)

- Another acceptable answer was that the dilute solution of ethanoic acid means that a less concentrated solution of NaOH can be used to neutralise it. Since NaOH is a caustic substance, it is safer to use a less concentrated solution.


## Question

## EXAM TIPI

Key words to use when explaining about the dilution of the vinegar are smaller percentage error.
(c) (i) Name a suitable indicator for this titration.

## Answer

Phenolphthalein.

## Question

(ii) State the colour change observed at the end point.

## Answer

The colour of the phenolphthalein change is from pink to colourless.

## Question

(d) (i) Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide in each $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion.

## Answer

## EXAM TIP!

When asked for a colour change, you must always state two colours and make it obvious what colour was present at the beginning and at the end. Also, the word 'clear' is not acceptable as a colour.

## Step 1

To calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide in each $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion, use formula No. 2 .

## Step 2

Input the information into the formula and solve:

$$
\text { No. of moles } \mathrm{NaOH}=\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000}=\frac{25 \times 0.09}{1000}=0.00225 \text { mole }
$$

Answer: There are 0.00225 mole NaOH in each $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion.

## Question

(ii) Calculate the number of moles of ethanoic acid in each $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of the diluted vinegar.

## Answer

Note from the question that $12.4 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the diluted vinegar were required to neutralise $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the NaOH solution. Since $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ and NaOH react in the ratio of 1:1, this means that the $12.4 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the diluted vinegar must also contain 0.00225 mole ethanoic acid.
$12.4 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ contain 0.00225 moles ethanoic acid
$1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ contains $\frac{0.00225}{12.4}=0.00018$ moles

### 13.4 Accuracy and precision in volumetric analysis

We have already learned in Chapter 12 that instruments such as burettes, pipettes and volumetric flask are manufactured to a high degree of accuracy. This means that we can use them to measure volumes that are very close to the actual or true volume.

For example, if the correct titration figure is $25.2 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ and your measurement is $25.2 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, then your measurement is accurate. When measuring the concentration of ethanoic acid in vinegar using a burette, pipette and volumetric flask, provided you carry out the recommended procedure for carrying out a titration, you can be confident that the result you obtain will be accurate. In other words, the value that you calculate for the concentration of ethanoic acid in vinegar is very close to the correct or true value of ethanoic acid in vinegar.

There is another word called precision that we meet in our study of chemistry, which needs to be distinguished from accuracy.

For example, suppose you measure the mass of an object three times on two different laboratory balances, Figure 13.4.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-246.jpg?height=916&width=1651&top_left_y=1692&top_left_x=273)
Figure 13.4 The balance on the left has been calibrated correctly at the factory and shows the true mass of 50.00 g each time a reading is taken. The balance on the right has not been calibrated correctly. It gives precise readings each time a reading is taken but they are inaccurate.

Note in Figure 13.4 that the true value of the mass is 50.00 g . The balance on the left-hand side has been properly calibrated at the factory and correctly gives the true value of 50.00 g each time a measurement is taken.

However, the balance on the right has not been calibrated properly and does not give accurate readings. Note in Figure 13.4 that all three measurements from the faulty balance are close together. We say that the measurements show precision. However, the fact that they do not give the true value of 50.00 g , means that there is a lack of accuracy in the readings of the faulty balance.

In short, accuracy means getting the correct or true result every time. Precision means getting results that are close together. Scientists always try to obtain results that are both accurate and precise.

Accuracy means how close a measurement is to the correct value. The correct value is often referred to as the 'true' or 'actual' value.

Precision means how close a set of repeated measurements are to each other.

Accuracy and precision are often explained using a dart board, Figure 13.5.

Some key differences between accuracy and precision are summarised in Table 13.3.

| Accuracy | Precision |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1. Refers to how close a measured value is to the correct value of the quantity being measured. | 1. Refers to how close the individual measurements are with each other. |
| 2. Focuses on the correct value. | 2. Focuses on the repeatability of measurements. |
| 3. Measurements are clustered around the correct value. | 3. Measurements clustered closely together. |

Table 13.3 Some differences between accuracy and precision

## Why are accuracy and precision important in volumetric analysis?

When carrying out a titration, accuracy and precise measurements are of great importance because you are using the volume of one solution to determine the concentration of another solution.

- Accurate measurements of the volumes of solutions that react together will ensure that the true value of the unknown concentration of the solution being analysed will be found.
- Inaccurate measurements will lead to a wrong value of concentration.
- Precision is all about consistency, i.e. that you get similar results every time that you repeat the titration.
- You may recall in Chapter 12 that we mentioned that the results of two accurate titrations should agree to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. This degree of precision tells you that your procedure is reliable, i.e. that your experimental technique is consistent. This increases the confidence in your findings.
The ability to follow a set of instructions in chemistry plays an important role in helping you to develop key laboratory skills. Following instructions exactly by using the correct masses and volumes of chemicals will help you to get accurate results. If you repeat a particular experiment, you will then get similar results, i.e. you will ensure precision in your results.

Accuracy and precision are also of importance in industrial chemistry. For example, chemists working in the pharmaceutical industry, Figure 13.6, must have the ability to follow experimental procedures very carefully. This ensures that every batch of a particular drug is made in exactly the same way so that the quality and effectiveness of the drug is maintained at the same high standards.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-247.jpg?height=2198&width=909&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1849)
Figure 13.5 The game of darts can be helpful to distinguish between accuracy and precision.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-247.jpg?height=617&width=916&top_left_y=2812&top_left_x=1839)
Figure 13.6 Chemists working in the pharmaceutical industry must follow detailed sets of instructions as part of laboratory procedures to ensure consistency and effectiveness of drug quality from one batch to the next.

When writing up laboratory reports of practical work in volumetric analysis, it is important that you mention if your measurements are both accurate and precise. This helps others understand the reliability of your results. It also confirms that the procedure that you followed is working well.

Carrying out the wide range of experiments in the Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook will help you to develop key laboratory skills and achieve accurate and precise results from your work in the laboratory.

## Example 13.3

## Question

The correct volume of a solution is $23.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. A student measured the volume of this solution three times and recorded the volumes as $23.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}, 23.6 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ and $23.7 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Are these results accurate, precise or both?

## Answer

- The results are not accurate, as they are different from the correct volume.
- The results are precise, as they are close to each other.


## Example 13.4

## Question

When carrying out an experiment to measure the concentration of ethanoic acid in vinegar, a student washed out the burette with deionised water but forgot to also wash it out with the solution that it was to contain. Would this error affect the accuracy, or precision, or both of the results obtained?

## Answer

- This error would affect the accuracy of the results.
- The water remaining in the burette would dilute the solution of ethanoic acid placed in the burette.
- Therefore, an inaccurate titration figure would be obtained.
- The inaccurate titration figure will give an inaccurate concentration of ethanoic acid in the vinegar.
- The error will not affect the precision of the results since, while the results will be inaccurate, they will be close together.


## Example 13.5

## Question

A student is carrying out an experiment to measure the concentration of ethanoic acid in vinegar. What precautions should be carried out to ensure that the result obtained is as accurate as possible?

## Answer

The following precautions will ensure accuracy:

1. Only use equipment which has a high degree of accuracy in measuring volumes of solutions, e.g. burette, pipette and volumetric flask.
2. Take volume readings at eye-level to prevent errors due to parallax and also read where the bottom of the meniscus touches the calibration mark.
3. Rinse glassware correctly, e.g. burettes and pipettes should first be rinsed with deionised water and then with the solutions they are to contain.
4. As you near the endpoint, add the solution drop-by-drop from the burette to obtain an accurate end point rather than overshooting the end point by adding too much solution from the burette.
5. When measuring unknown concentrations, always use standard solutions, i.e. solutions whose concentration is accurately known.

## Summary What I should know

Volumetric problems may be solved from first principle and also with the aid of our key formulas.
Number of moles $=\frac{\text { Mass (in grams) }}{\text { Relative molecular Mass }}$
Number of moles $=\frac{\text { volume } \mathrm{e}^{*} \times \text { molarity }}{1000}$
(*in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ )
$\frac{V_{a} \times M_{a}}{n_{a}}=\frac{V_{b} \times M_{b}}{n_{b}}$
Density $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Volume }}$
Accuracy means how close a measurement is to the correct value. The correct value is often referred to as the 'true or 'actual' value.

Precision means how close a set of repeated measurements are to each other.

# 14 Oxidation and Reduction

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-252.jpg?height=479&width=1267&top_left_y=514&top_left_x=185)

### 14.1 Introduction

One of the most famous statues in the world is the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor. When this statue was first built in 1886, it had a shiny brown colour due to its outside layer of copper metal sheeting, Figure 14.1. However, over the years, the statue turned green as the copper reacted with oxygen and other substances in the air to form a green substance called verdigris (from the Old French meaning 'green from grey'). This type of reaction is called an oxidation reaction.

The layer of copper metal is only 2.4 mm thick. When the statue was erected it was known that the verdigris would form. In fact, the verdigris protects the copper underneath from further corrosion. If the outer sheeting were made of iron, there was a danger that it would rust away.

In the early days of chemistry, oxidation was defined simply as follows:

## Oxidation is the addition of oxygen to a substance.

For example, when coal is burned, the chemical reaction that takes place may be described as the combining of the carbon in the coal with oxygen from the air to form the gas carbon dioxide.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-252.jpg?height=386&width=877&top_left_y=2916&top_left_x=188)

A similar oxidation reaction occurs when magnesium metal is burned in air, Figure 14.2.

```
magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide
    $\stackrel{2 \mathrm{Mg}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow \quad 2 \mathrm{MgO}}{\text { magnesium gains oxygen }}$
        ∴ OXIDATION
```


## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of the concepts of oxidation and reduction in chemistry.
- To make students familiar with a range of oxidation and reduction reactions in our everyday lives.
- To give students an appreciation of various ways of defining oxidation and reduction in chemistry.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-252.jpg?height=948&width=1180&top_left_y=1432&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 14.1 When the Statue of Liberty was gifted to the USA by France in 1886, it was a shiny brown colour due to the copper sheeting. However, over the years, the copper has reacted with oxygen and other substances in the air to form a new green substance called verdigris.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-252.jpg?height=812&width=1180&top_left_y=2799&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 14.2 The burning of magnesium metal in air is an example of an oxidation reaction, since magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

One of the most commonly observed oxidation reactions is the rusting of iron, Figure 14.3. This may be represented in a simplified form as:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-253.jpg?height=313&width=887&top_left_y=612&top_left_x=328)

Corrosion is a general name used to describe the deterioration (breaking down, wearing away) of metals due to chemical reactions with their environment.

Rusting is a specific type of corrosion that occurs in iron and in its alloys such as steel. (An alloy is a mixture of one metal with another metal or with carbon. Steel is a mixture of iron and carbon.) We will be studying corrosion and its prevention in more detail in Chapter 21.

Oxygen is the most abundant element by mass in the Earth's crust and in the human body. It is also one of the most reactive elements - it combines with the vast majority of the other elements. Oxygen is involved in many of the most important chemical reactions in our lives:

- Combustion. The burning (combustion) of fuels is an example of an oxidation reaction, Figure 14.4. For example, methane gas burns in oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.

$$
\underset{\text { methane }}{\mathrm{CH}_{4}}+\underset{\text { oxygen }}{2 \mathrm{O}_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{\substack{\text { carbon } \\ \text { dioxide }}}{\mathrm{CO}_{2}}+\underset{\text { water }}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-253.jpg?height=733&width=1183&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 14.3 Rusting is an example of an oxidation reaction. It causes the iron to form the brown oxide $\left(\mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}\right)$ of the metal which is commonly called rust.

Corrosion is any undesired process whereby a metal is converted to one of its compounds.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-253.jpg?height=899&width=1183&top_left_y=1546&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 14.4 The combustion of fuels is an example of an oxidation reaction. Fuels react with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.

- Respiration. You may recall when studying Junior Cycle Science that respiration is the release of energy from food in the cell of an organism. Respiration is another example of an oxidation reaction and may be described by the equation:

$$
\underset{\text { glucose }}{\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_{6}}+\underset{\text { oxygen }}{6 \mathrm{O}_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{\substack{\text { carbon } \\ \text { dioxide }}}{6 \mathrm{CO}_{2}}+\underset{\text { water }}{6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}+\text { Energy }
$$

Therefore, it is not surprising that chemists classify many chemical reactions in terms of the reaction with oxygen.

Chemists also discovered that it was possible to remove oxygen from some substances. For example, when hydrogen gas is passed over heated copper(II) oxide, it is found that copper metal is obtained.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-253.jpg?height=395&width=1228&top_left_y=3418&top_left_x=1536)

Since this type of reaction was often used to extract metals from their ores, it was referred to as a reduction reaction. The reason for this name was because a large amount of an ore of the metal was converted or reduced to a smaller mass of metal, Figure 14.5

Note that in the above reaction the copper(II) oxide has lost oxygen. Thus, reduction could be said to be the opposite of oxidation.
Reduction may be defined as the removal of oxygen from a substance. Since hydrogen was often used to remove the oxygen, reduction may also be defined as the addition of hydrogen.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-254.jpg?height=424&width=1186&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 14.5 The word 'reduction' referred to the fact that when a metal is extracted from its ore, the mass of metal is less than the mass of the original ore.

Reduction is the removal of oxygen or the addition of hydrogen.

### 14.2 Oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer

After the discovery of the electron, chemists began to take a closer look at various chemical reactions. It became clear that many chemical reactions involved the transfer of electrons. Let us again consider the oxidation of magnesium to magnesium oxide.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-254.jpg?height=251&width=858&top_left_y=1940&top_left_x=201)

We see that what is actually happening in this reaction is that the magnesium is losing electrons and the oxygen is gaining electrons. In fact, each magnesium atom is losing two electrons. Therefore, oxidation may also be defined in terms of electron loss.

Oxidation of an element takes place when it loses electrons.

Consider now the reduction of copper(II) oxide to copper metal.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-254.jpg?height=313&width=1134&top_left_y=3060&top_left_x=188)

We see that what is actually happening is that the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2 *}$ ion is gaining two electrons to become a copper atom. Thus, reduction may also be defined in terms of electron transfer.

Reduction of an element takes place when it gains electrons

The words OIL RIG ('oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons') may be used to help you remember these definitions, Figure 14.6.

If we think of oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons being transferred, it becomes clear that oxidation and reduction must always occur together. If one substance loses electrons (oxidation), there must be some other substance to accept (gain) these electrons (reduction).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-254.jpg?height=861&width=1156&top_left_y=2405&top_left_x=1442)
Figure 14.6 Oxidation is loss of electrons. Reduction is gain of electrons.

This may easily be seen in the reaction between sodium and chlorine to form sodium chloride.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-255.jpg?height=395&width=825&top_left_y=546&top_left_x=862)
Each Cl atom gains one electron

A redox reaction is a reaction in which both oxidation and reduction take place.

- This is like a transfer of money - one person gives you a $€ 10$ note and you receive the $€ 10$ note.
- So we see that oxidation reactions and reduction reactions always occur together.
- Therefore, it is more correct to refer to these types of reactions as oxidation-reduction reactions or redox reactions.
- Note also that in the above reaction, neither oxygen nor hydrogen is present.
- It is clear, therefore, that the definitions of oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer are broader than the previous definitions that described oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen and hydrogen.

If we take a closer look at the reaction between magnesium and oxygen to form magnesium oxide, we see that this is another example of an oxidation-reduction reaction.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-255.jpg?height=486&width=1072&top_left_y=1940&top_left_x=794)

An interesting reaction in which the results of the oxidation-reduction reaction can be easily seen is the reaction between zinc metal and copper ions, Figure 14.7.

- When zinc metal is left standing in copper sulfate solution, two observations are noted:
- The zinc becomes covered with a brown deposit.
- The blue colour of the solution (caused by the presence of $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ions) begins to fade.
- On analysing the brown deposit, it is found to be copper metal.
- This fading implies that the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are being used up.
- On analysing the solution in the beaker, it is found that $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ ions are present.

Chemists concluded:

- The zinc metal was being oxidised (losing electrons).
- The copper ions $\left(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\right)$ were being reduced (gaining electrons).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-255.jpg?height=897&width=1183&top_left_y=2636&top_left_x=1627)
Figure 14.7 When zinc metal is left standing in a solution containing copper ions, an oxidationreduction reaction takes place. This reaction causes copper metal to be deposited, and zinc goes into solution as $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ ions.

The above evidence led chemists to conclude that the following chemical reaction was taking place:

$$
\mathrm{Zn}+\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}+\mathrm{Cu} \downarrow
$$

Recall that the downward arrow after Cu means that the copper settles out of solution. An insoluble solid that settles out of solution is called a precipitate.

If we study this equation closely, we see that the Zn is oxidised and the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ is reduced:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-256.jpg?height=460&width=841&top_left_y=1067&top_left_x=654)

In this reaction, the zinc atom could not lose electrons (oxidation) without the presence of something to accept (gain) these electrons (i.e. the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ion). We say that the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ion is an oxidising agent. (Another name for an oxidising agent is oxidant.) An agent is someone or something that undertakes a

An oxidising agent is a substance that brings about oxidation in other substances. mission to get things done. In redox reactions, the oxidising agents have a mission to bring about oxidation, i.e. to take electrons from another species.

- If we look at the above equation, we see that the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ion (the oxidising agent) accepts two electrons from the Zn atom i.e. the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ion is itself reduced.
- This is a general characteristic of oxidising agents - the oxidising agent is always reduced.
- The substance that causes the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ion to be reduced is Zn .
- Therefore, we say that Zn is the reducing agent. (Another name for a reducing agent is a reductant.) In redox reactions, the reducing agents have a mission to bring about reduction, i.e. to add electrons to another species.
- In order for a substance to act as a reducing agent, it must donate

A reducing agent is a substance that brings about reduction in other substances. electrons to some other substance, e.g. in the above equation Zn gives two electrons to the $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ion.

- When it does this, the Zn itself is oxidised.
- This is a general characteristic of reducing agents - the reducing agent is always oxidised.

We can now indicate the oxidising and reducing agents in the above equation.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-256.jpg?height=489&width=1202&top_left_y=3180&top_left_x=488)

A common oxidising agent is hydrogen peroxide, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}$, which is used to bleach hair. The hydrogen peroxide converts the coloured pigment in the hair to a colourless hair 'pigment' that leaves the hair blonde - hence the expression 'peroxide blonde', Figure 14.8. The hydrogen peroxide solution used in hair salons is usually only about $3 \% \mathrm{w} / \mathrm{v}$ concentration. This is much more dilute than the concentrated solution of hydrogen peroxide that you find in laboratories.

Some everyday examples of oxidising agents are summarised in Table 14.1.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-257.jpg?height=655&width=1183&top_left_y=325&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 14.8 Hydrogen peroxide is a very useful oxidising agent. It oxidises the coloured pigments in hair to a blonde colour.

| Oxidising agent | Use | Reaction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hydrogen peroxide, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}$ | Bleaching hair | coloured hair pigment $+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow$ colourless hair 'pigment' $+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ |
| Iodine, $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ | Used to prevent infection of cuts; a solution of iodine in ethanol is called 'tincture of iodine' | live germ $+\mathrm{I}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}^{-}+$dead germ |
| Chlorine gas, $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ | Used in treating water to make it safe to drink | live germ $+\mathrm{Cl}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-}+$dead germ |
| Sodium hypochlorite, NaClO | Household bleach for bleaching clothes | coloured fabric + ClO- → Cl+ colourless fabric |

Table 14.1 Examples of oxidising agents.

Some examples of reducing agents are summarised in Table 14.2.

| Reducing agent | Use | Reaction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Carbon | Used to extract metals from their ores by removing oxygen from the ore | $\mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}+3 \mathrm{C} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Fe}+3 \mathrm{CO}$ iron ore iron metal |
| Aluminium | Used to extract metals from their ores by removing oxygen from the ore | $\mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}+2 \mathrm{Al} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Fe}+\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ iron ore iron metal |
| Sulfur dioxide, $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ | Used as a food preservative (E220) as it prevents the oxidation of natural sugars (food spoilage); also used in bleaching items, e.g. paper and textiles | Coloured form of dye + sulfur dioxide → colourless form of dye |
| Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid) | Vitamin C acts as a reducing agent by converting insoluble $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions into soluble $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions; this helps iron to be absorbed in the body | $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+$ vitamin $\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ |

Table 14.2 Examples of reducing agents

## Example 14.1

## Question

Define oxidation in terms of electron transfer. In the following example, indicate clearly, by showing electron loss or gain, which species is being oxidised and which is being reduced:
$2 \mathrm{KI}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{KCl}+\mathrm{I}_{2}$
What are the oxidising and reducing agents in the above reaction?

## Answer

Oxidation is the loss of electrons.
The electron loss and electron gain may be more easily seen if we ignore the $\mathrm{K}^{+}$ion ('spectator ion') on each side of the equation. All of the required information may then be summarised as follows:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-258.jpg?height=437&width=1186&top_left_y=1305&top_left_x=787)

- Once you have established what is oxidised and what is reduced, it is easy to pick out the oxidising and reducing agents.
- In this question, since the $\mathrm{I}^{-}$is oxidised, the oxidising agent must be the $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$.
- Similarly, since the $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ is reduced, the reducing agent must be $\mathrm{I}^{-}$.
- The question merely asks you to indicate the various items, so full marks are obtained for laying out your work as shown above.


### 14.3 Oxidation numbers: Keeping track of electrons

As chemistry developed, it became clear that the definitions of oxidation and reduction needed to be expanded further. We have already seen that oxidation-reduction reactions need not involve oxygen at all. It was also found that not all oxidation-reduction reactions involved electron transfer, i.e. ionic compounds were not formed in all redox reactions.

Consider, for example, the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen:

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

This reaction is very different from the reaction of magnesium with oxygen as no ions are formed. Water is a covalent compound.

- To keep track of the movement of electrons during chemical reactions in which covalent compounds are involved, chemists introduced the idea of oxidation numbers (also called oxidation states).
- Oxidation numbers are simply numbers that are assigned to atoms to help us decide whether or not oxidation and reduction have taken place and, if so, how many electrons have been lost and gained.

Oxidation number is the charge that an atom has or appears to have when electrons are distributed according to certain rules.

Oxidation number is also described as the charge that an atom appears to have in a compound if the bonding is assumed to be completely ionic.

For example, in the compound water, the two electrons in each of the single covalent bonds are counted as if they have been completely transferred to the more electronegative element, i.e. to the oxygen atom (E.N. of $\mathrm{H}=2.20$, E.N. of $\mathrm{O}=3.44$ ), Figure 14.9.

Since we have 'transferred ownership' (on paper) of two electrons from hydrogen to oxygen, we assign an oxidation number of -2 to the oxygen atom. Since each hydrogen atom has formally lost an electron, we assign an oxidation number of +1 to each of the hydrogen atoms. This may be indicated by writing:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbf{H}_{2} \mathbf{O} \\
& 2(+1)-2
\end{aligned}
$$

The electrons are assigned to the more electronegative element

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-259.jpg?height=352&width=317&top_left_y=524&top_left_x=2285)
Figure 14.9 When assigning oxidation numbers, the electrons are assigned to the more electronegative element.

Since oxidation numbers are not actual charges, they are usually written under the symbol of the element. This avoids confusion when dealing with charged species.

Chemists have developed rules to make it easy for us to assign oxidation numbers. We will now discuss these rules.

## Rules for assigning oxidation numbers

1. The oxidation number of any uncombined element is zero.

- An uncombined element is an element that is not bonded to another element, e.g. $\mathrm{Zn}, \mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{O}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$.
- This means that in $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ the oxidation number (O.N.) of hydrogen is zero, in sodium metal (Na) the O.N. of Na is 0 and in $\mathrm{F}_{2}$ the O.N. of F is 0 .

2. The oxidation number of an ion of an element is the same as its charge.

- This means that the O.N. of Br in the $\mathrm{Br}^{-}$ion is -1
- The O.N. of Fe in $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ is +2
- The O.N. of Na in $\mathrm{Na}^{+} \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$is +1
- The O.N. of Cl in $\mathrm{Na}^{+} \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$is -1
- The O.N. of Mg in $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} \mathrm{O}^{2-}$ is +2

3. The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the elements in a compound must add up to zero.

- For example, in NaCl the sum of the oxidation numbers is +1 (for sodium) added to -1 (for chlorine) to give a total of zero.
- Similarly, in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ the sum is $2(+1)$ for the hydrogen atoms added to -2 for the oxygen atom, giving a total of zero.

4. Oxygen always has an oxidation number of -2 . There are two exceptions. In peroxides it has an oxidation number of -1 and in the compound $\mathrm{OF}_{2}$ it has an oxidation number of +2 .

- In magnesium oxide, $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} \mathrm{O}^{2-}$, the oxidation number of oxygen is -2 .
- First exception to rule: In hydrogen peroxide, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}$, the oxygen is assigned an oxidation number of -1 . This is done in order that the sum of all of the oxidation numbers in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}$ will add up to zero, i.e. $2(+1)$ for the two hydrogen atoms and 2(-1) for the two oxygen atoms.
- Second exception to rule: A similar reason holds in the case of oxygen difluoride, $\mathrm{OF}_{2}$. Fluorine is the only element that is more electronegative than oxygen. Therefore, in the $\mathrm{OF}_{2}$ molecule, Figure 14.10, the electrons in the two covalent bonds are assigned to the fluorine atoms. Therefore, so that the sum of all of the oxidation numbers adds up to zero, the oxygen atom must be assigned an oxidation number of +2 .

5. Hydrogen is always assigned an oxidation number of +1 in its compounds. There is one exception. In the metal hydrides it is assigned the metal hydrides it is assigned an oxidation number of $\mathbf{- 1}$.

- For example, in $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ each H atom is assigned an oxidation number of +1 . It follows from Rule 3 above that the oxidation number of the N atom must be -3 .
- Exception to rule: In a metal hydride (e.g. NaH ) the H atom is assigned an oxidation number of -1 . The reason for this is because sodium hydride is an ionic compound, $\mathrm{Na}^{+} \mathrm{H}^{-}$. The oxidation number of -1 is assigned to the H atom because there is one negative charge on this atom (Rule 2).

6. The halogens always have an oxidation number of $\mathbf{- 1}$ in their compounds unless bonded to a more electronegative atom.

- For example, since fluorine is the most electronegative element in the Periodic Table, its oxidation number will always be -1 .
- Although chlorine usually has an oxidation number of -1 in its compounds, this is not the case when it is bonded to oxygen or fluorine both of which are more electronegative than chlorine. (E.N. of $\mathrm{O}=3.44$, E.N. of $\mathrm{F}=3.98$, E.N. of $\mathrm{Cl}=3.16$ ).
- For example, in $\mathrm{Cl}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ the oxidation number of each chlorine atom is +1 . In the compound $\mathrm{Cl}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}$, each chlorine atom has an oxidation number of +7 .

$$
\begin{array}{cc}
\mathbf{C l}_{\mathbf{2}} \mathbf{O} & \mathbf{C l}_{\mathbf{2}} \mathbf{O}_{\mathbf{7}} \\
2(+1)-2 & 2(+7) 7(-2) \\
\text { O.N. of } \mathrm{Cl}=+1 & \text { O.N. of } \mathrm{Cl}=+7
\end{array}
$$

- Thus, whereas the O.N. of fluorine is always -1 , the O.N. of the other halogens can vary depending on the particular compound.
- Note the difference in the way that the formulas $\mathrm{OF}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ are written. As a general rule, the more electronegative element is usually placed second.

7. In a compound that is composed of two different elements, the electrons are assigned to the more electronegative element. The oxidation number of the second element is calculated by balancing the overall charge on the molecule.

- For example, consider the compound $\mathrm{CS}_{2,}$ Figure 14.11. This compound has the same structure as $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$.
- Since the E.N. value of sulfur ( 2.58 ) is greater than the E.N. value of carbon (2.55), the four outer electrons of carbon are formally assigned to sulfur.
- Therefore the oxidation number of each sulfur atom $=-2$.
- This gives a total negative charge of -4 .
- Therefore, the O.N. of C=+4 to balance the charges so that the overall sum of oxidation numbers add up to 0 .

8. The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the elements in a polyatomic ion must equal the charge on the ion.

- A polyatomic ion consists of two or more atoms bonded together and functions as a single unit with an overall charge. We have already met polyatomic ions in Experiment 5.1, e.g. $\mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{-}, \mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ and $\mathrm{CO}_{3}{ }^{2-}$. (Ions such as $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}, \mathrm{Na}^{+}$and $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ are often referred to as simple ions.)
- The following example will illustrate the usefulness of this rule.

Note: Some elements nearly always have the same oxidation number in their compounds. Such elements are the alkali metals ( $\mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{K}$, etc.) which have an oxidation number of +1 . Similarly, the alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, etc.) have an oxidation number of +2 . You will find that the oxidation numbers of these two groups of elements will be very useful as reference points for assigning oxidation numbers to elements in their compounds.

## Example 14.2

## Question

What is the oxidation number of the N atom in the $\mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{-}$ion?

## Answer

- We know that the oxidation number of the O atom is -2 .
- Therefore, the negative charge due to three oxygen atoms is $3 \times(-2)=-6$
- But overall charge on ion = -1
- From rule 8 , adding the oxidation number of the N atom to -6 must equal -1 .
- Let $x=$ oxidation number of the N atom.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x+(-6)=-1 \\
& x=-1+6=5
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbf{N O}_{\mathbf{3}}^{-} \\
& +5 \quad 3(-2)
\end{aligned}
$$

O.N. of the N atom $=5$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-261.jpg?height=290&width=642&top_left_y=410&top_left_x=1953)
Figure 14.11 In carbon disulfide, since the E.N. value of sulfur is great than that of carbon, the four outer electrons of carbon are formally assigned to sulfur.

## Example 14.3

## Question

What is the oxidation number of each of the elements in $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}$ ?

## Answer

- Note that of the three elements in $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}$, only one (oxygen) is mentioned in the rules for assigning oxidation numbers.
- To work out the oxidation numbers of Cu and S , we need to know that there are two negative charges on the sulfate ion, i.e. $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$.
- This must mean that, in order to balance the charges, there must be two positive charges on the copper, i.e. $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$.
- Therefore, the oxidation number of copper is +2 .
- Now consider the $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ ion. The four oxygen atoms give a total negative charge of $4(-2)=-8$.
- The overall charge on the ion is -2 .
- Therefore, the oxidation number of the sulfur atom must be +6 .


## $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}$ <br> $+2+64(-2)$

## EXAM TIPI

It is always best to clearly state the oxidation numbers of the elements. In the above notation, it is not clear if the oxidation number of oxygen is 4 or -2 . To avoid any confusion in an exam, it is best to set out your work as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{CuSO}_{4} \\
+2+64(-2) \\
\text { O.N. of } \mathrm{Cu}=+2 \quad \text { O.N. of } \mathrm{S}=+6 \quad \text { O.N. of } \mathrm{O}=-2
\end{gathered}
$$

In Example 14.3, copper has an oxidation number of +2 . Since transition metals exhibit variable valency, the oxidation number of copper varies, e.g. in $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ the oxidation number of Cu is +1 , Figure 14.12.

We have already discussed the naming of transition metal compounds in Chapter 5. A summary of some examples is given in Table 14.3. The oxidation number (written in Roman numerals) is used in naming these compounds, e.g. FeO is called iron(II) oxide and $\mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ is called iron(III) oxide. Another way of stating this is to say that iron exists in an oxidation state of two ( +2 ) and an oxidation state of three (+3). In short, the Roman numeral tells us the oxidation state of the element.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-262.jpg?height=737&width=1118&top_left_y=2633&top_left_x=1458)
Figure 14.12 Copper(I) oxide is so called because copper has an oxidation number of 1 in $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. Copper has an oxidation number of 2 in copper(II) oxide, CuO .

| Formula of compound | Oxidation number of transition metal | Name of compound |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ | $\mathrm{Cu}=+1$ | Copper(I) oxide |
| CuO | $\mathrm{Cu}=+2$ | Copper(II) oxide |
| FeO | $\mathrm{Fe}=+2$ | Iron(II) oxide |
| $\mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ | $\mathrm{Fe}=+3$ | Iron (III) oxide |
| $\mathrm{MnO}_{2}$ | $\mathrm{Mn}=+4$ | Manganese(IV) oxide - commonly called manganese dioxide |
| $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ | $\mathrm{Mn}=+7$ | Potassium manganate(VII) - commonly called potassium permanganate |
| $\mathrm{V}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ | $\mathrm{V}=+3$ | Vanadium(III) oxide |
| $\mathrm{V}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{5}$ | $\mathrm{V}=+5$ | Vanadium(V) oxide |
| $\mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ | $\mathrm{Cr}=+3$ | Chromium(III) oxide |
| $\mathrm{K}_{2} \mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{7}$ | $\mathrm{Cr}=+6$ | Potassium dichromate(VI) |

Although we have only shown two oxidation states for each metal in Table 14.3, some elements have more than two oxidation states. For example, the metal vanadium has four oxidation states, Figure 14.13.

In your Leaving Certificate exam, you will only be asked to assign oxidation numbers up to the first 36 elements.

## Example 14.4

## Question

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-263.jpg?height=565&width=844&top_left_y=1770&top_left_x=1868)
Figure 14.13 Vanadium exists in four oxidation states.

What is the oxidation number of sulfur in $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ ?

## Answer

Each sodium atom has an oxidation number of +1 .
Each oxygen atom has an oxidation number of -2 .

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathbf{S}_{2} \mathbf{O}_{3} \\
& 2(+1) 2(x) 3(-2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\mathrm{x}=$ oxidation number of sulfur. The sum of all the oxidation numbers must be zero.
$2(+1)+2 x+3(-2)=0$
$2 \mathrm{x}=6-2=4$
$\mathrm{x}=2$
Oxidation number of sulfur $=+2$
Since oxidation numbers are assigned to help us 'keep track' of electrons on paper, we sometimes find that when we apply the rules, the oxidation number of an element may not work out to be a whole number. This is the case in Example 14.5.

## Example 14.5

## Question

What is the oxidation number of sulfur in $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}$ ?

## Answer

Each sodium atom has an oxidation number of +1 .
Each oxygen atom has an oxidation number of -2 .

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbf{N a}_{\mathbf{2}} \mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{4}} \mathbf{O}_{\mathbf{6}} \\
& 2(+1) 4(x) 6(-2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $\mathrm{x}=$ oxidation number of sulfur. The sum of all the oxidation numbers must be zero.
$2(+1)+4 x+6(-2)=0$
$4 \mathrm{x}=12-2=10$
$\mathrm{x}=2.5$
Oxidation number of sulfur = +2.5

## Note:

1. You may wonder what an oxidation number of 2.5 means. The 2.5 can be thought of as an average value of the oxidation numbers of the sulfur atoms. Not all atoms of sulfur in the $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}$ molecule are bonded in an identical way. This means that some $S$ atoms have a different oxidation number than other S atoms. The average oxidation number works out as 2.5 .
2. There are cases where an element may have an oxidation number of 0 even when it is in a compound, e.g. C has an oxidation number of 0 in sucrose, $\mathrm{C}_{12} \mathrm{H}_{22} \mathrm{O}_{11}$.
3. Note the distinction between valency and oxidation number. You may remember that we explained valency in Chapter 5 in terms of the number of atoms of hydrogen or any other monovalent element with which each atom of the element combines. Valency is just a number and does not carry any plus or minus charge. For example, the valency of carbon is 4 because it combines with four hydrogen atoms as in $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$. However, oxidation numbers can be positive or negative or zero. For example, the oxidation number of carbon in $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ is -4 , in $\mathrm{CCl}_{4}$ it is +4 , and in $\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ it is 0 .

Another difference between valency and oxidation number is that valency is always a whole number but oxidation numbers can be fractions.

### 14.4 Oxidation and reduction in terms of oxidation numbers

Oxidation numbers may be used to give very comprehensive definitions of oxidation and reduction.

The use of oxidation numbers to determine the species that are oxidised and reduced is shown in Examples 14.6 and 14.7.

## TEST YOURSELF:

Attempt Questions 14.3-14.5 and W14.1W14.8.

When an element is oxidised, its oxidation number increases, i.e. oxidation is an increase in oxidation number.

When an element is reduced, its oxidation number decreases, i.e. reduction is a decrease in oxidation number.

## Example 14.6

## Question

Using oxidation numbers, indicate the species oxidised and reduced in the reaction:
$2 \mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

## Answer

Assign oxidation numbers and indicate the elements that change oxidation number.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-265.jpg?height=493&width=864&top_left_y=872&top_left_x=1744)

## Example 14.7

## Question

Use oxidation numbers to determine whether or not the following is an oxidation/reduction reaction and, if so, indicate which species is being oxidised and which is being reduced:
$\mathrm{Cu}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO}_{4}+\mathrm{SO}_{2}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
[LCH]

## Answer

## Step 1

Write under each element the oxidation number of that element (using a pencil).

$$
\underset{0}{\mathrm{Cu}}+\underset{2(+1)+64(-2)}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}} \rightarrow \underset{+2+64(-2)}{\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}}+\underset{+42(-2)}{\mathrm{SO}_{2}}+\underset{2(+1)-2}{2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

## Step 2

Mark (in ink) those elements that show a change in oxidation number.

$$
\begin{array}{cl}
\mathrm{Cu}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} & \rightarrow \underset{+2}{\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}}+\mathrm{SO}_{2}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \\
0+6 & +4
\end{array}
$$

It now becomes clearer which elements are oxidised and which are reduced. Note that in particular example, one of the sulfur atoms is neither oxidised nor reduced (O.N. of $\mathrm{S}=+6$ in both $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4}$ ) and the other sulfur atom is reduced (O.N. of S in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}=+6$, O.N. of S in $\mathrm{SO}_{2}=+4$ ).
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-265.jpg?height=493&width=1117&top_left_y=3014&top_left_x=970)

In this example, sulfuric acid is the oxidising agent (and is therefore reduced) and copper is the reducing agent (and is therefore oxidised).

### 14.5 Balancing redox equations

In Section 10.4 we learned how to balance equations by inspection. This trial-anderror approach is fine for fairly simple equations. However, for more complicated equations, it is preferable to balance the equations in a more systematic manner. In the case of oxidation-reduction reactions, we use oxidation numbers to help us balance the equation.

The method is illustrated in the following examples.

## Example 14.8

## Question

Using oxidation numbers, balance the following equation:
$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

## Answer

## Step 1

Assign oxidation numbers to all atoms.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \\
& +74(-2)+2+1 \quad+2+3 \quad 2(+1)-2
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 2

Note which elements change oxidation number.

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \\
+7 & +2
\end{array}
$$

## Step 3

Show the number of electrons lost and gained.
An increase in oxidation number represents a loss of electrons. A decrease in oxidation number represents a gain of electrons.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-266.jpg?height=489&width=1222&top_left_y=2474&top_left_x=781)

## Step 4

Work out the ratio of oxidising agent to reducing agent.
In Step 3, we see that each $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ion must gain five electrons from the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2 *}$ ion. However, each $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ion can only lose one electron. Therefore, there must be five $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions for every one $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ion, i.e. $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$and $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ react in the ratio of $1: 5$.

Therefore, we can write:
$1 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
(The '1' before the $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$is usually omitted. It is written in here just to emphasise the ratio.)
Step 4 is a vital step. Therefore, it is best to just concentrate on getting this ratio correct and forget about everything else in the equation.

## Step 5

Balance the remaining items in the equation by the inspection method.
As a general rule, leave oxygen and hydrogen atoms as the last items to be balanced. From the above, we see that there is one Mn atom on the left-hand side (L.H.S) of the equation. Therefore, there must be one Mn atom on the right-hand side (R.H.S) of the equation.
$1 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Similarly, there are five iron atoms on the L.H.S. Therefore, there must be five iron atoms on the R.H.S.
$1 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
There are four oxygen atoms on the L.H.S. Therefore, there must be four oxygen atoms on the R.H.S.
$1 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Finally, there are eight hydrogen atoms on the R.H.S. Therefore, there must be eight H atoms on the L.H.S.
$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Always double check that the equation is balanced for atoms. If the equation involves ions, also check that the equation is balanced for charges

## 1. For atoms:

|  | L.H.S. | R.H.S. |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Mn | 1 | $1 \checkmark$ |
| Fe | 5 | $5 \checkmark$ |
| O | 4 | $4 \checkmark$ |
| H | 8 | $8 \checkmark$ |

## 2. For charges:

| $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ |  |
| :--- | :--- |
| Charge on L.H.S <br> $=1(-1)+5(+2)+8(+1)$ <br> $=+17$ | Charge on R.H.S. <br> $=1(+2)+5(+3)+4(0)$ <br> $=+17$ |

## EXAM TIPI

It is important that you use oxidation numbers to balance oxidationreduction equations.

You would be very unlikely to obtain the correct ratio of oxidising agent to reducing agent if you simply attempted to balance the equation by inspection.
Also, ensure that you indicate the correct charges on each of the species in the equation, as even one incorrect charge can lose many marks!

## Example 14.9

## Question

Using oxidation numbers, balance the following equation:
$\mathrm{Cu}+\mathrm{HNO}_{3}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+\mathrm{NO}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

## Answer

## Step 1

Assign oxidation numbers to all atoms.

$$
\underset{0}{\mathrm{Cu}}+\underset{+1+53(-2)}{\mathrm{HNO}_{3}}+\underset{+1}{\mathrm{H}^{+}} \rightarrow \underset{+2}{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}}+\underset{+2-2}{\mathrm{NO}}+\underset{2(+1)-2}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

## Step 2

Note which elements change oxidation number.

$$
\underset{0}{\mathrm{Cu}}+\underset{+5}{\mathrm{HNO}_{3}}+\underset{+2}{\mathrm{H}^{+}} \rightarrow \underset{+2}{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}}+\underset{+2}{\mathrm{NO}}+\underset{2}{\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}
$$

## Step 3

Show the number of electrons lost and gained.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-268.jpg?height=421&width=1170&top_left_y=1699&top_left_x=807)
gains 3 electrons

## Step 4

Work out the ratio of oxidising agent to reducing agent.
In order to have the same number of electrons lost and gained, bring this number up to six, i.e. 3Cu and $2 \mathrm{HNO}_{3}$.

$$
3 \mathrm{Cu}+2 \mathrm{HNO}_{3}+\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+\mathrm{NO}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

## Step 5

Balance the remaining items in the equation by the inspection method.

$$
3 \mathrm{Cu}+2 \mathrm{HNO}_{3}+6 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{NO}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Double check that the equation is balanced using tables for atoms and charges.

## 1. For atoms:

|  | L.H.S. | R.H.S. |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Cu | 3 | $3 \checkmark$ |
| N | 2 | $2 \checkmark$ |
| O | 6 | $6 \checkmark$ |
| H | 8 | $8 \checkmark$ |

2. For charges:

|  | $3 \mathrm{Cu}+2 \mathrm{HNO}_{3}+6 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{NO}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Charge on L.H.S. $=6(+1) =+6$ | Charge on R.H.S = 3(+2) $=+6$ |

[^0]
## Example 14.11

## Question

Using oxidation numbers, balance the following equation:
$\mathrm{I}_{2}+\mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}^{-}+\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}{ }^{2-}$

## Answer

## Step 1

Assign oxidation numbers to all atoms.

$$
\underset{0}{\mathrm{I}_{2}}+\underset{2(+2) 3(-2)}{\mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-}} \rightarrow \quad \stackrel{\mathrm{I}^{-}}{-1}+\underset{4(+2.5) 6(-2)}{\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}}
$$

## Step 2

Note which elements change oxidation number.

$$
\underset{+2}{\mathrm{I}_{2}}+\underset{-1}{\mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-}} \rightarrow \underset{+2.5}{\mathrm{I}_{4}^{-}}+\underset{\mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}}{\mathrm{S}_{2}^{2-}}
$$

## Step 3

Show the number of electrons lost and gained.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-269.jpg?height=499&width=798&top_left_y=1696&top_left_x=1126)

Each I atom gains 1 electron
$\therefore \mathrm{I}_{2}$ gains 2 electrons

## Step 4

Work out the ratio of oxidising agent to reducing agent.
In order to have the same number of electrons lost and gained, we need two $\mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-}$ ions for every one molecule of $\mathrm{I}_{2}$.

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}^{-}+\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}
$$

## Step 5

Balance the remaining items in the equation by the inspection method. 14.8-14.9 and W14.14-W14.25.

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}^{-}+\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}
$$

Double check that the equation is balanced using tables for atoms and charges.

## 1. For atoms:

|  | L.H.S. | R.H.S. |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| I | 2 | $2 \checkmark$ |
| S | 4 | $4 \checkmark$ |
| O | 6 | $6 \checkmark$ |

## 2. For charges:

| $\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}+\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2}$ |  |
| ---: | ---: |
| Charge on L.H.S. | $=2(-2)$ |
|  | $=-4$ | | Charge on R.H.S | $=2(-1)+1(-2)$ |
| ---: | :--- |
|  | $=-4$ |

Study SEC exam question 14.12 and model answer in the online resources.

## Summary What I should know

- Oxidation is the addition of oxygen to a substance.
- Reduction is the removal of oxygen from a substance or the addition of hydrogen to a substance.
- Oxidation of an element takes place when it loses electrons.
- Reduction of an element takes place when it gains electrons.
- An oxidising agent is a substance that brings about oxidation in other substances.
- A reducing agent is a substance that brings about reduction in other substances.
- Oxidation number is the charge that an atom has or appears to have when electrons are distributed according to certain rules.

Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number.
Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number.
Oxidation numbers may be used to balance redox equations.
