# 15 Volumetric Analysis: Oxidation-Reduction

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-272.jpg?height=1104&width=1274&top_left_y=527&top_left_x=182)

### 15.1 Introduction

In Chapters 12 and 13, we studied how volumetric analysis could be used to determine the concentrations of solutions of acids and bases. In Chapter 14, we saw that many reactions in chemistry may be classified as oxidation-reduction reactions. In this chapter, we will study how volumetric analysis may be used to determine the concentrations of oxidising and reducing agents.

The most important oxidising agent that we will come across in this course is potassium permanganate, which has the formula $\mathbf{K M n O}_{4}$, Figure 15.1. It is a strong oxidising agent and one of its uses is to remove iron ions from water. It oxidises soluble $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions to insoluble $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions which can then be filtered out of the water. It need only be present in very dilute concentrations (1-3 p.p.m). Therefore, the purple colour of the permanganate is not visible in the water. It is also used in dilute solutions in medicine as an antiseptic to treat fungal infections.

The more modern ('systematic') name for potassium permanganate is potassium manganate(VII) and you will see this name commonly used on Leaving Certificate exam papers. Since the name 'potassium permanganate' is so well known, we will use both terms throughout this chapter and in subsequent chapters.

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an introduction to volumetric analysis involving oxidation-reduction reactions.
- To provide students with the opportunity to investigate the role of oxidising and reducing agents in volumetric analysis.
- To enable students to determine the concentrations of substances being analysed in volumetric analysis involving oxidationreduction reactions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-272.jpg?height=1255&width=714&top_left_y=1933&top_left_x=1666)
Figure 15.1 Potassium permanganate is used to remove excess iron from water.

Before studying redox titrations, it is important to be familiar with some key points regarding potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)]. These points will be studied in the next section.

### 15.2 Potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)]: oxidising agent

The main points about potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] may be summarised as follows:

- Potassium permanganate is a purple-coloured solid.
- It is not a primary standard, as it cannot be obtained in a state of very high purity.
- It is unstable and decomposes in the presence of sunlight and heat.
- Therefore, the concentrations of potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] solutions vary over time.
- As a result of this, solutions of potassium permanganate must be standardised by titration against a primary standard solution.
- Potassium permanganate acts as an oxidising agent by gaining five electrons in acidic solution. The following is the reaction that takes place in acidic solution:

$$
\begin{array}{lc}
\mathbf{M n O}_{4}^{-+} & \mathbf{8 H ^ { + } + 5 e ^ { - }} \rightarrow \mathbf{M n}^{2+}+\mathbf{4 H}_{2} \mathbf{O} \\
\text { purple colourless }
\end{array}
$$

The above reaction is illustrated in Figure 15.2.
As a general rule, when dealing with redox reactions, the transfer of electrons is emphasised by writing the halfreactions rather than the fully balanced equations. The above half-reaction is so important and occurs so frequently in this course that it is recommended that you learn it off by heart.

- In order to get the permanganate to undergo the above reaction, it is necessary to add some dilute acid to supply the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions.
- When acidifying $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution, it is usual to use sulfuric acid. If HCl were used, the $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ions would be oxidised to $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ by the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$. If nitric acid were used, it could interfere with the reaction, as nitric acid is itself a strong oxidising agent.
- In neutral or basic solution, the above reaction does not take place, i.e. the manganese ion does not change from an oxidation state of +7 (purple) to +2 (colourless). Instead, the manganese ion changes from the oxidation state of +7 (purple) to +4 (brown).
- This oxidation state appears as a brown solid precipitate and is due to the formation of manganese dioxide, $\mathrm{MnO}_{2}$, Figure 15.3. The manganese dioxide is formed according to the reaction:

$$
\underset{\text { purple }}{\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+3 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow} \rightarrow \underset{\text { brown }}{\mathrm{MnO}_{2} \downarrow+4 \mathrm{OH}^{-}}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-273.jpg?height=760&width=1001&top_left_y=1510&top_left_x=1757)
Figure 15.2 As the acidified potassium permanganate solution is being added to the reducing agent, the manganese changes from an oxidation state of +7 (purple) to an oxidation state of +2 (colourless).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-273.jpg?height=785&width=997&top_left_y=2630&top_left_x=1761)
Figure 15.3 When the permanganate ion reacts with a reducing agent in neutral or basic solution, the manganese atom changes from an oxidation state of +7 (purple) to an oxidation state of +4 (brown).

- Potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] acts as its own indicator. It is said to be self-indicating. As explained above, it changes colour from purple to colourless when acting as an oxidising agent in acidic solution. This colour change enables us to detect the end point. (This will be explained in more detail later in this chapter.)
- Because of the intense purple colour of potassium permanganate solution, the bottom of the meniscus can be difficult to see. Therefore, it is usual to read the top of the meniscus, rather than the bottom of the meniscus, Figure 15.4.
- Because of the intense purple colour, its fairly low solubility and the fact that it is a good oxidising agent, we usually use fairly dilute solutions of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ in redox titrations. For example, 0.02 M solutions will frequently be used in the redox titrations on this course.

In the Leaving Certificate Chemistry course, we are required to study two examples of redox titrations. The first of these is the reaction between $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$and $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-274.jpg?height=1072&width=935&top_left_y=406&top_left_x=1644)
Figure 15.4 In the case of potassium permanganate solutions, it is normal to take the readings from the top of the meniscus.

### 15.3 The reaction of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$and $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions

As already stated, it is not possible to make up a solution of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ to an accurately known concentration by simply weighing out a certain amount of the solid and dissolving it in a known volume of solution. This is because $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ is not a primary standard.

- However, it is possible to determine the concentration of a $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution by titrating it against a solution containing $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions.
- $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ is an oxidising agent and, when added to a solution containing $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions (reducing agent), it converts the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions to $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions.

This is shown in the following half equations:
Oxidising agent: $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
(a)

Reducing agent: $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}$
(b)

- If we examine equation (a) above, we see that each $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ion can accept five electrons. However, each $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ion can lose only one electron.
- Therefore, five $\mathrm{Fe}^{2 *}$ ions will be required to react with one $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}{ }^{-}$ion, i.e. the ions react in the ratio of one $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ion to five $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions. Think carefully about this.
- To balance the electron transfer, we can write the above two equations as follows:

Oxidising agent: $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
Reducing agent: $5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-}$
Adding: $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
The important point to note from this equation is that $\mathbf{M n O}_{\mathbf{4}}{ }^{-}$ions react with
$\mathbf{F e}^{2+}$ ions in the ratio of 1:5. (We have already used this idea in the last chapter to balance redox equations). You will need to know this ratio for subsequent calculations.

We now consider some important points about the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ reducing agent in the reactions represented by the above equations:

- You might think that $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions for the titration would be obtained by dissolving crystals of iron(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 7 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ in water.
- However, it is not possible to use this compound as a primary standard because (i) the crystals tend to be oxidised slightly by the air and (ii) the crystals tend to lose their water of crystallisation when exposed to the air. The spontaneous loss of water of crystallisation to the air is known as efflorescence.

> Efflorescence is the spontaneous loss of water of crystallisation from a hydrated crystalline salt.

The word 'spontaneous' means it occurs on its own or naturally without any external intervention (e.g. heating) being necessary. Other examples of compounds that undergo efflorescence are $\mathrm{CuSO}_{4} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3} \cdot 10 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

> A substance is said to be hygroscopic if it has the ability to spontaneously absorb moisture from the surrounding air without dissolving into a liquid solution.

Examples of hygroscopic compounds are iron(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$, silica gel, $\mathrm{SiO}_{2}$ (used in packaging to absorb moisture) and concentrated sulfuric acid.

> Deliquescence is the spontaneous process by which a substance absorbs moisture from the atmosphere to the extent that it dissolves into a liquid solution.

Examples of deliquescent compounds are sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide.

- The anhydrous compound $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ cannot be used either because it takes in moisture from the air, i.e. it is hygroscopic.
- Instead of using iron(II) sulfate, we use a substance called ammonium iron(II) sulfate as a source of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions. This can be obtained in a high degree of purity, is not affected by the air, and so it can be used as a primary standard, Figure 15.5.
- The formula of ammonium iron(II) sulfate is $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. This is referred to as a 'double salt'. A double salt is a salt that consists of two different simple salts crystallised together in a fixed ratio within the same crystal structure.
- To remember its formula, write down the formula of iron(II) sulfate and put the formula of ammonium sulfate in front of it.
- The old name for ammonium iron(II) sulfate was 'ferrous ammonium sulfate'. This name is still widely used and is probably the name that appears on the container of the salt in the chemical store of your school.
- Even though ammonium iron(II) sulfate is hydrated, it is still used as a primary standard because it is very stable and does not spontaneously lose its water of crystallisation to the air.
- The high relative molecular mass of ammonium iron(II) sulfate (392.17) ensures that percentage errors due to slight inaccuracies in weighing will be reduced.
- When making up a solution of ammonium iron(II) sulfate, it is important that it is dissolved in water that contains dilute sulfuric acid. The sulfuric acid prevents the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions being oxidised to $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions by the oxygen in the air. $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions are more stable in the acidic solution and this makes them less likely to react with oxygen.

Make sure that you can explain the role of the dilute sulfuric acid, as it could be asked on an exam paper!

Figure 15.5 The formula of ammonium iron(II) sulfate is $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{FeSO} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. It can be used as a primary standard.

### 15.1 Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 11

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 11 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To prepare a standard solution of ammonium iron(II) sulfate and to use this solution to standardise a solution of potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] by titration

## Introduction

In this experiment, we will make up a standard solution of ammonium iron(II) sulfate. We will then use this standard solution to find out the exact concentration of a solution of potassium permanganate by titration.

## Key steps in procedure

- Some ammonium iron(II) sulfate is accurately weighed out on a clock glass using the laboratory balance.
- Using a graduated cylinder, dilute sulfuric acid is added to a beaker containing some deionised water.
- The ammonium iron(II) sulfate is transferred to the beaker taking all the usual precautions outlined in Chapter 12.


## Explanation

- The ammonium iron(II) sulfate is dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid as the sulfuric acid prevents the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions being oxidised to $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions by the oxygen in the air.


## Procedure (continued)

- The ammonium iron(II) sulfate solution is stirred to fully dissolve the crystals and, when dissolved, the solution is then transferred to a clean volumetric flask using a funnel.
- All the washings are transferred to the volumetric flask. The bottom of the meniscus of the solution is brought up to the mark with deionised water.
- The stoppered flask is inverted about 20 times.
- The pipette, burette and conical flask are washed with deionised water.
- The burette is washed with some of the potassium permanganate solution and filled with the aid of a funnel, Figure 15.6. The funnel is removed.
- The top of the meniscus of the potassium permanganate solution is adjusted so that it is level with the zero mark of the burette, taking the reading at eye level.
- A check is made to ensure that the tap and the space below the tap are also filled with the permanganate solution.
- Some of the ammonium iron(II) sulfate solution is transferred to a clean, dry beaker and the pipette is washed out with this solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-276.jpg?height=1433&width=1020&top_left_y=1969&top_left_x=1588)
Figure 15.6 Titration of potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] solution against a standard solution of ammonium iron(II) sulfate.

－Using a pipette filler，the pipette is filled to the mark with the ammonium iron（II）sulfate solution and this amount of ammonium iron（II）sulfate is placed in the conical flask．
－Using a graduated cylinder，some dilute sulfuric acid is added to the conical flask． The sulfuric acid should be in excess．

## Explanation

－The need for an excess of sulfuric acid is to ensure that a sufficient supply of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions is present so that all of the $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ions are reduced to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ ions according to the following half equation：

$$
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

If no acid（or insufficient acid）is added，a brown precipitate of $\mathrm{MnO}_{2}$ will be formed in the conical flask during the titration．

## Procedure（continued）

－The titration is carried out in the usual manner until a faint permanent pink colour is observed at the end point．

## Explanation

－The faint permanent pink colour at the end point may be explained as follows：as long as $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions are present in the conical flask，the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution that is run into the flask loses it colour．When all the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions have reacted，the next drop of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution gives a permanent pink colour．Therefore，at the end point，one single drop of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ from the burette will turn the solution in the conical flask a faint pink colour．The $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ is acting as its own indicator．

## Procedure（continued）

－One rough and two accurate titrations are carried out．The two accurate titration figures should agree to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ ．
－As $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ stains glassware，all glassware must be thoroughly washed out when all titrations are completed．

## Calculations

The exact concentration of the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution may be calculated using the average titration figure．The method of calculation is shown in Example 15．1．

You may have noticed that the first few drops of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ added to the conical flask are decolorised slowly but subsequent drops are decolorised more rapidly．This is due to an occurrence called autocatalysis（Chapter 17）．The reaction is catalysed by the $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ ions formed in the reaction．As soon as the $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ ions are formed，the rate of the reaction increases as the $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ ions are produced．

### 15.4 Solving volumetric problems in redox reactions

The general expression derived for solving volumetric problems involving acid-base reactions may also be used for solving volumetric problems involving redox reactions. (The derivation of this formula is the same as outlined for acid-base reactions.)

For redox reactions we write this expression as follows:
$\mathrm{V}_{0}=$ volume of oxidising agent ( $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ )
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{o}}=$ molarity of oxidising agent
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=$ number of moles of oxidising agent (from balanced equation)
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{r}}=$ volume of reducing agent ( $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ )
$\mathrm{M}_{\text {red }}=$ molarity of reducing agent
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=$ number of moles of reducing agent (from balanced equation)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-278.jpg?height=727&width=1489&top_left_y=833&top_left_x=1129)

The use of this equation is illustrated in the following examples.

## Example 15.1

## Question

A student made up a 0.12 M ammonium iron(II) sulfate solution and used this to standardise a solution of potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)]. $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the ammonium iron(II) sulfate solution were titrated against the potassium permanganate solution. The equation for the reaction is:
$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
The average titration figure was $23.75 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Calculate the concentration of the potassium permanganate solution in (a) moles per litre and (b) grams per litre.

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the molarity of the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution (oxidising agent)
From the balanced equation, we see that one mole of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$- reacts with
5 moles of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$, i.e. $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=1$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=5$.

## $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$( $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$

Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}}=23.75$

$$
\frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{r e d}}{n_{r}}
$$

$\mathrm{M}_{0}=$ ?
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=1$

$$
\frac{23.75 \times M_{0}}{1}=\frac{25 \times 0.12}{5}
$$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{r}}=25$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{K} & =39.1 \\
\mathrm{Mn} & =54.94 \\
4 \times \mathrm{O}=4 \times 16 & =64.00 \\
\hline M_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{KMnO}_{4} & =158.04
\end{array}
$$

$\mathrm{M}_{\text {red }}=0.12$

$$
M_{0}=\frac{25 \times 0.12}{5 \times 23.75}
$$

$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=5$

$$
\text { = } 0.0253 \text { moles per litre. }
$$

(a)

## Step 2

Convert to $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{L}$

$$
\begin{align*}
& \left.=0.0253 \times 158.04 \text { grams per litre (Rel. molecular mass } \mathrm{KMnO}_{4}=158.04\right) \\
& =3.998 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L} .  \tag{b}\\
& \text { (b) }
\end{align*}
$$

[^1]
## Example 15.2

## Question

A sample of iron(II) sulfate crystals $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \times \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ was analysed in order to find out the value of x . 6.42 g of the crystals were dissolved in deionised water to which some dilute sulfuric acid had been added, and the resulting solution was made up to $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ in a volumetric flask. $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ samples of this solution were titrated against $0.018 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution. The balanced equation for the reaction is:
$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
The average titration figure was $25.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Calculate the value of x in the above formula.

## Answer

When solving problems of this type, proceed as we did in the case of acid-base volumetric problems. First calculate the concentration of the iron(II) sulfate solution in moles per litre. Then relate this number of moles to the mass of substance dissolved and hence calculate the relative molecular mass of the hydrated salt. Once this is known, it is easy to calculate the value of x.

## Step 1

Calculate the molarity of the $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ solution (reducing agent)

$$
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} \quad \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}
$$

Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}}=25.5$

$$
\frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{r e d}}{n_{r}}
$$

$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{o}}=0.018$
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=1$

$$
\frac{25.5 \times 0.018}{1}=\frac{25 \times \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{red}}}{5}
$$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{r}}=25$
$\mathrm{M}_{\text {red }}=$ ?

$$
M_{\mathrm{red}}=\frac{25.5 \times 0.018 \times 5}{25}
$$

$$
n_{t}=5
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =0.0918 \mathrm{moles} / \text { litre } \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \\
& =0.023 \mathrm{moles} / 250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \mathrm{FeSO}_{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. by dissolving 6.42 g of the crystals in $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution, we obtain a solution which contains 0.023 moles.

## Step 2

Calculate the relative molecular mass of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot \times \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
From Step 1, 0.023 moles $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot \times \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=6.42 \mathrm{~g}$
1 mole $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \times \mathrm{xH}_{2} \mathrm{O}=\frac{6.42}{0.023} \mathrm{~g}=279.13 \mathrm{~g}$
$1 \mathrm{~mole} \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \times \mathrm{xH}_{2} \mathrm{O}=279.13 \mathrm{~g}$

## Step 3

Calculate the value of $x$ using the values of $M_{r}$ of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ and $M$, of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \times \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
151.92+18 x & =279.13 \\
18 x & =279.13-151.92=127.21 \\
x & =\frac{127.21}{18}=7
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $x=7$. The formula is $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 7 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{Fe} & =55.85 \\
\mathrm{~S} & =32.07 \\
4 \times \mathrm{O}=4 \times 16 & =64 \\
\hline M r \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} & =151.92
\end{array}
$$

## To determine the percentage of elemental iron in an iron tablet

## Introduction

In this experiment, we will measure the amount of iron(II) sulfate, $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$, in an iron tablet and then compare our result with the quantity stated on the packet. The quantity on the packet is usually stated in terms of milligrams of the anhydrous salt, e.g. 200 mg FeSO $_{4}$ per tablet.

The amount of iron(II) sulfate is measured by dissolving some tablets in dilute sulfuric acid and titrating the solution against standardised potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] solution. The potassium permanganate must be standardised immediately before use in this titration since, as already mentioned, $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ is unstable and is decomposed by the presence of light and heat, i.e. the concentration of the solution varies over time.

## Key steps in procedure

- Five tablets are placed on a clock glass and the total mass found using the laboratory balance. If the iron tablets are in the form of capsules, the contents of five capsules are emptied onto the clock glass and the total mass of the contents is found.
- The tablets are ground up using a mortar and pestle. This helps the iron sulfate to dissolve more quickly. Some dilute sulfuric acid is added to the mortar to make it easier to grind the tablets.
- Taking all the precautions outlined previously, the paste of acid and tablets is transferred to a beaker containing some dilute sulfuric acid.
- The solution is stirred to dissolve the iron sulfate in the paste.


## Observation

- It may be observed that the solution is cloudy rather than clear.


## Explanation

- The outer coating of the tablets may not dissolve easily and this may give a cloudy appearance to the solution. Do not worry about this as it will not affect your results. (Iron tablets often have a coating to slow down the rate at which they dissolve in the stomach. This reduces the chance of stomach upsets.)


## Procedure (continued)

- Taking all the precautions outlined in previous experiments, the solution of the tablets is transferred to a clean volumetric flask. The bottom of the meniscus of the solution is brought up to the mark with deionised water.
- The stoppered flask is inverted about 20 times.
- The pipette, burette and conical flask are rinsed with deionised water.
- The burette is washed with some of the potassium permanganate solution and filled with the aid of a funnel, Figure 15.10. The funnel is removed.
- The top of the meniscus of the potassium permanganate solution is adjusted so that it is level with the zero mark of the burette.
- A check is made to ensure that the tap and the space below the tap are filled with the permanganate solution.
- Some of the iron tablet solution is transferred from the volumetric flask to a clean, dry beaker. Using a pipette filler, the pipette is washed out with a small amount of this solution. The pipette is then filled to the mark with the iron tablet solution and this volume is pipetted into the conical flask.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-282.jpg?height=1355&width=886&top_left_y=436&top_left_x=1644)
Figure 15.10 Determining the percentage of elemental iron in iron tablets.

- Using a graduated cylinder, dilute sulfuric acid is added in excess to the conical flask (for the same reason as stated in the previous experiment).
- A titration is carried out in the usual way until a faint permanent pink colour is observed at the end point. One rough and two accurate titrations are carried out.


## Calculations

Using the average titration figure, the mass of iron in each tablet is calculated. The method of calculating is shown in Example 15.3.

## Example 15.3

## Question

A student was asked to analyse an iron tablet to determine if the amount of iron sulfate per tablet stated on the packet was correct. He dissolved five tablets whose total mass was 1.21 grams in dilute sulfuric acid and made the solution up to $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ in a volumetric flask. He then titrated $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portions of the resulting solution against 0.015 M potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)]. The average titration figure was $5.75 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Calculate (a) the mass of anhydrous $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ in each tablet, (b) the mass of elemental iron in each tablet, (c) the percentage of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ in each tablet and (d) the percentage of elemental iron in each tablet.

The equation for the reaction is:
$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the molarity of the $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ solution.
From the balanced equation, we see that one mole of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$reacts with five moles of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$, i.e. $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=1$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=5$.
$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}\left(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\right.$
Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}}=5.75$

$$
\frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{r e d}}{n_{r}}
$$

$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{o}}=0.015$
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=1$

$$
\frac{5.75 \times 0.015}{1}=\frac{25 \times \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{red}}}{5}
$$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{r}}=25$
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{red}}=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_{\text {red }} & =\frac{5.75 \times 0.015 \times 5}{25} \\
& =0.0173 \text { moles per litre }
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=5$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{Fe} & =55.85 \\
\mathrm{~S} & =32.07 \\
4 \times \mathrm{O}=4 \times 16 & =64 \\
\hline M_{r} \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} & =151.92
\end{array}
$$

## Step 2

Convert to $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{L}$
$=0.0173 \times 151.92 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$ (Rel. molecular mass $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}=151.92$ )
$=2.628 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$.

## Step 3

Calculate the mass of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ per $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.
From Step 2, in the $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask there are $\frac{2.628}{4}=0.657$ grams of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$.

## Step 4

Calculate the mass of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ per tablet.
Thus, since we used 5 tablets, 1 tablet contains $\frac{0.657}{5}$ grams of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}=0.131$ grams

## Step 5

Calculate the percentage of iron in $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$
The percentage of iron in $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ is $\frac{55.85}{151.92} \times 100=36.76 \%$

## Step 6

Calculate the percentage of $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$ and Fe per tablet.
Therefore, the mass of iron in each tablet is $36.76 \%$ of $0.131 \mathrm{~g}=0.048 \mathrm{~g}$
(b)

### 15.5 The reaction of iodine and sodium thiosulfate

The second type of redox titration that we will study in this course is the reaction between iodine and sodium thiosulfate. Sodium thiosulfate, $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$, is an important reducing agent used in chemistry, Figure 15.11.

For example, sometimes excess chlorine may be added when disinfecting swimming pools and sodium thiosulfate is used to reduce the excess chlorine to harmless chloride ions. It is also used in analysing the amount of certain substances dissolved in water (e.g. oxygen), for extracting gold, and as an antidote to cyanide poisoning.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-285.jpg?height=715&width=349&top_left_y=554&top_left_x=1732)
Figure 15.11 Sodium thiosulfate helps reduce excessive amounts of chlorine in swimming pool water.

We will be meeting sodium thiosulfate on many occasions in this course. The following is a summary of some important points about it:

- Sodium thiosulfate is commonly found in the form of a colourless crystalline solid of formula $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ called sodium thiosulfate pentahydrate, Figure 15.12. The pent part of the name refers to the five molecules of water in the formula. (The water content of sodium thiosulfate crystals is variable but the pentahydrate is the most common one.) These water molecules are not chemically bonded to the sodium thiosulfate molecule but are trapped within the crystal structure. If sodium thiosulfate pentahydrate is heated, the water of crystallisation is lost and a white powder is formed. This white powder is anhydrous $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$.
- The thiosulfate ion, $\mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-}$, has a structure similar to that of the sulfate ion, $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$, except that one of the oxygen atoms in the sulfate ion is replaced by a sulfur atom in the thiosulfate ion, Figure 15.13. (The prefix 'thio' means 'sulfur'.)
- Sodium thiosulfate is a reducing agent and reacts with iodine molecules, $\mathrm{I}_{2}$, to convert them to iodide ions, $\mathrm{I}^{-}$. The equation for the reaction is:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-285.jpg?height=457&width=1082&top_left_y=2832&top_left_x=608)
- The $\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}{ }^{2-}$ ion formed in the above reaction is called the tetrathionate ion. Its structure may be represented as shown in Figure 15.14.
Note that the thiosulfate ion (the reducing agent) is oxidised to the tetrathionate ion. This may be easily seen by assigning oxidation numbers.

$$
\begin{array}{cc}
\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-} & \rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}+2 \mathrm{I}^{-} \\
+2 & +2.5
\end{array}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-285.jpg?height=801&width=1103&top_left_y=1351&top_left_x=1657)
Figure 15.12 Sodium thiosulfate, $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$, is one of the most useful reducing agents in chemistry. These crystals are hydrated and have the formula $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} .5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-285.jpg?height=424&width=721&top_left_y=2500&top_left_x=2024)
Figure 15.13 The thiosulfate and sulfate ions

<img class="imgSvg" id = "mincxtkix8aysg410ym" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>

Figure 15.14 The tetrathionate ion, $\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}$.

- Sodium thiosulfate is not a primary standard, as it cannot be obtained in a sufficiently pure state and the crystals are efflorescent. Therefore, a solution of known concentration cannot be made up by weighing out a certain amount of the solid and dissolving it in a known volume of solution. A sodium thiosulfate solution is standardised by titrating it against a standard iodine solution.
- A standard solution of iodine cannot be made up by direct weighing. This is because iodine slightly vaporises (sublimes - changes directly from solid to vapour) even at room temperature. In addition, iodine is almost completely insoluble in water. For these two reasons, iodine is not a primary standard.
How therefore do we make up a standard solution of iodine? Stay tuned!
- A standard solution of iodine is obtained by reacting a standard solution of potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] with excess potassium iodide solution. Consider the reaction of acidified permanganate ions with iodide ions:

$$
\begin{align*}
& \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}  \tag{a}\\
& 2 \mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \tag{b}
\end{align*}
$$

In equation (a) we see that five electrons are gained. In equation (b), two electrons are lost. We can balance the electron gain and loss by multiplying (a) by 2 and (b) by 5 . This gives us:
(a) $\times 22 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+16 \mathrm{H}^{+}+10 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
(b) $\times 510 \mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow 5 \mathrm{I}_{2}+10 \mathrm{e}^{-}$

Adding
$\mathbf{2 M n O}_{\mathbf{4}}^{-}{ }^{-} \mathbf{1 0 I ^ { - }} \boldsymbol{+} \mathbf{1 6} \mathbf{H}^{+} \boldsymbol{\rightarrow} \mathbf{2 M n}^{2+} \boldsymbol{+} \mathbf{5 I}_{2} \boldsymbol{+} \mathbf{8} \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{2}} \mathbf{O}$
Excess potassium iodide is added for two reasons:

1. By having the $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ions in excess, all of the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ reacts completely with the $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ions to form the maximum amount of $\mathrm{I}_{2}$, i.e. the equivalent number of moles of $\mathrm{I}_{2}$.

- For every two moles of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ that react, five moles of $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ are formed.
- Thus, the amount of iodine formed in the above reaction is directly related to the amount of potassium permanganate.
- Therefore, if we use a standard solution of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$, we can easily work out the amount of iodine formed.
- This known amount of iodine formed is then titrated against a sodium thiosulfate solution to calculate the exact concentration of the sodium thiosulfate solution, i.e. to standardise the thiosulfate solution.

2. The presence of the $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ions helps to keep in solution the iodine that is produced.

- Iodine (non-polar) is only sparingly soluble in water (a polar solvent) but is readily soluble in potassium iodide solution.
- When iodine is added to KI solution, the $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ molecule reacts with the iodide ion to form an ion called the tri-iodide ion, $\mathrm{I}_{3}{ }^{-}$.
- The $\mathrm{I}_{3}{ }^{-}$ion, because it is charged, dissolves easily in water.

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+\mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{3}^{-}
$$

- The $\mathrm{I}_{3}$ - ion is identical in its chemical behaviour to $\mathrm{I}_{2}$.
- Therefore, solutions of $\mathrm{I}_{3}$ - may be treated as solutions of $\mathrm{I}_{2}$, i.e. a solution of iodine in potassium iodide may be treated as if it were a solution of iodine in water.

How is the end point detected in an iodine/thiosulfate titration?
As already stated, thiosulfate reacts with iodine according to the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}+2 \mathrm{I}^{-} \\
& \text {reddish } \\
& \text { brown } \\
& \text { colourless }
\end{aligned}
$$

As the thiosulfate solution is added to the iodine solution, the reddish-brown colour gradually turns yellow, then paler yellow, then paler still until the solution turns colourless, Figure 15.14.

Since there is no sudden colour change, this would make the end point very difficult to detect. Therefore, it is necessary to use an indicator to detect the end point accurately. The indicator used is starch. Starch indicator forms a blue-black colour with iodine, Figure 15.16. When all of the iodine has reacted with the thiosulfate, the blue-black colour suddenly disappears.

- When performing an iodine/thiosulfate titration, the starch is only added when most of the iodine has disappeared, i.e. when the reddish/brown colour of the iodine has become pale yellow.
- The reason for this is because if starch were added at an early stage in the titration, the iodine present would become strongly adsorbed on to the starch and this would make the titration less accurate, since the iodine would be desorbed slowly to react with the thiosulfate.
- In addition, when the pale yellow colour is observed, it tells us that the end point is near. Then, when the starch is added, the thiosulfate solution can be added drop by drop in order to obtain an accurate titration figure.
- The method of carrying out iodine/thiosulfate titrations is discussed again in the next experiment.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-287.jpg?height=851&width=1183&top_left_y=885&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 15.15 As the thiosulfate uses up the iodine, the colour of the solution in the conical flask becomes lighter.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-287.jpg?height=854&width=1180&top_left_y=1979&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 15.16 Starch solution forms a blue-black complex with iodine.

### 15.3 Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 13

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 13 in the Student Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

## To prepare a solution of sodium thiosulfate and to standardise it by titration against a solution of iodine

## Introduction

In this experiment, we will make up an approximate 0.1 M solution of sodium thiosulfate. We will then find the exact concentration of this solution by titrating it against a solution of iodine. The iodine solution is made by the reaction between acidified $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution (of known concentration) and excess iodide ions. The permanganate ions and iodide ions react in the conical flask as follows:

$$
2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+10 \mathrm{I}^{-}+16 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{I}_{2}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

The iodine formed is then reacted with sodium thiosulfate, which is added from a burette. The following reaction occurs:

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}+2 \mathrm{I}^{-}
$$

The experimental set up is illustrated in Figure 15.17.
It is important to use distilled water in this experiment, as tap water contains small quantities of chlorine (an oxidising agent) that may interfere with the result by increasing the amount of iodine present. Remember that chlorine oxidises iodide ions to iodine.

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{2}+2 \mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-}+\mathrm{I}_{2}
$$

Deionised water has all of the dissolved ions removed from tap water but could still contain some dissolved chlorine. Using distilled water will ensure a more accurate result but, if distilled water is not available, use deionised water instead.

## Key steps in procedure

- Some sodium thiosulfate is weighed out on a clock glass using the laboratory balance.
- Taking all the precautions outlined previously, the crystals are transferred to a beaker containing distilled water.
- The solution is stirred to fully dissolve the crystals

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-288.jpg?height=1397&width=926&top_left_y=1380&top_left_x=1650)
Figure 15.17 Experiment to standardise a solution of sodium thiosulfate

and, when dissolved, the solution is transferred to a clean volumetric flask with the aid of a funnel.

- All the washings are transferred to the volumetric flask. The bottom of the meniscus of the solution is brought up to the mark with deionised water.
- The stoppered flask is inverted about 20 times.
- The pipette, burette and conical flask are washed with deionised water.
- The burette is washed with some of the sodium thiosulfate solution and filled with the thiosulfate solution using a funnel. The funnel is removed.
- The bottom of the meniscus of the sodium thiosulfate solution is adjusted to the zero mark on the burette.
- A check is made to ensure that the tap and the space below the tap are filled with the sodium thiosulfate solution.
- A standardised $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution is poured into a clean, dry beaker. The pipette is washed with a small amount of this solution.
- Using a pipette filler, the pipette is filled to the mark with the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution and this amount of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution is added to the conical flask.
- Using a graduated cylinder, some dilute sulfuric acid is added to the conical flask, making sure that the acid is in excess.


## Observation

- The colour of the solution in the conical flask is purple.


## Explanation

- The purple colour is the colour of the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ before it takes part in the reaction.
- The sulfuric acid is added in excess to the potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] solution in the conical flask in order to supply sufficient $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions for complete reduction of the $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ions to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ ions according to the following half equation:

$$
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

## Procedure (continued)

- Using a graduated cylinder some potassium iodide solution is added in excess to the conical flask.


## Observation

- The solution in the conical flask turns a reddish-brown colour.


## Explanation

- The reddish-brown colour is due to the iodine that has been formed according to the equation:

$$
\begin{array}{lr}
2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+10 \mathrm{I}^{-}+16 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+ & 5 \mathrm{I}_{2}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \\
\text { purple } & \text { reddish-brown }
\end{array}
$$

- The potassium iodide is added in excess for the two reasons stated above: (i) to ensure that all of the potassium permanganate has reacted (has been reduced) to produce the corresponding amount of iodine according to the above equation, and (ii) to keep in solution the iodine that is produced.


## Procedure (continued)

- A titration is carried out in the usual manner.


## Observation

- As the titration proceeds, the dark brown colour of the iodine becomes less intense and gradually changes to a yellow colour and then to a pale yellow colour.


## Explanation

- As the sodium thiosulfate solution is added to the conical flask, a reaction takes place between the thiosulfate ions and the iodine according to the following equation:

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+\underset{\text { reddish-brown }}{2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-}} \rightarrow \underset{\text { colourless }}{\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}}+2 \mathrm{I}^{-}
$$

As the iodine becomes used up in the above reaction, the reddish-brown colour gradually becomes less intense and fades to a pale yellow colour.

## Procedure (continued)

- The titration is continued until the solution in the conical flask becomes pale yellow (straw colour).
- A few drops of starch indicator are added.


## Observation

- The solution in the conical flask turns a blue-black colour.


## Explanation

- The pale yellow colour tells us that there is very little iodine left in solution, i.e. that the end point is near.
- The blue-black colour is caused by the starch reacting with the small amount of iodine left in solution.


## Procedure (continued)

- The titration is continued by adding the thiosulfate solution drop by drop until the blue-black colour disappears.
- The titration figure is noted. One rough and two accurate titrations are carried out. The two accurate titration figures should agree to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.


## Explanation

- The fact that the blue-black colour disappears tells us that there is no more iodine left in solution. This means that all of the iodine has reacted with the thiosulfate, i.e. the end point has been reached.
- The colour changes observed in the various stages of this experiment are summarised in Figure 15.18.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-290.jpg?height=2124&width=2368&top_left_y=1230&top_left_x=221)


## Calculations

The method of calculating the concentration of the sodium thiosulfate solution in iodine/thiosulfate titrations is shown in Examples 15.4 and 15.5.

Example 15.4 shows you how to calculate the concentration of a sodium thiosulfate solution when you are given the concentration of the iodine solution. Example 15.5 shows you how to calculate the concentration of a sodium thiosulfate solution when you are given the concentration of the potassium permanganate solution, i.e. the type of calculation involved in Student Experiment No. 13 above.

## Exampte 15.4

## Question

$25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of a 0.045 M iodine solution (previously standardised) were titrated against a solution of sodium thiosulfate. The average titration figure was $27.45 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Calculate the concentration of the sodium thiosulfate solution in (a) moles per litre and (b) grams per litre of crystalline $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} .5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

The reaction between iodine and thiosulfate may be represented as:

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}+2 \mathrm{I}^{-}
$$

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the concentration of the sodium thiosulfate solution (reducing agent).
From the balanced equation, we see that two moles of thiosulfate (the reducing agent) react with one mole of iodine (the oxidising agent), i.e. $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=1$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=2$.

$$
\text { I. } \quad\left(\mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-}\right.
$$

Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{0}=25$
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{o}}=0.045$
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=1$

$$
\frac{25 \times 0.045}{1}=\frac{27.45 \times \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{red}}}{2}
$$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{r}}=27.45$
$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{red}}=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{M}_{\text {red }} & =\frac{25 \times 0.045 \times 2}{27.45} \\
& =0.082 \mathrm{moles} / \mathrm{L}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=2$

## Step 2

Convert to $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{L}$
$=0.082 \times 248.2 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$ (Rel. molecular mass of $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=248.2$ )
$=20.352 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \times \mathrm{Na}=2 \times 22.99 & =45.98 \\
2 \times \mathrm{S}=2 \times 32.07 & =64.14 \\
3 \times \mathrm{O}=3 \times 16 & =48.00 \\
10 \times \mathrm{H}=10 \times 1.008 & =10.08 \\
5 \times \mathrm{O}=5 \times 16 & =80.00 \\
\hline M_{r} \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} .5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} & =248.2
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: Concentration of sodium thiosulfate solution is:
(a) 0.082 moles per litre
(b) 20.352 grams $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ per litre.

## Example 15.5

## Question

$25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.02 M potassium permanganate are pipetted into a conical flask. Some dilute sulfuric acid and excess potassium iodide solution are then added and the liberated iodine is titrated against a solution of sodium thiosulfate of unknown concentration. The average titration figure is $18.7 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. Calculate the concentration of the sodium thiosulfate solution in (a) moles per litre and (b) grams per litre of crystalline $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

The reactions may be represented as:
$2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+10 \mathrm{I}^{-}+16 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{I}_{2}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}{ }^{2-}+2 \mathrm{I}^{-}$

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the molarity of the sodium thiosulfate solution (reducing agent)
From the balanced equations, we see that two moles of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$produce five moles of $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ and these five moles of $\mathrm{I}_{2}$ would then react with ten moles of $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$, i.e. $2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}{ }^{-} \equiv 5 \mathrm{I}_{2} \equiv 10 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-}$.
This means that $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=2$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=10$.

$$
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}\left(\mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-}\right.
$$

Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{o}}=25$

$$
\frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{r e d}}{n_{r}}
$$

$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{o}}=0.02$
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=2$

$$
\frac{25 \times 0.02}{2}=\frac{18.7 \times \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{red}}}{10}
$$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{r}}=18.75$
$\mathrm{M}_{\text {red }}=$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_{\text {red }} & =\frac{25 \times 0.02 \times 10}{2 \times 18.7} \\
& =0.1337 \text { moles per litre }
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=10$

## Step 2

Convert to $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{L}$
$=0.1337 \times 248.2 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$ (Rel. molecular mass of $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=248.2$ )
$=33.184 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$

$$
\begin{array}{|ll|}
\hline 2 \times \mathrm{Na}=2 \times 22.99 & =45.98 \\
2 \times \mathrm{S}=2 \times 32.07 & =64.14 \\
3 \times \mathrm{O}=3 \times 16 & =48.00 \\
10 \times \mathrm{H}=10 \times 1.008 & =10.08 \\
5 \times \mathrm{O}=5 \times 16 & =80.00 \\
\hline M_{r} N a_{2} S_{2} O_{3} .5 H_{2} \mathrm{O} & =248.2
\end{array}
$$

Answer: Concentration of sodium thiosulfate solution is:
(a) 0.1337 moles per litre
(b) 33.184 grams $\mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \cdot 5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ per litre.

[^2]
## Example 15.7

## Question

Acidified solutions of potassium permanganate liberate iodine from iodide solution according to the equation:
$2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+10 \mathrm{I}^{-}+16 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{I}_{2}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
When excess potassium iodide was added to $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of an acidified solution of potassium permanganate, it required $22.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.125 M sodium thiosulfate solution to reduce the iodine liberated. Calculate the mass of potassium permanganate in the $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution.

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the concentration of the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution.
$2 \mathrm{MnO}_{4}{ }^{-} \equiv 5 \mathrm{I}_{2} \equiv 10 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-}$, i.e. $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=2$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=10$.

$$
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} \mathrm{S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-}
$$

Given:
$\mathrm{V}_{0}=25$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{r e d}}{n_{r}} \\
& \frac{25 \times M_{0}}{2}=\frac{22.5 \times 0.125}{10}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{o}}=$ ?
$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}=2$
$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{r}}=22.5$
$\mathrm{M}_{\text {red }}=0.125$

$$
M_{0}=\frac{22.5 \times 0.125 \times 2}{25 \times 10}
$$

$\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}}=10$

$$
\text { = } 0.0225 \text { moles per litre }
$$

## Step 2

Convert to $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{L}$
$=0.0225 \times 158.04$ grams per litre (Rel. molecular mass of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}=158.04$ )
$=3.556$ grams per litre

## Step 3

Convert to $\mathrm{g} / 25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$
$=\frac{3.556}{1000} \times 25$
= 0.089 grams per $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$

\$\$

\$\$

Answer: Mass of $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ in $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution $=0.089$ grams.

## Summary What I should know

- Potassium permanganate [potassium manganate(VII)] is an oxidising agent.
- Potassium permanganate is not a primary standard.
- Potassium permanganate acts as its own indicator when it is used in titrations.
- Potassium permanganate oxidises $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions to $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions in acidified solution.
- One of the equations used for analysing data from titrations involving redox reactions is:
$\frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{\text {red }}}{n_{r}}$
Sodium thiosulfate is a reducing agent. It reduces iodine molecules to iodide ions.
A solution of sodium thiosulfate is standardised by titration against a solution of iodine.
Starch is used to detect the end point in an iodine/thiosulfate titration.

# 16 Oxidation-Reduction Volumetric Exam-Style Questions

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-297.jpg?height=453&width=1263&top_left_y=544&top_left_x=324)

### 16.1 Introduction

In Chapter 13, we learned that many problems in acid-base volumetric analysis can be solved from first principles. Having now studied the concepts of oxidation-reduction reactions in Chapters 14 and 15 , we will now see how we can apply this knowledge to solve problems in volumetric analysis involving oxidation-reduction reactions. As was done in Chapter 13, we will begin by studying some key formulas to help us solve these volumetric problems and we will also make use of first principles methods that do not require the use of any formulas. When solving a problem in an exam paper from first principles or by using formulas, always remember that it is very important to show all your work.

## OBJECTIVES

- To introduce students to a range of different types of questions in volumetric analysis involving oxidation-reduction reactions.
- To give students practice in solving oxidationreduction volumetric problems from first principles and also by using some key formulas.
- To ensure that students can identify and discuss potential sources of errors in practical work involving volumetric analysis.


### 16.2 Key formulas for solving volumetric problems

The same key formulas as used in Chapter 13 will be used in this chapter. These key formulas are summarised in Table 16.1. We will then show how these key formulas can be used in solving some volumetric problems in exam-style questions.

| Formula |  | Comment |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | Number of moles $=\frac{\text { Mass (in grams) }}{\text { Relative Molecular Mass }}$ | This is a very useful formula (Chapter 8) for calculating the number of moles of a substance when we know the relative molecular mass. It can also be manipulated to (i) calculate the mass if we know the number of moles and relative molecular mass <br> or <br> (ii) calculate the relative molecular mass if we know the mass and number of moles. |
| 2. | Number of moles $=\frac{\text { volume }{ }^{*} \times \text { molarity }}{1000}$ (*in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ ) | This is a very useful formula for calculating the number of moles when given a volume of solution and the molarity of the solution. |
| 3. | $\frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{r e d}}{n_{r}}$ | This is a very useful formula for calculating the unknown concentration of a solution from titration data. |
| 4. | Density $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Volume }}$ | This formula is very useful if we are given the density of a liquid and its volume and we need to calculate the mass of the liquid. |

Table 16.1 Some key formulas in volumetric analysis

## EXAM TIPI

Note that this question essentially asks for a definition of a primary standard. So make sure you know this definition!

Hydrated ammonium iron(II) sulfate can be used as a primary standard because it can be obtained in a stable, pure and soluble solid form so that it can be weighed out and dissolved in water to a solution of accurately known concentration. In addition, it does not absorb water (not hygroscopic) or does not lose water of crystallisation (not efflorescent).

## Question

(b) (i) Describe how you would prepare exactly $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of a standard solution containing 9.31 g of $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ (hydrated ammonium iron(II) sulfate) that was supplied on a clock glass.

## Answer

The detailed steps should be studied carefully in Experiment 11 of the Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook. The following is a summary of the main steps:

1. Dissolve the crystals in a beaker containing deionised water and dilute sulfuric acid.
2. Add the washings of the clock glass to the beaker.
3. Transfer the contents of the beaker to the $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask.
4. Use a funnel when transferring the contents of the beaker to the $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask.
5. Add the washings of the beaker, funnel and glass rod to the $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask.
6. Add deionised water to the volumetric flask until the water is near the graduation mark.
7. When the meniscus of the water is near the graduation mark of the volumetric flask, carefully use a dropper to add water.
8. Ensure that the bottom of the meniscus is on the graduation mark.
9. Stopper the volumetric flask.
10. Invert the stoppered flask about 20 times.

## Question

(ii) Why was dilute sulfuric acid added during the preparation of this standard solution?

## Answer

The sulfuric acid prevents the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions being oxidised to $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions by the oxygen in the air.

## Question

$$
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

In each titration, a little dilute sulfuric acid was added to a $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portion of the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ion solution in a conical flask before adding the potassium manganate(VII) solution from a burette. On average, $22.6 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution were required for complete reaction with $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the solution of the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions in excess acid.
(i) How was the end point of each titration detected?

Answer: A faint permanent pink colour is observed at the end point.

## Question

(ii) If insufficient acid was present in the conical flask, what would have been observed as the $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$ solution was added from the burette to the $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ion solution? Explain.
Answer: If insufficient acid was present in the conical flask, a brown solid precipitate would be observed.
This brown solid precipitate is due to the formation of manganese dioxide, $\mathrm{MnO}_{2}$.
(d) (i) Calculate the concentration of $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ in the standard solution in moles per litre.

## Answer

Relative molecular mass of $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=392.17$
Working from first principles: 392.17 g in 1 L solution $\rightarrow 1 \mathrm{M}$ solution

1 g in 1 L solution $\rightarrow \frac{1}{392.17} \mathrm{M}$ solution
9.31 g in 1 L solution $\rightarrow \frac{9.31}{392.17} \mathrm{M}$ solution
9.31 g in $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ solution $=\frac{9.31 \times 4}{392.17}$

$$
=0.095 \mathrm{M} \text { solution }
$$

The concentration of $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}=0.095 \mathrm{M}$

## Alternatively, using Formula 1:

Calculate $M_{r}$ of $\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \cdot \mathrm{FeSO}_{4} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
2 \times \mathrm{N}=2 \times 14.01 & =28.02 \\
20 \times \mathrm{H}=20 \times 1.008 & =20.16 \\
2 \times \mathrm{S}=2 \times 32.07 & =64.14 \\
14 \times \mathrm{O}=14 \times 16 & =224 \\
1 \times \mathrm{Fe}=1 \times 55.85 & =55.85 \\
\hline M_{r} & =392.17
\end{array}
$$

Number of moles $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Relative Molecular Mass }}=\frac{9.31}{392.17}=0.02374$ moles in $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask
Therefore, concentration in moles $/ \mathrm{L}=0.02374 \times 4=0.095 \mathrm{M}$ solution

(iii) Calculate the number of moles of potassium manganate(VII) reduced to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ by this quantity of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ion.

Answer: From the balanced equation, one mole of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ions reacts with 5 moles of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ions

$$
\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Therefore, number of moles of $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}{ }^{-}$ions $=\frac{0.002375}{5}=0.000475$ moles

## Example 16.2

## Question

Sodium thiosulfate is a reducing agent that reacts with iodine according to the following balanced equation:

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}^{2-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{I}^{-}+\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}^{2-}
$$

To determine the concentration of a sodium thiosulfate solution, a student titrated it against $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ portions of a standard iodine solution.
[LCH]
(a) Explain how iodine, a non-polar substance of very low water solubility, is brought into aqueous solution.

## Answer

lodine is brought into aqueous solution since, when added to KI solution, the $\mathrm{l}_{2}$ molecule reacts with the iodide ion. In this reaction, an ion called the tri-iodide ion $\left(\mathrm{I}_{3}{ }^{-}\right)$is formed. Since the $\mathrm{I}_{3}{ }^{-}$ion is charged, it dissolves easily in water.

$$
\mathrm{I}_{2}+\mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{3}^{-}
$$

## Question

(b) The iodine solution was made up in a $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ volumetric flask. Describe the procedure for measuring $25.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of this solution into a conical flask.

## Answer

The main steps for measuring $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of an iodine solution into a conical flask are:

1. Pour the iodine solution into a clean, dry beaker.
2. Obtain a 25 cm 3 pipette.
3. Rinse out the pipette with deionised water.
4. Also rinse out the pipette with the iodine solution.
5. Using a pipette filler, bring the bottom of the meniscus of the iodine solution to the graduation mark in the pipette.
6. Read the meniscus at eye level.
7. Allow the iodine solution in the pipette to drain into the conical flask.
8. When the discharge is complete, touch the tip of the pipette against the side of the conical flask.
9. Wait a few seconds before removing the pipette (draining time).
10. Allow the last drop in the pipette to remain there - do not blow it into the conical flask.

## Question

(c) Name a suitable indicator for this titration.

At what stage is the indicator added?
State the colour change at the end point in the presence of the indicator.

## Answer

- A suitable indicator is starch.
- The indicator is added when the solution in the conical flask is a pale yellow (straw) colour. The pale yellow (straw) colour tells you that nearly all the iodine is used up,


## EXAM TIPI

When you are asked for a colour change, you must always state the initial colour and the final colour, i.e. two colours! Also note that 'clear' is not accepted for 'colourless' as a clear solution can be coloured. i.e. the end point is near.

- The colour change at the end point is blue-black to colourless.

$500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of iodine solution contains 0.025 mole $\mathrm{l}_{2}$

25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3} \text { of iodine solution contains } \frac{0.025 \times 25}{500}=0.00125 \mathrm{~mole} \mathrm{l}_{2}
$$

## Question

(ii) Calculate the number of moles of sodium thiosulfate required to reduce this quantity of iodine.

## Answer

From the balanced equation $\mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}{ }^{2-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{l}^{-}+\mathrm{S}_{4} \mathrm{O}_{6}{ }^{2-}$
Two moles of thiosulfate react with every mole of iodine.
Therefore, $2 \times 0.00125=0.0025$ moles of sodium thiosulfate are required to react with 0.00125 mole $_{2}$.

## Question

(e) Explain why the use of distilled water instead of deionised water throughout this experiment would be likely to ensure a more accurate result.
Tap water contains small quantities of chlorine (an oxidising agent) that may interfere with the result by increasing the amount of iodine present. Deionised water has all of the dissolved ions removed from tap water, but deionised water could still contain some dissolved chlorine.

- A systematic error also arises if the wrong indicator is used for a particular titration. The correct indicator specified in the laboratory manual for each particular type of titration must always be used. Using the wrong indicator for each titration in a set of titrations to measure an unknown concentration will give rise to errors in detecting the end point. If the wrong indicator is used in a titration, the end point may be detected too early or too late. The reason for this is because different indicators change colour at different pH values. (We will explain this in more detail in Chapter 19.)
- A systematic error arises if the correct procedure for rinsing out glassware is not followed. The rinsings required are summarised in Figure 16.2.
- If a burette is only rinsed with deionised water, the water remaining in the burette will dilute the solution added to the burette. This 'more dilute' solution will introduce an error to the volume added at the end point since a greater volume of the diluted solution will be required for complete reaction.
- If a pipette is only rinsed with deionised water, the water remaining in the pipette will dilute the solution drawn into the pipette. This error will mean that a lower amount of solution will need to be added from the burette to completely react with the 'more diluted' solution from the pipette.
- If the conical flask is rinsed with the solution it is to contain, this means that an additional volume of solution (i.e. in addition to the solution that is added from the pipette) has been added to the conical flask. This error will result in a greater volume of solution having to be added to the conical flask from the burette to fully react with the solution in the conical flask.

These errors in rinsings are classified as systematic errors, as they always affect the results in a specific direction.

- Another example of a systematic error would be if the end point is always overshot. For example, suppose a student does not realise, when using $\mathrm{KMnO}_{4}$, that the end point is when a faint permanent pink colour is observed. Instead, the student always takes the end point when a strong purple colour is formed, Figure 16.3. Therefore, all of the titre readings will be too high, i.e. shifted in one direction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-304.jpg?height=1244&width=1261&top_left_y=2422&top_left_x=195)
Figure 16.2 Summary of rinsing required when using a burette, pipette and conical flask in volumetric analysis.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-304.jpg?height=1053&width=1134&top_left_y=2555&top_left_x=1487)
Figure 16.3 A systematic error arises if the end point is always overshot due to lack of knowledge about the correct colour change at the end point.

## The main points about systematic errors may be summarised as follows:

- Systematic errors are consistent, repeating errors that always lead to a deviation from the true value.
- Systematic errors shift all measurements consistently in one direction. In other words, systematic errors cause all measurements to be consistently too high or too low compared to the true value. In short, a characteristic of systematic errors is that they have a consistent bias in one direction.
- Systematic errors cannot be reduced or eliminated by repeated trials - they can only be corrected by undertaking measures such as fixing calibration of instruments or correcting wrong techniques.
- Systematic errors reduce accuracy, as all values are shifted in one direction.
- Systematic errors do not usually affect precision, as all the incorrect results could still be clustered close together.


## Systematic errors can be minimised when we:

- Ensure instruments are calibrated correctly before use.
- Use the correct indicators at all times.
- Read volumes of liquids in instruments such as burettes and pipettes at eye-level.
- Follow the correct procedure as outlined in laboratory manuals.


## 2. Random error

The word 'random' means that something is 'unpredictable or unplanned' or that it 'changes without any fixed pattern'. Unlike systematic errors, which happen the same way every time, random events have no pattern and can happen in different ways each time.

Examples of random errors are:

A random error is an unpredictable fluctuation in a measurement around the true value that occurs due to variations in experimental conditions and procedures.

- Air currents affecting the reading of an electronic balance can give rise to random errors each time the balance is used during the experiment.
- Uneven mixing of solutions in a volumetric flask or conical flask can also give rise to random errors. For example, when performing a titration, the conical flask must be continuously shaken in a similar manner during each trial of the titration. If the conical flask is shaken continuously during one trial and shaken very little during a second trial, this could give rise to a random error in trying to detect the end point.
- Similarly, when making up a solution in a volumetric flask, the flask needs to be inverted the same number of times to ensure thorough mixing. Otherwise, variations in the end point could be obtained since the concentration of the solution may not be uniform throughout the solution.
- Failure to wash down the sides of the flask with deionised water at regular intervals during each trial of the titration could also give rise to random errors.
- Human reaction time could cause variations in starting and stopping stopwatches when measuring times for reactions to take place. (This will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 17.)
- Fluctuations in room temperature that could affect the rate of the reaction could also cause random errors. (This will also be discussed in more detail in Chapter 17.)
- A random error could also occur if there is variation in the number of drops of indicator added during each trial of the titration. When we study the theory of how indicators work (Chapter 19), we will see that it is important to ensure that there is consistency in the number of drops of indicator added in each trial of the titration. The recommended number of drops in the laboratory manual should always be used consistently in each trial of the titration.
- A random error could also occur if there is a change in lighting conditions in the lab during the experiment. These changes could affect the difficulty or ease of determining the colour change, as intensity of colours can vary in the presence of bright sunlight or in a less bright environment. Figure 16.4.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-306.jpg?height=1795&width=2430&top_left_y=1132&top_left_x=188)
Figure 16.4 Lack of consistency in adding the same number of drops of indicator during each trial of the titration can give rise to random errors.

1. Incorrectly reading the volume of liquid in a burette or pipette could also be categorised as a random error. For example, if there is no consistency in reading the volume, i.e. in trial 1 of the titration the reading is taken at eye level with the meniscus, in trial 2 the reading is taken from above, and in trial 3 the reading is taken from below.
2. Misjudging the end point could also be categorised as a random error. For example, in one trial the titration could be stopped early and in the next trial the end point could be overshot. This leads to fluctuations around the true value.

The main points about random errors may be summarised as follows:

- Unlike systematic errors, which always shift the results in one direction, random errors cause measurements to fluctuate in both directions around the true value.
- Random errors are unpredictable and inconsistent.
- Random errors can be reduced by repeating measurements and averaging results. For example, you could overshoot the end point due to a random error in interpreting the colour change. This may be caused by a change in the lighting conditions of the room. The random error can be corrected by repeating the titration and averaging two values that agree to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.
- Random errors may not necessarily affect accuracy due to repeated measurements being taken and averaging of results.
- Random errors affect precision because random errors give rise to results that are scattered from each other rather than being clustered close together.
- Random errors can be minimised by keeping the room conditions the same (controlled conditions) throughout the experiment.
It is important in volumetric analysis that results are accurate and precise. By recognising systematic and random errors, we can take steps to minimise them.


## Example 16.3

## Question

A student prepares a solution using a volumetric flask but fails to ensure that the solution in the volumetric flask is mixed thoroughly by forgetting to invert the flask several times before using the solution in a titration.

## Question

(a) Explain the type of error introduced into the experiment.

## Answer

This introduces a random error because different samples could have different concentrations due to the incomplete mixing.

## Question

(b) Explain how this error will affect the titration results.

## Answer

Since different samples could have different concentrations in each trial of the titration, the titration figure in some trials may be high and in other trials may be low.

## Example 16.4

## Question

A student performs a titration three times. The rough titration figure was $22.4 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$, the second titration figure was $22.2 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ and the third titration figure was $22.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$. The true end point is $22.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.

## Question

(a) Is there evidence of a systematic error in carrying out the titration?

## Answer

Yes, there is a systematic error, as all the values are consistently lower than the true value of $22.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.

## Question

(b) Is there evidence of a random error in carrying out the titration?

## Answer

There is no evidence of a random error, as two results were obtained which agree to within $0.1 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$.

## Summary What I should know

Volumetric problems may be solved from first principle and also with the aid of key formulas.
Number of moles $=\frac{\text { Mass (in grams) }}{\text { Relative molecular mass }}$

Number of moles $=\frac{\text { volume } \mathrm{e}^{*} \times \text { molarity }}{1000}$
(*in $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ )
$\frac{V_{0} \times M_{0}}{n_{0}}=\frac{V_{r} \times M_{\text {red }}}{n_{r}}$
A systematic error is a consistent, repeating error that always occurs in one direction, i.e. it is always higher or always lower than the true value.

A random error is an unpredictable fluctuation in a measurement around the true value that occurs due to variations in experimental conditions and procedures.
