## (v) Catalysts

We have already seen in Experiment 17.1 that a substance called manganese dioxide, when added to hydrogen peroxide, helps the hydrogen peroxide to decompose more rapidly.

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{MnO}_{2}} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2}
$$

If you were to measure the mass of manganese dioxide present at the beginning of the experiment, you would find that the same mass of manganese dioxide would be present at the end of the experiment, i.e. the manganese dioxide is not used up in the reaction. We say that the manganese dioxide is a catalyst.

- Note that the definition uses the word 'alters' rather than 'speeds up'.
- This is because, while most catalysts are used to speed up reactions, some can be used to slow reactions down.
- Those catalysts that have a retarding effect are called negative catalysts or inhibitors. Glycerine is an example of a negative catalyst. It is sometimes added to hydrogen peroxide to slow down its rate of decomposition when it is being stored.

We will now study catalysts under the following headings:
(a) General properties of catalysts
(b) Types of catalysis
(c) Mechanisms of catalysis

## (a) General properties of catalysts

The general properties of catalysts may be summarised as follows:

- Catalysts play an active part in chemical reactions and are recovered chemically unchanged at the end of a reaction. For example, if the manganese dioxide used to catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide is examined before and after the decomposition reaction has taken place, it is found to have exactly the same chemical properties.
- Catalysts tend to be specific, i.e. a catalyst catalyses one particular reaction or sometimes a class of very similar reactions, e.g. platinum catalyses many hydrogenation (addition of hydrogen) reactions. However, other broadly similar reactions may not be catalysed, e.g. platinum may not catalyse other addition reactions. Biological catalysts called enzymes, which are produced by living cells, tend to be extremely specific.

For example, liver contains an enzyme called catalase. This enzyme decomposes hydrogen peroxide in living things. Hydrogen peroxide is highly toxic to living cells and is constantly being produced as a result of chemical reactions in the cells. It is essential that hydrogen peroxide be decomposed as soon as it is formed.

A catalyst is a substance that alters the rate of a chemical reaction but is not consumed in the reaction.

An enzyme is a substance that is produced by a living cell and acts as a biological catalyst.

The enzyme catalase acts so quickly to break down the hydrogen peroxide that it is the fastest enzyme known. The effect of the enzyme catalase on hydrogen peroxide is shown in Figure 17.26.

- Large amounts of enzymes are used in the manufacture of biological washing powders.
- These washing powders contain enzymes that catalyse the breaking down of the chemicals in food and other stains on clothing. Almost all of the enzymes in washing powders are hydrolases - enzymes that catalyse the breaking down (hydrolysis) of fats, proteins and carbohydrates.
- An enzyme called protease is used in washing

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-330.jpg?height=785&width=1180&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 17.26 Liver contains an enzyme called catalase which acts as a catalyst in the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

powders for its ability to digest protein-based stains, such as blood, at low temperatures.

Catalysts need only be present in very small amounts to function as catalysts. You may assume that in the reactions studied in this course, increasing the amount of catalyst does not significantly alter the rate of the reaction. The effect on the rate of altering the amount of catalyst varies depending on the reaction itself. The effect can only be determined by experiment.

- In the case of equilibrium reactions, a catalyst helps equilibrium to be achieved more quickly. However, it does not affect the position of equilibrium or the composition of the final mixture in an equilibrium reaction. This will be studied in more detail in Chapter 18.
- The action of a catalyst may be destroyed by certain substances called catalyst poisons, e.g. in the past when lead was added to petrol, it was found that the lead destroyed the catalysts in the catalytic converters in cars. Another example of a catalyst poison is arsenic. This is very dangerous because it inhibits the actions of certain enzymes in the body.

Some of the general properties of catalysts are summarised in Figure 17.27.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-330.jpg?height=1072&width=2430&top_left_y=2633&top_left_x=188)
Figure 17.27 Some general properties of catalysts

## (b) Types of catalysis

Chemists have discovered that there are three types of catalysis - homogeneous catalysis, heterogeneous catalysis and autocatalysis.

## (i) Homogeneous Catalysis

Homogeneous catalysis means catalysis in which both the reactants and the catalyst are in the same phase, i.e. there is no boundary between the reactants and the catalyst.

- Note the use of the word 'phase' in this definition. A phase is a specific state of matter that has uniform chemical and physical properties. For example, if you mix oil and water, they form two phases (an oil phase and a water phase). Even though both oil and water are in the same state of matter (liquid), they are in different phases because there is a boundary between them.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-331.jpg?height=1098&width=1183&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 17.28 The iodine snake is an example of homogeneous catalysis!

- An example of homogeneous catalysis is the 'iodine snake' experiment. In this experiment, some concentrated potassium iodide solution (the catalyst) is added to washing-up liquid and some hydrogen peroxide solution is then added. Potassium iodide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Both liquids are in the same phase, i.e. there is no boundary between them. The oxygen is quickly released and gets trapped in the washing-up liquid. Foam is produced and is carried out of the bottle in the form of a snake as shown in Figure 17.28,


## (ii) Heterogeneous Catalysis

- An example of this type of catalysis is the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (liquid) catalysed by manganese dioxide (solid). In this case there is a physical solid-liquid boundary between the manganese dioxide and the hydrogen peroxide, i.e. manganese dioxide does not dissolve in the hydrogen peroxide.
- Another example is the catalytic oxidation of methanol (liquid) by platinum (solid). The following is the reaction that occurs:

Heterogeneous catalysis is catalysis in which the reactants and the catalyst are in different phases, i.e. there is a boundary between the reactants and the catalyst.

$$
\underset{\text { Methanol }}{2 \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{OH}}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pt}} \underset{\text { methanal }}{2 \mathrm{HCHO}}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

Note the almost identical spelling of the two chemicals. Methanol is one of a family of chemicals called alcohols. Methanal is one of a family of chemicals called aldehydes. We will be studying these chemicals in more detail in Chapter 24. The experiment to demonstrate the oxidation of methanol to methanal is shown in Figure 17.29.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-331.jpg?height=717&width=769&top_left_y=2868&top_left_x=1982)
Figure 17.29 Methanol is oxidised to methanal using platinum as a catalyst. This is an example of heterogeneous catalysis.

The main points about this experiment may be summarised as follows:

## Key steps in procedure

- About $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of methanol are placed in a $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ conical flask. A piece of cardboard in the shape of a T-piece and covered with aluminium foil is suspended in the conical flask. The purpose of the aluminium foil is to prevent the cardboard catching fire.
- In the fume cupboard, the methanol is warmed to about $60^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and placed on a heat-resistant mat to keep it warm.
- A spiral of platinum wire (the catalyst) is held by a tongs and heated until it is red hot using a Bunsen burner.
- The hot spiral of platinum wire is quickly hung inside the conical flask.


## Observation

- The hot spiral, which will have cooled during the transfer, will begin to glow red hot again.
- There will be a number of mild 'pops' or mini explosions.
- A repeating cycle of occurrences takes place, i.e. the spiral glows, then there is a miniexplosion, the spiral cools down, then the spiral heats up again, then there is another miniexplosion, and so on.
- The smell of methanal may be noticed. Avoid smelling it directly as it is poisonous and produces tears.
- A flame may be observed in the flask.


## Explanation

- The T-piece acts as a chimney to allow waste gases to be swept away and more air to flow into the conical flask.
- The T-piece is covered in aluminium foil to prevent the cardboard being burned.
- The platinum glows because the reaction taking place is exothermic, i.e. it gives out heat.
- The glowing ceases for a while because carbon monoxide is formed due to incomplete combustion of the methanol. This carbon monoxide poisons the catalyst. Once the carbon monoxide leaves the platinum, the platinum again works as a catalyst and the glowing starts again.
- The flame inside the flask is caused by the hot wire igniting the methanol vapour. The flame is extinguished when the oxygen in the air inside the flask is used up.

The popping sounds are caused by hydrogen exploding. In the absence of sufficient oxygen, methanol is oxidised (catalytic dehydrogenation) to methanal and hydrogen gas:

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{OH} \rightarrow \mathrm{HCHO}+\mathrm{H}_{2}
$$

A photograph of the reaction taking place is shown in Figure 17.30.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-332.jpg?height=733&width=1180&top_left_y=1315&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 17.30 When methanol is oxidised to methanal, the heat given out in the exothermic reaction causes the platinum wire to glow.

## (iii) Autocatalysis

You may recall that we studied the reaction between permanganate ions and iron(II) ions in Chapter 15.
$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8 \mathrm{H}^{+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+5 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
In performing this titration, you may have observed that the first few drops of potassium permanganate were decolorised slowly but subsequent drops were decolorised more rapidly. This is because the reaction is catalysed by the $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ ions formed in the reaction. The type of catalysis where one of the products of the reaction catalyses the reaction itself is called autocatalysis.

Autocatalysis is catalysis in which one of the products of the reaction acts as a catalyst for the reaction.

- An autocatalytic reaction starts slowly but speeds up as the catalyst product starts to form.


## (c) Mechanisms of catalysis

Knowledge of catalysis is very important for chemists, as it helps them to speed up or slow down chemical processes in industry. A lot of research takes place into obtaining a clear picture of the mechanisms of catalysis, i.e. how catalysts work. It has been discovered that there are two general mechanisms which explain how catalysts work.

## 1. The intermediate formation theory

This theory may be summarised as follows:

- Arrhenius suggested that a catalyst works by forming an intermediate compound. Consider the general reaction:

$$
W+X \rightarrow Y+Z
$$

Arrhenius suggested that one (or sometimes more than one) of the reactants combines with the catalyst to form an intermediate compound. This intermediate compound may only exist for a very short time and may be difficult to detect.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-333.jpg?height=206&width=880&top_left_y=1901&top_left_x=419)

- This intermediate then reacts with the other reactant to give the final product and regenerate the catalyst.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \begin{array}{l}
{[\mathrm{WC}]+\mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathrm{Y}+\mathrm{Z}+\mathrm{C}} \\
\text { catalyst }
\end{array} \\
& \text { Overall reaction: } \mathrm{W}+\mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathrm{Y}+\mathrm{Z}
\end{aligned}
$$

- The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide catalysed by the presence of $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ions ('iodine snake' reaction) illustrates the formation of the intermediate.

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{I}^{-}} 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{O}_{2}
$$

## Step 1

One of the hydrogen peroxide molecules reacts with an $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ion to form the $\mathrm{IO}^{-}$intermediate, Figure 17.31.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-333.jpg?height=636&width=1177&top_left_y=683&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 17.31 The $\mathrm{IO}^{-}$ion is the intermediate formed when $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ions are used to catalyse the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}+\mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{IO}^{-}
$$

intermediate

## Step 2

The intermediate then reacts with another hydrogen peroxide molecule to form the products and regenerate the catalyst.

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}+\mathrm{IO}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{O}_{2}+\mathrm{I}^{-}
$$

Adding the equations in Steps 1 and 2 gives us the overall equation:

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{I}^{-}} 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{O}_{2}
$$

## Evidence for the Intermediate Formation Theory of Catalysis

An experiment that provides visual evidence for the Intermediate Formation Theory is the oxidation of a compound called potassium sodium tartrate (don't worry about the formula!) using hydrogen peroxide.

- This reaction is catalysed by the presence of $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ ions, which have a pink colour.
- Some potassium sodium tartrate is dissolved in hot water and some crystals of pink cobalt(II) chloride (the catalyst) are added.
- The beaker is placed on a tripod standing in a dish, Figure 17.32.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-334.jpg?height=909&width=2383&top_left_y=377&top_left_x=213)
Figure 17.32 (a) The hydrogen peroxide is about to be added to the potassium sodium tartrate. The pink colour is due to the presence of $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ ions.

(b) The green colour is evidence for the existence of an intermediate compound.
(c) The pink colour is restored again, indicating that the $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ ions have not been used up but have been reformed again at the end of the experiment.

## Observation

- The solution is pink at the start of the experiment due to the presence of $\mathrm{Co}^{2}+$ ions.
- After adding some 100 -volume hydrogen peroxide, fizzing is observed.
- The solution changes to a green colour.
- After a short while, the fizzing stops and the green colour changes back to a pink colour again.


## Explanation

- The colour change from pink to green indicates the formation of a new substance, i.e. the green colour is the colour of the new substance.
- The change of the green colour of the new substance back to the original pink colour suggests that the new substance is an intermediate.
- The fizzing of the solution while it is green suggests that the intermediate is reacting. (The fizzing is caused by carbon dioxide being given off.)
- The fact that the pink colour is restored at the end suggests that the $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ ions have not been used up but are reformed at the end of the reaction, i.e. the catalyst has been regenerated.


## 2. The Surface Adsorption Theory

Although some examples of heterogeneous catalysis may be explained in terms of the Intermediate Formation Theory, most heterogeneous catalysis reactions are explained using a theory called the

## Surface Adsorption Theory.

- We must be careful to distinguish between the words 'adsorption' and 'absorption'.
- We are familiar with the word 'absorption' to describe what happens when one substance moves into another, e.g. a sponge absorbing water.
- However, the word 'adsorption' refers to the accumulation of substances only at the surface of another substance, e.g. gas molecules accumulating on the surface of a solid.
- A good example of adsorption is in the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water in the presence of a platinum catalyst. At room temperature the two gases, hydrogen and oxygen, do not react. However, if we add some finely divided platinum to the mixture, it is found that the reaction proceeds rapidly.

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \xrightarrow{\text { Platinum }} 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}
$$

There are three main steps involved in the mechanism of this reaction.

## 1. Adsorption stage

- Hydrogen and oxygen molecules diffuse towards the surface and settle on (are adsorbed on) the surface of the pieces of platinum.
- The oxygen and hydrogen molecules are held on the surface of the platinum by temporary bonds formed between these molecules and the platinum, Figure 17.33.
- Since platinum is a transition metal, it has vacant d orbitals that help the molecules to form temporary bonds with it, i.e. the molecules are chemically attached to (chemisorbed on) the platinum.

Figure 17.33 Hydrogen and oxygen molecules are adsorbed on to the surface of the platinum. The adsorbed molecules form weak bonds with the metal atoms.

## 2. Reaction on surface

- Since the oxygen and hydrogen molecules are adsorbed on the surface, the higher concentration of these molecules on the surface of the catalyst makes it more likely that the molecules will collide with each other.
- This will result in bonds being broken and new bonds being formed, i.e. a chemical reaction will occur to form water molecules on the surface of the platinum.
- The reaction is helped by the fact that the covalent bonds holding the atoms together are weakened by the formation of new bonds between the reactants and the surface of the catalyst.


## 3. Desorption stage

- The final stage (called the desorption stage) is when the products leave the surface of the catalyst. In this case, the gaseous water molecules leave the surface of the catalyst and diffuse away from the catalyst.
- More reactants are then adsorbed on to the surface of the catalyst and the whole process repeats over and over again.
- It is found that the more finely divided the catalyst, the better is its performance. This is because there is a greater surface area on which adsorption can take place.

Note: The specific locations on the surface of the catalyst where the above steps take place are called the active sites of the catalyst.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-335.jpg?height=1052&width=1183&top_left_y=2656&top_left_x=1575)

## Poisoning of catalysts

Catalysts may not affect the rate of a reaction if they are made ineffective. As an example of this problem, let's study the catalysts that exist in vehicles with internal combustion engines. The exhaust fumes from vehicles which burn fuels such as petrol and diesel in the internal combustion engine are a major source of air pollution. These exhaust fumes contain carbon monoxide, CO, nitrogen monoxide, NO , nitrogen dioxide, $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ and unburned hydrocarbons (i.e. compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen).

The sources of these fumes may be summarised as follows:

- The carbon monoxide comes from the incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons in the fuel.
- The oxides of nitrogen in the exhaust fumes are commonly referred to as $\mathrm{NO}_{\mathrm{x}}$ compounds. These oxides of nitrogen are formed because, when any fuel is burned in air at high temperatures, some of the nitrogen gas in the air is oxidised to form nitrogen monoxide, NO , which reacts with more oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide, $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$.
- In former times, when leaded petrol was used as a fuel, lead compounds were also emitted in the exhaust fumes.
- The unburned hydrocarbons arise from the fact that some of the fuel is not burned in the engine and the hydrocarbons are emitted in the exhaust fumes.
- It is very important to reduce the above emissions as much as possible. Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas that is highly poisonous. The oxides of nitrogen, as well as being poisonous, also contribute to acid rain. The unburned hydrocarbons can give rise to smog.
- One method of converting these environmentally harmful gases into harmless gases is to place a catalytic converter into the exhaust system of a motor vehicle.

Looking at the catalytic converter from the outside, it appears just like an extra silencer box on the car's exhaust system, Figure 17.34.

A catalytic converter consists of a thin coating of the metals platinum, palladium and rhodium (the catalysts) on a ceramic or metal 'honeycomb' inside a stainless steel case, Figure 17.35. The catalysts are spread over the surface of the honeycomb, which has a huge surface area - as large as two or three football fields! The mixture of hot harmful gases (at a temperature of around $300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ) is then converted into much less harmful products.

A catalytic converter is a device in the exhaust system of a motor vehicle which contains catalysts to convert pollutants in the exhaust gases to less harmful substances.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-336.jpg?height=714&width=1268&top_left_y=2949&top_left_x=188)
Figure 17.34 A catalytic converter is fitted into the exhaust system of cars powered by fossil fuels to convert the harmful gases into less harmful ones.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-336.jpg?height=525&width=1098&top_left_y=3187&top_left_x=1513)
Figure 17.35 The main gases entering a catalytic converter and leaving a catalytic converter

The main reaction that happens in the catalytic converter is the reaction between the polluting gases themselves (carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide) to form carbon dioxide and nitrogen:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-337.jpg?height=180&width=811&top_left_y=592&top_left_x=332)

Also, the unburned hydrocarbons react with the nitrogen oxides to form carbon dioxide and nitrogen and water. Note that the pollutants are being converted to $\mathrm{CO}_{2}, \mathrm{~N}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$, all of which are naturally present in the air. The environmental benefits of catalytic converters may be summarised in the form of a table.

| Reactant | Product | Environmental benefit of removal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Carbon monoxide | Carbon dioxide | Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas. |
| Nitrogen monoxide | Nitrogen | Nitrogen monoxide is poisonous and contributes to acid rain. |
| Hydrocarbons | Carbon dioxide and water | Hydrocarbons cause smog and contribute to the greenhouse effect. |

Note also that the chemical equation describing what takes place in a catalytic converter is a good example of heterogeneous catalysis, since the reactants and the catalysts are in different phases.

Catalytic converters usually last for about 80,000 kilometres. They need to be replaced as a result of 'poisoning' of the catalyst and disintegration of the catalysts and the ceramic surfaces as a result of engine vibration and wear from fast-moving hot gases. However, when leaded petrol was used as a fuel, the catalytic converter had a very short life. It was ruined as the lead poisoned the surface of the catalysts.

- When a catalyst is 'poisoned', a lot of the surface of the catalyst is blocked off due to permanent bond formation between the metal and the substance acting as the catalyst poison. substance that makes a catalyst inactive.
- Catalytic poisoning takes place when substances chemically bind to the catalyst's surface. These block the active sites on the catalyst that help to break down the harmful exhaust gases.

The lead compounds are more strongly adsorbed on to the surface of the catalyst than the other compounds and thus 'poison the catalyst' or prevent the catalyst from doing its job. A lot of the surface of the catalyst is blocked off due to permanent bond formation between the catalyst and the substance acting as the catalyst poison. Although lead is no longer added to petrol, catalysts in catalytic converters can still be poisoned by other substances:

- Sulfur compounds: These compounds found in fuels or oil can coat the surface of the catalyst. Modern fuels usually have low amounts of sulfur but contamination can still occur.
- Phosphorus: If the engine burns oil, phosphorus compounds can enter the exhaust system and poison the catalyst.
- Plastic silicone compounds: These are used for sealants and, when burned, the silicon deposits can poison the catalyst.

When the converter is changed, it is possible to recover most of the catalysts and recycle them. Each catalytic converter contains only a few grams of the catalysts, Figure 17.36.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-338.jpg?height=1088&width=1802&top_left_y=599&top_left_x=188)
Figure 17.36. This photograph shows the ceramic honeycombs used in catalytic converters.

Note: Catalysts can also become saturated when the active sites on the catalyst are temporarily occupied by reactants or intermediates. Since the catalysts are now working at full capacity, the effectiveness of the catalysts is reduced as they are unable to deal efficiently with the high concentration of gases. Once the reactants are converted to products and are desorbed from the surface of the catalyst, the actives sites are freed up again.

Active sites may be compared to seats in a cinema. Each seat can accommodate a person (reactant molecule). If all seats are occupied, people have to wait until one becomes available. If someone spills ice cream on a seat (poisoning), that seat becomes unavailable to accommodate new arrivals.

## (vi) Pressure (for gaseous reactions)

For reactions in which all the reactants and products are gases, when you increase the pressure of the gaseous reactants, you compress the gas particles into a smaller volume. Therefore, the gas particles are closer together and they collide more frequently with each other. Since the particles collide more frequently with each other, there is a higher chance that more collisions will form products. Therefore, the reaction rate increases.

In general, for all-gaseous reactions, an increase in pressure results in an increase in reaction rate. We will be studying reactions between gases in more detail in the next chapter.

### 17.5 Collision theory and activation energy

Many of the observed facts about rates of reactions are interpreted using a theory called the Collision Theory. This theory was developed from the kinetic theory of gases in order to account for the factors that influence the rate of a reaction.

The basic assumptions of this theory are:

1. For a reaction to occur, the reacting particles must collide with each other.
2. A collision only results in the formation of products if a certain minimum energy is exceeded in the collision. Such a collision is called an effective collision.

- For an effective collision to take place, the particles must have sufficient energy (must be moving quickly) and must collide head on. If the collision is at the wrong angle, the particle may just glance against each other and no reaction will occur. In short, collisions need to be oriented correctly, Figure 17.37. Note that an ineffective collision and an effective collision are shown in Figure 17.37. In the effective collision, an O atom is formed. This oxygen atom can then collide with other $O$ atoms to form an oxygen molecule.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-339.jpg?height=652&width=1583&top_left_y=1748&top_left_x=442)
Figure 17.37 When molecules collide in the right orientation, there is a higher chance that bonds will break, and products will be formed.

- When an effective collision occurs between colliding particles, bonds are broken and new bonds are formed, i.e. the effective collision brings about a chemical reaction.
- This results in the formation of products. According to the collision theory, the rate of a reaction depends not only on the number of collisions per second that take place between the reacting particles, but also on the fraction of these collisions that are effective.

Suppose that one mole of oxygen gas and one mole of hydrogen gas are placed in a one litre container at room temperature and at a pressure of one atmosphere. It has been calculated that $1 \times 10^{30}$ collisions take place every second between the molecules. If every one of these collisions were to lead to chemical reaction, the reaction would be over in a fraction of a second. However, by experiment, this is found not to be the case.

Chemists conclude that it is not the total number of collisions that will determine the rate of reaction but rather the number of effective collisions.

An effective collision is one that results in the formation of products.

Suppose you were to measure the walking speeds of people in the street. You would find that some are walking very slowly, some are walking very quickly, and the majority are walking at moderate speeds. Similarly, if you were to calculate the amount of energy possessed by the molecules in a sample of gas, you would find that most of the molecules have an average kinetic energy, some have a lower than average kinetic energy and some have a higher than average kinetic energy. This distribution of kinetic energies of the molecules of a gas at $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is shown in Figure 17.38. This type of graph is called the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. James Maxwell and Ludwig Boltzmann calculated the proportion of molecules with a given energy at a particular temperature. They drew diagrams similar to that shown in Figure 17.38. The area under the curve gives the total number of molecules. Thus, the area shaded in red shows the total number of molecules whose energy is above the Activation Energy.

If the temperature of the gas is increased, the kinetic energies of the gas molecules will increase also due to the heat energy supplied. This will mean that a greater proportion of molecules will now have higher energies as shown in Figure 17.39. Note that there is an increase in the number of molecules at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ that have energies about the Activation Energy. In other words, the green-shaded area is bigger than the red-shaded area.

- This distribution of energy among the molecules in a sample of gas explains why it is that not all the collisions between molecules bring about a reaction.
- When molecules with low energies collide, they simply bounce apart without any reaction taking place.
- It is only those molecules with high enough energies when they collide that form the products.
- A certain amount of energy is necessary for a chemical reaction to occur when molecules collide, i.e. for the collision to be effective.
- This energy is called the Activation Energy and is defined as follows:

Thus, the collision theory explains why reactions are faster at higher temperatures because a greater number of collisions reach the Activation Energy, i.e. more of the collisions have enough energy for the reaction to occur. In short, at higher temperatures there are more effective collisions.

Note: An increase in temperature does not change the size of the Activation Energy itself, since this size depends on the nature of the reactants, i.e. it depends on the particular reaction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-340.jpg?height=561&width=1153&top_left_y=397&top_left_x=1393)
Figure 17.38 This graph shows the distribution of energies of the molecules in a sample of gas at a temperature of $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-340.jpg?height=590&width=1268&top_left_y=1198&top_left_x=1334)
Figure 17.39 Increasing the temperature causes a greater number of molecules to have energy in excess of the activation energy.

## The Activation

Energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur, i.e. the minimum energy required for effective collisions between particles to occur.

## Example 19.7

## Question

Give two reasons why the rate of a chemical reaction increases as the temperature rises.
Which of these reasons is the more significant? Why?
[LCH]

## Answer

The rate of a chemical reaction increases as the temperature rises for the following two reasons:

1. There is an increased number of collisions since the moving molecules have more energy (they are moving faster) at the higher temperature.
2. More of the collisions are effective at the higher temperature, i.e. the colliding molecules have the minimum Activation Energy needed to react.

The more significant reason is the second one above. The reason why this is more significant is because, if molecules with low energies collide, they simply bounce apart without any reaction taking place. Thus, an increase in the number of collisions will not necessarily lead to the reaction taking place. The important thing is that the rise in temperature must be great enough to ensure that the colliding molecules have enough energy to reach the Activation Energy.

It is also generally the case that, for a particular temperature rise, the increase in the number of collisions is far exceeded by the increase in the fraction of those collisions that are effective.

The size of the Activation Energy depends on the nature of the reactants.

- Some reactions have a large Activation Energy. This means that these reactions are slow or may not occur at all, since only a small fraction of the particles have enough energy to supply the Activation Energy.
- In other cases, a greater fraction of the molecules have sufficient energy to supply the Activation Energy.
- This means that a greater fraction of the collisions are effective, i.e. these reactions are fast.

Activation Energy is often represented as shown in Figure 17.40.

## This type of diagram is called a Reaction Profile Diagram or Energy Profile Diagram.

A Reaction Profile Diagram (Energy Profile Diagram) is a graph which shows the change in energy of a chemical reaction with time as the reaction progresses.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-341.jpg?height=1404&width=1160&top_left_y=1881&top_left_x=1588)
Figure 17.40 The size of the activation energy determines the rate of reaction.

- Note from the diagram that the Activation Energy is the difference in energy between the average energy of the reactant molecules and the energy of molecules in the activated complex.
- The activated complex is simply an intermediate substance formed by the collision of molecules with enough energy to react.
- Reaction profile diagrams may be compared to a ball being rolled up a slope. If the ball has a lot of energy going up the slope, it may go over the top and roll down the other side, i.e. a chemical reaction occurs. If the ball has only a small amount of energy, it will only go a little way up the slope before falling back down.
- A chemical reaction that gives out heat is called an exothermic reaction. This means that the products have less energy than the reactants. The energy change between reactants and products is represented by the symbol $\Delta H$, which is called the Heat of Reaction. For an exothermic reaction, $\Delta H$ represents the amount of heat given out. (We will be studying this in more detail in Chapter 21.) A reaction profile diagram for an exothermic reaction is shown in Figure 17.41.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-342.jpg?height=610&width=1157&top_left_y=2083&top_left_x=188)
Figure 17.41 A reaction profile diagram for an exothermic reaction. Note that the products have less energy than the reactants. The energy given out is represented by the symbol $\Delta \mathrm{H}$.

A chemical reaction that takes in heat energy is called an endothermic reaction. In this case the products have more energy than the reactants. An endothermic reaction may also be represented by a Reaction Profile Diagram, Figure 17.42.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-342.jpg?height=606&width=1160&top_left_y=732&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 17.42 A reaction profile diagram for an endothermic reaction. Note that the products have more energy than the reactants. The energy taken in is represented by the symbol $\Delta \mathrm{H}$.

We have already discussed how the Collision Theory explains how a rise in temperature increases the rate of reaction. This theory may also be used to explain why the other factors that we have studied in this chapter affect the rate of a reaction.
(i) Nature of reactants: Reactions with covalent compounds involve bond-breaking taking place during a collision. This breaking of bonds requires energy and hence these types of reactions have much higher activation energies than reactions which merely involve oppositely-charged ions colliding with each other in solution.
(ii) Particle size: The smaller the particle size, the more surface area is exposed and, therefore, the greater the number of collisions taking place. Since the number of collisions that take place is greatly increased, the number of these collisions that are effective will also increase.
(iii) Concentration: If the concentration of the reactants is increased, the number of collisions will also be increased because the particles are closer together. Therefore, the number of effective collisions will be increased, giving rise to an increased rate of reaction.

In some cases, an increase in concentration may not always affect the rate, Figure 17.43. For example, we have seen that the rate of reaction increases when a more concentrated solution of HCl is used to investigate the rate of reaction between HCl and Mg . However, if you keep increasing the concentration of HCl , a further increase may not necessarily increase the rate of reaction as the maximum number of collisions between hydrogen ions and the magnesium atoms on the surface of the magnesium are already taking place. In other words, the surface of the Mg metal is already saturated with hydrogen ions.

Another example of a reaction in which increasing the concentration does not affect the rate is the addition of silver nitrate solution to a solution containing chloride ions. You will recall that a precipitate of silver chloride forms immediately (Chapter 5). The reaction is very fast (or instantaneous) on mixing the two solutions. Therefore, even if you change the concentration of one or more of the reactants, the time to form the precipitate won't change.
(iv) Catalyst: A catalyst works by providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, Figure 17.44. Therefore, more reactant molecules now possess the energy required for effective collisions to occur. Therefore, the rate of reaction increases.

A reaction profile diagram may also be drawn to represent an endothermic reaction that is both catalysed and uncatalysed, Figure 17.45.
(v) Pressure: As already discussed, for reactions in which all the reactants and products are gases, when you increase the pressure of the gaseous reactants, you compress the gas particles into a smaller volume. Therefore, the gas particles are closer together and will collide more frequently with each other. Since the particles collide more frequently with each other, there is a higher chance that more collisions will be effective and form products. Therefore, the reaction rate increases.

In general, for all-gaseous reactions, an increase in pressure results in an increase in reaction rate.

Study Example 17.4 in the online resources.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-343.jpg?height=880&width=1167&top_left_y=374&top_left_x=1588)
Figure 17.43 When the HCl solution is already very concentrated, a further increase in concentration may not increase the rate of the reaction due to a type of 'saturation effect' at the surface of the metal. In other words, the maximum number of collisions between hydrogen ions and the magnesium atoms are taking place.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-343.jpg?height=721&width=1173&top_left_y=1770&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 17.44 A catalyst reduces the activation energy for a reaction. In this case, the reaction profile diagram is shown for both a catalysed and uncatalysed exothermic reaction.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-343.jpg?height=730&width=1173&top_left_y=2799&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 17.45 A reaction profile diagram is shown for a catalysed and uncatalysed endothermic reaction.

## Summary What I should know

- The rate of reaction is defined as the change in concentration per unit time of any one reactant or product.
- The instantaneous rate of reaction is the rate of reaction at any one particular time during the reaction.

The instantaneous rate is determined by measuring the slope of the tangent to the curve at that instant.

- By experiment, it is found that the rate of a reaction depends on the nature of the reactants, the particle size, the concentration, the temperature, the presence of a catalyst and pressure (for gaseous reactions).
- A catalyst is a substance that alters the rate of a chemical reaction but is not consumed in the reaction.
- Homogeneous catalysis is catalysis in which the reactants and the catalyst are in the same phase i.e. there is no boundary between the reactants and the catalyst.
- Heterogeneous catalysis is catalysis in which the reactants and the catalyst are in different phases i.e. there is a boundary between the reactants and the catalyst.

Autocatalysis is catalysis in which one of the products of the reaction acts as a catalyst for the reaction.

- The Intermediate Formation Theory and the Surface Adsorption Theory are used to explain how catalysts work.

A catalytic converter is a device in the exhaust system of a motor vehicle that contains catalysts to convert pollutants in the exhaust gases to less harmful substances.

A catalyst poison is a substance that makes a catalyst inactive.
An effective collision is one that results in the formation of products.
The Activation Energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur, i.e. the minimum energy required for effective collisions between particles to occur.

# 18 Chemical Equilibrium

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-346.jpg?height=1117&width=1271&top_left_y=511&top_left_x=185)

### 18.1 Introduction: What is equilibrium?

If you look up the word 'equilibrium' in a dictionary, you will find it explained using words such as 'state of balance'.

Imagine a metre stick is suspended at its point of balance (centre of gravity). The stick is said to be balanced or in equilibrium, Figure 18.1. Note that the stick is not tipping over to one side: it is staying still, or static. Therefore, this type of equilibrium is called static equilibrium. The entire system is not moving. Static equilibrium occurs when an object is at rest and does not move because all the forces acting on it are balanced.

Now imagine runners on a treadmill, as in Figure 18.2. They are running forward, but the treadmill belt is moving backward at the same speed. Because they are moving at the same speed as the treadmill, each runner stays in the same spot. The two opposing motions balance each other, so there is no overall change in position. This is an example of dynamic equilibrium. The word 'dynamic' implies movement.

Another example of a dynamic equilibrium is walking down an escalator at the same speed as it is moving up. There is no overall change in position because the two opposing motions are balanced.

In this chapter, we will consider chemical reactions in which a state of dynamic equilibrium exists.

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of the concept of chemical equilibrium.
- To provide students with the opportunity to carry out laboratory work involving a reaction at chemical equilibrium.
- To ensure that students know how to solve problems involving reactions at chemical equilibrium.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-346.jpg?height=350&width=1115&top_left_y=1985&top_left_x=1474)
Figure 18.1 The metre stick does not move because the forces acting on it are balanced. Since the metre stick does not move, this type of state of balance is called static equilibrium.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-346.jpg?height=877&width=1180&top_left_y=2662&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 18.2 The photograph shows an example of dynamic equilibrium. The speed of each runner in the forward direction is equal to the speed of the belt in the opposite direction. The word 'equilibrium' means 'state of balance'.

### 18.2 What is chemical equilibrium?

When magnesium ribbon is burned in air, a very bright light is observed and a white substance called magnesium oxide is formed. We may write this reaction as follows:

$$
\underset{\text { magnesium }}{2 \mathrm{Mg}}+\underset{\text { oxygen }}{\mathrm{O}_{2}} \rightarrow \underset{\text { magnesium oxide }}{2 \mathrm{MgO}}
$$

This reaction is a one-way process - it is very difficult to turn the magnesium oxide back into magnesium and oxygen. Chemists often say that the reaction 'goes to completion'. In other words, the reactants are completely converted to products.

However, by experiment, it is found that there are many chemical reactions that do not 'go to completion'. One example of this is the reaction between hydrogen gas and nitrogen gas.

In 1908 two German chemists, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch discovered that nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas reacted to form ammonia, Figure 18.3.
Ammonia is a gas used in the manufacture of fertilisers, cleaning agents, explosives and nylon.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-347.jpg?height=207&width=923&top_left_y=1770&top_left_x=507)

However, Haber discovered that the reaction did not go completely from left to right. He found that some of the ammonia that was formed actually decomposed to give back the nitrogen and hydrogen. In other words, he found that the above reaction takes place in both directions:

Fritz Haber
(1868-1934)

Figure 18.3

Carl Bosch (1874-1940)

The process to manufacture ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is called the Haber process or, more correctly, the Haber-Bosch process, after the chemist (Fritz Haber) and the chemical engineer (Carl Bosch) who developed the process.

- In the forward direction, it takes place to form ammonia.
- In the backward direction, it takes place so that ammonia breaks down to form nitrogen and hydrogen.
Since the above reaction takes place both in the forward and backward directions, it is said to be reversible.

A reversible reaction is one in which the products react to give back the reactants, i.e. the reaction is going in both directions.

Reversible reactions are also called equilibrium reactions and are indicated using the equilibrium arrow sign ( ⇌).

$$
\mathrm{N}_{2}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3}
$$

Chemical reactions such as the above involve a dynamic equilibrium. This means that nitrogen and hydrogen are continuously reacting together to form ammonia, while ammonia is continuously decomposing to form nitrogen and hydrogen. When this state of equilibrium has been reached, it is found that the rate of the forward reaction is the same as the rate of the backward reaction. Therefore, there is no change in the overall amounts of nitrogen or hydrogen or ammonia present in the container.

In general, if reactants A and B react together to form products C and D and a state of equilibrium is reached, we can represent this as follows:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-348.jpg?height=241&width=665&top_left_y=612&top_left_x=289)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-348.jpg?height=199&width=265&top_left_y=664&top_left_x=1005)

At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the backward reaction, i.e. $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{f}}=\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{b}}$
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-348.jpg?height=255&width=890&top_left_y=608&top_left_x=1588)

Chemical equilibrium is a state of dynamic balance in a reversible reaction where the rate of the forward reaction is the same as the rate of the backward reaction.

## Visualising chemical equilibrium

Studying Figure 18.4 will help you to understand the concept of equilibrium. This graph describes what happens to the concentrations of reactants and products when nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas are placed in a sealed container.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-348.jpg?height=922&width=1209&top_left_y=1445&top_left_x=188)
Figure 18.4 When equilibrium is reached at time $\boldsymbol{t}$ the concentrations of reactants and products become steady and no longer change with time.

Note the following:

- The initial concentrations of nitrogen and hydrogen have fixed values depending on the number of moles of these gases placed in the sealed container.
- The initial concentration of ammonia is zero since the nitrogen and hydrogen have not yet reacted together to form ammonia.
- As the reaction proceeds, the rate of the forward reaction decreases (since the concentrations of the nitrogen and hydrogen are decreasing) and the rate of the backward reaction increases (since the concentration of the ammonia is increasing) until eventually, at time $\boldsymbol{t}$, the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the backward reaction.
- At this stage, note carefully in Figure 18.4 , the concentrations of all three substances in the container become constant due to the fact that the nitrogen and hydrogen are continuously reacting to form ammonia and the ammonia is continuously decomposing to form nitrogen and hydrogen.
- When this stage is reached, the situation in the container is described as a dynamic equilibrium because the nitrogen and hydrogen are

In a dynamic state the reactants are continuously forming products and the products are continuously forming reactants.

A dynamic chemical equilibrium is the equilibrium that exists in a closed system of a chemical reaction when the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the backward reaction. The concentrations of the reactants and products remain the same. continuously forming ammonia, while the ammonia is continuously decomposing to form nitrogen and hydrogen. The term dynamic also indicates that neither the forward nor the backward reaction has actually stopped - both are still occurring.

When the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the backward reaction, the two reactions balance out and hence the name dynamic chemical equilibrium is used to describe what is happening.

The initial state and the dynamic equilibrium state for the above reaction are shown in Figure 18.5.

Initially, the gases are fed into the sealed metal container (reactor) in which the reaction takes place. At this stage, the reactor contains only molecules of nitrogen and hydrogen as they have not yet reacted. However, at equilibrium, the reactor contains a mixture of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-349.jpg?height=1473&width=2430&top_left_y=1064&top_left_x=328)

The container in which chemical reactions involving gases are carried out is usually sealed to ensure that gases cannot escape as equilibrium is being established. This system is called a closed system.

Note the following:

- A closed system means that no matter can enter or leave the container. In other words, the total amount of reactants and products remains constant within the system to allow a state of chemical equilibrium to be reached.
- In a closed system the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant at equilibrium because no substances can enter or leave the system. The concentrations are constant because the system is sealed and this prevents the addition or removal of reactants or products.
- Even though no matter can enter or leave a closed system, energy (e.g. heat or light) can still be exchanged with the surroundings in a closed system.
- The state of equilibrium can be achieved from either direction of the reaction. In other words, if ammonia were placed in the reactor initially, the same state of equilibrium would be established as if you started with nitrogen and hydrogen.


### 18.3 Le Chatelier's Principle

Many chemical processes involve equilibrium reactions. Therefore, for economic reasons, it is important for chemists to try to shift the equilibrium as much as possible to the right, i.e. to maximise the amounts of products formed. A French chemist called Henri Le Chatelier, Figure 18.6, studied many equilibrium reactions.

In 1888 Le Chatelier put forward a rule that allowed chemists to predict the direction taken by an equilibrium reaction if the conditions of the reaction were changed. This rule is known as Le Chatelier's Principle and may be stated as follows:

> Le Chatelier's Principle states that if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system readjusts to relieve the stress applied.

Figure 18.6

## Henri Le Chatelier <br> (1850-1936)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-350.jpg?height=336&width=340&top_left_y=462&top_left_x=2275)

Henri Le Chatelier was a very practical industrial chemist who worked as a mining engineer prior to his appointment in 1877 as Professor of General Chemistry at the School of Mines in Paris. He was particularly interested in finding ways to increase yields in industrial processes. This helped lead him to the discovery of the principle that bears his name.

In the above statement of Le Chatelier's Principle, the word 'stress' simply means a change in the conditions of the reaction, such as:

- A change in the concentration of either reactants or products
- A change in pressure
- A change in temperature.

In simple language, Le Chatelier's Principle tells us that if we change the conditions of a reaction that has reached a state of equilibrium, the equilibrium will be shifted in such a direction that the effect of the change will be minimised. When this has been achieved, a new state of equilibrium will have been set up.

## Demonstrating Le Chatelier's Principle

To demonstrate Le Chatelier's Principle, consider the reaction in which two molecules of nitrogen dioxide, $\mathrm{NO}_{2^{\prime}}$ join together to form a molecule of dinitrogen tetroxide, $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}$. Both of these substances are gases, as indicated in the following equation:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-350.jpg?height=427&width=1001&top_left_y=2552&top_left_x=644)

The forward reaction gives out heat (an exothermic reaction) and the backward reaction takes in heat (an endothermic reaction). Chemists use the symbol $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ to indicate whether a reaction gives out heat or takes in heat. For example, the above equation could also be written:

$$
2 \mathrm{NO}_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4(g)} \quad \Delta H=-58.1 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

The negative sign indicates that the reaction gives out heat in the forward direction.
You will learn more about $\Delta H$ in Chapter 21,

The effect of change of temperature on this reaction is illustrated in Figure 18.7.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-351.jpg?height=874&width=1902&top_left_y=468&top_left_x=328)
Figure 18.7 An experiment to demonstrate Le Chatelier's Principle

The three test-tubes contain an equilibrium mixture of nitrogen dioxide gas and dinitrogen tetroxide gas. The middle test-tube is at room temperature and contains an approximate equal mixture of the two gases. Hence the light-brown colour.

The test-tube on the left is placed in ice. The lowering of the temperature constitutes a stress.

To minimise the effect of the lowering of the temperature, the equilibrium is shifted in the direction that produces heat (Le Chatelier's Principle). Therefore, the for ward reaction predominates (exothermic) and this results in the production of more dinitrogen tetroxide.

Therefore the brown colour becomes pale yellow.
If you lowered the temperature even more - using liquid nitrogen - the contents of the test-tube would become almost colourless.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-351.jpg?height=431&width=1010&top_left_y=2685&top_left_x=410)

The test-tube on the right is placed in hot water.
In order to absorb the stress of increased temperature, the reaction that absorbs heat will predominate, i.e. the equilibrium is shifted in the backward direction as predicted by Le Chatelier's Principle. Therefore, more nitrogen dioxide is produced.

Therefore the contents of the test-tube turn dark-brown.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-351.jpg?height=304&width=1007&top_left_y=1549&top_left_x=1663)

## Effect of pressure change on reactions involving gases

In reactions in which all the reactants and products are gases, Le Chatelier found that in certain cases he was able to use changes in pressure to shift the direction of equilibrium in either the forward or backward direction. This may be illustrated by the reaction between nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas to form ammonia gas, Figure 18.8.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-351.jpg?height=949&width=1177&top_left_y=2558&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 18.8 If the pressure is increased, the equilibrium shifts to the side of the equation that has the smaller number of molecules. The smaller number of molecules occupies less volume and this helps to absorb the stress of increased pressure.

Le Chatelier's findings may be summarised as follows:
Le Chatelier's Principle predicts that in an all-gaseous reaction, an increase in pressure will favour the reaction that brings about a reduction in volume. This means it will shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules.

A change in the pressure on a system affects only an equilibrium reaction that has an unequal number of molecules of gaseous reactants and products. In Figure 18.8, the increase in pressure is relieved by the equilibrium being shifted to the side with the smaller number of molecules.

In all gaseous reactions in which there is the same total number of molecules on both sides of the equation, a change in pressure will have no effect on the position of equilibrium.

We have already seen in Chapter 17 that a catalyst alters the rate of a chemical reaction. In the case of a reaction that has reached a state of dynamic equilibrium, a catalyst increases (or in some cases decreases) the rate of both the forward reaction and the reverse reaction by the same amount. In other words, the catalyst enables the system to reach a state of equilibrium in a shorter time. However, adding a catalyst to an equilibrium reaction does not affect the position of equilibrium in the reaction or the composition of the equilibrium mixture. Thus, a catalyst does not alter the yield of product in an equilibrium reaction. In short, a catalyst speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached but it does not change the position of equilibrium.

## Example 18.1

## Question

The following reaction occurs in a closed vessel at a certain temperature. The forward reaction is exothermic.
$\mathrm{PCl}_{3(g)}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_{5(g)}$
What would be the effect on the concentration of $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ in the equilibrium mixture of:
(i) introducing more $\mathrm{PCl}_{3}$ into the mixture, (ii) increasing the pressure, (iii) increasing the temperature?
[LCH]

## Answer

(i) If more $\mathrm{PCl}_{3}$ is introduced into the container, the equilibrium will shift to the right to absorb the increase. Therefore, the concentration of $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ will increase.
(ii) Note that all of the substances in the above reaction are gaseous. There are two molecules on the left-hand side of the equation but only one on the right-hand side of the equation. If we increase the pressure, the equilibrium shifts to the side that has the smaller number of molecules (in accordance with Le Chatelier's Principle). Therefore, the equilibrium shifts to the right-hand side. Thus, the concentration of $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ increases.
(iii) We are told that the forward reaction is exothermic. This implies that the backward reaction is endothermic.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-352.jpg?height=226&width=603&top_left_y=3040&top_left_x=390)

If the temperature is increased, the equilibrium will be shifted in the backward direction in order to absorb this heat. Therefore, the concentration of $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ will decrease.

### 18.1 Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 18

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 18 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

To investigate how changes in (a) concentration and (b) temperature can affect the state of equilibrium in the reaction between iron (III) chloride and potassium thiocyanate

## Introduction

In this experiment we will investigate the effect of changes in (a) concentration and (b) temperature on the state of equilibrium in the following reaction:

$$
\underset{\text { yellow }}{\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+\mathrm{CNS}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \underset{\text { red }}{\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CNS})^{2+}}}
$$

We use iron (III) chloride ( $\mathrm{FeCl}_{3}$ ) as the source of the $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions and potassium thiocyanate (KCNS) as the source of the CNS- ions. $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions are yellow and CNS- ions are colourless. However, when the two ions combine, an equilibrium reaction is set up involving the production of the blood-red ferrothiocyanate ion. This is a complex ion of formula $\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CNS})^{2+}$.

## Part (a) To investigate the effect of concentration

## Key steps in procedure

- About $5 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of iron (III) chloride solution and one drop of potassium thiocyanate solution are mixed in a test-tube.


## Observation

A red colour is observed, Figure 18.9.

Figure 18.9 The red colour is due to the presence of the $\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CNS})^{2+}$ ion. This means that the equilibrium lies on the right-hand side of the equation shown above.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-353.jpg?height=642&width=479&top_left_y=1888&top_left_x=1224)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-353.jpg?height=642&width=486&top_left_y=1888&top_left_x=1712)
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-353.jpg?height=642&width=480&top_left_y=1888&top_left_x=2200)

## Explanation

The red colour is caused by the formation of $\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CNS})^{2+}$ as follows:

$$
\underset{\text { yellow colourless }}{\mathrm{FeCl}_{3}}+\underset{\text { red }}{\mathrm{Ce}\left(\mathrm{CNS}^{-}\right)}
$$

Since the red colour is observed, the equilibrium must lie on the right-hand side of the above equation.

- Some dilute hydrochloric acid is added until the red colour disappears.


## Explanation

In keeping with Le Chatelier's Principle, the red colour disappears as the equilibrium is shifted to the left-hand side to absorb the $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ions added.

- Add some potassium thiocyanate solution.


## Observation

A red colour is observed.

## Explanation

In keeping with Le Chatelier's Principle, the solution becomes red because the equilibrium is shifted to the right-hand side to absorb the CNS-ions added.

## Part（b）To investigate the effect of temperature

In this part of the experiment，we will investigate the effect of temperature on the equilibrium：
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-354.jpg?height=252&width=1033&top_left_y=618&top_left_x=891)

## Key steps in procedure

－Mix together about $10 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of a solution of iron（III）chloride and a drop or more of potassium thiocyanate solution in a test－tube．

## Observation

A red colour is formed．

## Explanation

The equilibrium lies on the right－hand side of the above equation．
－The solution is divided among three test－tubes．One test－tube is placed in hot water， one test－tube is placed in ice，and the third test－tube is left at room temperature．

## Observation

－The red colour changes to yellow in the test－tube placed in hot water，Figure 18．10． The colour change is difficult to see．
－The yellow colour changes to red in the test－tube placed in ice．This colour change is difficult to see．

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-354.jpg?height=851&width=1632&top_left_y=1992&top_left_x=315)
Figure 18．10 The red colour changes to yellow when the equilibrium mixture is placed in boiling water． The red colour becomes more intense when the equilibrium mixture is placed in ice．

## Explanation

In the case of the test－tube placed in hot water，the equilibrium shifts to the left （direction of endothermic reaction）in order to absorb the added heat．Therefore，the red colour changes to yellow．This is in keeping with Le Chatelier＇s Principle．

In the case of the test－tube placed in iced water，the equilibrium shifts to the right （direction of exothermic reaction）in order to replace the heat that has been removed． Therefore，the colour changes to red．This is in keeping with Le Chatelier＇s Principle．

We conclude that adding heat favours the direction of the endothermic reaction （in which heat is absorbed）and removing heat favours the direction of the exothermic reaction（in which heat is liberated）．

### 18.4 Using Le Chatelier's Principle to optimise product yield

As a case study, we now consider how Le Chatelier's Principle is applied to maximise yield in the industrial manufacture of ammonia. Ammonia is one of the most important chemicals manufactured by the chemical industry. Ammonia is used to manufacture fertilisers, explosives and cleaning agents. Approximately 80\% of all ammonia produced is used to manufacture fertilisers, Figure 18.11.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-355.jpg?height=805&width=1183&top_left_y=1250&top_left_x=325)

The key points about the manufacture of ammonia may be summarised as follows.

Ammonia is manufactured by reacting nitrogen (obtained from the air) with hydrogen (usually obtained from natural gas). The reaction may be summarised as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{Fe} \\
\mathrm{~N}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(g)} \quad \Delta H=-92.4 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{gathered}
$$

In words, this may be written as:
iron (catalyst)
nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonia
The amount of ammonia produced depends on the temperature and the pressure inside the reaction vessel.

Le Chatelier's Principle in action: Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch used Le Chatelier's Principle to figure out the best conditions for making ammonia. As seen in the above equation, there are four moles of reactants (on the left) and only two moles of ammonia (on the right), Figure 18.12. According to Le Chatelier's Principle, at high pressure, the equilibrium will shift to the right, producing more ammonia. By experiment, this is found to be true.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-355.jpg?height=867&width=1121&top_left_y=400&top_left_x=1601)
Figure 18.12 An increase in pressure causes the equilibrium to be shifted from left to right.

Pressure compromise: A high-pressure plant is expensive both to build and to maintain and the improvement in yield is not worth the extra cost. Also, with high-pressure plants there is a danger of gas leaks and other safety problems when dealing with gases under high pressure, e.g. explosions. Therefore, a compromise pressure of approximately $\mathbf{2 0 0}$ atmospheres is used in the production of ammonia to ensure a relatively good yield of ammonia while also reducing the cost of a high-pressure plant.

Temperature conditions: The negative value of $\Delta \mathrm{H}$ in the above equation tells us that the reaction is exothermic (releases heat) going from left to right. Therefore, if we lower the temperature in the reaction vessel, Le Chatelier's Principle tells us that the equilibrium will be shifted to the right, i.e. more ammonia will be produced. However, it is found that, if the temperature is too low, the rate of the reaction is too slow, i.e. the system takes a long time to come to equilibrium.

Temperature compromise: At low temperature, we would succeed in getting a high yield of ammonia (the mixture of the three gases in the reaction vessel could consist of about 90\% ammonia) but the ammonia would be produced too slowly to be economically viable. Therefore, a compromise temperature of approximately $\mathbf{5 0 0}^{\boldsymbol{\circ}} \mathbf{C}$ is used in practice to ensure a satisfactory yield of ammonia while also ensuring that the reaction does not take too long.

In short, Le Chatelier's Principle tells us that the best conditions to maximise the yield of ammonia in the Haber process are high pressure and low temperature. However, in practice, a balance is needed between yield and reaction speed.

The Haber process involves a method of removing the ammonia as it is formed (thus pushing the equilibrium to the right) and continuously feeding in new reactants.

## Role of catalysts in industrial processes

In industrial processes, catalysts make a very valuable contribution to the economy of the process. For example, in the Haber process, the percentage conversion of nitrogen and hydrogen to ammonia under the above conditions at which a typical plant operates is small. However, using a catalyst enables the same percentage conversion to be achieved in a much shorter time, i.e. it brings the system to equilibrium more quickly. In addition, it allows the reaction to be carried out at a lower temperature than would be the case if no catalyst were present. This increases the productivity of the plant and hence makes the process more economical.

### 18.5 The equilibrium constant

So far we have discussed equilibrium from a descriptive point of view. We have seen how various factors can affect the position of equilibrium and shift it to the left or to the right. When a system reaches a state of equilibrium, chemists and chemical engineers need to know the exact concentrations of reactants and products that exist in the equilibrium mixture. In some cases, it is possible to determine these concentrations by experiment. In other cases, it is necessary to determine these concentrations by performing calculations. In this section, we consider how chemists and chemical engineers perform calculations relating to systems that have reached a state of equilibrium.

By experiment, it has been discovered that, provided the temperature remains constant, there is a simple mathematical relationship between the concentrations of the reactants and products in an equilibrium mixture. This simple relationship is based on a law known as the Law of Chemical
Equilibrium or the Equilibrium Law. Consider the reaction in which a moles of reactant $A$ react with $\mathbf{b}$ moles of reactant B to form $\mathbf{c}$ moles of product C and $\mathbf{d}$ moles of product D at equilibrium.

$$
a A+b B \rightleftharpoons c C+d D
$$

It has been found by experiment that the concentrations of all species at equilibrium are related by the expression:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-356.jpg?height=343&width=942&top_left_y=787&top_left_x=1477)
$K_{c}$ is called the equilibrium constant. (The ' $K$ ' represents the constant and the subscript ' $C$ ' stands for concentration since the value of $K$ depends on the concentrations of the reactants and products at equilibrium.) The square brackets represent concentration measured in moles per litre.

It is very important for you to be able to write correct equilibrium constant expressions when given the balanced equation.

Note the following points carefully:

- The products are always written above the line (in the numerator) and the reactants are always written below the line (in the denominator).
- The concentrations of the products are multiplied together. The concentrations of the reactants are multiplied together. The multiplication sign is usually omitted.
- The concentration of each species is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.
- Thus, the equilibrium constant expression for the reaction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{N}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(g)} \\
& \text { is } K_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right]^{2}}{\left[\mathrm{~N}_{2}\right]\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]^{3}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Every equilibrium reaction has its own value for $K_{c}$ at the particular temperature at which the reaction takes place. For example, at $458^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ the value of $K_{\mathrm{c}}$ for the reaction $\mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{I}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{HI}$ is 46 (approximately).

By experiment it is found that this $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}$ value of 46 is always obtained no matter what concentrations of hydrogen and iodine are put into the container and allowed to reach equilibrium at that temperature, Figure 18.13.

Instead of putting hydrogen and iodine into the

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-357.jpg?height=473&width=1169&top_left_y=377&top_left_x=1582)
Figure 18.13 The equilibrium $\mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{I}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{HI}$ can be set up starting either with a mixture of hydrogen and iodine or with hydrogen iodide on its own in the container.

container, you could inject hydrogen iodide gas into the container and let it stand until equilibrium is reached. You could then determine the equilibrium concentrations of each of the three gases in the mixture by experiment. The results from five such experiments are given in Table 18.1. Note that a similar value for $K_{c}$ is obtained in each case.

| Expt. No. | Initial concentrations (moles/litre) |  |  | Equilibrium concentrations (moles/litre) |  |  |  |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
|  | $\left[\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{2}}\right] \times \mathbf{1 0}^{-\mathbf{2}}$ | $\left[\mathrm{I}_{2}\right] \times 10^{-2}$ | $[\mathrm{HI}] \times 10^{-2}$ | $\left[\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{2}}\right] \times \mathbf{1 0}^{-\mathbf{2}}$ | $\left[\mathrm{I}_{2}\right] \times 10^{-2}$ | $[\mathrm{HI}] \times 10^{-2}$ | $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^{2}}{\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]\left[\mathrm{I}_{2}\right]}$ |
