Table 18.1 The results of five experiments carried out to determine the equilibrium constant for the reaction $\mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{I}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{HI}$

Some important points about $K_{\mathrm{c}}$ may be summarised as follows:

- In the above example, the value of 46 for $K_{c}$ tells us that the numerator is much greater than the denominator, i.e. the concentration of the product is much greater than that of the reactants. The value for $K_{c}$ gives us an idea of how far the equilibrium is pushed to the right, i.e. how far a reaction goes to completion. The larger the value of $\boldsymbol{K}_{\mathbf{c}}$, the greater is the extent to which the equilibrium is pushed towards the products. A low value of $K_{c}$ tells us that only a small fraction of the reactants has been converted to products.
- In the preceding sections, we have used the term position of equilibrium to describe equilibrium reactions. When we say that the position of equilibrium lies on the right-hand side of the equation, this means that the reaction has a large equilibrium constant. If the equilibrium lies on the left of the equation, the reaction has a small equilibrium constant.
- You may find it helpful to think of the equilibrium constant $K_{c}$ as a measure of the ratio between products and reactants when a reaction reaches equilibrium. If $K_{c}$ has a high value, this means that the side of the products is favoured. If $K_{c}$ has a low value, this means that the side of the reactants is favoured.


## Temperature: The only factor affecting the value of $\boldsymbol{K}_{\mathbf{c}}$

Whenever a value of $K_{c}$ for a particular reaction is quoted, the temperature is usually stated. This is because the value of $K_{c}$ depends on temperature. In fact, temperature is the only factor that affects the value of $K_{c}$. Changing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in a particular direction.

Think of the equilibrium constant $K_{c}$ as a measure of the balance between products and reactants when a reaction reaches equilibrium. If $K_{c}$ has a high value, this means that the side of products is favoured. If $K_{c}$ is low, this means that the side of reactants is favoured.

A change in temperature determines whether the equilibrium reaction is pushed in the forward or backward direction.

- If the forward reaction is endothermic, then raising the temperature will push the reaction in the forward direction (to absorb the added heat). This produces more products and, therefore, the value of $K_{c}$ will increase. If the temperature is lowered, this will push the reaction in the backward direction (to produce more heat). This decreases the concentration of products and, therefore, the value of $K_{c}$ will decrease.
- If the forward reaction is exothermic, then raising the temperature will push the reaction in the backward direction (to absorb the added heat). This decreases the concentration of products and, therefore, the value of $K_{c}$ will decrease. If the temperature is lowered, this will push the reaction in the forward direction (to produce more heat). This increases the concentration of products and, therefore, the value of $K_{c}$ will increase.

For example, consider the reaction:

$$
\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}
$$

For this reaction at $127^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, K_{c}$ has a value of 4390 . At $327^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, K_{c}$ has a value of 4.03 . At $527^{\circ} \mathrm{C}, K_{\mathrm{c}}$ has a value of 0.03 .

## Why does a change in concentration of reactants and products not affect the value of $K_{c}$ ?

- Changing the concentrations of reactants or products only shifts the position of the equilibrium to either favour the reactants or the products and reestablish equilibrium (Le Chatelier's Principle). For example: If you add more reactants, the system will shift toward producing more products until the original ratio of concentrations is restored. Conversely, if you add more products, the reaction shifts to produce more reactants until the original ratio of concentrations is restored.
- Even though the concentrations of individual reactants and products may increase or decrease as the reaction shifts, their ratio at equilibrium remains the same. This means that the equilibrium constant $K_{c}$ does not change.
- In short, $K_{c}$ is not affected by the starting amounts of reactants or products because the value of $K_{c}$ depends on the concentrations at equilibrium - not the specific concentrations at any given time before equilibrium is re-established.

As shown in Table 18.1, at constant temperature, a new state of equilibrium is always reached with the same approximate value of $K_{c}$.

## Why does a change in pressure (for gaseous reactions) not affect the value of $K_{c}$ ?

Changing pressure affects the position of equilibrium in reactions involving gases with unequal number of moles on either side of the equation. The equilibrium will shift to accommodate the change and re-establish equilibrium. This shift in equilibrium due to pressure change helps to counteract the pressure change and re-establish equilibrium. However, it does not change the ratio of the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium. Therefore, the value of $K_{c}$ will be unchanged.

## Why does a catalyst have no effect on the value of $K_{c}$ ?

- A catalyst helps a reaction to reach equilibrium more quickly, i.e. a catalyst only affects the rate of a reaction by speeding up the time taken to reach equilibrium.
- A catalyst alters the rate of the forward and backward reactions equally. In other words, in the presence of a catalyst, the products are produced and used up at the same rate. Therefore, a catalyst does not change the overall ratio of concentrations of products to reactants at equilibrium.
- In short, a catalyst has no effect on the composition of the equilibrium mixture. Therefore, a catalyst has no effect on the value of the equilibrium
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-359.jpg?height=398&width=564&top_left_y=1175&top_left_x=2200)
constant $K_{\mathrm{c}}$.


## How do I work out the units of $K_{\mathrm{c}}$ ?

The units of $K_{c}$ depend on the reaction itself.
For example in the reaction:
$\mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{I}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{HI}$
The units of $K_{c}$ can be found by proceeding as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_{c} & =\frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^{2}}{\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]\left[\mathrm{I}_{2}\right]} \\
& =\frac{(\text { moles } / \mathrm{L})^{2}}{(\text { moles } / \mathrm{L})(\text { moles } / \mathrm{L})}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the units cancel out, there are no units for $K_{c}$ in this particular case.

However, for the reaction:
$\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}$
$K_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right]^{2}}{\left[\mathrm{~N}_{2}\right]\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]^{3}}$
$K_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{(\mathrm{moles} / \mathrm{L})^{2}}{(\mathrm{moles} / \mathrm{L})(\mathrm{moles} / \mathrm{L})^{3}}$
$K_{c}=\frac{1}{(\text { moles } / \mathrm{L})^{2}}$
Therefore, the units in this case are (moles/L)-2.

When stating a value for $K_{c}$ it is essential to give the equation to which it refers. For example, we have already seen that at $458^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the value of $K_{c}$ for the equilibrium $\mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{I}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{HI}$ is 46 approx.

$$
K_{c}=\frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^{2}}{\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]\left[\mathrm{I}_{2}\right]}=46
$$

However, if we write the equilibrium reaction as $2 \mathrm{HI} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{I}_{2}$ then the new $K_{c}$ (represented as $K_{c}^{\prime}$ ) will be:

$$
K_{c}^{\prime}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]\left[\mathrm{I}_{2}\right]}{[\mathrm{HI}]^{2}}=\frac{1}{46}
$$

If the equilibrium reaction is written as $1 / 2 \mathrm{H}_{2}+1 / 2 \mathrm{I}_{2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HI}$, then a different value of $K$ (represented as $K^{\prime \prime}{ }_{\mathrm{c}}$ ) will be obtained.

$$
K^{\prime \prime}{ }_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{[\mathrm{HI}]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]^{1 / 2}\left[\mathrm{I}_{2}\right]^{1 / 2}}=\sqrt{46}
$$

While the value of the equilibrium constant gives us information about the extent of a reaction, it tells us nothing about the rate of a reaction. In other words, $K_{c}$ tells us how far a reaction has gone but not how fast the reaction goes.

## Example 18.2

## Question

Phosphorus(V) chloride decomposes into phosphorus(III) chloride and chlorine at a temperature of 500 K according to the following balanced equation.

$$
\mathrm{PCl}_{5(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_{3(g)}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}
$$

(a) When the temperature of the equilibrium mixture is increased, the phosphorus(V) chloride decomposes further. Is the reaction endothermic or exothermic? Justify your answer.
(b) What changes, if any, would an increase in pressure have on the value of $K_{c}$ ? Explain.

## Answer

(a) The forward reaction is endothermic. The reason for this is that the system responds to absorb the heat added. Since the $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ decomposes further, this means that the forward reaction absorbs heat, i.e. the forward reaction must be endothermic.
(b) The increase in pressure will have no effect on $K_{c}$,

The reason for this is that the value of $K_{c}$ is always constant at constant temperature.

### 18.6 Calculations using the Law of Chemical Equilibrium

Chemists and chemical engineers make great use of the Law of Chemical Equilibrium to deduce information about systems that have reached a state of equilibrium. The following examples demonstrate some of these uses.

## (a) To calculate the value of $K_{\mathrm{c}}$ given equilibrium concentrations

## Example 18.3

## Question

The reaction:
$\mathrm{N}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}$
was allowed to reach equilibrium at $450^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in a one litre container. It was found that there were 13.6 moles $\mathrm{N}_{2}, 1.0$ mole $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ and 1.5 moles $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ in the container when equilibrium had been established. Calculate the value of $K_{c}$ at this temperature.

## Answer

To solve this problem simply write the equilibrium constant expression for the reaction and substitute in the appropriate values. Since we are told that the container is one litre, then the concentrations given are automatically in moles per litre.

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_{c} & =\frac{\left[N H_{3}\right]^{2}}{\left[\mathrm{~N}_{2}\right]\left[\mathrm{H}_{2}\right]^{3}} \\
& =\frac{(1.5)^{2}}{(13.6)(1.0)^{3}}=0.165
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $K_{c}=0.165$

## Example 18.5

## Question

The thermal decomposition of phosphorus pentachloride is represented by the following equation:
$\mathrm{PCl}_{5(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_{3(g)}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}$
A mass of 20.85 g of phosphorus pentachloride was heated at 523 K in a closed 8-litre vessel. When the reaction had come to equilibrium at that temperature, it was found that 80\% of the pentachloride had dissociated.
(i) What is meant by chemical equilibrium? Why is it described as a dynamic process?
(ii) What would be the effect, if any, on the percentage decomposition of the phosphorus pentachloride if the reaction were carried out at a higher pressure?
(iii) Calculate $K_{\varepsilon}$ for the reaction.
[LCH]

## Answer

(i) Chemical equilibrium is a state of dynamic balance where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.

It is described as a dynamic process because both the forward and reverse reactions are still taking place even though the overall reaction seems to have stopped.
(ii) Less $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ would have dissociated since, according to Le Chatelier's Principle, at higher pressure the equilibrium is pushed to the left-hand side of the above equation due to the fact that there is a smaller number of moles on the left-hand side of the equation.
(iii) No. of moles of $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Rel. molecular mass }}=\frac{20.85}{208.22}=0.100$

Since $80 \%$ of $\mathrm{PCl}_{5}$ dissociates, then the number of moles of $\mathrm{PCl}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$ will be $80 \%$ of 0.1 mole i.e. 0.08 mole.

|  | $\mathrm{PCl}_{5(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_{3(g)}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2(g)}$ |  |  |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Initially | 0.1 | 0 | 0 |
| At equil. | $0.1-0.08$ | 0.08 | 0.08 |
|  | $=0.02$ |  |  |
| Conc. at equil. $(\mathrm{V}=8 \mathrm{~L})$ | $\frac{0.02}{8}$ | $\frac{0.08}{8}$ | $\frac{0.08}{8}$ |
|  | $=[0.0025]$ | $=[0.01]$ | $=[0.01]$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{PCl}_{3}\right]\left[\mathrm{Cl}_{2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\right]} \\
& \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{(0.01)(0.01)}{(0.0025)}=0.04
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=0.04$

## (b) To calculate the equilibrium concentrations given the value of $K_{c}$

## SEC exam question 18.7

## Question

An oxide of nitrogen is nitrogen dioxide ( $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ ), a brown compound which forms an equilibrium mixture with colourless dinitrogen tetroxide ( $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}$ ), as described by the following balanced chemical equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}

The photograph shows the equilibrium mixture at five different temperatures.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-362.jpg?height=890&width=1137&top_left_y=1253&top_left_x=221)

## Question

(i) Is the conversion of $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ to $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}$ (the forward reaction) exothermic or endothermic? Justify your answer.

## Answer

The forward reaction is exothermic.

- As the temperature increases, the brown colour gets darker.
- Therefore, there is more $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ and less $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}$ at higher temperature.
- Therefore, the increase in temperature favours the backward reaction.
- Therefore, the backward reaction must be endothermic since according to Le Chatelier's Principle, the equilibrium is shifted in such a way that the added heat is absorbed.
- Therefore the forward reaction must be exothermic.

Write out the concentrations:

$$

$x=$ no of moles of $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ that react.

## Step 2

Input data into equilibrium expression.
$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{NO}_{2}\right]^{2}}$
$0.5=\frac{1+\mathrm{x}}{(2-2 \mathrm{x})^{2}}$

## Step 3

Solve for x .
$0.5=\frac{1+x}{4-8 x+4 x^{2}}$
$0.5\left(4-8 x+4 x^{2}\right)=1+x$
$2-4 x+2 x^{2}=1+x$
$2-1-4 \mathrm{x}-\mathrm{x}+2 \mathrm{x}^{2}=0$
$2 \mathrm{x}^{2}-5 \mathrm{x}+1=0$
$\mathrm{x}=\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^{2}-4 a c}}{2 a}$
$\mathrm{x}=2.28$ or $\mathrm{x}=0.219$

## Step 4

Determine which x is chemically possible.
For $\mathrm{x}=2.28$ : this is not possible as we started with only 2 moles $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$.
For $\mathrm{x}=0.22$ :
$\left[\mathrm{NO}_{2}\right]:=2-2 \mathrm{x}=2-2(0.22)=1.56 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$
$\left[\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\right]: 1+\mathrm{x}=1+0.22=1.22 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$
Answer: $\mathrm{NO}_{2}=1.56$ moles, $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}=1.22$ moles
TEST YOURSELF: Attempt Questions 18.3-18.6 and W18.6-W18.19.

## Summary What I should know

Chemical equilibrium is a state of dynamic balance where the rate of the forward reaction is the same as the rate of the backward reaction.

In a dynamic state, the reactants are continuously forming products and the products are continuously forming reactants.

In a closed system the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant at equilibrium because no substances can enter or leave the system.

Le Chatelier's Principle states that, if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system readjusts to relieve the stress applied.

Le Chatelier's Principle predicts that in an all-gaseous reaction, an increase in pressure will favour the reaction that results in a reduction in volume, i.e. it will shift the reaction towards the side with the smaller number of molecules.

Le Chatelier's Principle predicts that the best conditions to maximise the yield of ammonia in the Haber Process are high pressure and low temperature.

The Law of Chemical Equilibrium states that for:
$\mathrm{aA}+\mathrm{bB} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{cC}+\mathrm{dD}$
$K_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{[\mathrm{C}]^{\mathrm{c}}[\mathrm{D}]^{\mathrm{d}}}{[\mathrm{A}]^{\mathrm{d}}[\mathrm{B}]^{\mathrm{b}}}$
The Law of Chemical Equilibrium may be used in calculations involving systems at equilibrium.

## Why is the ionic product of water temperature dependent?

Let's take a closer look at the dissociation of water.
$\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-} \quad \Delta \mathrm{H}=+55.8 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

- Note that the forward reaction is endothermic.
- When you increase the temperature, then according to Le Chatelier's Principle, the equilibrium will shift from left to right to absorb the added heat.
- Therefore more $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions and more $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions are produced.
- Therefore $K_{w}$ increases, Figure 19.0.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-366.jpg?height=691&width=1170&top_left_y=1468&top_left_x=1451)
Figure 19.0 As the temperature increases, note that the value of $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{w}}$ increases.

Note from the graph:

- The value of the ionic product of water depends on temperature.
- As the temperature is increased, the value of the ionic product of water also increases.


## Calculating the concentration of $\mathbf{H}^{+}$ions in pure water

Let us now calculate the actual concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in pure water.

$$
K_{\mathrm{w}}=\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=1.0 \times 10^{-14}
$$

Since $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]$then $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]^{2}=1.0 \times 10^{-14}$
Therefore, $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-14}}=1.0 \times 10^{-7}$

$$
\text { and }\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=1.0 \times 10^{-7}
$$

In other words, for a neutral solution at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ :

$$
\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=1.0 \times 10^{-7}
$$

Now consider what happens when an acid (e.g. HCl ) is added to the water. The acid increases the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions. However, since $K_{w}$ is a constant, the value of $K_{w}$ cannot change.

$$
K_{\mathrm{w}}=\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=1.0 \times 10^{-14}
$$

Therefore, if the value of [ $\mathrm{H}^{+}$] increases (to say $10^{-5}$ ), the value of [ $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$] must decrease (to say $10^{-9}$ ) so that the two values multiplied together will equal $1.0 \times 10^{-14}$.

In other words, for an acidic solution:

$$
\begin{array}{ll} 
& {\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]>\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]} \\
\text {e.g. } & \left(10^{-5}\right)>\left(10^{-9}\right)
\end{array}
$$

Now consider what happens when a base (e.g. NaOH ) is added to water. The base increases the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions. However, since the value of $K_{\mathrm{w}}$ is a constant, then the value of $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$must decrease in order to satisfy the equation:

$$
K_{\mathrm{w}}=\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=1.0 \times 10^{-14}
$$

Therefore, if the value of [ $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$] increases (to say $10^{-6}$ ), the value of [ $\mathrm{H}^{+}$] must decrease (to say $10^{-8}$ ) so that the two values multiplied together will equal $1.0 \times 10^{-14}$.

In other words, for a basic solution:

$$
\begin{array}{ll} 
& {\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]<\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]} \\
\text {e.g. } & \left(10^{-8}\right)<\left(10^{-6}\right)
\end{array}
$$

The relationship of [ $\mathrm{H}^{+}$] to levels of acidity and basicity at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ may be summarised as shown in Figure 19.1.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-367.jpg?height=405&width=2270&top_left_y=3232&top_left_x=325)
Figure 19.1 If $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]>10^{-7}$, the solution is acidic. If $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]<10^{-7}$, the solution is basic. If $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=10^{-7}$, the solution is neutral. All concentrations are measured in moles per litre.

### 19.3 Measurement of acidity: The pH scale

You will have discovered when reading the previous page that expressing concentrations of solutions in terms of hydrogen ion concentrations is a bit confusing! Chemists don't like having to use numbers like $10^{-7}$ to express the concentrations of hydrogen ions in solution. It was for this reason that in 1909 a Danish chemist called Søren Sørensen devised an easier method to express the degree of acidity of a solution, Figure 19.2.

- Sørensen was working for a Danish brewery and decided to introduce a simpler method of reporting levels of acidity in beer.
- Instead of reporting that a solution contains 0.00001 (or $10^{-5}$ ) moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions per litre, he referred to the solution as 'having a pH of 5 '.
- To do this, he had to get rid of the power in the expression $10^{-5}$ and also to get rid of the negative sign in the power.
Therefore, he defined pH as follows:

Figure 19.2

## Søren Sørensen

(1868-1939)
Søren Sørensen was born in Copenhagen, Denmark. He studied chemistry at the University of Copenhagen. In 1909 he became famous when he suggested a system for making it easier to write the concentrations of hydrogen ions in solution. The pH system that he introduced is now one of the fundamental concepts in chemistry.
$\mathbf{p H} \boldsymbol{=} \boldsymbol{-} \boldsymbol{\operatorname { l o g }}_{\mathbf{1 0}}\left[\mathbf{H}^{+}\right]$where the square brackets indicate concentration in moles per litre.
The above definition of pH may also be stated in words as follows:
The pH of a solution is the negative logarithm to the base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration measured in moles per litre.

- The ' p ' in pH stands for 'power' and the ' H ' in pH refers to the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion. Thus, pH may be roughly translated as 'power of hydrogen ions'.
- The log to the base 10 in the above definition of pH ensures that the powers of ten do not appear in the pH scale. The negative sign in the above definition of pH ensures that all pH values are positive.


## Example 19.1

## Question

A solution has a concentration of $10^{-4}$ moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions per litre. What is the pH of this solution?
Answer
$\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log _{10}\left(10^{-4}\right)=-(-4)=+4 \quad$ Answer: $\mathrm{pH}=4$

Studying Table 19.2 may help you to see the relationship between concentration in moles/litre of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions and pH .

| Solution | [ $\mathrm{H}^{+}$] | pH |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A | $0.001=1 \times 10^{-3}$ | 3 |
| B | $0.000001=1 \times 10^{-6}$ | 6 |
| C | $0.0000001=1 \times 10^{-7}$ | 7 |
| D | $0.000000001=1 \times 10^{-9}$ | 9 |
| E | $0.000000000001=1 \times 10^{-12}$ | 12 |

Table 19.2 Note that a pH value is simply the number in the power with the negative sign changed to a positive sign.

From Table 19.2 we see that solution A has the highest concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions and the lowest pH . Solution E has the lowest concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ ions and the highest pH. Studying Figure 19.3 may help you to understand this.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-369.jpg?height=740&width=1173&top_left_y=725&top_left_x=332)
Figure 19.3a A low pH indicates a high concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-369.jpg?height=766&width=1173&top_left_y=1640&top_left_x=332)
Figure 19.3b A high pH indicates a low concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions.

Solution C has the same concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions as pure water. Thus, a pH of 7 indicates a neutral solution at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The relationship between concentration in moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions per litre and pH is summarised in Figure 19.4.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-369.jpg?height=284&width=1160&top_left_y=2962&top_left_x=341)
Figure 19.4 The concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in solution (measured in moles per litre) and the corresponding pH values

Note from Figure 19.4 that, as the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions increases, the pH value decreases. Also, as the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions decreases, the pH value increases.

Therefore, at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, we can say that:
The pH of an acidic solution is less than 7.
The pH of a basic (alkaline) solution is greater than 7.
The pH of a neutral solution is equal to 7.
Note: In all subsequent calculations involving pH , you will be using a scientific calculator. Make sure you know how to use it to enter powers, obtain logs, and obtain antilogs.

## Example 19.2

## Question

Calculate the pH of a solution whose hydrogen ion concentration is $7.1 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$.

## Answer

$\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log _{10}\left(7.1 \times 10^{-7}\right)=6.15$
Answer: pH = 6.15

## Example 19.3

## Question

Calculate the hydrogen ion concentration (in moles per litre) of a solution whose pH is 3.7.

## Answer

$\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=3.7$
$\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-3.7$
$\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\operatorname{antilog}(-3.7)=1.995 \times 10^{-4}$
Answer: $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=1.995 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$

## The temperature dependence of $\boldsymbol{K}_{\mathbf{w}}$

If you examine Table 19.1, you will observe that the value of $K_{\mathrm{w}}$ increases with increasing temperature. This must mean that the self-ionisation of water is endothermic, since it is favoured by higher temperatures:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-369.jpg?height=238&width=570&top_left_y=3112&top_left_x=1608)

- Since the forward reaction is favoured as the temperature is increased, more hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions will be formed.
- Therefore, the value of $K_{\mathrm{w}}$ increases and the pH of pure water decreases as the temperature increases, Table 19.3. This is also illustrated in Figure 19.5.
- Since the pH decreases as temperature is increased, you might think that water would become more acidic at higher temperatures.
- However, this is not found to be the case in practice. A solution is acidic if there is an excess of hydrogen ions compared to hydroxide ions.
- In the case of pure water, there is always the same number of hydrogen ions as hydroxide ions present.
This is because, for every $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion that is formed when a molecule of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ dissociates, an $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ion is also formed.
- Therefore, pure water is always neutral regardless of its temperature, since the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$and $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions are always present in equal concentrations.
- Always remember that the neutral value for pH is calculated from $K_{w}$. Therefore, if $K_{w}$ changes, then the neutral value also

| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0 | $0.11 \times 10^{-14}$ | 7.47 |
| 10 | $0.30 \times 10^{-14}$ | 7.27 |
| 20 | $0.68 \times 10^{-14}$ | 7.08 |
| 25 | $1.01 \times 10^{-14}$ | 7.00 |
| 30 | $1.47 \times 10^{-14}$ | 6.92 |

| 90 | $36.0 \times 10^{-14}$ | 6.22 |
| 100 | $51.3 \times 10^{-14}$ | 6.14 |

Table 19.3 The pH of pure water decreases as the temperature increases.

changes.

- Since at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ the pH value of pure water is 6.14 , then the neutral value of the pH at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is 6.14 and not 7 .
It is possible to measure the pH of a substance by a number of methods. One method that you may have come across at Junior Cycle level is to use universal indicator paper, i.e. paper that turns a different colour depending on the pH of the solution into which it is dipped, Figure 19.6. Universal indicator solution may also be used.

The colour of the paper or solution is then matched against a chart of colours supplied with the indicator. We will be studying indicators in more detail in section 19.7.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-370.jpg?height=1293&width=1763&top_left_y=2555&top_left_x=175)

## Measuring pH using pH sensors and dataloggers

A modern method of measuring pH is to use a pH sensor and datalogger, Figure 19.7. Prior to the development of modern pH sensors and datalogging technology, instruments called pH meters were used. However, pH meters are rarely used now.

The pH sensor is sensitive to the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in solution. The pH sensor is placed in the solution whose pH is to be measured and the pH is then read off directly on a computer or mobile phone. The pH values of some common substances are shown in Figure 19.8.

### 19.4 Strengths of acids and bases

In Chapter 11, we defined an acid as a proton donor. We learned that different acids donate protons to different extents. Using the Brønsted-Lowry theory, we defined a strong acid as follows:

A strong acid is a good proton donor, i.e. it is almost completed dissociated in water.

Acids such as $\mathrm{HCl}, \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ are classified as strong acids because they are good proton donors, i.e. they are almost completely dissociated in water.
$\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$
Note that the equilibrium arrow ↩ is not used for this equation since the reaction goes almost completely from left to right. (By experiment it is found that there is about $99.996 \%$ dissociation.)

You may recall that in Chapter 11 we learned that many acids are described as weak acids and we defined a weak acid as follows:

A weak acid is a poor proton donor, i.e. it does not fully dissociate in water.

Weak acids have a small tendency to donate protons, e.g. when ethanoic acid (acetic acid) is added to water, it does not fully dissociate in the water. In fact only about $1,3 \%$ of the ethanoic acid molecules are dissociated in a 0.1 M solution and the following equilibrium is set up:

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-371.jpg?height=533&width=1163&top_left_y=377&top_left_x=1587)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-371.jpg?height=2378&width=1173&top_left_y=1155&top_left_x=1591)
Figure 19.8 The approximate pH values of some common substances

## Acid dissociation constant

In order to represent the strength of an acid, chemists use the symbol $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ which is known as the acid dissociation constant. For the general case of an acid HA undergoing dissociation:

$$
\mathrm{HA} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{A}^{-}
$$

The acid dissociation constant, $K_{2}$, is defined as:

$$
K_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{A}^{-}\right]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}
$$

Sometimes, the formation of the hydronium ion, $\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}$, is shown in the equilibrium reaction.

$$
\mathrm{HA}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}+\mathrm{A}^{-}
$$

In this case, $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is written as:

$$
K_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{A}^{-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{A}}\right]}
$$

- Note that $\left[\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right]$ does not appear in the $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ expression. This is because $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is defined purely in terms of the dissociation of the acid. (The [ $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ ] would be included if you were simply asked to write $K_{\mathrm{c}}$ for the reaction.)
- Acid dissociation constants derive from equilibrium constants for particular acids by assuming that $\left[\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right]$ is constant.
- Acid dissociation constants are constant for each particular acid and only vary with temperature. Remember this point about varying with temperature, as we will come back to it again later on in this chapter.
- The value of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ gives us an accurate measure of the extent to which an acid is dissociated. In other words, it tells us how strong the acid is. For example, for an acid such as hydrochloric acid, which is almost completely dissociated in water, the value of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is very large. This is because, for a strong acid, the concentrations of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions and $\mathrm{A}^{-}$ions in solution are very large.
- On the other hand, for a weak acid such as ethanoic acid, little dissociation occurs and therefore the concentrations of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$and $\mathrm{A}^{-}$ions are small. Therefore, the value of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is small.
The values of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ for some acids are listed in Table 19.4.

| Name of acid | Type of acid | Formula | $K_{a}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hydrochloric acid | Strong acid | HCl | $1 \times 10^{7}$ |
| Nitric acid | Strong acid | $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ | $1 \times 10^{5}$ |
| Sulfuric acid | Strong acid | $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ | $1 \times 10^{3}$ |
| Hydrofluoric Acid | Weak acid | HF | $6.6 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| Methanoic acid | Weak acid | HCOOH | $1.8 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| Ethanoic acid | Weak acid | $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$ | $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ |
| Benzoic acid | Weak acid | $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{COOH}$ | $6.3 \times 10^{-5}$ |

Table 19.4 The dissociation constants of some acids at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The value of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ provides an accurate measure of the extent to which an acid dissociates, i.e. the strength of that acid.

- Strong acids have relatively large values of $K_{a}$.
- Weak acids have small values of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$.
- As a general rule, if the value of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is less than $10^{-2}$, the acid is classified as a weak acid.

[^3]Acid dissociation constants allow us to compare the relative strengths of different acids. For example, in the case of ethanoic acid $\left(\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}\right)$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ :

$$
K_{a}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}\right]}=1.8 \times 10^{-5}
$$

Similarly, in the case of hydrofluoric acid (HF) at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ :

$$
K_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{F}^{-}\right]}{[\mathrm{HF}]}=6.6 \times 10^{-4}
$$

Since $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ for hydrofluoric acid is greater than that of ethanoic acid, we conclude that HF is a stronger acid than $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$.

In Chapter 11, we learned about strong bases and weak bases. We defined a strong base as follows:

A strong base is a good proton acceptor.
Sodium hydroxide ( NaOH ) and potassium hydroxide $(\mathrm{KOH})$ are examples of strong bases, since they accept protons readily.

$$
\text { e.g. } \mathrm{NaOH}+\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}
$$

The equilibrium arrow is not used for this equation, since the reaction goes almost completely from left to right, as NaOH is a good proton acceptor.

We also learned in Chapter 11 that a weak base is defined as follows:

A weak base is a poor proton acceptor.

For a weak base, we can write the dissociation as follows:

$$
\mathrm{BOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{~B}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-}
$$

In this case, $K_{b}$, the base dissociation constant, is written as:

$$
K_{b}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{B}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]}{[\mathrm{BOH}]}
$$

For example, magnesium hydroxide is a weak base that is slightly soluble in water and dissociates in water as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_{2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-} \\
K_{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]^{2}}{\left[\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}\right]}
\end{gathered}
$$

The most common weak base that we will meet in this course is ammonia, $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$. The reaction of ammonia with water may be written as:

$$
\mathrm{NH}_{3}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-}
$$

Since the ammonia molecule has a poor tendency to accept a proton, the equilibrium lies on the left-hand side. The value of $K_{b}$, the base dissociation constant, gives an indication of the degree of dissociation.

$$
K_{b}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right]}
$$

The value of $K_{\mathrm{b}}$ for ammonia is only $1.74 \times 10^{-5}$. This confirms that ammonia is a weak base. The values of $K_{b}$ for some bases are listed in Table 19.5.

| Name of base | Type of base | Formula | $K_{\mathrm{b}}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sodium hydroxide | Strong base | NaOH | Very large ( $\infty$ ) |
| Potassium hydroxide | Strong base | KOH | Very large ( $\infty$ ) |
| Barium hydroxide | Strong base | $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ | Very large ( $\infty$ ) |
| Ammonia | Weak base | $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ | $6.6 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| Aniline (phenylamine) | Weak base | $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{NH}_{2}$ | $4.3 \times 10^{-10}$ |

Table 19.5 The dissociation constants of some bases at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The value of $K_{\mathrm{b}}$ provides an accurate measure of the extent to which a base dissociates, i.e. the strength of that base.

- Strong bases have relatively large values of $K_{\mathrm{b}}$.
- Weak bases have small values of $K_{\mathrm{b}}$.

The larger the value of $K_{b}$, the higher is the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$and the stronger is the base.

- As a general rule, if the value of $K_{b}$ is less than $10^{-2}$, the base is classified as a weak base.


## Relative strengths of conjugate acid-base pairs

Consider the reaction of the strong acid HCl with water:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-374.jpg?height=272&width=1020&top_left_y=686&top_left_x=221)

Since HCl is a strong acid, the reaction goes almost completely from left to right, i.e. there is little tendency for the $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ion to accept a proton and push the reaction in the backward direction. Since the $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ion is a poor proton acceptor, we say it is a weak conjugate base.

A strong acid has a weak conjugate base.

Now consider the reaction of ethanoic acid (weak acid) and water:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-374.jpg?height=327&width=1180&top_left_y=660&top_left_x=1438)

Since the equilibrium lies on the left-hand side, this implies that the $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$ion has a great tendency to accept a proton and push the equilibrium to the left. This means that the $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$ion is a good proton acceptor, i.e. it is a strong base.

A weak acid has a strong conjugate base.
From studying a large number of acid-base reactions, chemists have deduced the following general statements.

The stronger the acid, the weaker is its conjugate base. The weaker the acid, the stronger is its conjugate base.

## Example 19.4

## Question

Define (a) acid, (b) conjugate pair, in terms of the Brønsted-Lowry theory.
Sulfuric acid dissociates in water as follows: $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}+\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}$
Why is (i) sulfuric acid considered to be a strong acid, (ii) the conjugate base of sulfuric acid described as a weak base? Show, by means of an equation, that the conjugate base of sulfuric acid can itself act as an acid.
[LCH]

## Answer

(a) An acid is a proton donor.
(b) A conjugate acid-base pair is any pair consisting of an acid and a base which differ by one proton.
(i) Sulfuric acid is a strong acid because it is a good proton donor, i.e. it is almost fully dissociated into ions in aqueous solution.
(ii) The conjugate base of sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{HSO}_{4}{ }^{-}$, is described as a weak base because it is a poor proton acceptor, i.e. it has little tendency to accept a proton to form $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$. Since $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ is a strong acid, the equilibrium $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}+\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}$lies very much on the right-hand side.

The following equation shows that the conjugate base of sulfuric acid can itself act as an acid:

$$
\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{O}^{+}+\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}
$$

Do not get confused between the words 'concentrated' and 'strong'. As already discussed in Chapter 12, a concentrated solution is one that contains a large amount of solute in a given volume of solution. In chemistry, the word 'strong' refers to the extent to which an acid can donate $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions. Unfortunately, in everyday speech we use the word 'strong' to mean concentrated. Instead of asking for a cup of strong coffee, you should really ask for a cup of concentrated coffee! Table 19.6 summarises how the terms concentrated, dilute, strong and weak differ in this context.

| ACIDS AND BASES |  |
| :--- | :--- |
| STRENGTH | CONCENTRATION |
| A strong acid is a good proton donor. | A concentrated solution of a strong acid contains a large amount of acid dissolved in a small amount of water. A dilute solution of a strong acid contains a small amount of acid dissolved in a large amount of water. |
| A strong base is a good proton acceptor. | A concentrated solution of a strong base contains a large amount of base dissolved in a small amount of water. A dilute solution of a strong base contains a small amount of base dissolved in a large amount of water. |
| A weak acid is a poor proton donor. | A concentrated solution of a weak acid contains a large amount of acid dissolved in a small amount of water. A dilute solution of a weak acid contains a small amount of acid dissolved in a large amount of water. |
| A weak base is a poor proton acceptor. | A concentrated solution of a weak base contains a large amount of base dissolved in a small amount of water. A dilute solution of a weak base contains a small amount of base dissolved in a large amount of water. |


![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-375.jpg?height=925&width=613&top_left_y=944&top_left_x=2145)
Table 19.6 It is important that you understand the terms concentrated, dilute, strong and weak when studying the properties of acids and bases.

## pH is a measure of acidity but not of acid strength

- Measuring the pH of a solution does not allow us to distinguish between a strong acid and a weak acid.
- The pH of a solution tells us the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in moles per litre in that solution.
- Imagine adding a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (strong acid) into a large volume of water. You could adjust the volume of water so that the pH of the final solution is 5.0, i.e. there are $1 \times 10^{-5}$ moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions per litre, Figure 19.9.
- Now imagine adding a larger amount of concentrated ethanoic acid (acetic acid), a weak acid, into a smaller volume of water. You could adjust the volume of water so that the pH of the final solution is 5.0 .
- In short, making up a dilute solution of a strong acid, or a concentrated solution of a weak acid, can give the same pH value.

While strong acids fully dissociate and weak acids only partly dissociate in water, the final pH of their solutions only depends on the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions per litre (and the temperature of course, but let's assume that the temperature is constant). The pH sensor that is inserted into the solution measures the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions per litre and it does not matter how they got there! Think carefully about this!

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-375.jpg?height=688&width=1281&top_left_y=2936&top_left_x=1474)
Figure 19.9 Measurement of pH alone does not allow us to distinguish between a weak acid and a strong acid. The dilute solution of sulfuric acid (strong acid) and the concentrated solution of ethanoic acid (weak acid) have the same pH .

## Example 19.5

## Question

A teacher was left gasping for air on reading a statement written in a student's exam script that said, 'Solutions of strong acids always have a low pH.' Explain why this statement is not correct.

## Answer

- pH depends on the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in solution.
- A strong acid is defined as a good proton donor.
- A strong acid is almost fully dissociated into ions in aqueous solution.
- If you take, say, one drop of a strong acid such as HCl or $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$, and dilute it by adding it to a large volume of water, the resulting concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions will be very low.
- The pH of this solution could be around 4 or 5 or even higher, depending on how dilute the solution is.
- For example, the pH of a 0.00001 M solution of $\mathrm{HCl}=5$. In other words, the dilute solution of this strong acid does not have a low pH.
- On the other hand, the pH of a 0.1 M solution of the weak acid ethanoic acid (acetic acid) = 2.9. In other words, the more concentrated solution of this weak acid had a lower pH than the more dilute solution of the HCl (strong acid).
- Therefore, it is incorrect to say that solutions of strong acids always have a low pH. This confuses the level of acidity present in solution with the strength of an acid. The pH is determined by the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in solution - not by whether the acid is a strong acid or a weak acid.

It is possible to work out on paper the pH of a solution if we have certain information about that solution. In this course, you are required to be able to calculate the pH of solutions of (a) strong acids and strong bases and (b) weak acids and weak bases. We now consider these two types of calculation.

### 19.5 Calculating the pH of strong acids and strong bases

Calculating the pH of strong acids and strong bases is very straightforward, since strong acids and strong bases can be assumed to be fully dissociated in water. The following examples will illustrate the method used.

## Example 19.6

## Question

Calculate the pH of a 0.01 M HCl solution.

## Answer

Since the acid is fully dissociated, the 0.01 mole of HCI will give 0.01 mole of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in solution.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{HCl} & \rightarrow \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-} \\
1 \mathrm{~mole} & \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~mole} \\
\therefore 0.01 \mathrm{~mole} & \rightarrow 0.01 \mathrm{~mole} \\
\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right] & =-\log _{10}(0.01)=2
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: pH = 2

## Exampte 19.7

## Question

Calculate the pH of a solution containing 5 g of sulfuric acid in $250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution.

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the concentration of the acid in grams per litre.
$5 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} / 250 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=20 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} / \mathrm{L}$

## Step 2

Convert this mass to number of moles.
No. of moles of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Rel molecular mass }}=\frac{20}{98.086}=0.204$
i.e. concentration of $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}$ solution $=0.204 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 \times \mathrm{H}=2 \times 1.008 & =2.016 \\
1 \times \mathrm{S}=1 \times 32.07 & =32.07 \\
4 \times \mathrm{O}=4 \times 16.00 & =64.00 \\
\hline M_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} & =98.086
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 3

Calculate the concentration of moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions per litre.

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}
$$

1 mole $\rightarrow 2$ moles $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions
$\therefore 0.204$ mole $\rightarrow 0.408$ mole $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions

## Step 4

Calculate the pH .
$\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log _{10}(0.408)=0.3893$
Answer: $\mathrm{pH}=0.3893$
A similar method is used to find the pH of a solution of a strong base. We know from our study of the ionic product of water at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ that: $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=10^{-14}$

Taking the negative log of each term: □ $\mathrm{pH}+\mathrm{pOH}=14$

Thus, pOH is defined in a similar fashion to pH :

$$
\mathrm{pOH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]
$$

## Example 19.8

## Question

Calculate the pH of a 0.15 M NaOH solution.

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the number of moles of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions in solution.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{NaOH} & \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-} \\
1 \text { mole } & \rightarrow \quad 1 \text { mole } \\
\therefore 0.15 \text { mole } & \rightarrow \quad 0.15 \text { mole }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 2

Calculate the pOH .

$$
\mathrm{pOH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=-\log _{10}(0.15)=0.82
$$

## Step 3

Calculate the pH .
$\mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH}=14-0.82=13.18$
Answer: $\mathrm{pH}=13.18$

Note that to calculate the pH of a solution of a base, we first work out the pOH and subtract this value from 14.

$$
\mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH}
$$

## Example 19.9

## Question

Calculate the pH of a solution containing 9 g of potassium hydroxide, KOH , in $500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution.

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the concentration of the KOH in grams per litre.
$9 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{KOH} / 500 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=18 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{KOH}$ / litre

## Step 2

Convert grams per litre to moles per litre.
No. of moles of $\mathrm{KOH}=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Rel. molecular mass }}=\frac{18}{56.108}=0.3208$
Therefore, concentration of $\mathrm{KOH}=0.3208 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$

## Step 3

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
1 \times \mathrm{K}=1 \times 39.1 & =39.1 \\
1 \times \mathrm{O}=1 \times 16.00 & =16.00 \\
1 \times \mathrm{H}=1 \times 1.008 & =1.008 \\
\hline M_{r} \mathrm{KOH} & =56.108
\end{array}
$$

Calculate the number of moles per litre of OH -ions in solution

$$
\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{~K}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-}
$$

1 mole $\rightarrow \quad 1$ mole
$\therefore 0.3208 \mathrm{~mole} \rightarrow 0.3208 \mathrm{~mole} \mathrm{OH}^{-}$

## Step 4

Calculate the pOH .
$\mathrm{pOH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=-\log _{10}(0.3208)=0.4938$

## Step 5

Calculate the pH .
$\mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH}=14-0.4938=13.5062$
Answer: pH = 13.5062

## Example 19.10

## Question

Calculate the pH of a 0.01 M solution of calcium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$. Assume that the calcium hydroxide is fully dissociated.

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the number of moles of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions per litre.

$$
\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}
$$

$$
1 \text { mole → } 2 \text { mole }
$$

$\therefore 0.01$ mole $\rightarrow \quad 0.02$ mole

## Step 2

Calculate the pOH

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pOH} & =-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] \\
& =-\log _{10}(0.02) \\
& =1.7
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 3

Calculate the pH

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pH} & =14-\mathrm{pOH} \\
& =14-1.7 \\
& =12.3
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: pH = 12.3

Note: Since the pH scale is a logarithmic one, a difference in one pH unit corresponds to a ten-fold difference in the concentration, Table 19.7.

## (a)

| Concentration of <br> HCl solution | $\mathbf{p H}$ |
| :--- | :---: |
| 1.0 M | 0 |
| 0.1 M | 1 |
| 0.01 M | 2 |
| 0.001 M | 3 |
| 0.0001 M | 4 |


(b)
| Concentration of <br> NaOH solution | $\mathbf{p H}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1.0 M | 14 |
| 0.1 M | 13 |
| 0.01 M | 12 |
| 0.001 M | 11 |
| 0.0001 M | 10 |


Table 19.7 The logarithmic nature of the pH scale is illustrated by studying the pH values of (a) solutions of HCl of various concentrations and (b) solutions of NaOH of various concentrations.
