### 19.6 Calculating the pH of weak acids and weak bases

To calculate the pH of a solution of a weak acid or weak base, we must know the extent to which the acid or base dissociates. This depends on the value of the dissociation constant for the acid or base. $\left(K_{\mathrm{a}}\right.$ or $\left.K_{\mathrm{b}}\right)$ and also on the concentration of the solution. To explain how the pH is calculated, we will first work out the pH of a solution from first principles, and then use this to deduce a general expression for solving similar problems.

## Example 19.11

## Question

Calculate the pH of a 0.1 M solution of ethanoic acid given that the value of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

## Answer

Let $\mathrm{x}=$ number of moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions produced.

|  | $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}$ | + | $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ |  |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Initially | $[0.1]$ | $[0]$ |  | $[0]$ |
| At equil. | $[0.1-x]$ | $[x]$ |  | $[x]$ |

Now write the dissociation constant ( $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ ) expression for this reaction and substitute the above equilibrium concentrations into the expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_{a} & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}^{-}\right]\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}\right]} \\
1.8 \times 10^{-5} & =\frac{(x)(x)}{(0.1-x)}
\end{aligned}
$$

To make it easier to solve this equation, we make the assumption that $0.1-x \approx 0.1$. This is a valid assumption since, for a weak acid, the amount of dissociation is very small.

Thus, the above expression now simplifies to:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{(x)(x)}{0.1} & =1.8 \times 10^{-5} \\
x^{2} & =1.8 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.1 \\
x & =\sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.1}=1.3 \times 10^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e. $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=1.3 \times 10^{-3}$
$\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log _{10}\left(1.3 \times 10^{-3}\right)=2.9$
Answer: pH = 2.9

In the above problem, we obtain a very simple expression at the end.

$$
x=\sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.1}
$$

We can write a more general expression as:

$$
\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{a}} \times M_{\text {acid }}}
$$

where $\mathrm{M}_{\text {acid }}$ is the concentration of the acid in moles per litre.
This is a very useful formula for finding the concentration of hydrogen ions (in moles per litre) in a solution of a weak acid when given the value of $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ and the concentration of the acid in moles per litre. It is important to remember that all concentrations are measured in moles per litre.

Similarly, it can be shown that the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions in a solution of a weak base is given by:

$$
\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=\sqrt{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}} \times \mathrm{M}_{\text {base }}}
$$

where $\mathrm{M}_{\text {base }}$ is the concentration of the base in moles per litre.
The two formulas above are well worth learning off, as they are not given in the Formulae and Tables booklet and they greatly simplify the calculations involved in determining the pH values of weak acids and bases, as shown in the following examples.

## Example 19.12

## Question

Calculate the pH of a 0.1 M solution of methanoic acid (formic acid) given that $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ for this acid is $2.1 \times 10^{-4}$.
[LCH]

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the [ $\mathrm{H}^{+}$] by substitution in the formula:
$\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{a}} \times \mathrm{M}_{\text {acid }}}=\sqrt{2.1 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.1}=\sqrt{0.000021}=0.0046$

## Step 2

Calculate the pH .
$\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log _{10}(0.0046)=2.34$
Answer: $\mathrm{pH}=2.34$

## Example 19.13

## Question

Find the pH of an aqueous solution containing 1.48 g of propanoic acid $\left(\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{COOH}\right)$ in
$200 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of solution, given that the dissociation constant $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ for propanoic acid is $1.36 \times 10^{-5}$.
[LCH]

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the concentration of the propanoic acid in $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{L}$.
$1.48 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{COOH} / 200 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=1.48 \times 5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}=7.4 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{L}$

## Step 2

Calculate the number of moles of propanoic acid per litre (molarity of solution).
Rel. molecular mass $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{COOH}=74.078$
No. of moles $=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Relative molecular mass }}=\frac{7.4}{74.078}=0.0999$

$$
\begin{aligned}
3 \times \mathrm{C}=3 \times 12.01 & =36.03 \\
6 \times \mathrm{H}=6 \times 1.008 & =6.048 \\
2 \times \mathrm{O}=2 \times 16.00 & =32.00 \\
\hline M_{r} \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4} & =74.078
\end{aligned}
$$

$\therefore \mathrm{M}_{\text {acid }}=0.0999 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$

## Step 3

Calculate the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in moles $/ \mathrm{L}$.
$[\mathrm{H}+]=\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{a}} \times M_{\text {acid }}}=\sqrt{1.36 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.0999}=\sqrt{1.3586 \times 10^{-6}}=0.0012$

## Step 4

Calculate the pH .
pH $=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log _{10}(0.0012)=2.92$
Answer: pH = 2.92

## Summarising the factors that affect the pH of a solution

As we conclude our study of pH , it may be helpful to summarise the two main factors that affect the pH of a solution, as these are specifically mentioned on the syllabus.

## 1. Concentration of $\mathbf{H}^{\boldsymbol{+}}$ ions

Since $\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$, the first and most obvious factor that determines the pH of a solution is the concentration of hydrogen ions measured in moles per litre (mol/L).

- When comparing two solutions of the same acid, the more concentrated the solution, the higher the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{*}$ ions - and therefore, the lower the pH .
- Similarly, for two solutions of the same base, the more concentrated the solution, the greater the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions - and therefore, the higher the pH .
- However, the actual concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$or $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions also depends on whether the acid or base is strong or weak.
- A strong acid has a large Ka value and dissociates more in water, producing more $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions.
- A strong base has a large $K_{b}$ value and produces more $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions in solution.
- Therefore, when comparing two different acids that have equal concentrations:
- If acid $A$ is strong and acid $B$ is weak, acid $A$ will have a larger $K_{a}$ and produce more $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions.
- As a result, the pH of acid A will be lower than the pH of acid B , Figure 19.10.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-382.jpg?height=1121&width=1700&top_left_y=2047&top_left_x=501)
Figure 19.10 Both acids are of equal concentration but the stronger acid produces more $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in solution and, therefore, has a lower pH than the weak acid.

- Similarly, comparing two different bases of equal concentration:
- If base A is strong and base B is weak, base A will have a larger $K_{\mathrm{b}}$ and produce more $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions than base B .
- Therefore, the pH of base A will be higher than the pH of base B .

Since strong acids and strong bases dissociate in solution to give more ions than weak acids and weak bases, we can use a conductivity sensor to distinguish between strong acids and weak acids and also distinguish between strong bases and weak bases. To ensure a fair test, we compare the conductivity of a 0.01 M solution of hydrochloric acid (strong acid) and a 0.01 M solution of ethanoic acid (weak acid), Figure 19.13. (Dilute solutions are used as the conductivity of strong acids is very high.)

A conductivity sensor is placed in each solution in turn and the results are displayed on a computer screen. Note that the conductivity of the strong acid $(12,014.0)$ is much higher than that of the weak acid (213.0). (The units of conductivity are micro siemens per cm, but you do not need to worry about these units.)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-384.jpg?height=1003&width=2007&top_left_y=1084&top_left_x=188)
Figure 19.13 The conductivity of the weak acid is much lower than that of a solution of a strong acid of the same concentration. Conductivity depends on the number of ions in solution. Since the strong acid produces more ions in solution than the weak acid, the conductivity of the strong acid is much higher than the weak acid.

## Limitations of the pH scale

We have seen that the concept of pH is extremely useful in chemistry and is one of the foundations of the study of chemistry. However, it is helpful to be aware of some limitations of the pH scale.

1. Limited to $\mathbf{0 - 1 4}$. The pH scale is limited to the $0-14$ range even though, in theory, pH values outside this range are possible. We will give examples of this in the next point.
2. Limited to dilute solutions ( $<\mathbf{1}$ M). The pH scale does not work with very concentrated solutions. For example, the pH of 1 M HCl is 0 and that of 1 M NaOH is 14 . It is found that once the concentration goes above 1 M , complete dissociation does not always occur, i.e. you cannot predict the actual number of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$or $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions in solution. Therefore, calculations of pH for solutions of concentration greater than 1 M are not accurate. For example, if you calculate the pH of 10 M HCl solution using the formula $\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$, you obtain a pH value of -1 . Similarly, if you calculate the pH value of 10 M NaOH solution, you obtain a pH value of 15. However, these calculations are based on the assumption that full dissociation occurs and this is not the case with very concentrated solutions. In short, pH is limited to dilute solutions of 1 M or less.
3. Limited to aqueous solutions. The pH scale is limited to solutions in which substances are dissolved in water (aqueous solutions). However, chemical reactions can occur in other types of solvent, such as ethanol and liquid ammonia. These need not concern us in this course.

### 19.7 Acid-base indicators

In Chapter 12, we saw that acid-base indicators were used to find the end point when carrying out a titration. We now consider the theory used to explain how these indicators work, and we discuss how to choose an indicator for a particular titration.

An acid-base indicator is a substance that changes colour according to the pH of the solution in which it is placed.

The main points about acid-base indicators may be summarised as follows:

- Many natural dyes act as indicators, e.g. the dye in red cabbage, elderberry juice and blackberry juice. Examples of indicators that you meet in the school laboratory are litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein, Figure 19.14. Litmus is obtained from plants called lichens that grow on cliffs and trees. Acid-base indicators are often simply referred to as 'indicators'.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-385.jpg?height=1612&width=2426&top_left_y=1406&top_left_x=332)
Figure 19.14 Methyl orange, litmus and phenolphthalein are common acid-base indicators.

- Most indicators are weak acids in which the colour of the undissociated molecule is different from that of the dissociated molecule. (In reality, the dissociated molecule is the negative ion of the indicator.) Suppose we represent the indicator litmus as HIn. Litmus has a red colour in an acidic solution and is blue in an alkaline solution.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-385.jpg?height=213&width=414&top_left_y=3528&top_left_x=1061)
- HIn represents the acid form of the indicator and In- represents the conjugate base of the indicator. If $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions from an acid are added to blue litmus, the blue litmus turns red. This is because, in accordance with Le Chatelier's Principle, the above equilibrium shifts from right to left in order to absorb the added $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions. Therefore, the red colour of the Hin predominates. In other words, the blue litmus turns red.
- If a base containing $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions is added to red litmus, the $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions react with the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in the above equilibrium reaction to remove them to form water. In accordance with Le Chatelier's Principle, more $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions must be formed and, therefore, the equilibrium is shifted to the right. Thus, the blue colour of the Inions predominates. In other words, the red litmus turns blue.
- A small number of indicators are weak bases that dissociate slightly as follows:

$$
\mathrm{XOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{X}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-}
$$

- The undissociated XOH part has a different colour to the dissociated X+ part. Addition of acid removes some of the $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions from the right-hand side as water, and thus the equilibrium shifts to the right. Therefore, the colour of $\mathrm{X}^{+}$ predominates in acidic solution.
- Addition of base increases the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions on the right-hand side and this shifts the equilibrium to the left-hand side. Hence the colour of XOH predominates in basic solution.
- When an indicator is used in a titration, there is usually very little of it used, e.g. only two or three drops of an indicator are added to $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the solution in the conical flask. Therefore, the indicator makes a negligible contribution to the $\mathrm{H}^{+}\left(\right.$or $\left.\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right)$ion concentration.
- The molecules of indicators tend to be rather complicated, with lots of benzene rings! Some examples of these molecules are shown in Figure 19.15. (Litmus is actually a mixture of a number of dyes but the structure common to many of the dyes is shown in Figure 19.15.) You do not have to remember the structures of any of these molecules. They are simply included to brighten up your lives!
<img class="imgSvg" id = "mincxtmzwnl2q3b9uaf" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>
<img class="imgSvg" id = "mincxtnc5zfwyd1vc5j" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>

Phenolphthalein (colourless form)
<img class="imgSvg" id = "mincxtno47hxtnqlmjo" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"/>

Litmus (common structure)

Figure 19.15 The molecules of the indicators litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein are fairly complicated. There is no need to remember them!

## Range of an indicator

Because our eyes have limited sensitivity to colour changes, it is found that indicators need a change of about two pH units in order for us to see a distinct change from one colour to another. The pH interval over which there is a clear change of colour for a particular indicator is called

The range of an indicator is the pH interval over which there is a clear change of colour for that indicator. the range of the indicator.

Each indicator has its own range, and examples of the ranges of common indicators are given in Table 19.8.

| Name of indicator | Approx. range | Acid colour (lower pH) | Base colour (higher pH) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Methyl orange | 3-5 | red | yellow |
| Litmus | 5-8 | red | blue |
| Phenolphthalein | 8-10 | colourless | pink |

Table 19.8 The ranges of some common indicators

From Table 19.8 we can conclude the following:

- Methyl orange has a distinct red colour below a pH of 3 and a distinct yellow colour above a pH of 5 . Between a pH of 3 and 5 , the indicator is neither distinctly red nor yellow but an intermediate colour.
- Litmus has a definite red colour below a pH of 5 and a definite blue colour above a pH of 8 .
- Phenolphthalein is colourless below a pH of 8 and has a definite pink colour above a pH of 10.
It is recommended that you learn Table 19.8 by heart, as this information will be very useful to you.
- The pH ranges of different indicators vary, i.e. indicators change colour over widely differing pH values. This is because each indicator has its own dissociation constant value.
- You may recall that universal indicator is a mixture of indicators that gives a gradual change in colour over the entire range of the pH scale, Figure 19.16. A few drops of universal indicator are added to a solution whose pH is to be measured and the colour observed is compared with a colour chart supplied with the universal indicator. This gives an approximate value of the pH of the solution.

Figure 19.16 Universal indicator has been added to solutions whose pH ranges (left to right) from 1 to 14. The colour observed is then compared with a pH colour chart supplied with the indicator.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-387.jpg?height=848&width=1873&top_left_y=3004&top_left_x=1035)

## Measuring pH accurately using a pH sensor

The most accurate way of measuring pH is to use an instrument called a pH sensor, Figure 19.17. A pH sensor is also called a pH probe or pH electrode. It is a more accurate way of measuring pH than using pH indicators for the following reasons:

1. Precise numerical value. A pH sensor always gives a precise numerical value for pH , e.g. $\mathrm{pH}=4.72$. It does this by measuring the voltage set up by hydrogen ion concentration and converts this to an exact digital pH measurement. Since a pH sensor is measuring electrical signals, it works perfectly and accurately regardless of the colour of the solution.
2. Removes subjectivity. A pH sensor does not rely on subjective colour interpretation, which can vary between people when estimating shades of colour using pH indicators. The colour of pH indicators can also be affected by the colour of the solution itself or by lighting in the room. pH indicators may suggest that the pH of a solution is approximately $3-4$ but a more accurate value is not possible as you are only judging shades of colour.

As a result, pH sensors are ideal for scientific experiments where high precision is needed. For example, in a titration you may wish to know when the pH of the solution is exactly equal to 7 . Only a pH sensor can give this level of precision.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-388.jpg?height=1157&width=1886&top_left_y=1731&top_left_x=188)
Figure 19.17 A pH sensor is the most accurate way to measure pH values. This wireless PASCO pH sensor connects to a laptop or mobile phone using Bluetooth.

## Calibrating pH sensors: accuracy and precision

Before using pH sensors in an experiment, we must calibrate the sensor. Calibration is the process of ensuring that the pH sensor is giving accurate pH readings. To do this, we set the pH sensor to correct pH values using solutions of known pH values.

## Why is calibration necessary for pH sensors?

- The pH sensor is a very sensitive, accurate and delicate instrument and must always be handled with great care.
- A pH sensor responds to the concentration of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in solution.
- Over time, the sensitivity of the pH probe can drift due to wear and tear (ageing) of the sensor, contamination of the sensor with previous solutions, or drying out of the glass bulb of the sensor.
- One of the most common causes of drift is the drying out of the glass bulb due to incorrect storage. When not in use, a pH sensor must always be stored in the storage solution supplied with the pH sensor. Otherwise, the pH sensor can dry out in the air and will not function properly. The pH sensor then has to be left stored for several hours in the storage solution to get it functioning again.
When calibrating a pH sensor, we usually use two different buffer solutions. See Figure 19.18.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-389.jpg?height=1483&width=2427&top_left_y=891&top_left_x=328)
Figure 19.18 This pH sensor is being calibrated using buffer solutions of pH 3 and pH 10.

## A buffer solution is one that resists change in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or base.

In other words, the pH of a buffer solution stays constant, even if we add small amounts of acid or base. Buffer solutions are ideal for calibrating pH sensors since buffer solutions have a known, fixed pH . To calibrate the pH sensor, we must have a standard reference, i.e. something we know is correct. Buffer solutions are our standard references in calibration.

You may recall in Chapter 13 that we explained that accuracy means how close a measurement is to the correct value. The correct value is often referred to as the 'true' or 'actual' value. Since calibration adjusts the sensor's response to match known standards of pH buffer solutions, this makes the reading accurate.

After the electrode has been calibrated, repeated readings could be taken to test for precision. You may recall in Chapter 13 that precision means how close a set of repeated measurements are to each other. For example, if you place the pH electrode in deionised water and obtain readings of 7.00, 7.01 and 7.00, you know that these readings are both accurate and precise. However, if you were to obtain readings of 7.40, 6.35 and 6.91, you would know that these readings are neither accurate nor precise.

## Carrying out a pH titration

It is quite easy to follow the changes in pH as a titration is carried out. Such an experiment is called a $\mathbf{p H}$ titration and the experimental set up is shown in Figure 19.19.

The main points about this experiment may be summarised as follows:

- The base is placed in the burette and the acid is placed in a beaker. This is done to allow us to start with a low pH value and work upwards.
- You will recall that we used a conical flask when previously carrying out titrations. We do not use a conical flask when performing pH titrations as the narrow mouth of the conical flask would make it difficult to insert the pH sensor properly - it would get in the way of the burette. The beaker is better for pH titrations as it allows the pH sensor to be kept upright or resting against the side of the beaker when the tip of the pH sensor is immersed in the solution. But how do we stir the solution in the beaker during the titration? Stay tuned!
- The solution in the beaker is kept stirred by placing a small magnetic stirring bar in the beaker. Since we are not using a conical flask, shaking the beaker could cause spillages and could damage the pH sensor. Instead, the solution in the beaker is stirred with the aid of the magnetic stirring bar. The beaker is placed on a laboratory magnetic stirrer and this keeps the stirring bar rotating.
- A pH sensor is placed in the acid solution. As already explained, the pH sensor is a device that measures the hydrogen ion concentration in a solution and displays the corresponding pH value.
- The pH sensor measures the pH as the base is added from the burette to the acid in the beaker.
- The pH sensor is connected to a computer or mobile phone using Bluetooth wireless technology.
- A graph of pH versus time is plotted for the solution in the beaker with the aid of the datalogging software. A graph showing change of pH related to volume of base added is obtained. This graph is

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-390.jpg?height=916&width=1212&top_left_y=761&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 19.19 In carrying out a pH titration, the acid is usually placed in a beaker and the base is placed in a burette. The pH is measured using a pH sensor. The pH sensor is connected to the laptop using Bluetooth technology. The datalogging software in the laptop or mobile phone detects the signal from the pH sensor and displays the information on the screen.

A photograph of this experiment being carried out is shown in Figure 19.20.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-390.jpg?height=825&width=1212&top_left_y=2304&top_left_x=1435)
Figure 19.20 A pH titration enables us to follow the changes in pH as the titration proceeds.

called a $\mathbf{p H}$ titration curve.

- Note that no indicator is used in this titration. It is not necessary as we are measuring the pH directly using the pH sensor and, therefore, can see the end point from the pH titration curve.

We will now consider each of the four possible types of acid-base titration.

## 1. Titrating a strong acid against a strong base

Consider the pH changes that take place when we titrate a strong acid against a strong base, Figure 19.21.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-391.jpg?height=1170&width=1586&top_left_y=807&top_left_x=514)
Figure 19.21 This graph shows the pH changes observed as a strong acid is titrated against a strong base. The acid is placed in the beaker so that the graph starts with a low pH . Litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein are all suitable indicators for this titration.

What indicator would be suitable for this titration?

- Any indicator that has one colour at a pH of around 3 and another colour at a pH of around 10 will identify the end point accurately.
- In other words, we need an indicator that has one colour at the bottom of the steep vertical part of the curve and another colour at the top of the steep vertical part of the curve.
- Chemists often express this idea by saying that the end point must be 'sharp', i.e. a very small addition of acid or base (one drop) must cause a complete colour change in the indicator.
- Referring to Table 19.8, we see that all three indicators satisfy this criterion. Therefore, all three indicators would be suitable for carrying out a titration of a strong acid against a strong base.
- Litmus is not as reliable as the other two indicators, and hence is not usually used in accurate work.

When carrying out titrations, we used the idea of end point.

> The end point is the moment during a titration when the indicator changes colour.

There is another point that chemists refer to when discussing pH titration curves.
The equivalence point in an acid-base titration is the point at which the acid and the base have reacted in exact proportions according to the balanced equation.

In other words, the equivalence point is the point in the reaction at which both acid and base have reacted in exactly equal amounts according to the mole ratio in the balanced equation. Neither the acid nor the base is present in excess. For example, if you study Figure 19.20, the equivalence point for the strong acid-strong base reaction is at $\mathrm{pH}=7$. This occurs when 25 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ of 0.1 M NaOH have been added to $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.1 M HCl . At this stage, the same number of moles of acid has reacted with an equal number of moles of base to form a neutral solution of sodium chloride.

In short, the end point is an observable concept and the equivalence point is a chemical concept.

A pH titration could also be carried out by adding the acid to the base. In this case, the pH titration curve starts at a high pH as shown in Figure 19.22.

## 2. Titrating a strong acid against a weak base

Consider how the pH changes when a strong acid is titrated against a weak base, Figure 19.23.

What indicator would be suitable for this titration?

- In this titration, $0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NH}_{3}$ solution is slowly added to $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 0.1 M HCl .
- Note that the curve is almost vertical from pH values of 3-7 approximately.
- Therefore, any indicator which has one colour at $\mathrm{pH}=3$ and another colour at $\mathrm{pH}=7$ will identify the end point accurately.
- Referring to Table 19.8 , we see that the only one of the three indicators that would be suitable is methyl orange as it is the only indicator whose range lies within the steep vertical part of the graph.
- Litmus would not be suitable as it would not have completely changed colour until a pH of 8 had been reached.
- Phenolphthalein would not be suitable as its range is completely outside the 3-7 range. In fact, phenolphthalein would not begin to change colour until a pH of 8 was reached.
This pH titration could also be carried out by adding the acid to the base. In this case, the pH titration curve starts at a higher pH as shown in Figure 19.24.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-392.jpg?height=896&width=1235&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=1380)
Figure 19.22 This graph shows the pH changes observed as a strong acid is titrated against a strong base. The base is placed in the beaker so that the graph starts with a high pH.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-392.jpg?height=893&width=1238&top_left_y=1487&top_left_x=1383)
Figure 19.23 This graph shows the pH changes observed as a strong acid is titrated against a weak base. The acid is placed in the beaker so that the graph starts with a low pH . Methyl orange is a suitable indicator for this titration.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-392.jpg?height=896&width=1235&top_left_y=2689&top_left_x=1383)
Figure 19.24 This graph shows the pH changes observed as a strong acid is titrated against a weak base. The base is placed in the beaker so that the graph starts with a higher pH than in the previous diagram

## 3. Titrating a weak acid against a strong base

We now study how the pH changes when titrating a weak acid against a strong base, Figure 19.25.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-393.jpg?height=1055&width=1492&top_left_y=651&top_left_x=325)
Figure 19.25 This graph shows the pH changes observed as a weak acid is titrated against a strong base. The acid is placed in the beaker so the curve starts at a low pH . Phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for this titration.

What indicator would be suitable for this titration?

- In this titration, 0.1 M NaOH is slowly added to $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of $0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{CH} \mathrm{CHOOH}_{3} \mathrm{COO}$.
- Note that the curve is almost vertical from pH values of 7-10 approximately.
- Therefore, we need an indicator which has one colour at $\mathrm{pH}=7$ and another colour at $\mathrm{pH}=10$ to identify the end point accurately.
- From Table 19.8, we see that phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for this titration as it is colourless at a pH of 7 and pink at a pH of 10, i.e. its range lies within the steep vertical part of the graph.
- Neither of the other two indicators would be suitable as they are outside the $7-10$ range.

This pH titration could also be carried out by adding the acid to the base. In this case, the pH titration curve starts at a higher pH , as shown in Figure 19.26.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-393.jpg?height=964&width=1336&top_left_y=2780&top_left_x=406)
Figure 19.26 This graph shows the pH changes observed as a weak acid is titrated against a strong base. The base is placed in the beaker so that the graph starts with a higher pH than in the previous diagram.

## 4. Titrating a weak acid against a weak base

Consider how the pH changes when titrating a weak acid against a weak base, Figure 19.27.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-394.jpg?height=974&width=1557&top_left_y=579&top_left_x=182)
Figure 19.27 This graph shows the pH changes observed as a weak acid is titrated against a weak base. The acid is placed in the beaker so that the graph starts with a low pH. There is no suitable indicator for this titration as there is no sudden increase in the pH at any stage of the titration.

What indicator would be suitable for this titration?

- In this titration, $0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NH}_{3}$ is slowly added to $25 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of $0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}$.
- Note that the pH rises so gradually that there is no sudden jump in the pH value at any stage of the titration.
- The graph looks more like a gentle slope rather than having a sharp jump in pH .
- Therefore, it is not possible to detect the end point using an indicator as there would be no large sudden jump in pH to cause a sudden colour change.
- This type of titration could not be used to determine the concentration of a solution of a weak acid or a weak base.
- Instead, the weak acid is titrated against a strong base and the weak base is titrated against a strong acid.

This pH titration could also be carried out by adding the acid to the base. In this case, the pH titration curve starts at a higher pH as shown in Figure 19.28.

## NOTE

When carrying out the above pH titrations, we kept the concentrations of all acids and bases constant at 0.1 M . This was done in order to ensure a fair test. In other words, it allows us to make a fair comparison between the titration curves.

## EXAM TIPI

When asked to identify pH titration curves, it is helpful to write on the curve the lower and upper limits of the vertical part of the curve. For example, curve D has a vertical part of the curve from pH 3 to pH 10 . Therefore, this must be the titration curve for a strong acid-strong base titration.
(ii) Explain why it is difficult to carry out an accurate weak acid-weak base titration.

It is difficult to carry out an accurate weak acid-weak base titration because:

- The pH rises so gradually that there is no sudden jump in the pH value at any stage of the titration.
- The graph looks more like a gentle slope rather than having a sharp jump in pH.
- Therefore, it is not possible to detect the end point using an indicator.
- There would be no large sudden jump in pH to cause a sudden colour change in the indicator.
(iii) Explain why the student used a pH meter rather than universal indicator to measure the pH .

The sensor in a pH meter is a more accurate way of measuring pH than using universal indicator for the following reasons:

1. Precise numerical value. A pH sensor always gives a precise numerical value for pH, e.g. $\mathrm{pH}=4.72$. Since a pH sensor is measuring electrical signals, it works perfectly and accurately regardless of the colour of the solution.
2. Removes subjectivity. A pH sensor does not rely on subjective colour interpretation, which can vary between people when estimating shades of colour using pH indicators. The colour of universal indicator can also be affected by the colour of the solution itself or by lighting in the room. Universal indicator may suggest that the pH of a solution is approximately $3-4$, but a more accurate value is not possible as you are only judging shades of colour.
(iv) Name one variable which the student should have kept constant to make sure that she could make a fair comparison between the titrations.

The concentration of the acid and the concentration of the base should be kept constant to ensure a fair comparison between the titration curves.

## Summary What I should know

- $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{w}}=\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] . \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{w}}$ is called the ionic product of water.
$\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$where the square brackets indicate concentration in moles per litre.
The pH of an acidic solution is less than 7 . The pH of an alkaline solution is greater than 7. The pH of a neutral solution is equal to 7 at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

The stronger the acid, the weaker is its conjugate base. The weaker the acid, the stronger is its conjugate base.
$\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\sqrt{K_{a} \times[a c i d]}$ and $\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=\sqrt{K_{a} \times[\text { base }] \text { are useful expressions for calculations involving }}$ weak acids and weak bases.

Acid-base indicators are substances that change colour according to the pH of the solution in which they are placed.

When titrating a strong acid against a strong base, methyl orange, phenolphthalein and litmus are suitable indicators.

When titrating a strong acid against a weak base, methyl orange is a suitable indicator.
When titrating a weak acid against a strong base, phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator.

### 20.1 Introduction

Water is one of the most abundant and most important chemicals on Earth. About 80\% of the Earth's surface is covered with water and it makes up about two-thirds of our body mass. Water is essential for life. We could survive for several weeks without food, but we could not live for more than a few days without water. In fact, we need to take in about two litres of water every day in order to stay healthy.

One of the most important properties of water is that it is an excellent solvent. Each day we use large quantities of water for various purposes drinking, washing, flushing the toilet and watering the garden. Industry uses vast quantities of water for cooling, manufacturing various products and

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of sources of water contamination and its consequences.
- To give students an appreciation of the importance of providing clean water for human use.
- To give students an understanding of the consequences of the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect.
generating electricity. We take water very much for granted and yet it is one of the most important items that we require. In the first part of this chapter, we will study the importance of water in our environment. In the second part of the chapter, we will continue our studies of the environment by taking a close look at the greenhouse effect.


### 20.2 Water - A finite resource

You may recall in studying science at Junior Cycle that you learned about the way in which water circulates around the Earth. This may be represented by the water cycle, Figure 20.1.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-400.jpg?height=1606&width=2342&top_left_y=2187&top_left_x=224)
Figure 20.1 The water cycle represents the way that water circulates through the oceans, atmosphere and Earth.

As you can see from the water cycle, it seems that water is everywhere - in the oceans, clouds, rivers and underground. However, you may be surprised to learn that:

- About $97 \%$ of all the water on Earth is saltwater. This is not of much use to us for drinking without spending a lot of money to remove the dissolved salts.
- Of the remaining $3 \%$ of water (which is freshwater), about two-thirds of this water is locked away in glaciers and ice caps or is deep underground.
- Only about $1 \%$ of all water on Earth is easily accessible in our rivers and lakes and in groundwater near the surface of the earth.

Therefore, water is often referred to as a finite or limited resource, since there is a limited amount of water that is available to us on Earth. Even though water is being recycled as shown in Figure 20.1, the total amount of freshwater available to us does not increase. As the population of the world increases, the demand for clean water rises. It would be of some help if the supply of available freshwater stayed the same. Unfortunately, the supply is actually decreasing due to increasing levels of contamination.

### 20.3 Causes of water contamination

Water contamination may be defined as follows:
The six causes of water contamination that are on our course are

Water contamination is the introduction of substances into water that makes it unsafe for consumption or harmful to ecosystems. summarised in Table 20.1.

|  | Cause | Chemistry involved | Biochemical consequences |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | Sewage | This contains high levels of organic matter, e.g. carbohydrates, proteins, fats and urea. | Levels of oxygen dissolved in water are decreased by bacterial decomposition. Biochemical Oxygen Demand (explained later) is increased resulting in fish kills. |
| 2. | Industrial effluent | This could contain organic solvents or toxic chemicals. | Toxic substances can accumulate in food chains and damage organs in aquatic life. This can also alter pH and temperature of water and harm ecosystems. |
| 3. | Agricultural effluent | Runoff water from farms may contain nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers, and also may contain pesticides. | Nitrates and phosphates act as nutrients and cause excessive growth of algae (algal bloom). Decomposition of algae causes eutrophication (explained later). Pesticides can be toxic to aquatic life. |
| 4. | Microplastics | These are tiny plastic particles ( $<5 \mathrm{~mm}$ ) whose chemical composition is harmful to health. They can transport toxins. | These are ingested by aquatic organisms, who mistake them for food. Microplastics can kill organisms and can be transferred up the food chain to affect human health. |
| 5. | Heavy metals | These are metals such as mercury, lead and cadmium. They can end up in water through improper disposal of batteries, electronic waste, industrial waste and mining. | Heavy metals interfere with the actions of enzymes in the human body and can cause damage to the kidneys and liver. They can also cause neurological damage. $\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}$ ions mimic $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ ions, interfering with the functioning of nerves and bone development as well as causing brain damage, especially in children. |
| 6. | Acidification | Acid rain or acidic industrial discharges can lower the pH of water. | Acidic conditions interfere with enzyme function and damage tissues, Organisms such as shellfish are badly affected, as the acid destroys their protective shells. Acidification can also release toxic metals from compounds. |

Table 20.1 Summary of the main causes of water contamination

Note the term biochemical consequences used as a heading in the table above. Biochemical consequences of water contamination refer to the chemical and biological effect that contaminants have on living organisms and on the environment. In other words, the biochemical consequences of chemical changes in the water result in the harming or killing of living things. Let us now discuss in more detail the concept of Biochemical Oxygen Demand in point 1 of Table 20.1.

## Biochemical Oxygen Demand

Dissolved oxygen is often referred to as 'the breath of life under water'. Dissolved oxygen in rivers, lakes and the sea is vital for the survival of fish and other forms of life, Figure 20.2.

- Since the $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ molecule is nonpolar, the solubility of oxygen in water (a polar solvent) is quite low and depends on the temperature of the water. For example, at $10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ the solubility of oxygen is $11.3 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{ppm})$ whereas at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ the solubility of oxygen drops to $9.2 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}$. (The fact that solubility of gases in water drops with increase in temperature is observed when water is heated. As the water is heated, bubbles of air are seen to come out of solution.)

Now consider what happens when organic waste is discharged into a waterway. Examples of organic waste are domestic sewage, animal slurry, silage effluent from farms, effluents from food processing factories, milk and industrial waste. When the organic waste is discharged into the water, the bacteria and other organisms that are naturally present in the water are provided with nutrients. These nutrients cause the organisms to multiply into large numbers. As the organisms break down the waste into compounds such as carbon dioxide and water, they use up the oxygen dissolved in the water.
organic matter + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

- If a considerable amount of organic waste is present, it is possible that the dissolved oxygen level in the water will be reduced so much that fish life in the water may be reduced or possibly killed off completely. For example, trout and salmon need an approximate concentration of 5 ppm of dissolved oxygen in order to survive.
- The dissolved oxygen used up by bacteria may not be replaced fast enough by more oxygen from the air dissolving in the water.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-402.jpg?height=1462&width=1095&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1520)
Figure 20.2 Fish absorb dissolved oxygen from the water through their gills. The air pump produces bubbles that stir the water and help fresh air to mix with the water so that oxygen levels are maintained.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-402.jpg?height=763&width=1098&top_left_y=2190&top_left_x=1520)
Figure 20.3 This dissolved oxygen sensor measures the concentration of dissolved oxygen in the water.

- If the dissolved oxygen drops to zero concentration, anaerobic bacteria (bacteria that do not require oxygen) will take over and the river will become foul-smelling due to the presence of hydrogen sulfide gas, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$.

The concentration of dissolved oxygen is measured using a dissolved oxygen sensor, Figure 20.3.

The release of substances into the environment that damage the environment is called pollution. In the early 1900s, the Royal Commission on Sewage Disposal introduced a test to measure the demand that water has for dissolved oxygen. This test is called the Biochemical Oxygen Demand test or, more simply, the B.O.D. test. It is simply a method used by chemists to indicate the level of pollution in a sample of water.

The main points about the B.O.D. test may be summarised as follows:

- The B.O.D. test is carried out by completely filling two bottles with the water to be tested.
- The measurement of dissolved oxygen is carried out immediately in one of the bottles so that the oxygen content does not increase due to photosynthesis by plant material in the water or decrease due to respiration by microorganisms in the water.
- The second bottle is incubated at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in darkness for five days, Figure 20.4.
- The second bottle is kept in darkness to prevent photosynthesis taking place, as this would increase the level of oxygen in the water.
- The purpose of the fixed temperature of $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is because a fixed temperature is required for a valid comparison of different water samples as the amount of oxygen dissolved in water depends on temperature. Also, the rate at which oxygen is consumed by microorganisms depends on temperature.
- When the five-day period has elapsed, the amount of dissolved oxygen remaining in the second bottle is measured.
- The B.O.D. is the difference in the two dissolved oxygen levels, as this is the amount of oxygen that has been used up during the test. B.O.D. is measured in $\mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{ppm})$ of oxygen.

Examples of B.O.D. values are given in Table 20.2. Note that the higher the B.O.D. is, the more polluted the water. A high B.O.D. value means that there is a large amount of organic waste in the water and, as this organic waste is acted on by bacteria, the level of oxygen becomes depleted.

## Biochemical oxygen demand (B.O.D.) is defined as:

- The amount of dissolved oxygen
- Consumed by biological (biochemical) action
- When a sample of water is kept at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
- In the dark
- For five days.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-403.jpg?height=922&width=1177&top_left_y=885&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 20.4 Two samples of water are needed to calculate the B.O.D. of a water sample.

| B.O.D. (mg/L) | Example |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1-2 | Clean water |
| 20-40 | Treated sewage |
| 100 | Polluted water (fish die) |
| 300 | Raw sewage |
| 500 | Brewery effluent |
| 30000 | Pig slurry |
| 54000 | Silage effluent |

Table 20.2 Some examples of B.O.D. values

Most of the fish kills in Ireland are caused by silage and slurry effluent being discharged into rivers and lakes.

The B.O.D. test may be used to measure the level of pollution in effluents. However, because of the low solubility of oxygen in water $(9.2 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}$ at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), water samples with B.O.D. values greater than $9 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}$ must be diluted by a fixed amount with well-oxygenated, pure water. This is done in order to ensure that dissolved oxygen will be present throughout the five-day period of the test and that a measurable amount of oxygen (at least 2 ppm ) will be left after the five-day period. Fresh distilled water is used for diluting the sample and the mixture must be well-shaken for a few minutes in order to oxygenate the water fully. If the effluent is not diluted, it is possible that all of the oxygen will be used up before the five days have elapsed.

Since B.O.D levels about $9.2 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{L}$ are not actually possible (as this is the maximum concentration of dissolved oxygen at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), values greater than this are generated when the figure obtained in the experiment is multiplied by an associated dilution factor.

Let us now discuss the concept of eutrophication mentioned in point 3 of Table 20.1.

## Eutrophication

The level of dissolved oxygen in water may also be reduced if the water is overloaded with plant nutrients, especially nitrate ions ( $\mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{-}$) and phosphate ions $\left(\mathrm{PO}_{4}{ }^{3-}\right)$.

This 'over-enrichment' is called eutrophication (a Greek word meaning 'well nourished').

> Eutrophication is the enrichment of water with nutrients, leading to excessive growth of algae and other plants.

The main points about eutrophication may be summarised as follows:

- Eutrophication may occur naturally or artificially.
- Natural eutrophication occurs mainly in lakes and is caused by a gradual increase in nitrogen and phosphorus levels caused by sediments building up in these lakes.
- Artificial eutrophication is caused by a sudden increase in nitrate and phosphate nutrients resulting from artificial fertilisers being washed into rivers and lakes, or by domestic sewage or waste from intensive farming entering these waterways.
- As the nitrate and phosphate levels rise, they are absorbed by plants and many of these plants and floating algae undergo rapid growth.
- The rapid growth gives rise to algal blooms that cover much of the surface of the water with a green scum, Figure 20.5.
- The algae are short-lived and when they decay a heavy oxygen demand is placed on the water due to increased activity by microorganisms.
- This increased activity causes the dissolved oxygen level to fall and many forms of animal life in the water are killed.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-404.jpg?height=1221&width=2179&top_left_y=2640&top_left_x=188)

There is some concern about the levels of nitrate ions in water. It is thought that high levels of nitrates may cause stomach cancer and also infant deaths.

We now discuss microplastics as mentioned in point 4 of Table 20.1

## Microplastics

The main points about microplastics may be summarised as follows:

- Microplastics are tiny plastic particles of size less than 5 mm . This term is used to distinguish them from larger plastic waste.
- They are dangerous to human health as many plastics contain harmful chemicals which can end up in water and food.
- Since microplastics are so small, they can be eaten by fish and other aquatic organisms. Therefore, they can enter the food chain and cause damage to human health.
- Microplastics come from a variety of sources, e.g. cosmetics, personal care products, synthetic clothing (such as polyester and nylon) and food packaging, Figure 20.6. Although waste from our homes is treated in wastewater (sewage) treatment plants, not all microplastics are removed in these treatment plants and so they enter rivers, lakes and oceans.
- Microplastics can also enter rivers, lakes and oceans from runoff water from roads, e.g. tyres are made from synthetic rubber and this releases microplastics. These particles accumulate on roads and are washed into the storm-water drainage system, which carries the untreated water into rivers, lakes and oceans.
- We will see later how water for drinking-water treatment plants is taken from rivers and lakes. Since microplastics are so small, it is possible that not all microplastics are removed in the drinking-water treatment process and, therefore, could end up in tap water in our homes.
- It is also possible for microplastics to enter the drinking water supply from plastic pipes in the water distribution system. Plastic pipes (e.g. PVC) can degrade over time, especially if they contain water under pressure.
- Primary microplastics are intentionally manufactured to be very small, for example, the tiny plastic beads shown in Figure 20.6 Secondary microplastics are formed when larger plastics (e.g. plastic bags) break down.
- Microplastics are known to persist in the environment at high levels, e.g. rivers, oceans and in soil.
- One of the big problems about microplastics is that, like all plastics, they degrade very slowly and can take hundreds or thousands of years to fully degrade.

Let us now take a look at heavy metals mentioned in point 5 of Table 20.1.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-405.jpg?height=962&width=1310&top_left_y=2532&top_left_x=1448)
Figure 20.6 These microplastics came from an exfoliating skin scrub and are so small that many of them fit on the tip of a finger.

## Acidification

The main points about acidification may be summarised as follows:

- The main source of acidification is caused by acid rain and acidic industrial discharges directly into waterways, Figure 20.9.
- The acidic water can dissolve metals such as $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ ions and heavy metals from rocks and sediments. These metals damage fish gills and cause fish kills.
- The change in pH affects aquatic life, since many species cannot survive at pH lower than 5. The low pH interferes with enzyme activity, salt balance and ion transport in cells.
- Organisms such as shellfish and snails are badly affected, as the acid destroys their protective shells.
- In general, there is a decline in biodiversity as many species are unable to survive at the lower pH .

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-407.jpg?height=1638&width=1183&top_left_y=1673&top_left_x=325)

### 20.4 Water treatment

It has been estimated that each household in Ireland uses about 300 litres of water each day. The water supplied to each of our houses by Uisce Éireann around the country must fulfil certain criteria. It must be attractive looking (i.e. colourless), it must be odourless, it must be safe to drink (no active bacteria present) and it must be fluoridated. In order to ensure that the quality of domestic water supplies is of an adequate standard, it is necessary to carry out certain procedures on the water taken from a river or lake. Water treatment plants have been set up throughout the country. The various stages in the process of water treatment may be summarised as follows:

## 1. Screening

- The water (usually taken from a river or lake) is passed through a wire mesh to remove any floating debris such as twigs, leaves and plastic bags.


## 2. Flocculation

The water that comes directly from the river or lake is often called 'raw' water because it is unsafe to drink. It may be cloudy due to the presence of suspended particles in the water. The second stage involves the removal of these suspended particles from the water.

- The word 'flocculation' means coagulation. It comes from a Latin word floccus, meaning tuft or clump - like a tiny piece of cotton wool.
- Very small suspended solids in the water can be made to form larger particles (called 'flocs') by adding certain chemicals to the water. This process is called flocculation.
- Chemicals that bring about flocculation are called flocculating agents.
- The most commonly used flocculating agent is aluminium sulfate, $\mathrm{Al}_{2}\left(\mathrm{SO}_{4}\right)_{3}$. The addition of aluminium sulfate to the water causes the suspended solids to coagulate or stick together, Figure 20.10.
- The amount of aluminium sulfate added to the water must be controlled, as excess aluminium sulfate affects the taste of water and causes corrosion of pipes.
- Tiny particles suspended in the water may be too small to settle out of the water on their own. Therefore, the water may look cloudy. Flocculating agents cause these to clump together and make them easier to remove by sedimentation or filtration.
- The flocs fall to the bottom of the tank in which flocculation takes place. The sludge formed is pumped out of the tanks and treated elsewhere.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-408.jpg?height=974&width=661&top_left_y=423&top_left_x=1849)
Figure 20.10 Aluminium sulfate is a flocculating agent and is added to water to coagulate suspended particles in the water.

Flocculation is the coming together (coagulating or clumping) of small, suspended particles in water into larger particles.

A flocculating agent is a chemical added to water to coagulate suspended particles and thus help sedimentation to take place.

## 3. Sedimentation (also called settling)

- The water is now passed into large settling tanks. The water flows in at the bottom of these large tanks and rises up slowly to the surface where the clear water is allowed to overflow (decant) into channels, Figure 20.11.
- The water is allowed to rise up towards the surface very slowly to allow maximum settlement to take place at the bottom of the tank due to gravity. Heavier particles sink faster than lighter ones.
- Over $90 \%$ of the suspended particles are removed in the sedimentation stage. If these particles were not removed, the water would look cloudy. Removing the large particles at the beginning of the treatment process is important, as it makes later steps such as filtration more efficient and less costly.
- This process is entirely physical, i.e. no chemicals are added at this stage.
- The substance formed at the bottom of the tank is called sludge. This sludge contains decaying vegetation, leaves, algae and clay. The sludge is pumped out of the tanks and treated elsewhere.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-409.jpg?height=1372&width=1883&top_left_y=1497&top_left_x=328)
Figure 20.11 Settling tanks at Inniscarra Water Treatment Plant, Co. Cork.

Note: As a result of increased demand for water in recent years, modern water treatment plants do not have the capacity to store vast quantities of water. Therefore, flocculation is carried out before sedimentation as described above. If you visit an old water treatment plant, you may find that steps 2 and 3 are in reverse order.

## 4. Filtration (sand and microfiltration membranes)

- In the next stage, the water is then passed through large beds of sand to physically remove suspended solids by filtration, Figure 20.12. You may recall the process of filtration from your study of Junior Cycle science.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-410.jpg?height=591&width=1740&top_left_y=761&top_left_x=227)
Figure 20.12 Any remaining suspended solids are removed by filtration. The diagram shows sand filtration in operation.

These filter beds remove any remaining suspended solids. In sand filtration, water is passed through layers of coarse and fine sand. As water flows through the layers of sand, the suspended particles get trapped in the spaces between the grains of sand. Thus, the sand acts just like a sieve or filter paper to remove the suspended solids. The sand is supported on a layer of gravel and the layers of sand are cleaned regularly. Some filtration tanks are shown in Figure 20.13.

In some water treatment plants, a process called microfiltration is carried out. This is similar to sand filtration except that a plastic membrane with tiny pores is used. The tiny pores are usually between 0.1 and 10 micrometres $\left(10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}\right)$ in diameter. A micro metre $(\mu \mathrm{m})$ is one-millionth of a metre. Microfilters are made from strong durable plastic materials called polymers (Chapter 24).

Water is forced through the membrane under pressure. The pores are so small that not only are suspended solids removed, but also bacteria are removed. However, it does not remove viruses since these are small enough to get through the pores.

- The water that comes out of the filter beds is now clear. However, it is not fit to drink as it may still contain harmful bacteria (if only a sand filter is used) or viruses. This problem is dealt with in the next stage.
- Note that at this stage, suspended solids have been removed by three methods:
(i) sedimentation (settling), (ii) flocculation and (iii) filtration.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-410.jpg?height=906&width=1547&top_left_y=2721&top_left_x=1071)
Figure 20.13 These large filtration tanks contain filter beds of sand that remove any remaining suspended solids.

Filtration is a method of separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using a material that allows the liquid to pass through, but not the solid.

## 5. Chlorination

- This step is an important disinfection step. Chlorine is added to the water in order to sterilise it, i.e. to kill any harmful microorganisms in the water.

Chlorine reacts with water to form an acid called hypochlorous acid. This acid kills the microbes.

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{HOCl}+\mathrm{HCl}
$$

hypochlorous acid

- The chlorine need only be present in small quantities (approximately 0.5 ppm ). If too much chlorine is added, it gives the water an unpleasant taste and smell. The amount of chlorine gas added to the water is carefully controlled, Figure 20.14. Sufficient chlorine must remain in the water to ensure that the water is kept safe for drinking when it is being distributed to our homes. Water can get contaminated in pipes or reservoirs. The amount of chlorine still present in the water is called the chlorine residual. This residual is important to ensure ongoing disinfection while the water is being stored or distributed.
- The effectiveness of the chlorine treatment is continually monitored by examining the water for the presence of microorganisms in the water.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-411.jpg?height=711&width=1183&top_left_y=2327&top_left_x=325)
Figure 20.14 The chlorine gas in these cylinders is injected continuously into the water to kill bacteria.

## 6. Fluoridation

- By law, all water treatment plants in Ireland must include fluoridation as part of the water treatment process. This involves adding small quantities (about 1 ppm) of fluorine compounds to the water.
- Examples of fluorine compounds commonly added are sodium fluoride, NaF, and hexafluorosilicic acid, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SiF}_{6}$.
- Water is fluoridated because it has been shown that the presence of fluoride ions in water helps to reduce tooth decay. It does this by strengthening the enamel of teeth.
- The level of fluoridation is carefully controlled in the water treatment plant as excess fluoride in water gives rise to a condition known as fluorosis which causes staining of teeth, Figure 20.15.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-411.jpg?height=929&width=1183&top_left_y=1002&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 20.15 In some parts of the world there is an excess of fluoride ions found naturally occurring in the water supply, and this causes teeth to be stained. This condition is known as fluorosis. These photos show the teeth of a person with fluorosis, before and after treatment.

## 7. pH Adjustment

pH sensors are used in the laboratories of water treatment plants in order to monitor the pH of water taken from rivers and lakes.

- Water coming from limestone areas tends to be basic with a pH of about 7.8. Water coming from sandstone areas and bogs tends to be acidic and could have a pH as low as 5.8 .
- The optimum pH of water for distribution to homes and factories is about 7.2. Therefore, Uisce Éireann has to alter the pH of the water before distributing it to homes and factories.
- If the water supply is slightly acidic, it may cause corrosion of pipes. Therefore, the pH has to be raised above 7 and a substance such as calcium hydroxide (lime) is commonly used for this. The amount of calcium hydroxide added must be controlled, as adding too much could affect the taste of the water.
- If the water contains high levels of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ or $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ ions ('hard' water), Uisce Éireann may soften it by adding in substances such as sodium carbonate (a base). If this causes the pH to be too high, it is lowered using dilute sulfuric acid or carbon dioxide. Care has to be taken to avoid adding excess sulfuric acid, as this could cause corrosion in pipes.

A summary of the chemicals added to water during the treatment process is given in Table 20.3.

| Name of chemical | Purpose | Problems caused by adding excess |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Aluminium sulfate | Coagulation of small suspended particles | Taste of water affected; corrosion of pipes |
| Chlorine | Sterilise water (kill harmful microorganisms) | Taste and smell of water affected |
| Fluorine compound (e.g. sodium fluoride or hexafluorosilicic acid) | Reduce tooth decay | Staining of teeth |
| Calcium hydroxide | Raise pH | Hardness of water |
| Sodium carbonate | Soften water | Taste of water affected |
| Sulfuric acid | Lower pH | Corrosion of pipes |

Table 20.3 Summary of chemicals used in water treatment

## 8. Ultraviolet (UV) treatment

When discussing the use of chlorine in water treatment plants, we saw that chlorine was used to disinfect water. In some water treatment plants, ultraviolet (UV) radiation is used as a final disinfection step. UV treatment involves exposing water to UV radiation of a specific wavelength to kill microorganisms in the water. It is often used in addition to chlorination rather than as a complete replacement. Some of the advantages and disadvantages of UV treatment compared to chlorination are given in Table 20.4.

| Advantages of UV treatment | Disadvantages of UV treatment |
| :--- | :--- |
| - Does not use any chemicals, so it is more environmentally friendly. No need to transport, handle or store hazardous, toxic chlorine. | - UV lamps have high maintenance (contain mercury), consume electricity and need regular cleaning and replacement. |
| - No chlorine residual in the water. | - If there are any suspended particles in the water, these can shield the microorganisms from UV light. |
| - It kills some organisms such as cryptosporidium, which are resistant to chlorine. | - It has been found that some microorganisms can repair and reverse the destructive effects of UV radiation. |

Table 20.4 Comparing some advantages of UV treatment relative to chlorine, with some disadvantages of UV treatment of water.

The treated water that leaves the treatment plant is then stored in reservoirs for distribution throughout the water supply network.

## Energy and environmental impact of water treatment

As already discussed, access to clean, safe drinking water is essential for public health. However, it is important to bear in mind that there is a high cost to the water treatment process, which is summarised in Figure 20.16.

Therefore, we need to avoid wasting water and we need to use it as efficiently as possible. Energy must be used in the water treatment plant to produce drinking water for distribution to our homes. Some examples of how this energy is used are:

- Pumping water from rivers and lakes into the water treatment plant
- Pumping water through each stage of the process within the water treatment plant
- Stirring and mixing chemicals during the flocculation process
- Pumping sludge out of the flocculation tanks
- Cleaning sand filters and membrane filters using pressure pumps for water
- Operating all the equipment in the laboratories and administration buildings
- Pumping water over long distances from the water treatment plant throughout the water supply network - often against the force of gravity.


## Positive environmental impacts of safe drinking water production

- Public health, e.g. waterborne diseases such as cholera and typhoid are eliminated in the water treatment process.
- The availability of tap water means that we do not have to rely on bottled water. This lowers plastic waste and transportation costs and pollution caused by this transportation.


## Negative environmental impacts of safe drinking water production

- Energy consumption (as described above).
- Chemical usage: the production and transport of these chemicals has an environmental impact, e.g. carbon dioxide emissions and use of resources to manufacture chemicals.
- Generation of sludge in the sedimentation and flocculation stages - this needs to be disposed of properly.
- Wastewater from washing sand filters and membrane filters.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-413.jpg?height=2322&width=1176&top_left_y=377&top_left_x=1647)
Figure 20.16 Summary of stages in treatment of drinking water

Modern water treatment plants have introduced sustainable practices to reduce environmental impact. These are summarised in Table 20.5.

| Feature | Traditional treatment plant | Modern treatment plant |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Energy | Energy from burning fossil fuels | Renewable energy - solar energy and wind energy are used to generate electricity. |
| Disinfection | Chlorination | UV disinfection takes place. |
| Sludge handling | Sent to landfill | Sludge is dried out and is used for making bricks. It is also added to soil as compost. |
| Monitoring of efficiency | Manual monitoring using digital systems done periodically | Sensor technology and artificial intelligence systems provide real-time monitoring of plant efficiency and detection of leaks. |
| Times when pumps operating | Pumps in operation continuously | Pumping of the water from the river or lake is scheduled for times when renewable energy is available. Energy from solar and wind sources is stored in batteries to power pumps. When treatment plants are designed, there is maximum use of gravity to move water around the plant. |

Table 20.5 Comparing traditional water treatment plants with more modern water treatment plants

For example, solar panels help to reduce emissions of carbon dioxide and hence reduce the carbon footprint of water treatment plants. The reason for this is because solar panels reduce the need for electricity generated from fossil fuels such as natural gas, oil and coal. The burning of these fossil fuels produces carbon dioxide, which is a greenhouse gas. (This topic will be discussed in more detail later on in this chapter.)

Solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity. During this process, no fuels are burned and no carbon dioxide is released into the air.

## Deionised and distilled water

Since deionised water is so easily and cheaply produced, its use is far more widespread than that of distilled water. However, there is a slight difference between deionised water and distilled water. Distilled water is the purest form of water as all dissolved and suspended solids as well as dissolved gases have been removed from the water. Deionised water is not as pure as distilled water as deionised water normally contains dissolved gases and non-ionic material. These non-ionic substances, which do not dissociate into ions when dissolved in water, are often organic material that may be dissolved in the water. For some specialised industries (e.g, the electronics industry) the water must not contain any organic materials as this affects the purity of the silicon chips being manufactured. Therefore, in recent years, resins have been developed that remove organic material from water as well as ions.
