### 20.5 The carbon cycle

When studying Junior Cycle science, we learned that all living things contain carbon and that carbon plays an important role in our lives. Our body is constantly 'burning' compounds of carbon to keep us alive in the process of respiration. Every time we breathe, we exhale carbon dioxide.

We also learned that plants depend on carbon to stay alive. Plants take in carbon dioxide and make glucose and oxygen from it during the process of photosynthesis.

We also learned that the Earth is surrounded by a layer of gases called the atmosphere. This layer reaches up to 100 km above the surface of the Earth. Carbon is present in the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Although the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air is only 0.04 per cent approximately, it plays a very important role in our climate.

Some methods by which carbon dioxide is added to the atmosphere by carbon sources are summarised in Figure 20.17.

Figure 20.17 Summary of ways by which carbon dioxide is added to the atmosphere
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-415.jpg?height=1362&width=2433&top_left_y=1370&top_left_x=325)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-415.jpg?height=1108&width=1492&top_left_y=2767&top_left_x=325)
Figure 20.18 Summary of ways in which carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere.

Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by methods such as dissolving in water and by being used up in the process of photosynthesis, Figure 20.18. These systems are often called carbon sinks.

> A carbon sink is a system that absorbs more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases.

Comparing Figure 20.17 and Figure 20.18 we see that carbon sinks are the opposite to carbon sources.
As mentioned previously, the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is fairly constant at $0.04 \%$ approximately. Studying the carbon cycle (Figure 20.19) will help you to understand why this is the case. The carbon cycle shows us how carbon (in carbon dioxide and other compounds) is recycled through various processes. Note that the left-hand side of the diagram summarises the carbon sources. The right-hand side of the diagram summarises the carbon sinks.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-416.jpg?height=1245&width=1776&top_left_y=836&top_left_x=188)
Figure 20.19 The carbon cycle describes the process in which carbon continuously travels from the atmosphere to the Earth and back again into the atmosphere.

As shown in Figure 20.19, since trees absorb carbon dioxide from the air in the process of photosynthesis, forests are good examples of carbon sinks. Similarly, peatlands and wetlands are good carbon sinks. As soil is waterlogged and oxygen is limited, the dead plants in peatlands and wetlands don't fully decompose but accumulate and lock up carbon. If peatlands are dried out, the peat is exposed to air. The oxygen causes the peat to decompose and this releases carbon dioxide and methane to the air.

The carbon cycle is a natural process and, in a balanced system, the natural processes in the system recycle carbon efficiently. This helps to maintain a stable climate. However, in recent years scientists have expressed concern at the increasing levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. They are worried that this may lead to what is commonly called 'global warming'. This is discussed in the next sections.

### 20.6 The natural greenhouse effect

You may have noticed that when a car is parked in the sun, there is an increase in temperature inside the car. The car is behaving like a garden greenhouse that traps some of the energy radiated from the Sun. The plants inside a greenhouse are kept at a higher temperature than they would be if kept outside the greenhouse.

Similarly, the Earth's atmosphere acts like a greenhouse. The Sun emits radiation which is simply energy that travels through space in the form of waves. This radiation (mainly visible and ultraviolet radiation) falls on the Earth and warms up the Earth. The Earth loses some of this heat as it cools down. However, the atmosphere helps to trap some of the energy being lost, i.e. the atmosphere helps to keep the Earth warm, Figure 20.20.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-417.jpg?height=959&width=2182&top_left_y=367&top_left_x=330)
Figure 20.20 The Earth's atmosphere acts like a greenhouse. It helps to trap some of the heat being lost from the Earth as it cools down.

This trapping of the Sun's energy by the atmosphere is called the greenhouse effect. This effect is a completely natural occurrence.

> The natural greenhouse effect is the process by which certain gases in the Earth's atmosphere trap some of the heat energy from the Sun. This process keeps our planet warm enough to support life.

The greenhouse effect was discovered by John Tyndall, Figure 20.21.

The radiation from the sun consists of visible and ultraviolet radiation. This radiation enters the car and warms up items such as the seats and dashboard. These items re-radiate infrared radiation. Infra-red radiation is an invisible radiation, but we can feel it as heat. However, the heat gets trapped inside the car because the car windows prevent the infra-red radiation passing through it. Similarly, the plants and soil inside the greenhouse do not allow the infra-red radiation to pass through the walls of the greenhouse.

Let's now take a closer look at what happens in the case of the Earth. The surface of the Earth absorbs the visible and ultraviolet radiation from the Sun and warms up. The Earth then emits infra-red radiation. This is where the chemistry starts. As you are aware, the main gases in the atmosphere are oxygen and nitrogen. However, other gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane, and oxides of nitrogen also exist in the atmosphere. These other gases absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and re-radiate it

## John Tyndall <br> (1820-1893)

Figure 20.21
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-417.jpg?height=330&width=336&top_left_y=1471&top_left_x=2428)

John Tyndall was born in Leighlinbridge, Carlow. He was an outstanding teacher and lectured in the Royal Institution, London where his lectures drew great crowds. He studied the ability of gases to absorb heat and found that certain gases such as water vapour absorb heat very well and keep the Earth warm. In addition to his discovery of the greenhouse effect, he also explained why the sky is blue. The Tyndall National Institute UCC is named in his honour.
in all directions. As shown in Figure 20.20, some of the infra-red radiation goes into space but some is sent back to the Earth's surface. This is what keeps the Earth warm enough to support life.

The natural greenhouse effect is very beneficial to us. Without this natural greenhouse effect, a lot of heat energy would be lost from the Earth into outer space. This would cause the average temperature of the air just above the surface of the Earth to fall from about $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to about $-15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ (the temperature it would be if there were no atmosphere). The greenhouse effect is very important - without it the Earth would be covered by a thick sheet of ice, and life on Earth could not exist! The Moon is approximately the same distance from the Sun as the Earth. The Moon has no atmosphere surrounding it and the average surface temperature is about $-18^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

### 20.7 Greenhouse gases and greenhouse factors

As discussed already, it is found that some gases in the atmosphere are particularly good at absorbing the heat energy (mainly infra-red radiation) given off as the Earth cools down. Such gases are commonly referred to as greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide and water vapour are the main greenhouse gases. The other significant greenhouse gases are methane, dinitrogen oxide (nitrous oxide) and CFCs. Although the most abundant gases in the atmosphere are nitrogen $(78 \%)$ and oxygen $(21 \%)$, they are not greenhouse gases as they do not absorb the infra-red radiation emitted by the Earth.

Each type of greenhouse gas traps different amounts of heat. This is related to the molecular structure of each greenhouse gas and how the chemical bonds of these molecules absorb infra-red radiation. To give us a measure of how different greenhouse gases trap different amounts of heat, we use the term the greenhouse factor.

Thus, the greenhouse factor of a gas tells us how much heat is trapped by an individual gas in the atmosphere compared to the same amount of carbon dioxide. Since carbon dioxide is given a greenhouse factor of 1 , then if a gas has a greenhouse factor of, say, 30 , it means that the gas traps 30 times more

The greenhouse factor is a measure of the greenhouse effect caused by a particular gas, relative to the same amount of carbon dioxide, which is taken as the standard and is assigned a value of 1 . heat per molecule than $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$.

Scientists use greenhouse factors to compare how much heat a greenhouse gas traps in the atmosphere over a fixed period of time (usually 100 years) compared to carbon dioxide. To do this, they define a term called Global Warming Potential (GWP).

The global warming potentials for some greenhouse gases (over a 100-year period) are listed in Table 20.6.

| Greenhouse gas | Chemical formula | Global Warming Potential (100 years) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Carbon dioxide | $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ | 1 |
| Methane | $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ | 30 |
| Nitrous oxide (dinitrogen oxide) | $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ | 273 |
| Fluorinated gases (e.g. CFCs) | Various (e.g. CFC-13 has formula $\mathrm{CClF}_{3}$ ) | 4750-14400* |

Table 20.6 The main greenhouse gases and their corresponding Global Warming Potential values (*The actual value depends on the particular CFC.)

Note that carbon dioxide is the reference gas with a Global Warming Potential of 1 .

Global Warming Potential is very useful because it takes into account not only how strongly the gas traps heat, but also how long the gas stays in the atmosphere.

- Most water vapour comes from natural evaporation from sources such as oceans, lakes and plants. As the Earth gets warmer (due to $\mathrm{CO}_{2}, \mathrm{CH}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ ), more water vapour evaporates, and the warmer air holds more water vapour. We don't emit water vapour directly into the atmosphere in a way that affects our climate in the long term. In other words, the concentration of water in the atmosphere depends on temperature, not direct emissions. Therefore, it would not make sense to assign it a GWP value in the same way that we assign to gases that we add directly to the atmosphere.
- Water vapour stays in the atmosphere for just a few days or weeks before condensation takes place and it falls as rain. This is in contrast to gases such as $\mathrm{CO}_{2}, \mathrm{CH}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$, which can stay in the atmosphere for many years. The short lifetime of water means that it is not possible to compare water vapour to other gases over a 100-year period, as required in calculating GWP values.


### 20.8 The enhanced greenhouse effect

It is of great concern to everybody that increasing concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere are causing the Earth to get warmer.
This occurrence is called the enhanced greenhouse effect.
In other words, the enhanced greenhouse effect takes place when extra greenhouse gases increase the amount of heat trapped in the Earth's atmosphere above the natural level.

The extra warming that results from the enhanced greenhouse effect is called global warming.

Evidence for the enhanced greenhouse effect may be summarised as follows:

## 1. Rising carbon dioxide levels

The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere plotted against time since 1958 is shown in Figure 20.23.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-420.jpg?height=1157&width=1574&top_left_y=2519&top_left_x=188)
Figure 20.23 Accurate measurements of the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere have been made in Hawaii since 1958. The rising levels are giving cause for concern.

The levels of carbon dioxide in the Earth's atmosphere are rising as a result of more fossil fuels being burned due to increasing industrialisation. The rise in levels of carbon dioxide became particularly obvious in the 1970s and has caused considerable debate about the effect of the carbon dioxide increase on the Earth's climate. Over the past 100 years, the amount of fossil fuels being burned has increased by about $4 \%$ each year. It has been estimated that the burning of fossil fuels in Ireland produces an average of about 16,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year.

In Figure 20.23, note that within any one year the levels rise and fall. This is because, as plants grow in the spring and summer, photosynthesis uses up carbon dioxide, causing the level in the atmosphere to fall. In the winter and autumn, the level of carbon dioxide rises again as less photosynthesis is occurring as plants decay.

The contribution of greenhouse gases to global warming is shown in Figure 20.24.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-421.jpg?height=1108&width=1063&top_left_y=406&top_left_x=1591)
Figure 20.24 The main greenhouse gases (other than water vapour) and the approximate contribution they make to the greenhouse effect

## 2. Global temperature rise

Since 1880 the average surface temperature of the Earth has risen by over $1.1^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Most of this increase has occurred since 1970. The speed of global temperature rise cannot be explained by natural factors alone. However, it can be explained when human influences on emissions of greenhouse gases are taken into consideration.

## 3. Matching of climate computer models

Computer models are used to study the Earth's climate. When only natural factors are included, the models do not match the observed warming. However, when human emissions are included, the models accurately match the temperature rise. This is very strong evidence that human activity is responsible for the enhanced greenhouse effect.

Water vapour is also a greenhouse gas and has a greater overall effect than carbon dioxide due to its higher concentration. (You may have noticed that, if there are no clouds in the sky, the nights can be very chilly. This is because heat is rapidly escaping from the Earth as there is little water vapour to redirect the escaping infrared radiation back to the Earth.) However, the global concentration of water vapour is not affected to any great extent by human activities. The amount of water vapour in the atmosphere depends on temperature and is controlled by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle.

On the other hand, it is found that the rate of 'turnover' of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is quite slow. As already mentioned, this 'turnover' rate of carbon dioxide is referred to as the residence time for carbon dioxide. Although the sea can dissolve a lot of carbon dioxide, the top few hundred metres of sea water mix very slowly with deeper waters. This means that, when carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it can take hundreds of years before it penetrates deep down in the ocean and is precipitated as calcium carbonate. Thus, although the oceans will eventually dissolve much of the increased levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, this will take a long time. It is estimated that carbon dioxide has a residence time of about 100 years, i.e, the average molecule of carbon dioxide remains in the atmosphere for about 100 years. Photosynthesis is the process that removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere at the greatest rate. However, this cannot keep pace with the rate at which carbon dioxide is being released into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels.

The concentration of other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere are also affected by human activity, e.g. methane (from natural gas leakage, landfill rubbish dumps, swamps, paddy fields and ruminants), dinitrogen oxide (use of nitrogenous fertilisers) and CFCs (from old fridges, foams and aerosol sprays). Although there are only very small amounts of CFCs in the atmosphere, each molecule has a big effect, since CFCs have a large greenhouse factor. Therefore, it is important that steps are taken to limit the amounts of these substances released into the atmosphere.

## Consequences of the enhanced greenhouse effect

The consequences of the enhanced greenhouse effect are illustrated in Figure 20.25 and may be summarised as follows:

1. Global warming. The Earth's average surface temperature is rising and most of this increase has occurred since the 1970s. Since water expands as the temperature increases, it is expected that sea levels will rise. It is also expected that sea levels could be affected by the melting of glaciers in the Arctic and Antarctic regions. Global sea levels have risen by about 20 cm since 1900. This could be quite serious and could adversely affect the homes and livelihoods of people in low-lying countries such as the Netherlands and Bangladesh.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-422.jpg?height=925&width=1898&top_left_y=2526&top_left_x=184)
Figure 20.25 Some consequences of the enhanced greenhouse effect

2. Climate changes and more extreme weather events. It is expected that, as the temperature of the atmosphere is increased, more violent weather disturbances will be observed - storms will be more frequent and more violent. This is because more energy will be contained in the air and water vapour at the Earth's surface. Climate conditions in general will become more extreme, and data from climate conditions in the past will be less reliable.
3. Changes in precipitation (rain, snow, hail) patterns. As the temperature of the atmosphere is increased, the warmer air will increase evaporation of water. Since water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas, increased levels of water vapour will result in increased warming. Warmer air can hold more moisture and, therefore, heavier rain can fall. Therefore, some regions of the world will experience more intense rainfall and flooding will result.

However, in some subtropical regions, rising temperatures increase evaporation from soil, which increases the occurrence of droughts. More prolonged droughts are now being experienced in many regions
4. Ocean acidification. This term refers to the ongoing decrease in the pH of the Earth's oceans caused by the dissolving of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere in water. Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid:

$$
\mathrm{CO}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}
$$

As greater quantities of carbon dioxide dissolve in the oceans, this makes it more difficult for marine organisms to survive. For example, the shells or exoskeletons of many marine organisms such as oysters, clams and mussels are built from calcium carbonate. Carbonic acid reacts with calcium carbonate to give off carbon dioxide. Thus, the organisms die as the solid shell or exoskeleton is destroyed.

$$
\underset{\text { solid }}{\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{CO}_{3}} \rightarrow \underset{\text { soluble }}{\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{HCO}_{3}^{-}}
$$

5. Ecosystems and biodiversity. The rising temperature of the Earth and the change in weather patterns can disrupt the balance in many natural ecosystems. Some animals may be forced to migrate to cooler areas and those that cannot move or adapt quickly enough may decline in population or become extinct. Climate change may cause droughts and floods which destroy habitats, e.g. ice melting in polar regions. These changes can impact on food supply, e.g. fewer pollinators result in fewer crops. Also, the decline in the marine population can result in lower availability of fish.

## Other greenhouse gases

So far, we have studied the main greenhouse gases. There are two other categories of greenhouse gases listed on the syllabus that we are studying. We will now briefly discuss these.

## NOx greenhouse gases

The term 'NOx gases' refers to two gases called nitrogen monoxide ( NO ) and nitrogen dioxide ( $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ ). (The old name for nitrogen monoxide was nitric oxide.) These gases are emitted when fossil fuels such as petrol and diesel are burned at high temperature in car engines, Figure 20.26. Do not confuse these gases with the gas $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ (nitrous oxide or dinitrogen oxide) which contributes to the greenhouse effect as a result of nitrogenous fertilisers.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-423.jpg?height=603&width=1378&top_left_y=3040&top_left_x=1380)
Figure 20.26 NOx gases contribute to the enhanced greenhouse effect both directly and indirectly due to the formation of ozone near the surface of the Earth.

The impact of NOx on the enhanced greenhouse effect is a bit complicated but the following are the key points:

- Nitrogen monoxide is not considered a greenhouse gas by itself. However, on emission from car engines, it reacts with the air to form nitrogen dioxide.

$$
2 \mathrm{NO}+\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{NO}_{2}
$$

- Nitrogen dioxide does contribute to the enhanced greenhouse effect but only very weakly compared to the other greenhouse gases.

In addition to this direct effect on the enhanced greenhouse effect, the NOx gases also indirectly contribute to the greenhouse effect because they help form ozone in the lower atmosphere. (You may have heard of ozone because of its importance in the upper atmosphere in protecting us from harmful UV radiation.) The ozone in the lower atmosphere acts as a greenhouse gas which helps to trap heat near the Earth's surface.

## Sulfur oxides

Sulfur dioxide ( $\mathrm{SO}_{2}$ ) and sulfur trioxide ( $\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ ) do not significantly contribute to the greenhouse effect. They are not direct greenhouse gases as they do not trap heat directly. The gases are produced by burning fossil fuels containing sulfur and also in volcanic eruptions.

These gases react in the atmosphere to form aerosols - tiny droplets of sulfuric acid suspended in air. These aerosols reflect sunlight back into space, causing a cooling effect.

### 20.9 The significance of the carbon cycle in relation to natural and human-influenced climate change and sustainability

The above topic is listed on the Leaving Certificate chemistry curriculum. You could be asked an essay-style question on this topic, similar to that given on the SEC sample exam paper. Therefore, in your essay, it is important to cover some key points. The mind map shown in Figure 20.27 may be of assistance to you or you may prefer to draw your own mind map.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-424.jpg?height=960&width=1882&top_left_y=2786&top_left_x=187)
Figure 20.27 Mind map summarising some key points about the significance of the carbon cycle in relation to natural and human-influenced climate change and sustainability

- Outline what the carbon cycle is all about and refer to carbon in the atmosphere, oceans, land and living things.
- Refer to key processes such as photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, decomposition and the dissolving of carbon dioxide in oceans and waterways.
- Discuss why the carbon cycle is important for climate and how, under natural conditions, a balanced system exists that keeps the concentration of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ at a stable level.
- Explain what happens when the carbon cycle is disrupted by human influences (e.g. burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests) that add more carbon to the cycle than the natural systems (natural carbon sinks) can handle.
- Explain that trees are natural carbon sinks. When they are cut down, less $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ is absorbed due to loss of photosynthesis and the burning or decay of the tree releases the stored carbon as $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$.
- Explain that more $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ in the atmosphere results in a more intense greenhouse effect and that this gives rise to global warming and climate change.
- State that sustainability is the use of a resource so that it does not run out.
- Explain that to live sustainably we need to understand the carbon cycle and ensure that it is kept in balance.
- Outline that sustainability involves reducing carbon emissions, e.g. move away from burning fossil fuels to generate electricity and switch to renewable energy. Also we need to protect carbon sinks such as oceans and forests and to plant trees to offset emissions.
- Outline some consequences of the enhanced greenhouse effect - rise in sea levels, climate change, effect on agriculture.


### 20.10 Solutions to anthropogenic influences on the atmosphere

The word 'anthropogenic' comes from the Greek words anthropos, meaning 'human being' and gen- meaning 'be produced'. In the English language, it means 'resulting from human activity'. Thus, we now study the possible solutions to the changes in the composition of the atmosphere that are caused by human actions.

The main anthropogenic influences on the atmosphere and possible solutions to the impacts of these influences are summarised in Table 20.7. You are advised to study Table 20.7 carefully as the topic of possible solutions to anthropogenic influences on the atmosphere is specifically mentioned on the syllabus that we are studying.

| Human activity | Influence on atmosphere | Possible solutions |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Burning fossil fuels | This releases greenhouse gases (mainly $\mathrm{CO}_{2}, \mathrm{CH}_{4}$ and $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ ). | - Switch to renewable energy sources such as solar, wind and hydroelectricity. <br> - Improve energy efficiency in buildings (better insulation), industry (recycling of energy) and transport (greater fuel efficiency) <br> - Phase out fossil fuels such as coal, natural gas and oil. |
| 2. Deforestation and draining of peatlands and wetlands | There are fewer trees and peatlands are drained. This results in less carbon dioxide being taken out of the atmosphere. | - Create more carbon sinks by planting more trees. <br> - Protect peatlands and wetlands as these are good carbon sinks. |
| 3. Transportation | Transportation using fossil fuels emits greenhouse gases (e.g. $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ ). | - Use sustainable transport (e.g. cycling, walking and public transport). <br> - Use biofuels to achieve lower carbon footprint. |
| 4. Agriculture | Agricultural activity produces $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ from livestock and $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ from fertilisers. | - Reduce methane production inside animals with the aid of special feeds. <br> - Breed animals that naturally produce less methane. <br> - Install biogas systems to collect methane from animal manure and food waste. Biogas can be used to fuel vehicles or inject into natural gas pipelines. <br> - Use fertilisers more efficiently (correct amount at the correct time) and plant nitrogen-fixing crops to reduce the need for artificial fertilisers. |
| 5. Industrial processes | Industrial activity produces $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ from burning fossil fuels for energy and chemical reactions. Cement production is a major emitter of $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$. <br> $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ is emitted in the manufacture of nitric acid and nylon. | - Switch from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources. <br> - Improve energy efficiencies in industrial plants, e.g. better insulation, more efficient motors and more efficient production methods. <br> - Install a carbon capture system. |
| 6. Waste and landfills | $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ is released when organic matter is broken down by bacteria in the absence of oxygen (anaerobic respiration or fermentation). | - Install pipes in landfills to collect methane. The biogas can be burned to generate electricity instead of allowing it to escape into the atmosphere. $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ formed has lower GWP than $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$. <br> - Reduce food waste. <br> - Recycle carbon-based materials such as paper and wood. |

Table 20.8 Summary of some possible solutions to anthropogenic influences on the atmosphere

The term carbon capture (mentioned in point 5 in Table 20.8) is also called carbon capture and storage. This is a process where carbon dioxide is trapped before it enters the atmosphere and then stored safely (often underground).

Carbon capture is a way of trapping carbon dioxide gas before it goes into the atmosphere, and storing it so that it cannot contribute to global warming.

## CARBON CAPTURE PROCESS

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-427.jpg?height=1577&width=2202&top_left_y=683&top_left_x=442)
Figure 20.28 Some industries install carbon capture systems which trap carbon dioxide before it goes into the atmosphere.

Carbon capture is used in power plants and factories that produce carbon dioxide (usually by burning fossil fuels), Figure 20.28. The carbon dioxide is removed from chimneys after burning has taken place. It is compressed into a liquid and transported via pipelines or trucks. It is then pumped into oil or gas fields that are no longer in use.

Recall that methane is a very powerful greenhouse gas and traps about 30 times more heat than carbon dioxide. Therefore, even if methane is burned to form carbon dioxide and water, the global warming effect is lessened.

Note that many of the suggested solutions in Table 20.8 involve us as individuals contributing to sustainability. You may recall in your study of Junior Cycle Science meeting the idea of carbon footprint.

A carbon footprint tells us how much we are adding to climate change by the way we travel, shop, recycle and other activities in our everyday lives.

Carbon footprint is a measure of the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere as a result of the activities of a particular individual, organisation or community through burning fossil fuels.

## Summary What I should know

- Water contamination is the introduction of substances into water that make it unsafe for consumption or harmful to ecosystems.
- Biochemical oxygen demand (B.O.D.) is defined as the amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by biological (biochemical) action, when a sample of water is kept at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, in the dark, for five days.
- Eutrophication is the enrichment of water with nutrients leading to excessive growth of algae and other plants.
- Flocculation is the coming together (coagulating) of small, suspended particles in water into larger particles.
- Treatment of drinking water involves screening, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, chlorination, pH adjustment and UV treatment.
- Water treatment has energy and environmental impacts.
- The carbon cycle describes the process in which carbon continuously travels from the atmosphere to the Earth and back again into the atmosphere.
- The natural greenhouse effect is the process by which certain gases in the Earth's atmosphere trap some of the heat energy from the Sun. This process keeps our planet warm enough to support life.
- The enhanced greenhouse effect is an intensification of the Earth's natural greenhouse effect due to increased concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere caused by human activities, such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation.

# 21 Thermochemistry

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-430.jpg?height=1108&width=1218&top_left_y=524&top_left_x=186)

### 21.1 Introduction

The transfer of energy between chemical substances plays an important part in our lives. For example, the burning of fuels in air releases large amounts of energy to provide us with heat for our homes or fuel for transport. The reaction of glucose and oxygen during respiration in the cells of our bodies releases energy to keep us active and alive. Photosynthesis occurs when plants absorb energy from sunlight to enable carbon dioxide and water molecules to react together to form glucose molecules. The branch of chemistry which studies the heat changes that occur during chemical reactions is called thermochemistry.

Thermochemistry is the study of heat changes that occur during chemical reactions.

Thermochemistry is also called chemical thermodynamics from the study of engines and the relationship between heat and movement. We will find that the study of thermochemistry will be a great help to us in areas such as predicting whether a reaction gives off heat or takes in heat, Figure 21.1, or comparing fuels to decide which are the most efficient ones to use.

Enthalpy (H) is the total heat content that is stored in a chemical system.

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of energy changes that occur during chemical reactions.
- To provide students with the opportunity to investigate energy changes in combustion and neutralisation experiments in the laboratory.
- To ensure that students know how to carry out calculations on energy changes involved in chemical reactions.
- To give students an appreciation of trends in energy changes in the combustion of hydrocarbons and primary alcohols.


### 21.2 Enthalpy and enthalpy change

The word 'enthalpy' is used to describe the total heat content of a chemical system (both reactants and products). The symbol for enthalpy is $H$ (H for heat) and it is measured in kilojoules (kJ).

Whenever we use the term chemical system we are referring to the reactants and products. When we speak about heat being lost to the 'surroundings', we mean what is outside the chemical system. For example, if we mix two chemicals in a beaker and heat is generated, it is often said that this heat is 'lost to the surroundings', e.g. to the air in the laboratory.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-430.jpg?height=828&width=1232&top_left_y=2773&top_left_x=1383)
Figure 21.1 This instant cold-pack works by mixing together two chemicals inside the packet. The temperature falls when these two chemicals react together.

It is impossible to directly measure the enthalpy of reactants or products. The reason for this is because enthalpy refers to the total energy stored in a substance. This total energy is rather complicated, as energy is stored in chemical bonds, energy is stored as kinetic energy in moving particles, energy is stored as particles vibrate, and energy is also related to how particles collide against the sides of containers.

So instead of trying to measure enthalpy itself, we focus on what we can measure. We can easily measure the enthalpy changes that take place during a chemical or physical process. The symbol for enthalpy change is $\Delta H$ and it is measured in kilojoules (kJ). The symbol $\Delta$ is pronounced 'delta' and is often used in mathematics to indicate change.

You may wonder why the definition includes reference to 'constant pressure'. In most experiments, the pressure of the system does not change. For example, chemical reactions carried out in open containers such as beakers and conical flasks take place at atmospheric pressure. If an experiment is being carried out in a closed container, then some energy might be lost in changing the volume of the system, e.g. pushing against the plunger of a syringe. In short, by carrying out experiments under constant pressure, we ensure that any energy changes are due only to loss or gain of heat energy.

## Thermochemical equations

Chemists use the symbol $\Delta H$ ('delta $\mathrm{H}^{\prime}$ ) to indicate the heat change taking place when a chemical reaction occurs. For example, hydrogen is a fuel that burns in oxygen to form water. We can write a balanced equation as follows:

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=-242 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

- Equations such as the above are called thermochemical equations.
- This equation tells us that when one mole of hydrogen reacts with half a mole of oxygen to form one mole of steam, 242 kilojoules of heat are released.

By convention, a negative value of $\boldsymbol{\Delta} \mathbf{H}$ indicates an exothermic reaction. Any chemical reaction that produces heat is called an exothermic reaction. ('Ex' is the Latin word for 'out of'.)

- A positive value of $\Delta H$ indicates an endothermic reaction.
- The kJ stands for kilojoules. The SI unit of energy is the joule (J). Since one joule of heat energy is rather small, heat changes when molar quantities react are normally measured in kilojoules ( $1 \mathrm{~kJ}=1000 \mathrm{~J}$ ).
- The $\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ in the above equation indicates that we are working in moles rather than molecules, i.e. the heat measured refers to 1 mole of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ reacting with half a mole of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ to form 1 mole of water $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.
- The $\Delta H$ value above is commonly referred to as the enthalpy of reaction and is defined as follows.

Enthalpy of reaction $(\Delta H)$ is the heat change when the numbers of moles of reactants indicated in the balanced equation for the reaction react completely at constant pressure.

Enthalpy change $(\Delta \boldsymbol{H})$ is the overall energy exchanged with the surroundings when a chemical reaction or physical change is carried out at constant pressure.

If the numbers of moles in the balanced equation are changed, then the enthalpy of reaction also changes. For example, if we burn twice the number of moles of hydrogen, the enthalpy of reaction is doubled:

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=-484 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

Note: The physical states of the reactants and products (solid, liquid or gas) are always given in thermochemical equation. Sometimes you may also see (aq) to indicate that the substance is dissolved in water. States of reactants and products are included because changing the physical states of either reactants or products can alter the value of $\Delta H$.

Thermochemical equations must be balanced, the value of $\Delta H$ must be written in and the physical states of reactants and products must be given. In books of data containing these thermochemical equations, the temperature at which the given enthalpy of reaction is measured is always stated. This is usually $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

## Exothermic reactions

Enthalpy changes can be illustrated on Enthalpy Profile Diagrams, Figure 21.2. Note that Enthalpy Profile Diagrams are similar to the Reaction Profile Diagrams that we met in Chapter 17 except that, instead of emphasising activation energy, we are now emphasising enthalpy changes. In Figure 21.2, the enthalpy of the reactants is greater than that of the products. Therefore, heat is given out when the reaction takes place.

Some examples of exothermic reactions are:
(i) Combustion. The term combustion is used to describe a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen to produce heat (and often light). Combustion is the scientific term for the everyday word 'burning'. The term combustion explains the chemistry of what happens when burning takes place.

One of the most important properties of fuels is that they burn in air. The burning of fuels always produces heat. An example of a combustion reaction is the burning of methane (found in natural gas), Figure 21.3.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(\theta)} \Delta H=-890.3 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
& \text { methane oxygen } \begin{array}{l}
\text { carbon water } \\
\text { dioxide }
\end{array}
\end{aligned}
$$

An exothermic reaction is a chemical reaction that produces heat. Since heat is lost to the surroundings, the enthalpy of the products is smaller than the enthalpy of the reactants.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-432.jpg?height=809&width=1181&top_left_y=686&top_left_x=1436)
Figure 21.2 Enthalpy profile diagram for an exothermic reaction

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-432.jpg?height=662&width=747&top_left_y=1712&top_left_x=1438)
Figure 21.3 The combustion of natural gas with oxygen in the air results in the formation of carbon dioxide and water.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-432.jpg?height=766&width=1072&top_left_y=2415&top_left_x=1500)
Figure 21.4 Enthalpy profile diagram for combustion of methane

The above reaction may be represented on an Enthalpy Profile Diagram as shown in Figure 21.4.
(ii) Respiration. This is the biochemical process in which energy stored in glucose is released for use in cells. It occurs in all living cells. This 'burning' of glucose inside our bodies supplies us with the energy we need.

$$
\underset{\text { glucose }}{\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_{6(s)}}+\underset{\text { oxygen }}{6 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)}} \rightarrow \underset{\substack{\text { carbon } \\ \text { dioxide }}}{6 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}}+\underset{\text { water }}{6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l j}} \Delta \mathrm{H}=-2801 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

As this reaction involves oxygen gas, this process is also known as aerobic respiration. Anaerobic (without oxygen) respiration can also occur in cells, and also results in the release of energy.
(iii) Rusting. As you are aware, the rusting of iron is a very slow process, so it is not very obvious that it is an exothermic process. It may be described by the following equation:

$$
\underset{\text { iron }}{4 \mathrm{Fe}_{(s)}}+\underset{\text { oxygen }}{3 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)}} \rightarrow \underset{\text { iron }(\text { III }) \text { oxide }}{2 \mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3(s)}} \Delta H=-1,650 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

Another common exothermic reaction is the neutralisation process when acids and bases react. We will study this in more detail later on in this chapter.

## Endothermic reactions

Not all chemical reactions give out heat. In some cases, a drop in temperature is observed when a chemical reaction occurs. In these cases, heat is taken in from the surroundings. You will notice the drop in temperature if you hold a beaker of water at room temperature and add sherbet to it. Heat is taken in from your hand. Such a reaction is called an endothermic reaction. ('Endon' is the Greek word for 'inside'.) An endothermic reaction is one that takes in heat.

If you study Figure 21.5, you will see that the enthalpy of the products is greater than that of the reactants. In other words, heat is taken in when the reaction takes place.

An endothermic reaction is a chemical reaction that takes in heat. Since heat is taken in from the surroundings, the enthalpy of the products is greater than that of the reactants.

Some examples of endothermic reactions are:

## (i) Thermal decomposition

In some chemical reactions, heating a chemical causes it to break down into similar substances. The use of heat to break down a substance is called thermal decomposition.

> Thermal decomposition is a chemical reaction in which heat is applied to a single compound to cause it to break down into two or more simple substances.

Since energy is absorbed in the form of heat, thermal decomposition reactions are almost always endothermic. (There are a few exceptions in the case of some explosives but these need not concern us in this course.)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-433.jpg?height=1085&width=1600&top_left_y=2689&top_left_x=1158)
Figure 21.5 Enthalpy profile diagram for an endothermic reaction

An example of a thermal decomposition reaction is the decomposition of limestone (calcium carbonate) to lime (calcium oxide). Lime is used in agriculture and in the construction industry.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-434.jpg?height=267&width=1346&top_left_y=612&top_left_x=188)

This reaction plays an important role in the manufacture of cement, Figure 21.6.
The enthalpy profile diagram for the thermal decomposition of limestone is shown in Figure 21.7.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-434.jpg?height=685&width=1229&top_left_y=1184&top_left_x=188)
Figure 21.6 Limestone is placed in this large rotary kiln and is heated to convert it to lime. This endothermic reaction is important in the manufacture of cement.

In Junior Cycle science, you learned that when photosynthesis takes place, energy is absorbed in the form of sunlight by plants to make glucose. Since energy is absorbed, photosynthesis is another example of an endothermic reaction.

$$
6 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \longrightarrow \underset{\text { glucose }}{\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{12} \mathrm{O}_{6(\mathrm{~s})}+6 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \Delta H=+2801 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}}
$$

In photosynthesis, the chlorophyll in plants allows light energy from the Sun to be absorbed and converted into chemical energy. The chemical energy is stored in the chemical bonds of glucose, Figure 21.8.

## Physical changes and enthalpy changes

So far we have been discussing chemical changes. A chemical change is a change that results in the formation of one or more new substances. You may recall that in Junior Cycle, you also learned about physical changes.

A physical change is a change that does not result in the formation of any new substance.

Changes of state also result in enthalpy changes. Changes of state are not classified as exothermic or endothermic reactions, since they are merely physical changes rather than chemical reactions. It is more correct to refer to them as exothermic or endothermic processes.

Some examples of physical changes are:
(i) Melting. When ice melts, energy is absorbed to overcome the intermolecular forces between the water molecules in the crystal lattice. It is found that 6.01 kJ of energy are absorbed for every mole of ice ( 18.02 g ) that melts. This quantity is called the enthalpy of fusion of ice. 'Fusion' is just another word for melting.

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \Delta H_{\text {fus }}=+6.01 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

The enthalpy of fusion ( $\Delta H_{\text {fus }}$ ) is the energy absorbed when one mole of a solid melts to become a liquid at constant pressure.
(ii) Boiling. When water boils, energy is absorbed to overcome the intermolecular forces between the water molecules. It is found that 40.7 kJ of energy are absorbed for every mole of water that is converted to steam. This quantity is called the enthalpy of vaporisation of water.

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \Delta \mathrm{H}_{v a p}=+40.7 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

The enthalpy of vaporisation ( $\Delta H_{\text {vop }}$ ) is the energy absorbed when one mole of a liquid boils to become a gas at constant pressure.

Note that the enthalpy of vaporisation is higher than the enthalpy of fusion. This is because not only must the intermolecular forces between the water molecules be overcome, but also the particles must be fully separated in the gas.

Enthalpy of vaporisation can be demonstrated if you put a few drops of a volatile liquid such as ether or propanone on the back of your hand. You will feel a drop in temperature because the heat energy needed to change the liquid to a gas comes from your hand.

When steam is converted to water (condensation) this entire large amount of energy ( $40.7 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ) is released. A burn from steam can be more harmful than a burn from boiling water, Figure 21.9. Boiling water is never hotter than $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ but steam could be at much higher temperatures. If the hot steam condenses on your skin, the excess energy of the gaseous molecules is lost (in the form of heat) when they become a liquid.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-435.jpg?height=1000&width=1180&top_left_y=1901&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 21.9 A burn caused by steam is more severe than that caused by boiling water, since more heat is released when the hot steam condenses on skin.

(iii) Dissolving. In many cases, dissolving a salt in water is simply a physical change. For example, if sodium chloride is dissolved in water there is a slight fall in temperature and the solution is slightly cool to touch.

$$
\mathrm{NaCl}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{-} \Delta H_{\mathrm{sol}}=+3.9 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

However, if calcium chloride is dissolved in water there is a rise in temperature and the solution feels hot to touch.

$$
\mathrm{CaCl}_{2(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca}_{(a q)}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{Cl}_{(a q)}^{-} \quad \Delta H_{s o l}=-81.3 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

An 'infinitely dilute solution' means that the ions are well separated from each other in solution and do not interact with each other as they are surrounded by water molecules. In practice, this is achieved by dissolving a small number of grams of the salt in a fairly large volume of water (about $200 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ ) to ensure

Enthalpy of solution ( $\Delta H_{\text {sal }}$ ) is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and standard atmospheric pressure. a dilute solution. Then the temperature change is measured. By taking the volume of water into account and the mass of solute added, the heat of solution can be calculated. Since this experiment is not on our course, you need not worry about the details of how enthalpy of solution is measured in practice.

We have already stated that in many cases, dissolving a salt in water is simply a physical change. However, in other cases, when the substance is added to water, a chemical reaction may occur. We have already studied some of these reactions with water in Chapter 7.

## Standard conditions for measuring enthalpy changes

Enthalpy changes for various chemical reactions are listed in databases around the world. Therefore, it is important that these values of enthalpy changes are measured under the same conditions. The conditions chosen by chemists are the normal conditions that are found in a science laboratory. These conditions are:

- Standard temperature for measuring enthalpy changes $=25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}(298 \mathrm{~K})$
- Standard pressure $=$ atmospheric pressure $=1.01325 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$
(SEC Formulae and Tables booklet)
Note that the standard temperature for enthalpy is different to the standard temperature that we met when discussing the properties of gases, i.e. standard temperature for gases $=273.15 \mathrm{~K}$.


### 21.3 Heat of combustion

The term enthalpy of reaction is a general term used for any type of chemical reaction. In some cases a different term is used to indicate the particular type of chemical reaction being considered. As already stated, a reaction in which a substance is burned is called a combustion reaction. Consider the reaction in which carbon is burned in oxygen to form carbon dioxide:

$$
\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)} \quad \Delta H=-394 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

The heat change in this reaction $\left(-394 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$ is called the heat of combustion of the reaction. It is defined as follows:

Note: In keeping with the syllabus documentation, the terms heat and enthalpy are used interchangeably in this textbook. The term heat of combustion may also be called enthalpy of combustion.

The phrase 'completely burned in excess oxygen' is important in the definition of

The heat of combustion of a substance is the heat change when one mole of the substance is completely burned in excess oxygen. heat of combustion. This is because some elements have more than one oxide, e.g.

$$
\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=-111 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

This value of $\Delta H$ is not the heat of combustion of carbon, since complete combustion of carbon in excess oxygen forms carbon dioxide, not carbon monoxide.

Another important phrase in the definition of heat of combustion is 'one mole'. Consider the thermochemical equation to describe what happens when butane from a gas cylinder is burned when using a gas cooker:

$$
2 \mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{10(g)}+13 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 8 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+10 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=-5754 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

Is $-5754 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ the heat of combustion of butane? It is not since, by definition, the heat of combustion involves one mole of the substance being burned.
Therefore, the heat of combustion of butane is $-\frac{5754}{2}=-2877 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$.
This may be represented by the following thermochemical equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{10(g)}+61 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \\
& \Delta H=-2877 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Heats of combustion are accurately measured using an instrument called a bomb calorimeter. A calorimeter is any container used for the determination of heat changes. (The name comes from an old unit of energy called the calorie, 1 calorie = 4.18 joules.) As the bomb calorimeter is not on your course, we will not discuss the details of how it works. However, we will meet the name 'calorimeter' again, so remember this name!

Some examples of heats of combustion of various fuels are given in Table 21.1.

| Fuel | Formula | Heat of combustion $\boldsymbol{\Delta} \boldsymbol{H}$ measured in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Methane | $\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}$ | -890 |
| Ethane | $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{6(g)}$ | -1560 |
| Propane | $\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{8(g)}$ | -2220 |
| Butane | $\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{10(\mathrm{~g})}$ | -2877 |
| Hexane | $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{14(0)}$ | -4194 |
| Ethanol | $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}$ | -1371 |
| Carbon | $\mathrm{C}_{(s)}$ | -394 |
| Hydrogen | $\mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}$ | -286 |

Table 21.1 Heats of combustion of some fuels

## To investigate the heat of combustion of a series of alcohols using spirit burners

## Introduction

In this experiment, we will measure the amount of energy released when a certain mass of an alcohol is burned in air. The amount of heat will be measured by heating a known mass of water in a container made of copper. The container is called a calorimeter. Copper is usually used as it is a good conductor of heat. By measuring the temperature rise caused by heating a certain amount of water, we can calculate the heat of combustion of the alcohol.

The heat of combustion of a substance is the heat change when one mole of the substance is completely burned in excess oxygen. The heats of combustion of the first six primary alcohols are summarised in Table 21.2

| Name of alcohol | Formula | Balanced equation for combustion | $\boldsymbol{\Delta} \boldsymbol{H}_{\text {combustion }}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Methanol | $\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{OH}$ | $2 \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+3 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+4 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \quad \Delta H=-1452 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ | $-726 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ |
| Ethanol | $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}$ | $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+3 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \quad \Delta H=-1367 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ | $-1367 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ |
| Propan-1-ol | $\mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{7} \mathrm{OH}$ | $2 \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{7} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+9 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 6 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+8 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \quad \Delta H=-4042 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ | $-2021 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ |
| Butan-1-ol | $\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{9} \mathrm{OH}$ | $\mathrm{C}_{4} \mathrm{H}_{9} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+6 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+5 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \quad \Delta H=-2676 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ | $-2676 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ |
| Pentan-1-ol | $\mathrm{C}_{5} \mathrm{H}_{11} \mathrm{OH}$ | $2 \mathrm{C}_{5} \mathrm{H}_{11} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+15 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 10 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+12 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \Delta \mathrm{H}=-6662 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ | $-3331 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ |
| Hexan-1-ol | $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{13} \mathrm{OH}$ | $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{13} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}+9 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 6 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+7 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=-3984 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ | $-3984 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ |

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-438.jpg?height=785&width=942&top_left_y=2487&top_left_x=351)

## Key steps in procedure

- The apparatus is set up as shown in Figure 21.10.
- The copper calorimeter is clamped directly above the spirit burner.
- A draught shield is placed around the apparatus.


## Explanation

- The purpose of the draught shield is to improve the accuracy of the experiment. In the lab, air currents can blow the flame of the burner sideways. This disperses the heat. We need to keep the heat from the burner concentrated on the calorimeter. Our calculations assume that all the heat from the burning alcohol is used to heat the water.
- The heatproof mat protects the surface of the bench in case the glass spirit-burner may crack due to heat generated by the burning wick.


## Key steps in procedure (continued)

- A graduated cylinder is used to place a known volume (depending on the capacity of the calorimeter) of water in the copper calorimeter.
- Fill the spirit burner to about half its capacity with the alcohol being investigated.
- Place the cap on the spirit burner and find the total initial mass of the spirit burner and alcohol.


## Explanation

- We need an exact volume of water to calculate the heat transferred to the water.
- We need to know the initial mass of the alcohol in order to calculate the mass of alcohol burned.
- We need to keep the cap on the spirit burner to avoid loss of alcohol by evaporation.


## Key steps in procedure (continued)

- Place the spirit burner under the calorimeter, remove the cap and light the wick.
- Allow the alcohol to burn and heat the water.
- From time to time, stir the water gently using a glass rod.
- When the temperature has risen by a certain amount (e.g. $40^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), extinguish the flame and replace the cap on the spirit burner.
- Find the new mass of the spirit burner and cap.


## Explanation

- The water is stirred with the glass rod during heating to ensure even distribution of heat.
- We need to know the initial temperature of the water and the final temperature. The temperature rise will help us to calculate the heat transferred from the burning alcohol to the water.
- We need to find the new mass of the spirit burner and cap in order to find the mass of alcohol that has been burned.


## Calculations

- The heat gained by the water in the combustion of the alcohol is calculated using the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Heat gained } & =\text { mass of water × specific heat capacity of water × rise in temperature of water } \\
& =m \times c \times\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$m=$ mass of water in kg.
$c=$ specific heat capacity of water in $\mathrm{J} \mathrm{kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$
$t_{2}-t_{1}=$ temperature rise

The specific heat capacity (c) of a substance is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K . For example, the specific heat capacity of water is $4200 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$. (This can also be written as $4.2 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$.) This means that it takes 4200 joules of heat to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water from, say, $19^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

In carrying out the experiment, we assume that all the heat produced by the burning alcohol goes towards the raising of the temperature of the water in the copper calorimeter.

- Knowing the heat liberated when a certain mass of alcohol was burned, it is then possible to calculate the amount of heat that would be liberated when one mole of the alcohol is completely burned in excess oxygen, i.e, the heat of combustion of the alcohol. The answer you get is an approximation and, therefore, may not be the one quoted in data books of heats of combustion.

When writing up an account of this experiment in your laboratory notebook, discuss the possible sources of error and steps that you took to ensure the accuracy of your results. These are outlined in the Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook
A sample calculation is given in Example 21.1.

## Example 21.1

## Question

A group of students performed an experiment to measure the heat of combustion of methanol. They used a copper calorimeter containing $80 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of water. The initial temperature of the water was $21.0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the final temperature was $63.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The mass of the spirit burner and methanol before heating was 154.62 g and after heating was 154.01 g . Assuming that all the energy released by the burning alcohol went into heating the water, calculate the heat of combustion of methanol. The specific heat capacity of water is $4200 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$. Density of water is $1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}$.

## Answer

Initial temperature of water: $21.0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
Final temperature of water: $63.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
Initial mass of spirit burner and fuel: 154.62 g
Final mass of spirit burner and fuel: 154.01 g
Specific heat capacity of water: $4200 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$

## Step 1

Calculate the mass of methanol burned.
Mass burned = mass before burning - mass after burning

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =154.62 \mathrm{~g}-154.01 \mathrm{~g} \\
& =0.61 \mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 2

Convert the mass of methanol to moles

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { No. of moles methanol } & =\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Relative molecular mass }} \\
& =\frac{0.61}{32.042} \\
& =0.0190 \text { mole }
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 \times \mathrm{C}=2 \times 12.01 & =12.01 \\
4 \times \mathrm{H}=4 \times 1.008 & =4.032 \\
1 \times \mathrm{O}=1 \times 16.00 & =16.00 \\
\hline M_{r} \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{OH} & =32.042
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 3

Convert mass of water to kilograms.
$80.0 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of water $=80.0 \mathrm{~g}=0.08 \mathrm{~kg}$

## Step 4

Calculate the temperature rise.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Temperature rise } & =\text { final temperature }- \text { initial temperature } \\
& =63.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}-21.0^{\circ} \mathrm{C} \\
& =42.5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 5

Calculate the heat absorbed by the water.
Heat gained $=$ mass × specific heat capacity × rise in temperature

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =m \times c \times\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right) \\
& =0.08 \times 4200 \times 42.5 \\
& =14,280 \mathrm{~J} \\
& =14.28 \mathrm{~kJ}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 6

Calculate the heat of combustion in kJ per mole.
0.0190 mole of methanol releases 14.28 kJ

Therefore, 1 mole of methanol would release $\frac{14.28}{0.0190} \mathrm{~kJ}$

$$
\text { = } 751.58 \mathrm{~kJ}
$$

Answer: Heat of combustion $\boldsymbol{\Delta} \boldsymbol{H}_{\text {comb }} \boldsymbol{=} \mathbf{- 7 5 1 . 5 8 ~ k J ~ m o l} \boldsymbol{\mathrm { H }}^{-\mathbf{1}}$

## EXAM TIPI

The most common error in exams is for students to forget to convert grams of water to kilograms when substituting into the equation to calculate the heat gained. It is important to have the mass of the water heated in kg, since the units of specific heat capacity involve kg.

### 21.4 Bond enthalpy

Let us now consider what determines the value of $\Delta H$ for a particular reaction. Suppose we consider the combustion of methane:

$$
\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=-890 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

As already discussed in Chapter 5, when a chemical reaction occurs, bonds are broken and new bonds are formed. Energy is required to break a bond and energy is released when a bond is formed. If we examine the left-hand side of the above equation, we see that four $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bonds and two $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ bonds must be broken, Figure 21.11.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-442.jpg?height=988&width=1808&top_left_y=1145&top_left_x=188)
Figure 21.11 This diagram shows bond-breaking and bond-making for the combustion of methane in oxygen.

The energy involved in breaking bonds is called the bond enthalpy (also called bond dissociation enthalpy or bond dissociation energy) and is defined as follows:

> Bond enthalpy is the average energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond and to separate the neutral atoms completely from each other.

Note that the definition always refers to the bondbreaking process. For example, consider the single covalent $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}$ bond in the $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ molecule:

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{(g)}+\mathrm{H}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=+436 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

Note that we are breaking the single covalent bond between two hydrogen atoms in a molecule of hydrogen gas. Both hydrogen atoms then become separate hydrogen atoms. The bond enthalpy value tells us that it takes 436 kJ of energy to break one mole of H - H bonds.

Bond enthalpy values are measured from studying spectra of molecules and also from values of heats of reaction. They were used by Linus Pauling to draw up a table of electronegativity values
(Chapter 6). Pauling realised that chemical bonds are like 'store rooms' for chemical energy. Some average bond enthalpy values are listed in Table 21.3. Bond enthalpy values tell you how much energy is needed to break different bonds. The higher the bond enthalpy value for a particular bond, the stronger the bond.

| Bond | Average bond enthalpy value in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| C-H | +412 |
| C-C | +348 |
| $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}$ | +614 |
| $\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}$ | +839 |
| $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}$ | +463 |
| $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ | +498 |
| $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$ | +799 |
| $\mathrm{N} \equiv \mathrm{N}$ | +945 |

Table 21.3 Average bond enthalpy values for some bonds

- Note that bond enthalpy values are always given as bond enthalpy per mole of bonds broken.
- The same quantities of energy would be released when the bonds are formed.
- The + sign is placed before each average bond enthalpy value to emphasise that energy is needed to break bonds. In other words, bond breaking is an endothermic process.
- The reason that the bond enthalpy values in Table 21.3 are average values is because it is found that the bond enthalpy value for a particular bond can vary. For example, the energy to break the first $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bond in methane is not the same as that required to break any of the other $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bonds.

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3(g)}+\mathrm{H}_{(g)} & \Delta H=+435 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
\mathrm{CH}_{3(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{H}_{(g)} & \Delta H=+444 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
\mathrm{CH}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{(g)}+\mathrm{H}_{(g)} & \Delta H=+444 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
\mathrm{CH}_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{(g)}+\mathrm{H}_{(g)} & \Delta H=+339 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Therefore, average bond enthalpy of the methane } \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H} \text { bond } \\
& =\frac{435+444+444+339}{4} \\
& =\frac{1662}{4} \\
& =415.5 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

## What decides whether a particular reaction is exothermic or endothermic overall?

Whether a particular reaction is exothermic or endothermic overall depends on bond enthalpy values.

- Breaking bonds in reactants always requires energy, i.e. it is always an endothermic process. The amount of energy needed depends on the bond enthalpies of the bond being broken.
- Forming bonds in products always releases energy, i.e. it is always an exothermic process. The amount of energy released depends on the bond enthalpies of the new bonds formed.

The $\Delta H$ for the overall reaction depends on the total energy needed to break bonds and the total energy released when bonds are formed.
$\Delta H$ for overall reaction $=$ Total energy required to break bonds - total energy released in forming bonds.

- If more energy is released when forming bonds than is used to break the bonds ⇒ exothermic reaction.
- If more energy is used to break bonds than is released when new bonds are formed ⇒ endothermic reaction.

In short, the value of $\Delta H$ for a particular reaction is dependent on the amount of energy that is needed to break the bonds and the amount of energy that is liberated when the new bonds are formed.

We now study how we can analyse a given reaction involving covalent molecules to predict the value of $\Delta H$ for that reaction using average bond enthalpy values.

## Example 21.2

## Question

Methane reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water as shown in the following equation:
$\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2_{(g)}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2_{(g)}}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)}$
Using the standard bond enthalpy values for the $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bond, the $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ double bond, the $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$ double bond and the O - H bond given in Table 21.3, calculate the enthalpy of reaction.

## Answer

When answering questions of this type, it is helpful if you write out the equation in a similar form to that shown in Figure 21.12. This will help you to avoid mistakes in identifying bonds that are broken and bonds that are made when the reaction takes place.

Note that Figure 21.12 is a simplified version of

Figure 21.11. Use these types of simplified diagram to help you fill in the parts of Table 21.4 and Table 21.5. Be sure to show all your work so that you can maximise your marks in an exam.

## Step 1

Calculate the energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants.

Energy needed to break bonds (Reactants)
| Bond and quantity | Bond enthalpy ( $\mathbf{k J ~ m o l}^{-\mathbf{1}}$ ) | Total energy ( $\mathbf{k J}$ ) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $4 \times \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ | 412 | $4 \times 412=1648$ |
| $2 \times 0=0$ | 498 | $2 \times 498=996$ |
|  | Total energy in | 2644 |


Table 21.4 Calculate the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants.

## Step 2

Calculate the energy released when bonds are made in the products.

Energy released by making bonds (Products)
| Bond and quantity | Bond enthalpy ( $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ) | Total energy (kJ) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $2 \times \mathrm{C}=0$ | 799 | $2 \times 799=1598$ |

|  | Total energy out | 3450 |

Calculate the enthalpy of reaction by substituting the values into the equation:
$\Delta H$ for overall reaction $=$ Total energy required to break bonds total energy released in forming bonds $=2644-3450=-806 \mathrm{~kJ}$
