### 21.5 Enthalpy of neutralisation

We have already learned (Chapter 11) that neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water.
e.g. $\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

We have also seen that the essential reaction taking place in this neutralisation reaction is:
$\mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$

Neutralisation reactions are nearly always exothermic. When discussing heat changes involved in neutralisation reactions, the term enthalpy of neutralisation is used. This term is defined as follows:

Enthalpy of neutralisation is the heat change when one mole of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions from an acid reacts with one mole of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions from a base.

Enthalpy of neutralisation is measured in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$. Consider the enthalpy of neutralisation of a number of strong acids and strong bases when dilute solutions of these acids and bases react together:
$\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\Delta H=-57.1 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{KCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\Delta H=-57.2 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$\mathrm{HNO}_{3}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaNO}_{3}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\Delta H=-57.3 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$\mathrm{HNO}_{3}+\mathrm{KOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{KNO}_{3}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\Delta H=-57.3 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
You will observe that the enthalpy of neutralisation is almost the same in all cases. This is because, if we ignore 'spectator' ions, the essential reaction occurring is the same in all cases. ('Spectator' ions are ions that do not take part in the actual chemical change. They are unchanged on both the reactant and product sides of the chemical equation.)

For example, if we take a close look at the reaction between nitric acid and potassium hydroxide, we see that the reaction that occurs simply involves a proton and a hydroxide ion coming together to form water.
$\mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{-}+\mathrm{K}^{*}+\mathrm{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{K}^{+}+\mathrm{NO}_{3}{ }^{-}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\mathbf{H}^{+}+\mathbf{O H}^{-} \rightarrow \mathbf{H}_{2} \mathbf{O}$
$\boldsymbol{\Delta} \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol{=} \mathbf{- 5 7} \mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-\mathbf{1}}$
However, consider the reaction between a strong acid and a weak base or between a weak acid and a strong base:
$\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{OH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{Cl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\Delta H=-52.2 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
$\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
$\Delta H=-55.2 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
When either a weak acid or a weak base is involved, the numerical value of $\Delta H$ is usually less than $57 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. This is because weak acids and weak bases do not fully dissociate in water. For complete neutralisation to occur and form one mole of water, the weak acid or base must become fully dissociated. This dissociation requires energy, i.e. it is endothermic. Therefore, the heat released will be less than 57 kJ since a certain quantity of heat is required to cause complete dissociation of the acid or base.

### 21.2 Experiment

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 20 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

## Student Experiment No. 20

## To determine the enthalpy of reaction for a neutralisation reaction

## Introduction

In this experiment, a known number of moles of hydrochloric acid is mixed with an equal number of moles of sodium hydroxide in an insulated container. The rise in temperature of the mixture is then measured and, from this, the enthalpy of reaction is calculated.

In order to get a significant temperature rise, the solutions of HCl and NaOH that are used in this experiment are more concentrated ( 1 M ) than those you used in carrying out titrations ( 0.1 M ). Therefore, great care must be taken when handling these solutions. They must not be allowed to come in contact with your skin or eyes. As always, safety glasses should be worn throughout the experiment. The corrosive symbol on this page is important!

## Key steps in procedure

- Using a graduated cylinder, a known volume of hydrochloric acid solution is placed in a polystyrene cup, Figure 21.13.
- The same volume of sodium hydroxide of the same concentration is placed in a second polystyrene cup.
- The volumes and concentrations of HCl and NaOH used are recorded.
- Both solutions are allowed to stand until they are at the same temperature.
- The temperature of each solution is recorded.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-446.jpg?height=1206&width=984&top_left_y=2099&top_left_x=485)
Figure 21.13 Measuring the enthalpy of reaction for the neutralisation reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide

- The sodium hydroxide solution is quickly added to the hydrochloric acid solution and care is taken to avoid any loss of liquid due to splashing.
- A lid is immediately placed on the polystyrene cup in which the two solutions have been mixed.
- The solution is stirred continuously.
- The maximum temperature reached by the mixture is recorded.


## Observation

- A rise in temperature is observed.


## Explanation

- More concentrated solutions of HCl and NaOH are used than were used in titrations in order to obtain a significant temperature rise in this experiment. If 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaOH were used, the temperature rise would be small and would be difficult to accurately measure.


## Calculations

- The heat given out in the reaction is calculated using the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { Heat given out } & =\text { mass × specific heat capacity } \text { × rise in temperature } \\
& =m \times c \times\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$\mathrm{m}=$ mass of solution in kg.
$\mathrm{c}=$ specific heat capacity of solution in $\mathrm{J} \mathrm{kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$
$\mathrm{t}_{2}-\mathrm{t}_{1}=$ temperature rise
In carrying out the experiment we assume that all the heat generated goes towards the raising of the temperature of the solution and that no heat is absorbed by the plastic container, i.e. the plastic container has negligible heat capacity.

Knowing the heat liberated when the number of moles of acid used was neutralised, it is now possible to calculate the amount of heat that would be liberated when one mole of the acid is neutralised, i.e. the enthalpy of reaction for the neutralisation of 1 mole of HCl by NaOH .

In carrying out the calculations the following points are worth noting:
In general, it is assumed that the density of the solution is the same as the density of water, i.e. that $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of the solution have a mass of 100 g or 0.1 kg .

You will always be given the specific heat capacity of the solution, e.g. when carrying out the calculations for the above experiment, the specific heat capacity of the solution is $4060 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$.

If the acid and base are at two different temperatures at the beginning of the experiment, use the average value when carrying out calculations.

## EXAM TIPI

The most common error in exams is for students to forget to convert grams to kilograms when substituting into the above equation. It is important to have the mass of the solution in kg since the units of specific heat capacity involve kg.

The answer you get may not be the one quoted in data books of heats of reaction for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. When writing up an account of this experiment in your laboratory notebook, discuss the possible sources of error and steps that you took to ensure the accuracy of your results. These are outlined in the Laboratory Notebook accompanying this textbook.

The method of calculating the enthalpy of reaction for a neutralisation reaction is shown in Example 21.3.

## Example 21.3

## Question

A student carried out an experiment to measure the enthalpy of neutralisation of nitric acid by sodium hydroxide in a container made of plastic of negligible specific heat capacity. She used $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 1.0 M nitric acid and $100 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 1.0 M sodium hydroxide. The initial temperature of both of the solutions was $15.6^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and the final temperature of the solution was $22.4^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Given that the specific heat capacity of the solution is $4080 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$, calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation. (Assume that the density of the solution is $1 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}$.)

## Answer

## Step 1

Convert grams to kg .
Mass of solution $=200 \mathrm{~g}=0.2 \mathrm{~kg}$.

## Step 2

Calculate the temperature rise.
Temperature rise $=22.4-15.6=6.8^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

## Step 3

Calculate the heat given out.
Specific heat capacity $=4080 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$
Heat given out $=$ mass × specific heat capacity × temp rise

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =0.2 \times 4080 \times 6.8 \\
& =5548.8 \text { joules }
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 4

Calculate the number of moles of acid that were neutralised.
Number of moles of $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ that were neutralised $=\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000}=\frac{100 \times 1}{1000}=0.1$

## Step 5

Calculate the enthalpy of reaction.
0.1 mole of $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ that is neutralised gives 5548.8 joules of heat

Therefore, 1 mole of $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ that is neutralised gives $5548.8 \times 10=55,488 \mathrm{~J}=55.488 \mathrm{~kJ}$ of heat
Since for $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}, 1$ mole of acid gives 1 mole of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions
∴ Enthalpy of neutralisation is $-55.488 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
i.e. $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaNO}_{3}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \quad \Delta H=-55.488 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Answer: Enthalpy of neutralisation $=-55.488 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

If you use a diprotic acid such as sulfuric acid, you must take care in the calculations when determining the enthalpy of neutralisation, since one mole of acid gives two moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions,
e.g. $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}+2 \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_{2} \mathrm{SO}_{4}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.
This is illustrated in Example 21.4.
Study Example 21.4 in the online resources.

## Example 21.5

## Question

In an experiment to measure the enthalpy of reaction for the reaction between sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid, a student added $50 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ of 1.0 M HCl solution to the same volume of 1.0 M NaOH solution in a polystyrene foam cup.

Calculate the total number of moles of acid neutralised in this experiment.
Taking the total heat capacity of the reaction mixture used in this experiment as $420 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$, calculate the heat released in the experiment if a temperature rise of $6.7^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ was recorded.

Hence, calculate the enthalpy of reaction for $\mathrm{NaOH}+\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$
[LCH]

## Answer

## Step 1

Calculate the number of moles of acid neutralised.
Number of moles of HCl $=\frac{\text { volume × molarity }}{1000}=\frac{50 \times 1}{1000}=0.05$ moles

## Step 2

Calculate the heat given out in the reaction.
Heat given out $=$ Heat capacity × Rise in temperature

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =C \times\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right) \\
& =420 \times 6.7 \\
& =2814 \text { joules } \\
& =2.814 \mathrm{~kJ}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 3

Calculate the heat given out by one mole of HCl .

In some cases, you may not be given the specific heat capacity of the solution but rather given the heat capacity of the overall system. The symbol for heat capacity is $\mathbf{C}$. The heat capacity of an object is the amount of heat needed to change its temperature by 1 K .

Heat given out $=$ heat capacity × rise in temperature $=C \times\left(t_{2}-t_{1}\right)$.
0.05 mol of HCl releases 2.814 kJ when neutralised

⇒ 1 mol would release $\frac{2.814}{0.05} \mathrm{~kJ}$ when neutralised $=56.28 \mathrm{~kJ}$
i.e. the enthalpy of reaction is $-56.28 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Answer: Enthalpy of reaction $=-56.28 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

## EXAM TIP!

Remember to include the negative sign when writing down the final answer!

### 21.6 Enthalpy of formation

Sometimes chemists need to know the amount of energy absorbed or released when a compound is formed from its elements, e.g. the amount of energy released when water is formed from hydrogen and oxygen. Knowledge of this energy is very important when designing fuel cells as sources of power, Figure 21.14. The bus is powered by the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water. We will be discussing fuel cells in more detail in Chapter 22.

TEST YOURSELF: Attempt Questions 21.4 and W21.10 -W21.12.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-449.jpg?height=584&width=1183&top_left_y=2936&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 21.14 The reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water releases energy. The energy released is used to provide the power needed by this bus.

This enthalpy change that takes place when a compound is formed from its elements is called the enthalpy of formation and is defined as follows:

The enthalpy of formation of a compound is the heat change that takes place when one mole of a compound in its standard state is formed from its elements in their standard states.

The standard state of an element or compound is its normal form at $\mathbf{2 5}^{\boldsymbol{\circ}} \mathbf{C}$ and at normal atmospheric pressure. (Another reminder! Do not confuse this temperature with the standard temperature that we met when discussing the properties of gases, i.e. standard temperature for gases $=273.15 \mathrm{~K}$.) Thus, the standard state of oxygen is the gaseous state, that of water is the liquid state, and that of magnesium is the solid state - because these are the states in which these substances exist at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and standard pressure.

We will use water as an example to illustrate the concept of heat of formation. The heat of formation of water is found to be $-285.8 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$. This may be represented as follows:

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)} \quad \Delta H=-285.8 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

Note that one mole of water in its normal liquid state is formed in this reaction.
The following equation does not represent the heat of formation of water:

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \quad \Delta H=-241.8 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

This is because the water formed in the second equation above is in the gaseous state. At $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ the normal state of water is liquid.

Similarly, the following equation does not represent the heat of formation of water:

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(\theta)} \quad \Delta H=-571.6 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

This is because the above equation shows the heat change that takes place when two moles of water are formed from its elements.

The heats of formation of most compounds have negative values of $\Delta H$. The reason for this is that energy is given out when the compound is formed from its elements, Table 21.6. We would expect this since compounds are generally more stable than the elements from which they are formed.

| Compound | Heat of formation $\boldsymbol{\Delta} \boldsymbol{H}$ measured in $\mathbf{k J} \mathbf{~ m o l}^{\mathbf{1}}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}$ | -74.9 |
| $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{6(g)}$ | -84.7 |
| $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}_{(l)}$ | -278 |
| $\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}$ | -394 |
| $\mathrm{NH}_{3(a)}$ | -46.2 |
| $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(t)}$ | -285.8 |

Table 21.6 Heats of formation of some compounds

By definition, enthalpy of formation of a compound is the heat change that takes place when one mole of a compound in its standard state is formed from its elements in their standard states. Since an element in its standard state is already in that form, no formation is required, so the enthalpy change is zero. In short, the enthalpy of formation of any element in its standard state is zero.

A common error in exams is for students to write the heat of formation equations incorrectly. Study the following examples carefully, and note that in some cases it is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 2 \mathrm{C}_{(s)}+\mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \\
& 1 / 2 \mathrm{~N}_{2(g)}+11 / 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH}_{3(g)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$1 / 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{C}_{(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{~N}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{HCN}_{(g)}$
$3 \mathrm{C}_{(s)}+11 / 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{~N}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{3} \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{~N}_{(g)}$ necessary to introduce fractions in order to have 1 mole on the right of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta H=+227 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
& \Delta H=-46 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
& \Delta H=+130 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
& \Delta H=+194.5 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 21.7 Hess's Law

Imagine that you are climbing a mountain and that there are various paths to reach the top of the mountain. Regardless of what path you take, you will reach the same height at the top of the mountain. Germain Hess, Figure 21.15, discovered something similar about heat changes in chemical reactions.

Hess studied the heat changes involved in a wide variety of different chemical reactions. He found that the quantity of heat produced in going from one substance to another was the same no matter what route was taken. In 1840 he announced his results in what is now called Hess's Law:

In other words, the amount of heat liberated or absorbed in a chemical reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one or in several steps, Figure 21.16.

Consider the routes for converting carbon and oxygen to carbon dioxide, Figure 21.17.

Route 1: $\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}$
$\Delta H_{1}=-394 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Route 2: $\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{(g)}$

$$
\Delta H_{2}=\times \mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

Route 3: $\mathrm{CO}_{(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}$
$\Delta H_{3}=-283 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
In Route 1, carbon is converted directly to carbon dioxide $\left(\Delta H_{1}=-394 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$. In Route 2, carbon monoxide is first formed $\left(\Delta H_{2}=x \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$. In the next step the carbon monoxide is further oxidised to carbon dioxide $\left(\Delta H_{3}=-283 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right)$.

## EXAM TIPI

When writing enthalpy of formation equations, always make sure you have one mole of product on the right-hand side of the equation!

Figure 21.15

## Germain Hess <br> (1802-1850)

Germain Hess was born in Geneva and became professor of chemistry in St Petersburg University, Russia. He is known as the founder of thermochemistry, as he measured the heat changes that took place in many chemical reactions.

Hess's Law states that if a chemical reaction takes place in a number of stages, the sum of the heat changes in the separate stages is equal to the heat change if the reaction is carried out in one stage.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathbf{A} \rightarrow \mathbf{B} \rightarrow \mathbf{C} \rightarrow \mathbf{D} \\
\Delta \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{A} \rightarrow 0}=\Delta \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{~B}}+\Delta \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}}+\Delta \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{C} \rightarrow 0}
\end{gathered}
$$

Figure 21.16 Diagrammatic representation of Hess's Law

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-451.jpg?height=493&width=783&top_left_y=3053&top_left_x=1884)
Figure 21.17 Hess's Law may be used to calculate the unknown enthalpy of reaction.

According to Hess's Law, the heat change for the single-step reaction is the same as the heat change for the two-step reaction.
i.e. $\Delta H_{1}=\Delta H_{2}+\Delta H_{3}$

$$
-394=x-283
$$

$x=-394+283=-111 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
i.e. $\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{(g)}$
$\Delta H_{2}=-111 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Thus, Hess's Law may be used to indirectly find the value of the enthalpy of reaction of a chemical reaction that may be difficult to measure directly in the laboratory. For example, it is difficult to measure experimentally the heat of formation of CO , since some $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ is also formed. However, the value may be calculated very accurately using Hess's Law.

In short, Hess's Law is very useful in chemistry because:

- Using Hess's Law, we can use enthalpy values that we can measure in the lab to calculate enthalpy values that we cannot measure in the lab.
- Therefore, it gives us a method for finding an enthalpy change indirectly.

Hess's Law is really just a re-statement of the more general Law of Conservation of Energy as applied to heat changes involved in chemical reactions.

The relationship between Hess's Law and the Law of Conservation of Energy is often illustrated in a simple energy profile diagram as shown in Figure 21.18. This energy profile is another way of representing the cycle type of diagram show in Figure 21.17.

The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed but can only be converted from one form of energy into another.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-452.jpg?height=893&width=1599&top_left_y=2142&top_left_x=221)
Figure 21.18 This energy profile diagram emphasises the relationship between Hess's Law and the Law of Conservation of Energy.

The great usefulness of Hess's Law is that it allows thermochemical equations to be added, subtracted, multiplied or divided to calculate unknown heats of reaction. For this reason, it is one of the most useful laws in thermochemistry.

We will now look at some examples of Hess's Law calculations to help you gain skills in carrying them out. When solving problems using Hess's Law, you are advised to approach them in a systematic fashion as shown in the examples that follow. If you approach the problem in a haphazard fashion you could end up 'going around in circles'.

## Example 21.6

## Question

Calculate the heat of formation of methane from the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{C}_{(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)} \\
& \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \\
& \mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta H=-393 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
& \Delta H=-286 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \\
& \Delta H=-879 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

[ LCH]

## Answer

In this example we are asked to calculate the heat of formation of a compound using other heats of formation and one enthalpy of reaction

## Step 1

Write down the equation you require. We need to write the equation for the heat of formation of methane. Thus, one mole of methane must be on the right-hand side of the equation.
The elements from which methane is formed must be on the left-hand side of the equation.
The equation must be balanced. The required equation is:
$\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}$

$$
\Delta H=?
$$

We must now build up each part of this equation (i.e. $\mathrm{C}, 2 \mathrm{H}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ ) using the given equations (a), (b) and (c) above.

## Step 2

Introduce C. [C is in (a) above.]
(a) $\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}$

$$
\Delta H=-393 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

## Step 3

Introduce $2 \mathrm{H}_{2}$. We have $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ in (b) above Therefore, multiply (b) by 2 . Remember to also multiply $\Delta H$ by 2 .
(b) $\times 2: 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}$
$\Delta H=-572 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

## Step 4

Get the left-hand side of the required equation by adding (a) to the above equation:
(a) $\mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{s})}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}$

$$
\Delta H=-393 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

(b) $\times 2: 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}$

$$
\Delta H=-572 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

(d) $\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}$

$$
\Delta H=-965 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

## Step 5

Introduce $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$. We have $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$ on the left-hand side of equation (c). We need it on the right-hand side of the required equation in the box above. Therefore, reverse equation (c), remembering to also reverse the sign of $\Delta H$.
(c) reversed: $\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \quad \Delta H=+879 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

## Step 6

Now add (c) reversed to (d) above:
(d)

$$
\mathrm{C}_{(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}
$$

$$
\Delta H=-965 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

(c) reversed: $\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)}$

$$
\Delta H=+879 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

$\mathrm{C}_{(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \theta_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \theta_{(g)}+\mathrm{CH}_{4(g)}+2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \quad \Delta \mathrm{H}=-86 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
i.e. $\mathrm{C}_{(s)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{4(g)} \Delta H=-86 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Answer: $\Delta H=-86 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

## Example 21.7

## Question

Calculate the enthalpy of reaction of the following reaction:
$2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)} \Delta H=$ ?

You are given the following heats of formation:
(a) $\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}$
$\Delta H=-21 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
(b) $\mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{s})}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO}_{2(g)}$
$\Delta H=-297 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
(c) $\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)}$
$\Delta H=-286 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

## Answer

Note that in this example we are asked to calculate the enthalpy of reaction using heats of formation of reactants and products.

## Step 1

The required equation is:

$$
2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{~S}_{(s)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(i)} \quad \Delta H=?
$$

## Step 2

Introduce $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}$ by reversing (a) and multiplying by 2 .
(a) reversed: $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{S}_{(s)}$
$\Delta H=+21 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
(a) rev $\times 2: 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{(s)}$
$\Delta H=+42 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

## Step 3

Introduce $\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)}$ by reversing (b).
(b) reversed: $\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{(s)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}$

$$
\Delta H=+297 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
$$

## Step 4

Add (a) rev $\times 2$ to (b) reversed.
(a) rev $\times 2: 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}$
$\Delta H=+42 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
(b) reversed: $\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{S}_{(s)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}$
$\Delta H=+297 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
(d): $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+5 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}$
$\Delta H=+339 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

## Step 5

We already have 3 S on the right-hand side of the equation. Therefore, the only remaining item to be introduced is the $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. This is done by multiplying (c) by 2 and adding it to (d).
(c) $\times 2: 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}$
$\Delta H=-572 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
(d): $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}$
$\Delta H=+339 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Add: $2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+3 \mathrm{~S}_{(\mathrm{s})}+\mathrm{O}_{2(g)}$
i.e. $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+\mathrm{SO}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 3 \mathrm{~S}_{(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}$
$\Delta H=-233 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Answer: $\Delta H=-233 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

As we come near to completing our study of thermochemistry, note that the change in enthalpy for particular processes can be determined in three ways:

1. By measurement in the laboratory
2. Using values of bond enthalpy data
3. Using standard heats of formation of reactants and products.

### 21.8 Trends in $\boldsymbol{\Delta} \boldsymbol{H}$ values for complete combustion of hydrocarbons and primary alcohols

As discussed in Chapter 23 (see the Assessment and Exam Guide), a hydrocarbon is a compound that contains carbon and hydrogen only. In this course, we need to know how to write balanced equations for the complete combustion of hydrocarbons and primary alcohols. Let's begin by studying the complete combustion of some hydrocarbons.

## Complete combustion of hydrocarbons

Complete combustion means that when a hydrocarbon burns in oxygen, there is sufficient oxygen present to produce only carbon dioxide and water as products. In other words, all the carbon atoms in the hydrocarbon are oxidised to carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen atoms are oxidised to water. On the contrary, incomplete combustion means that there is insufficient oxygen present. When insufficient oxygen is present, carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon (soot) are formed.

The balanced equations for the complete combustion of the first six alkanes are shown in Table 21.7. You are expected to construct these balanced equations yourself and you will get plenty of practice in balancing equations in the workbook accompanying this textbook. Once you get in the practice, balancing these equations will be a piece of cake!

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

| Ethane | $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{6}$ | $2 \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{6(g)}+7 \mathrm{O}_{2_{(g)}} \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{CO}_{2(g)}+6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(g)}$ | $\Delta H=-3120 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ | $-1560 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ |

- There is a steady increase in the quantity of heat (enthalpy of combustion) as the number of carbon atoms increases.
- This steady increase in the size of $\Delta H_{\text {combustion }}$ is almost linear as shown in Figure 21.19.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-455.jpg?height=1042&width=1359&top_left_y=2819&top_left_x=1399)

## Why is there an increase in the size of the enthalpy of combustion for the alkanes every time a $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ unit is added?

- Every time you move from one alkane to the next (methane to ethane, ethane to propane) you add one $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ group.
- The larger alkane of a consecutive pair has two additional C-H bonds and one additional C-C bond compared to the previous alkane, Figure 21.20.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-456.jpg?height=330&width=1156&top_left_y=898&top_left_x=244)
Figure 21.20 Adding a $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ unit causes one additional $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ molecule and one additional $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ molecule to be formed on complete combustion. These product molecules are very stable and, therefore, more energy is released when the alkane is burned for every $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ unit added.

- When the larger of the two consecutive alkanes undergoes complete combustion, these additional bonds are broken and new bonds are formed. Additional $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ bonds in oxygen must also be broken. As already discussed, breaking bonds is endothermic.
- However, additional $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$ bonds in $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{O}$ bonds in $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ are also formed when the larger of the two alkanes burns. As already discussed, making bonds is exothermic.
- In particular, the $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$ double bonds formed in the carbon dioxide molecule are very strong. Therefore, the $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ molecule is very stable and a lot of energy is released when additional quantities of it are formed.
- In summary, for the additional $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ unit in the larger alkane (of two successive alkanes), the energy required for the extra bond breaking upon complete combustion is more than offset by the energy released when making the bonds in the additional $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ formed.
- If you study the final column in Table 21.7, the increase in energy released on complete combustion is an average of about $650 \mathrm{~kJ}^{-1}$ mole ${ }^{-1}$ for each $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ unit added. It is approximately constant for each $\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ unit added because the same set of bond breaking and bond making energy changes are involved every time.

## Why do primary alcohols have lower heats of combustion than the corresponding alkanes?

- All alcohols have the -OH functional group. In other words, an oxygen atom is already present in the molecule, Figure 21.21.
- The carbon atom bonded to the -OH group is already partially oxidised.
- Therefore, less energy is released when the primary alcohol is fully oxidised to carbon dioxide and water. In other words, when an alcohol burns, fewer bonds to oxygen need to be formed compared to an alkane of the same number of carbon atoms.
- Recall that according to Hess's Law, the energy released on complete combustion of an alkane to carbon dioxide and water is the sum of the energy released when (i) one oxygen atom is added to convert the alkane to a primary alcohol ( $\Delta H_{2}$ in Figure 21.22) and (ii) the energy released in the complete combustion of that primary alcohol to carbon dioxide and water ( $\Delta H_{3}$ in Figure 21.22).

Figure 21.21 Comparing methane and methanol, we see that methanol has an O-H group.

Figure 21.22 Since alcohols already contain an O atom, less energy is released on complete combustion compared to alkanes.

- Therefore, because alcohols already contain an O atom, they release slightly less energy on combustion than the corresponding alkanes.

## Why do alkenes and alkynes have lower heats of combustion than the corresponding alkanes?

The reason for this may be explained as follows:

- There are fewer H atoms in alkenes and alkynes than in alkanes with the same number of carbon atoms, Figure 21.24. This means that alkenes and alkynes form fewer $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ molecules during combustion. Since the $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ molecule is quite stable, the reaction to form $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ is highly exothermic. Forming less $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ means less energy is released.
- Also in the complete combustion of any of the alkenes or alkynes, a double or triple bond must be broken. Both $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}$ bonds are strong and a lot of energy is required to break them. Therefore, there is less energy released than when an alkane with the same number of carbon atoms is burned.
- Alkynes have the lowest hydrogen content and a very strong $\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}$ bond. Therefore, an alkyne has the lowest value of heat of combustion compared to the alkane or alkene with the same number of carbon atoms.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-459.jpg?height=355&width=1596&top_left_y=3340&top_left_x=364)
Figure 21.24 Alkenes and alkynes molecules have fewer hydrogen atoms than alkanes with the same number of carbon atoms.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-460.jpg?height=1508&width=2433&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=188)

# 22 Electrochemistry

## OBJECTIVES

- To give students an understanding of how electricity is produced in galvanic cells and batteries.
- To make students familiar with the system for listing metals in order of their tendency to be oxidised.
- To ensure that students know the chemical reactions that take place in lithium-ion rechargeable batteries and in fuel cells.
- To provide students with the opportunity to investigate the use of electricity to bring about chemical reactions.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-462.jpg?height=803&width=700&top_left_y=1408&top_left_x=1433)
Figure 22.1 Galvani found that the frog's leg twitched when the nerves in the leg came in contact with two metals.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-462.jpg?height=600&width=1108&top_left_y=2256&top_left_x=1487)
Figure 22.2 Alessandro Volta invented the first battery.

Electrochemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies the relationship between chemical reactions and electricity.

Electrochemistry may be divided into two areas:
(i) The use of chemical reactions to produce an electric current (cells or batteries)
(ii) The use of an electric current to bring about chemical reactions (electrolysis).

So let's begin our study of electrochemistry by having a closer look at the use of chemical reactions to produce an electric current.

### 22.2 Galvanic (Voltaic) cells

We have learned that Volta showed that electricity is produced whenever two different metals are immersed in a conducting solution. We can show this in the laboratory by placing a piece of zinc in a solution of zinc ions and a piece of copper in a solution of copper ions. We link the two solutions using a 'salt bridge', Figure 22.3, and it is observed that a current flows in the connecting wire.

Note the following terms that are commonly used in electrochemistry:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-463.jpg?height=818&width=1183&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 22.3 This galvanic cell generates a voltage of 1.1 volts.

Electrode: The solid conductor (usually a metal or graphite) that carries the electricity into or out of the cell. In the cell shown in Figure 22.3, the electrodes are the strips of zinc and copper.

Electrolyte: The solution that contains ions and can conduct electricity. In the cell shown in Figure 22.3, the electrolytes are zinc sulfate and copper sulfate.

A cell in which a chemical reaction results in the production of an electric current is called a galvanic cell or a voltaic cell in honour of Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta. In the above cell, a voltage of about 1.1 volts registers on the voltmeter. You may recall from your study of Junior Cycle science that two or more cells connected together is called a battery.

Let's take a closer look at how redox reactions cause an electric current to flow, Figure 22.4.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-463.jpg?height=997&width=1763&top_left_y=2174&top_left_x=341)
Figure 22.4 Oxidation takes place at the zinc electrode. Reduction takes place at the copper electrode. These redox reactions cause electrons to flow from zinc to copper.

A galvanic cell consists of two half-cells. The current arises because oxidation occurs at one half-cell and reduction occurs at the other half-cell. If you examine Figure 22.4, you will see that each half-cell consists of a metal electrode that is dipping into a solution containing its own metal ions. Also, each half-cell is connected to the other half-cell by a wire and a salt bridge.

Oxidation. At the zinc electrode, zinc atoms lose electrons and form $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ ions, i.e. an oxidation reaction takes place:

$$
\mathrm{Zn}_{(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}_{(a q)}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

These electrons flow through the wire to the copper electrode.
Reduction. At the copper electrode, copper ions accept electrons to become copper atoms, i.e. a reduction reaction takes place to form copper metal:

$$
\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}{ }_{(a q)}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}_{(s)} \downarrow
$$

$$
\text { Overall reaction : } \mathrm{Zn}_{(s)}+\mathrm{Cu}_{(a q)}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn}_{(a q)}^{2+}+\mathrm{Cu}_{(s)} \downarrow
$$

- The salt bridge allows ions to flow between the two half-cells without the two solutions mixing directly with each other. It helps to maintain a balance of ions in each part of the cell. The salt bridge could simply consist of a piece of filter paper that has been soaked in a substance such as a solution of potassium chloride or potassium nitrate. Since $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ ions build up in the zinc half-cell, then negative ions will move from the salt bridge into the zinc half-cell to maintain balance of ions. Since $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are removed from solution in the copper half-cell, positive ions will move from the salt bridge into the copper half-cell to maintain balance of ion.
- The electrode at which oxidation occurs is called the anode. (Think of the two vowels $O$ and $A$ to help you remember this.) In a galvanic cell, the anode is negative and it loses electrons which flow around the wire in the circuit. Think of the electrons going away from the anode in a galvanic cell. Zinc is the anode in the galvanic cell shown in Figure 22.4. The phrase 'the anode is eaten away' may help you to remember that when oxidation occurs, the solid zinc metal is converted to $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$ ions in solution.
- The electrode at which reduction occurs is called the cathode. In a galvanic cell, the cathode is positive and it accepts electrons coming from the anode. Think of electrons coming to the cathode. Copper is the cathode in the galvanic cell shown in Figure 22.4. The acronym CROA may also be of help.

We can now define a galvanic cell in terms of oxidation-reduction reactions.
A galvanic (voltaic) cell is a device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy through oxidation-reduction reactions that occur within it.

- Note that a galvanic cell consists of two half-cells.
- A half-cell in electrochemistry is one part of the cell where either oxidation or reduction occurs.
- It typically consists of a metal electrode dipping into a solution containing ions of that metal. (Don't get confused between the cell that you meet in electrochemistry and the cell that you meet when studying biology!)

TEST YOURSELF: Attempt Questions 22.1 and W22.1-W22.2.

### 22.3 The electrochemical series

We have seen that the voltage generated by the zinc-copper cell is 1.1 volts. If we could assign a particular fraction of this voltage to each individual halfcell, we would then have a measure of the tendency for each of the above two reactions to occur. However, you cannot measure the voltage of a single half-cell because current will only flow when two half-cells are connected together. Chemists overcome this problem by choosing a particular half-cell as the standard with which to compare other half-cells. The half-cell chosen as the reference is called the hydrogen half-cell. This consists simply of a piece of platinum metal immersed in a 1 M solution of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions. Hydrogen gas (at atmospheric pressure) is then bubbled over the platinum electrode. A standard half-cell of any other element consists of an electrode of the element immersed in a 1 M solution of its ions.

- Some metals have a greater tendency to lose their outer electrons than other metals, e.g. if zinc is replaced by magnesium in the cell in Figure 22.4, a much higher voltage is observed. This is because magnesium has a far greater tendency to lose electrons than zinc.
- The standard electrode potential value for a metal is the voltage recorded when the standard half-cell of that metal is connected to a standard hydrogen half-cell as shown in Figure 22.5.
- Chemists use the standard electrode potential of a metal to describe the tendency of the metal to lose electrons, i.e. the tendency for a metal to be oxidised.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-465.jpg?height=750&width=1248&top_left_y=2044&top_left_x=325)
Figure 22.5 The hydrogen half-cell on the left is used to measure the standard electrode potential of copper.

Each element in turn may be connected to the standard hydrogen electrode and the standard electrode potential of the element measured. It is then possible to draw up a table of the elements in order of their standard electrode potentials. Such a table is called the electrochemical series.

The electrochemical series is a list of elements in order of their standard electrode potentials, i.e. in order of the decreasing tendency for the element to be oxidised (lose electrons) under standard conditions.

Part of the electrochemical series is shown in Table 22.1. You need to know the order of these metals relative to hydrogen. Your teacher will probably award a bar of chocolate to the student in the class who creates the best mnemonic to help remember the order - so get working on this!

## The electrochemical series and corrosion

Since metals near the top of the electrochemical series tend to lose electrons readily, these metals are reactive and corrode easily.

Corrosion is any undesired process whereby a metal is converted to one of its compounds.

Metals such as potassium and sodium have to be stored under oil to prevent them reacting with moisture or oxygen in the air. If a piece of potassium or sodium is removed from the jar of oil and sliced in two, a white powder is seen to form quickly on the metal, Figure 22.8. The sodium or potassium forms an oxide of the metal, i.e. it corrodes.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-467.jpg?height=636&width=776&top_left_y=1419&top_left_x=325)
Figure 22.8 Sodium metal is near the top of the electrochemical series. Therefore, it is oxidised quickly when it comes in contact with oxygen in the air.

The most common example of corrosion we see around us is the corrosion of iron and steel. As you are aware, if iron and steel are not treated, they will slowly be converted to rust. Rust is an oxide of iron of formula $\mathrm{Fe}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \times \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$. (The amount of water of crystallisation can vary.) Rusting requires the presence of both oxygen and water.

As a general rule, the metals high up in the electrochemical series corrode more quickly than those low down in the series. There are some notable exceptions to this. For example, aluminium is quite high in the electrochemical series but does not appear to corrode. In fact, aluminium does corrode but the oxide of aluminium formed, $\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$, sticks firmly to the metal surface and prevents further corrosion.

There are several ways of preventing corrosion:

1. Painting and greasing. Painting is very useful for large structures such as bridges. However, the painting has to be done fairly frequently as corrosion will take place if the metal is scratched. When this happens, the bare metal is then exposed to air and water. For moving parts of machinery, oil and grease are very useful for preventing corrosion.
2. Galvanising. In this case, a coating of zinc is used to cover iron or steel to protect the iron or steel from corrosion. Such iron is called galvanised iron (named after Galvani). Since zinc is higher than iron in the electrochemical series, it corrodes in preference to the iron, thus protecting the iron. Items such as metal buckets and wheelbarrows are often made from galvanised iron. In addition, galvanised iron is used in building sheds and barns.
3. Coating of surface with another metal. In some cases, the iron or steel is coated with a very unreactive metal, e.g. 'tin' cans are made of steel coated with tin. The unreactive tin protects the steel. Chromium is also used as a surface coating, e.g. taps and bathroom fittings all consist of steel coated with chromium to prevent corrosion and also to give a nice shiny finish.
4. Using sacrificial anodes. In this method of preventing corrosion, the iron is placed in contact with a metal that is more easily oxidised, e.g. a block of zinc is bolted to iron. In this case, the zinc corrodes rather than the iron, i.e. the zinc is sacrificed to protect the iron. Sometimes, large pieces of zinc are attached to the steel hulls of ships or underground pipes, Figure 22.9. The zinc is oxidised, i.e. the zinc becomes the anode and the anode is eaten away. The zinc needs to be replaced from time to time. The steel of the hull is, therefore, the cathode and cannot corrode. This method of protection is also called cathodic protection because the steel is being protected by making it the cathode of the cell.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-467.jpg?height=730&width=958&top_left_y=2672&top_left_x=1575)
Figure 22.9 Zinc is bolted onto the steel hull. Since zinc is higher in the electrochemical series, it corrodes in preference to the steel hull. Zinc is the sacrificial anode.

### 22.4 Primary (non-rechargeable) and secondary (rechargeable) cells

As already discussed, a galvanic cell produces a flow of electrons as a result of chemical reactions taking place at the anode and cathode. You may recall from your study of electricity in Junior Cycle science that a battery is a collection of two or more cells connected together. For example, when four 1.5 volt zinc-carbon cells are connected in series, the total voltage is 6 V , Figure 22.10. (Connecting the cells in series means that the positive end of one cell is connected to the negative end of another cell.)

In everyday speech we often use the terms cell and battery to mean the same thing, but you need to be clear on the difference. Each of the units shown in Figure 22.10 is a cell and it is only when the cells are connected together that we have a battery.

So called 'zinc-carbon' cells and 'alkaline' cells are types of cells commonly used in items such as remote-control devices, flashlights and wall clocks. These cells are examples of primary cells because they are non-rechargeable.

A primary cell is a type of galvanic cell that is designed for single use only. When the chemical reactions that take place inside a primary cell have been completed, the cell cannot be recharged as the chemical reactions are irreversible.

As you are aware, the battery in your mobile phone can be recharged, Figure 22.11. A typical smartphone contains one 'lithium-ion' cell. Since lithium-ion cells can be recharged, they are classified as secondary cells.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-468.jpg?height=1020&width=1528&top_left_y=2369&top_left_x=188)
Figure 22.11 Lithium-ion cells are classified as secondary cells since they can be recharged.

[^4]![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-468.jpg?height=1091&width=825&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1790)
Figure 22.10 Each of the cells shown has a voltage of 1.5 V . When the four cells are connected in series, the total voltage is $4 \times 1.5 \mathrm{~V}=6 \mathrm{~V}$.

A lithium-ion cell has a voltage of about 3.8 volts. Smartphones usually contain just one lithium-ion cell since a voltage of about 3.8 V is sufficient to power the electronics in the smartphone. The use of a single cell also reduces the size and mass of the smartphone. The invention and development of lithium-ion batteries has revolutionised the world of electronics, Figure 22.12.

Figure 22.12
| John Goodenough | $(1922-2023)$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Stanley Whittingham | $(1941-)$ |
| Akira Yoshino | $(1948-)$ |


![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-469.jpg?height=330&width=867&top_left_y=735&top_left_x=1344)

The Nobel Prize in chemistry was awarded in 2019 to John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino for their work in developing the lithium-ion battery. The Nobel citation stated that 'this rechargeable battery laid the foundation of wireless electronics such as mobile phones and laptops. It also makes a fossil fuel-free world possible, as it is used for everything from powering electric cars to storing energy from renewable sources.'

Another example of a secondary cell is the lead-acid battery used in cars. This consists of six 2 V cells in series and has a voltage of about 12 volts.

A comparison between primary and secondary cells is summarised in Table 22.2.

| Feature | Primary cell | Secondary cell |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Rechargeable | No | Yes |
| Chemical reactions | Not reversible | Reversible |
| Usage | Single use only | Can be reused many times |
| Voltage of one cell | 1.5 V (approx.) depending on type of cell | 3.8 V (approx.) for lithium-ion cell; 2 V for lead-acid |
| Environmental impact | Higher impact on environment | Lower impact since can be reused |
| Example | Zinc-carbon, alkaline, lithium | Lithium-ion, lead-acid |

Table 22.2 Comparing a primary cell and a secondary cell

Note in Table 22.2 that non-rechargeable batteries also include lithium batteries. These contain lithium metal or lithium compounds and are commonly found in watches, cameras and calculators. We will not be studying these in this course, as rechargeable lithium-ion cells are far more important.

Let's now take a closer look at a lithium-ion cell. To understand how a lithium-ion cell works, we first discuss what happens when the lithium-ion cell is being used to power a device. Then we will look at what happens when a lithium-ion cell is being recharged.

## The lithium-ion cell when being used to supply electricity to power a device (discharging)

We will tell the story in a number of stages and let's assume we are describing the lithium-ion cell in a mobile phone.

## Stage 1: The parts of the cell

If you study the diagram in Figure 22.13, you will see that there are two electrodes in the lithium-ion cell.

## The carbon electrode

- The electrode on the left is made of carbon in the form of graphite. Graphite is an allotrope of carbon and will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 23. The carbon electrode is the negative electrode (anode) during discharge of the cell.
- Graphite consists of flat layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons (Chapter 23). Before the mobile phone is switched on, layers of lithium ions are inserted in between these layers. The layered structure of graphite is perfect for hosting the lithium ions. The technical term used to describe the hosting of the lithium ions is intercalation. This word was originally used for inserting extra days into a calendar. In chemistry it is used to describe inserting lithium ions between layers of particles such as atoms.


## The cobalt oxide electrode

- The electrode on the right is made of a substance called cobalt oxide, $\mathrm{CoO}_{2}$. This is the positive electrode (cathode) during discharge of the cell.


## The electrolyte

- This is a liquid or gel solution. It consists of lithium salts dissolved in an organic solvent. An organic solvent has to be used as lithium reacts with water.
- The electrolyte allows $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions to pass through but does not allow electrons to pass through it.
- The electrolyte is in contact with both the anode and the cathode to ensure that $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions can move in both directions between the anode and the cathode.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-470.jpg?height=1068&width=1622&top_left_y=563&top_left_x=996)
Figure 22.13 Diagram of lithium-ion cell when current is being drawn from it to operate an electronic device

## The separator (barrier)

- It is a thin plastic film. It may also be called the barrier.
- It allows $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions to pass through it in both directions.
- It prevents electrons from flowing directly between the electrodes. This would short circuit the cell.


## Stage 2: Reaction at carbon electrode: electron flow

- When the mobile phone is switched on, the carbon electrode is connected to the cobalt oxide electrode via the external circuit.
- The following spontaneous oxidation reaction occurs at the anode:

Reaction at carbon electrode (anode):

$$
\mathrm{LiC}_{6} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{C}_{6}
$$

The reaction is spontaneous because lithium, being at the top of the electrochemical series, has a strong tendency to lose electrons. Recall, that lithium is so reactive that it must be stored under oil to prevent it coming in contact with the oxygen in the air, Figure 22.14.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-471.jpg?height=609&width=1180&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=325)
Figure 22.14 Lithium, similar to sodium and potassium, is so reactive that it has to be stored under oil, to prevent it spontaneously reacting with the oxygen in the air.

$\mathrm{LiC}_{6}$ is not a chemical compound but a formula indicating that for every six carbon atoms in the graphite structure, there is one lithium ion between the layers of carbon atoms. Think of the layers of carbon atoms like individual pages stacked vertically with lithium ions between the pages. When the lithium is stored within the graphite in this form, it is very stable.

- The electrons that are released in the above reaction flow from the carbon electrode of the cell into the external circuit of the mobile phone and then to the cobalt oxide electrode. Note in Figure 22.13 that the direction of flow of electrons is from the carbon electrode (negative) to the part of the mobile phone that require energy and then to the cobalt oxide (positive) electrode.


## Stage 3: Lithium-ion flow

- We have seen in stage 2 that the electrons leave the carbon anode and travel to the cobalt oxide cathode through the external circuit. It is clear from the equation for the reaction that takes place at the carbon anode, for each electron that leaves the carbon anode, a $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ion is left behind.
- As you continue to use your mobile phone, $\mathrm{Li}{ }^{+}$ ions are building up at the carbon anode.
- Negative charge is building up at the cobalt oxide cathode.
- If the $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions did not move, the flow of electrons would stop due to this charge imbalance.
- Therefore, to balance the charge and keep the battery electrically neutral overall, $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions move from the carbon through the electrolyte and separator to the cobalt oxide cathode.

Note the difference between electron flow and lithium-ion flow. Electrons flow through the external circuit and $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions flow though the internal electrolyte.

## Stage 4: Reaction at cobalt oxide electrode

- At the cathode, the electrons that arrive via the external circuit combine with the $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions that arrive via the internal electrolyte. This may be written as:


## Reaction at cobalt oxide electrode (cathode):

$\mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{LiCoO}_{2}$
Lithium cobalt oxide

- This reduction reaction ( $\mathrm{Co}^{4+}$ in $\mathrm{CoO}_{2}$ to $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ in $\mathrm{LiCoO}_{2}$ ) is important as it allows the lithium ions to be held in the crystal lattice of lithium cobalt oxide. Similar to the way that lithium ions were stored in the carbon electrode (anode), lithium ions are also stored in the cobalt oxide (cathode).
- Chemists have discovered that the $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ions are small enough to fit in (intercalate) between the gaps of the much larger cobalt ions in the crystal lattice of lithium cobalt oxide. The $\mathrm{Li}^{+}$ ions are only inserted into the gaps. They do not form strong bonds - this is important when we need to reverse the reaction in the process of recharging the battery.


## Stage 5: The overall process involved in discharging the lithium-ion cell

We can summarise the above two reactions as follows:

Reaction at carbon anode: $\mathrm{LiC}_{6} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{C}_{6}$ Reaction at cobalt oxide cathode:
$\mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{LiCoO}_{2}$
Overall: $\mathrm{LiC}_{6}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{6}+\mathrm{LiCoO}_{2}$
This equation tells us that the overall result is the transfer of lithium ions from the carbon electrode to the cobalt oxide electrode. This transfer releases electrical energy to power the device. When the above reaction stops, there is no longer any source of power for the mobile phone and the cell needs to be recharged. If you understand the above stages, then understanding the recharging process is a piece of cake, since it is just the reverse of everything above!

## The lithium-ion cell when being recharged

When the lithium-ion cell is being recharged, an external power source (the charger) forces electrons in the opposite direction, Figure 22.15. Note that electrons are now entering the carbon electrode. This causes the redox reactions at the carbon electrode and the cobalt oxide electrode to be reversed.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-472.jpg?height=1007&width=1893&top_left_y=703&top_left_x=188)
Figure 22.15 This diagram shows a lithium-ion cell when it is being recharged.

- Electrons from the charger cause the reaction at the electrodes to be reversed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Reaction at cobalt oxide electrode: } \mathrm{LiCoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2} \\
& \text { Reaction at carbon electrode: } \mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{C}_{6} \rightarrow \mathrm{LiC}_{6} \\
& \hline
\end{aligned}
$$

Overall: $\mathrm{C}_{6}+\mathrm{LiCoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{LiC}_{6}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2}$
A summary of the discharging and charging of a lithium-ion cell is given in Table 22.3

| Feature | Discharging (cell is supplying power to a device) | Charging (energy from an external source is used to store power in the cell) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Electron flow | Carbon electrode → external circuit <br> → cobalt oxide electrode | Cobalt oxide electrode → external circuit <br> → carbon electrode |
| Li ${ }^{+}$flow | Carbon electrode → electrolyte <br> → cobalt oxide electrode | Cobalt oxide electrode → electrolyte <br> → carbon electrode |
| Reaction at carbon electrode | $\mathrm{LiC}_{6} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{C}_{6}$ <br> Oxidation <br> (Anode) | $\mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{C}_{6} \rightarrow \mathrm{LiC}_{6}$ <br> Reduction <br> (Cathode) |
| Reaction at cobalt oxide electrode | $\mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{LiCoO}_{2}$ <br> Reduction <br> (Cathode) | $\mathrm{LiCoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li}^{+}+\mathrm{e}^{-}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2}$ <br> Oxidation <br> (Anode) |
| Overall reaction | $\mathrm{LiC}_{6}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}_{6}+\mathrm{LiCoO}_{2}$ | $\mathrm{C}_{6}+\mathrm{LiCoO}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{LiC}_{6}+\mathrm{CoO}_{2}$ |
| Type of reaction | Redox reactions are spontaneous. <br> Galvanic cell. | External energy is used to force the reactions to take place in the opposite direction. <br> Electrolysis of $\mathrm{LiCoO}_{2}$. Electrolytic cell. |

Table 22.3 Summary of the discharging and charging of a lithium-ion cell

The cell is often called a 'rocking chair' cell as the lithium rocks between the carbon electrode and the cobalt oxide electrode.

As we come near the end of our story about the lithium-ion cell, make sure that you can summarise the function of the following three components:

## Functions of carbon electrode

- Enables oxidation to take place when cell is in use to power devices.
- Releases lithium ions and electrons when cell is in use to power devices.
- Enables reduction to take place when cell is being recharged.
- Stores lithium ions when the cell is charged.


## Functions of cobalt oxide electrode

- Enables reduction to take place when cell is in use to power devices.
- Receives electrons and lithium ions when cell is in use to power devices.
- Enables oxidation to take place when cell is being recharged.
- Stores lithium ions when cell is in use to power devices.


## Functions of electrolyte

- Allows movement of lithium ions from anode to cathode and cathode to anode.
- Does not allow movement of electrons through it. Electrons must move in external circuit to power the device.
- We now discuss briefly the life cycle of a lithium-ion cell.


## The life cycle of a lithium-ion cell

## Mining

- In some countries such as Chile, Argentina and Bolivia, lithium is extracted from salty liquids (called brines) found underground or near the Earth's surface. The salty liquid is pumped from the ground and poured into large pools to allow the water to evaporate, Figure 22.16. After the precipitation of other salts, the liquid that remains consists of about $25 \%$ lithium chloride.
- In Australia a lithium-containing mineral called spodumene is blasted out of open pits. Most of this is sent to China where the lithium metal is extracted.
- Since extraction from brines uses energy from the Sun, it is a more sustainable method than rock mining, which requires a lot of heavy machinery for crushing and transporting the rocks containing the lithium.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-473.jpg?height=506&width=1177&top_left_y=1738&top_left_x=1578)
Figure 22.16 This photo shows large pool of salty liquids called brines in the Atacama Desert, Chile. The water is allowed to evaporate leaving behind salts from which lithium and other metals can be extracted.

## Disposal of lithium-ion batteries

One of the major problems with improper disposal of lithium-ion batteries is the fire hazard associated with this type of battery, Figure 22.18.

Fires can be caused by physical damage to the battery. If the battery is crushed or punctured, it is possible that the separator between the electrodes will be damaged. This can cause an internal short circuit, and the heat generated can cause a fire. The battery is flammable because of the organic solvents in the electrolyte. Also, if the battery is damaged, it is possible that the lithium may react with water to release flammable hydrogen gas.

Other problems caused by the improper disposal of lithium-ion

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-474.jpg?height=701&width=877&top_left_y=371&top_left_x=1738)
Figure 22.18 This fire was caused by a damaged lithium-ion battery in the laptop.

batteries are the leaching of metals such as cobalt and copper into the soil and waterways.

## Recycling of lithium-ion batteries

Recycling of lithium-ion batteries is quite complex and expensive. Lithiumion batteries contain the metals lithium, cobalt and copper. In addition, they contain carbon, plastic separators and flammable organic electrolytes.

Batteries are often glued or sealed into items such as mobile phones and laptops. This means that disassembling them by hand can be slow and dangerous. It is estimated by some researchers that only 5\% to 10\% of lithiumion batteries are properly recycled worldwide. A lot of research is currently being undertaken to develop new systems to extract the metals from lithiumion batteries. In addition, manufacturers are being encouraged to design lithium-ion batteries that are easier to disassemble.

### 22.5 Fuel cells

In recent years a lot of research is being undertaken to move away from depending on the burning of fossil fuels to generate electricity or as fuels in our cars. One area in which this research is taking place is in the development of fuel cells. A fuel cell is a very efficient type of galvanic cell.

A fuel cell is a device that converts the chemical energy stored in a fuel directly into electrical energy. A fuel cell needs a continuous supply of chemicals.

There is no combustion involved in a fuel cell. Fuel cells work by using oxidation-reduction reactions to produce electricity.

To explain the operation of a fuel cell, let's consider the hydrogen fuel cell, Figure 22.19.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-475.jpg?height=1128&width=1254&top_left_y=1588&top_left_x=332)
Figure 22.19 A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell

Unlike batteries which are stores of energy, fuel cells can generate electricity (energy) continuously as long as the fuel and an oxidising agent are supplied.

The main points about the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell may be explained as follows:

Step 1: Hydrogen gas at the negative electrode

- The fuel is hydrogen and the oxidising agent is oxygen - usually oxygen from the air.
- Hydrogen gas $\left(\mathrm{H}_{2}\right)$ is fed to the negative electrode (anode).
- The anode is made of porous carbon containing a platinum catalyst.
- The porous carbon helps the gas to flow through it.
- The platinum catalyst helps the following oxidation reaction to take place:
Reaction at negative electrode:

$$
\mathrm{H}_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{(a q)}^{+}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

- Carbon conducts electricity. Therefore, the electrons produced at the anode, can flow through an external circuit to the cathode (positive electrode).
- The function of the anode is to provide a site for the above oxidation reaction to take place.


## Step 2: Movement of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions through the electrolyte

- The $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions produced at the negative electrode travel through an electrolyte to the positive electrode.
- The electrolyte is a solid plastic membrane - it looks like a small plastic sheet. It is of a special type of plastic which allows $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ ions to pass through it as the ions travel from the negative electrode to the positive electrode.
- The electrolyte is commonly called a proton exchange membrane.
- The membrane blocks electrons from passing through it. This forces the electrons to flow in the external circuit.
- The membrane also prevents the hydrogen and oxygen from mixing.
- The membrane has to be kept moist to allow the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions to pass through it.
- Note that the electrolyte has three functions:
(i) to allow $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions to pass through it.
(ii) to prevent electrons from passing through it.
(iii) to prevent the hydrogen and oxygen from mixing.


## Step 3: Oxygen gas at the positive electrode

- Oxygen gas is fed in at the positive electrode (cathode). The oxygen is supplied in air rather than as pure $\mathrm{O}_{2}$.
- The cathode is made from a similar material to the anode, i.e. porous carbon containing a platinum catalyst.
- The $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions that have travelled from the anode through the membrane react with the oxygen gas and electrons from the external circuit to make water.
The platinum catalyst helps to improve the efficiency of this reaction.
The reduction reaction that takes place at the positive electrode (cathode) may be summarised as follows:
- Reaction at positive electrode: $1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)}+2 \mathrm{H}^{+}{ }_{(a q)}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(b)}$
- Overall reaction: $\mathrm{H}_{2(g)}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{(l)}$
- Note that in the overall reaction, water is the only product, i.e. zero carbon emissions.

Other fuel cells that use methanol and methane as fuels instead of hydrogen also exist. However, these need not concern us in this course.

## Fuel cells and transport

A photograph of a fuel cell in a hydrogen-powered car is shown in Figure 22.20. A single hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell produces a voltage of only about 0.7 V . Therefore, in a typical car there are about 300-400 of these fuel cells connected together.

The car contains a high-pressure hydrogen tank. Hydrogen gas is fed into the negative side of the stack of fuel cells. Oxygen is supplied by air that is drawn in through vents. The electricity is generated as described above and is used to power the electric motor that turns the wheels of the car. Hydrogen-powered cars move smoothly and quietly - similar to electric cars. While electric cars require batteries to be recharged, the tanks in cars with fuel cells need to be refilled with hydrogen gas.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-476.jpg?height=629&width=861&top_left_y=1696&top_left_x=1757)
Figure 22.20 This car contains a fuel cell that is powered by hydrogen gas. The fuel cell provides the electricity to power the motor that turns the wheels of the car.

In Table 22.4 we compare a chemical cell with a fuel cell. Study this table carefully, as comparing a chemical cell with a fuel cell is one of the learning outcomes listed on the syllabus.

| Feature | Chemical cell | Fuel cell |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. Source of energy | Reactants are stored inside the cell. | The fuel and oxidising agent are continuously fed into the cell. |
| 2. Supply of reactants | Once all the reactants have been used up, the cell no longer works. | No limit to supply of reactants as the fuel and oxidising agent are continuously supplied. |
| 3. Charging | Primary cells cannot be recharged. Secondary cells can be recharged. | No need for recharging as the fuel is continuously supplied. |
| 4. Environmental impact | Environmental impact can be high due to extraction of metals (mining) and disposal problems. | Water is the only product in hydrogen fuel cells. Environmental impact low especially if using 'green hydrogen'. |

Table 22.4 Comparing a chemical cell with a fuel cell

Note that the same type of energy conversion takes place in both a chemical cell and a fuel cell, i.e. chemical energy is converted to electrical energy using redox reactions.

Figure 22.21 Green hydrogen is hydrogen that is produced by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity from wind or solar energy.

You may have heard the term green hydrogen being used when speaking about the use of hydrogen as a fuel, Figure 22.21. Hydrogen is a colourless gas but the 'green' refers to hydrogen gas that has been manufactured by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity that has been generated from wind or solar energy. (We will be studying how water is split into hydrogen and oxygen in the next section.) This manufacturing process does not release any carbon dioxide and hence does not damage the environment. Hydrogen may also be produced industrially by burning fossil fuels but hydrogen from this source would not be classified as green hydrogen.

The principle of a car being powered by fuel-cell technology may be demonstrated by means of a toy car, Figure 22.22. Firstly, hydrogen and oxygen gases are generated by splitting the water into these two gases. The two gases are stored in small onboard tanks. Once sufficient gases are collected, the hydrogen fuel cell powers the electric motor of the toy car - and off it goes!

There are still some challenges in using hydrogen as a fuel. For example, hydrogen is a flammable gas and forms an explosive mixture with air. It has to be stored under high pressure. In Ireland there is still no infrastructure in
