### 22.6 Electrolytic cells

When discussing the recharging of lithium-ion cells we saw that the electric current from the charger could bring about chemical reactions. In other words, the lithium-ion cell was acting as an electrolytic cell.

An electrolytic cell is a system in which electricity is used to cause a chemical change that would not happen on its own.

- Therefore, when a lithium-ion cell is discharging, it is acting as a galvanic cell.
- When a lithium-ion cell is being recharged, it is acting as an electrolytic cell.
- A lot of our knowledge about electrolytic cells comes from the work of Michael Faraday, Figure 22.24.


## Michael Faraday <br> (1791-1867)

Figure 22.24
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-478.jpg?height=342&width=351&top_left_y=1619&top_left_x=1025)

Michael Faraday was one of the greatest science teachers who ever lived. He was a lecturer in chemistry at the Royal Institution in London. His lectures in which he demonstrated lots of experiments drew such large crowds that Albemarle Street where the Royal Institution is located became the first one-way street in London.

- Michael Faraday introduced the word 'electrolysis' into the language of chemistry.
- The word 'electrolysis' comes from two Greek words electro and lysis which roughly translated mean 'splitting up using electricity'.

Electrolysis is the use of electricity to bring about a chemical reaction in an electrolyte, i.e. a chemical reaction is produced when an electric current is passed through an electrolyte.

## ![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-478.jpg?height=102&width=128&top_left_y=3131&top_left_x=195) <br> \section*{NOTE}

During electrolysis, the electrode where reduction occurs is still called the cathode and the electrode where oxidation occurs is still called the anode. In other words, CROA applies to both galvanic cells and electrolytic cells.

We can define an electrolyte as follows:
An electrolyte is a compound which when molten or dissolved in water will conduct an electric current.

The term electrolyte is also used to describe the solution through which a current passes by means of the movement of ions.

An electrolyte can be a conducting liquid or gel.
When carrying out electrolysis experiments, the electrodes we use are usually made of carbon or platinum. This is because these are unreactive and do not react with the electrolyte, Figure 22.25.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-478.jpg?height=756&width=928&top_left_y=1468&top_left_x=1556)
Figure 22.25 When carrying out electrolysis experiments, we use electrodes made of carbon or platinum. This is because these are unreactive and do not react with the electrolyte.

- In most cases, the electrodes do not react with the electrolyte into which they are dipping, i.e. the electrodes merely carry the current in and out of the electrolyte.
- Such electrodes are called inert electrodes.
- As mentioned above, the most common inert electrodes are graphite (carbon) and platinum.

We now study three examples of electrolysis reactions.

### 22.2A Experiment

## Student Experiment No. 22

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 22 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

## To investigate the electrolysis of acidified water using inert electrodes

## Introduction

The main points about this experiment may be summarised as follows:

- An electric current is passed through water to which has been added some dilute sulfuric acid. The sulfuric acid is added to assist the water to conduct electricity.
- The electrolysis reaction is carried out in a Hofmann voltameter or in the type of voltameter that uses inverted test-tubes to collect gases, Figure 22.26.
- A voltameter is an apparatus used to study the conduction of electricity through an electrolyte. Do not confuse this name with the name voltmeter, which is an instrument used to measure voltage.
- The volume of gas collected at the negative electrode is twice that collected at the positive electrode.
- Samples of each of the two gases are collected and tests are performed on them well away from the apparatus. It is found that the gas at the positive electrode relights a glowing splint, i.e. it is oxygen.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-479.jpg?height=984&width=1160&top_left_y=1093&top_left_x=1546)
Figure 22.26 Electrolysis of water may be carried out in a Hofmann voltameter or using inverted test-tubes.

The gas formed at the negative electrode ignites with a 'pop', i.e. it is hydrogen.

- The ratio of hydrogen gas to oxygen gas is 2 : 1 as consistent with the formula $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$.

The reaction that occurs at the electrode connected to the negative end of the battery is:
Negative electrode: $\quad 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2}$
The $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions from the sulfuric acid are attracted to the negative electrode. At the negative electrode, each $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion accepts an electron to form a H atom (reduction). Two hydrogen atoms then combine to form a hydrogen molecule.

The reaction which occurs at the electrode conned to the positive end of the battery is:
Positive electrode: $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}$

This may also be written as: $\quad \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}-2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2}$
The next few paragraphs are very important. We suggest you have a cup of strong coffee or a large bar of chocolate before you start reading!

You will recall when discussing galvanic cells that the electrode at which oxidation occurs is called the anode. Also, the electrode at which reduction occurs is called the cathode. We used the acronym CROA to help you remember this. We also learned that in a galvanic cell, the anode was the negative electrode and the cathode was the positive electrode. However, in electrolysis, you will see from the explanations that follow that the cathode is the negative electrode and the anode is the positive electrode.

Let's now take a close look at the reactions that occur in the electrolysis of water.
$\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions are attracted to the electrode that is connected to the negative end of the battery and the following reduction reaction occurs:

Negative electrode (reduction): $2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2}$
Electrons are removed from the water molecules that are near the electrode connected to the positive end of the battery (oxidation).

Positive electrode (oxidation): $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}$
This destabilises the water molecule and causes it to break down as shown above. Thus, oxygen gas is evolved at the positive electrode.

Using the acronym CROA, the electrode at which reduction occurs is called the cathode. In the electrolysis of water, reduction occurs at the negative electrode. Therefore, in electrolysis, the cathode is the negative electrode. This is the opposite of the situation in galvanic cells where the cathode was the positive electrode.

Using the acronym CROA, the electrode at which oxidation occurs is called the anode. In the electrolysis of water, oxidation occurs at the positive electrode. Therefore, in electrolysis the anode is the positive electrode. This is the opposite of the situation in galvanic cells where the anode was the negative electrode.

The reason why the signs are reversed in electrolysis is because the flow of electrons is reversed. In galvanic cells, the flow of electrons resulted from spontaneous chemical reactions. In other words, the reactions happened naturally on their own. However, in electrolysis, we have to force the reactions to occur by applying a voltage to reverse the flow of electrons compared to a galvanic cell.

Negative electrode (reduction): $\quad 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2}$
Positive electrode (oxidation): $\quad \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}$
Overall reaction: $\quad \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2}+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_{2}$
Conclusion: Water has been split into hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis.
Two $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions are removed at the negative electrode and two $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions are produced at the positive electrode. Therefore, the amount of sulfuric acid in the voltameter remains constant and the overall result is that water is broken down into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.

Note: You may wonder why the $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ ions from the sulfuric acid do not lose their two negative charges by a chemical reaction at the positive electrode. This does not happen because the $\mathrm{SO}_{4}{ }^{2-}$ ions are very stable and cannot be forced to react at this low voltage. If we had used hydrochloric acid, the $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ions in solution would lose their electrons at the positive electrode. This would interfere with the electrolysis of water and would cause chlorine gas to be evolved at the positive electrode instead of oxygen.

- What is essentially happening in any electrolysis reaction is that chemical reactions are occurring at each electrode. The battery'pumps' electrons on to the negative electrode where they are gained by some species, i.e. a reduction reaction occurs at the negative electrode.
- At the positive electrode, a chemical reaction occurs that involves a loss of electrons, i.e. an oxidation reaction occurs.

## Student Experiment No. 22

## To investigate the electrolysis of copper(II) chloride solution using inert electrodes

## Introduction

The main points about this experiment may be summarised as follows:

- Some copper(II) chloride solution is poured into a beaker.
- Two carbon electrodes are placed into the solution and connected to the DC power supply, Figure 22.27.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-481.jpg?height=754&width=1043&top_left_y=1184&top_left_x=452)
Figure 22.27 Electrolysis of copper(II) chloride solution

- The power supply is switched on and observations noted.
- It is observed that a brown solid is formed at the electrode connected to the negative end of the power supply.
- This solid is copper metal.

Negative electrode (reduction at cathode): $\quad \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$

- It is observed that bubbles of gas are collected at the electrode connected to the positive end of the power supply.
- If the gas is tested with moist blue litmus paper, it is observed that the litmus paper is bleached. This suggests that the gas is chlorine.

Positive electrode (oxidation at anode): $\quad 2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl}_{2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}$
Overall reaction: $\quad \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}+\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$

## Conclusion

During electrolysis of copper(II) chloride solution, copper metal is deposited at the cathode and chlorine gas is released at the anode. Note that since electrons are being removed from one electrode and given up at the other electrode, there is a complete circuit, Figure 22.27a.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-481.jpg?height=1066&width=1144&top_left_y=1181&top_left_x=1562)
Figure 22.27a Since electrons are being removed from one electrode and given up at the other electrode, there is a complete circuit.

## 2225 Experinent

## Student Experiment No. 22

Full details of the procedure for carrying out this experiment are given in Experiment 22 in the Student Laboratory Notebook.

To investigate what happens when an electric current is passed through a solution of potassium iodide using inert electrodes

## Introduction

In this electrolysis experiment, a gas is given off at only one electrode. The experiment may be carried out conveniently in the apparatus shown in Figure 22.28. The iodine that is formed is more easily seen if platinum electrodes are used.

The main points about this experiment may be summarised as follows:

- Some potassium iodide solution is placed in the apparatus shown and a few drops of phenolphthalein indicator are added. The solution is colourless.
- As the electrolysis proceeds, a brown colour is observed at the positive electrode, Figure 22.29.
- The brown colour at the positive electrode is due to the formation of iodine. The negative iodide ions in the water are attracted to the positive electrode ('unlike charges attract'). At the positive electrode, each iodide ion loses an electron to form an iodine atom. Two iodine atoms then join together to form an iodine molecule.


## Positive electrode (oxidation at anode):

$$
2 \mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-}
$$

Oxidation is occurring at the positive electrode since electrons are being lost.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-482.jpg?height=681&width=1039&top_left_y=920&top_left_x=1540)
Figure 22.28 Iodine and hydrogen gas are formed when a solution of potassium iodide is electrolysed.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2025_12_01_c7e4081cc58a01ef3097g-482.jpg?height=695&width=1040&top_left_y=1855&top_left_x=1536)
Figure 22.29 Electrolysis of KI solution is taking place in this voltameter.

- A pink colour is observed at the negative electrode and a gas is evolved. The gas is collected in a test-tube and is found, on analysis, to be hydrogen. The fact that the phenolphthalein turns pink implies that the solution is turning alkaline ( $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions present). Phenolphthalein is pink in a base and colourless in an acid. These facts lead chemists to conclude that the following reaction occurs at the negative electrode:
Negative electrode (reduction at cathode): $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}+2 \mathrm{e}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2}+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
Reduction occurs at the negative electrode as electrons are being gained.
Overall reaction: $2 \mathrm{I}^{-}+2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{2}+\mathrm{H}_{2}+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}$


## Conclusion

When a solution of potassium iodide undergoes electrolysis, the products are iodine, hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions.

Thus, what is actually happening at the negative electrode is that water molecules are being forced to accept electrons from the negative electrode. These extra electrons cause the molecules to be destabilised, and they break up to form hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions.

### 22.7 Concluding points

We began our study of electrochemistry by discussing galvanic (voltaic) cells and completed our study by discussing electrolytic cells. Both types of cells may be classified under the general category of electrochemical cell.

An electrochemical cell is any system that converts chemical energy into electrical energy or electrical energy into chemical energy by means of a redox reaction.

In other words, an electrochemical cell is a device that either (i) uses chemical reactions to produce electricity or (ii) uses electricity to cause chemical reactions to take place. In both cases, electrons move from one substance to another, i.e. oxidation-reduction reactions occur.

The final learning outcome that needs to be covered in this chapter is the following learning outcome specified in the syllabus:

- Students should be able to research a role of electrochemistry in an area related to sustainability and technology in everyday life.

In specifying the depth of treatment associated with this learning outcome the following two points are given:

- How electrochemistry could provide more sustainable uses of energy, such as electrochemical cells and the use of rechargeable batteries.
- Electrolysis and its potential for hydrogen production as a fuel, for example, through electricity generated from sustainable sources.

Your teacher may provide this research investigation as homework for you. When carrying out your research the following guidelines may be of assistance:

- Begin with a clear focus and choose one main area to research, such as:
- Electrochemical cells and rechargeable batteries (e.g. lithium-ion batteries in electric vehicles).
- Electrolysis for hydrogen fuel production (especially using renewable electricity).
- Make sure that you understand the basic scientific concepts explained in this chapter:
- Key terms such as redox reactions, anode, cathode, galvanic cells and electrolytic cells.
- Be able to explain how redox reactions and ion flow are involved in galvanic cells and electrolytic cells.
- Make the link to sustainability:
- Explain how the technology reduces the dependence on fossil fuels.
- Examine the environmental impact of materials used (e.g. materials in batteries).
- Compare and contrast the use of items such as petrol cars versus electric cars.
- Include real-world examples:
- Research how these new technologies (e.g. electric battery technology and hydrogen for transport) are being brought into use in other countries.
- Compare what is happening in other countries with what is happening in Ireland.
- Use reliable sources:
- Scientific websites (websites from reputable government organisations and professional bodies).
- Reputable news articles on green technology innovations.
- Avoid blogs or commercial sites.
- Analyse the material that you have gathered:
- What are the advantages and limitations of the technology?
- Are there economic or practical challenges in large-scale use?
- Summarise your conclusions and recommendations (e.g. in a PowerPoint presentation):
- Use diagrams of galvanic or electrolytic cells.
- Define all scientific terms used.
- Connect your research to everyday applications or current events.

## Summary What I should know

- A galvanic (voltaic) cell is a device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy through oxidation-reduction reactions that occur within it.
- The electrochemical series is a list of elements in order of their standard electrode potentials, i.e. in order of the decreasing tendency for the element to be oxidised (lose electrons) under standard conditions.
- A metal will displace another metal that is below it in the electrochemical series from a solution of its ions.
- A primary cell is a type of galvanic cell that cannot be recharged.
- A secondary cell is a type of galvanic cell that can be recharged.
- A fuel cell is a device that converts the chemical energy stored in a fuel fed into the fuel cell directly into electrical energy.
- Electrolysis is the use of electricity to bring about a chemical reaction in an electrolyte.
- An electrolytic cell is a system in which electricity is used to cause a chemical change that would not happen on its own.
- The electrode at which reduction occurs is called the cathode and the electrode where oxidation occurs is called the anode (CROA).

In a galvanic cell, the cathode is the positive electrode, and the anode is the negative electrode. However, in an electrolytic cell, the cathode is the negative electrode, and the anode is the positive electrode.

An electrochemical cell is any system that converts chemical energy into electrical energy or electrical energy into chemical energy by means of redox reactions.
